title: A film betrayed by Context?
review:
I think the main problem with this version of "War of the Worlds" is context.

To explain a little further - Taken on its own, "War of the Worlds" is a fairly decent piece of cinema: The actors (even the usually stilted Cruise), play their parts relatively well and with a fair degree of realism, the story is well-paced and the action sequences are well-directed in portraying the Martian purge of Earth from the (exceptional) everyman/every-family perspective. The CGI and visual effects aren't over done either, even in the more visually-intensive scenes...

HOWEVER it's when you place the film into context, that things start to go wrong...

For a start, "War of the Worlds" is part of an alarming trend amongst Hollywood film-makers to apparently negate claims of plagiarism, by using phrases such as "Based on the novel by" or "Suggested in the novel by" - Attempting to hide the fact that they are simply plundering older works for film ideas and using the names to provide marketable Kudos. "War of the Worlds" is not an adaptation by anyone's standard, its association with the work from which it steals its name is there to justify the use of the original's structure, characters and overall story-telling concepts.

Unfortunately, this intentional plagiarism is rife in Spielburg's effort, which at best could be described as a synthesis of several works and at worst, outright and systematic laziness. Having dealt with the obvious origins that provide the film with the majority of its material, you'll also find elements taken directly from the 1953 film version, such as the use of shields, the design elements of the Martian Tripods/Scanners/etc, and the remaking of several iconic scenes (The basement and final defeat sequences) - Even the homage in the opening 30 minutes, that sees a war machine rising from out of a church (reminscent of the end scene of the 1953 movie, where one crashes into a church) do not make this any the more forgivable.

There are other niggles that might be a little more tenuous but nonetheless give pause for thought - The wail of the Warmachines and Cruise's destruction of one, both seem to echo similar sounds and scenes from the British 1980's TV series "The Tripods" based on books by John Christopher - One of the Warmachines in that work is also destroyed by grenades thrown into the cockpit. This is without mentioning the facts that scenes of the Warmachines in the current movie spreading the Red Weed and feeding, instantly remind the watcher of the Machines farming humans in the Matrix Trilogy, and the aliens themselves bear a shocking resemblance to the Greys in "Independence Day" from 1996! When you thrown in some glaring continuity errors (Working Camcorders after an EMP blast?), some gaping plot-holes (The link to Mars is never made explicit, nor is a reason given why the aliens buried war machines under the surface instead of taking over at that point, or how said vehicles escaped detection with the construction of modern civilisation above them), and Spielburg's propensity to provide needlessly happy endings (I'll concede that in the original, the Narrator finds his wife & cousin unharmed, but in this 'adaptation' the survival of the son at the end beggars belief and belittles the audience) and the film is cast in a completely different and none to favourable light...

Whilst others might say the box office figures speak for themselves, this of course is sophistry - You don't know what you're getting with a movie until you sit down and see it, so by then it's too late to show your disdain by not viewing - Besides, even forewarned, people would still go just to see what the fuss was about! All in all? A disappointment, and a sizable one at that - Not so much on technical merits, but more on philosophical points...

title: What a disappointment !!
review: I saw the trailer a few months ago and i was sure that this movie is gonna be one of this years highlights. How wrong was I!! The special effects are really good. But what else ? Nothing. Tom Cruise is just running. He's not fighting against the Aliens how I would expect it from a real hero (except the one scene with the grenades). Compared to other alien invasion movies like Independence Day or Signs the movie loses in terms of 'Let's watch it again'. The first hour is really good. But then it's just getting boring as hell. And then the fight is over without a real climax. Within one minute it's all over. The paramecium saves the world. What a disappointment !! Now I know why critics were not allowed to write something in advance about this movie... I didn't read the novel and so I also didn't really know what to expect. Mr. Spielberg - better do Indiana Jones 4 now to let me believe in your skills again :-)

title: Bad emotions
review: Big surprise here: Tom Cruise cannot act, Steven Spielberg cannot do feelings. So ignore the characters and enjoy the destruction. We did have a discussion as to whether Tim Robbins can act, but one person won the argument by suggesting that Tom Cruise brings other actors down, down, down. The scenes that really ruin it are: the peanut butter sandwich family get together (they had electricity; did no one think that checking out TV and radio stations might have been better than working out their dysfunctional family problems?), the son running after army trucks (let him go, one less character to hate), that ghastly screaming girl (only when she was in the Martian cage did she shut up, so I say bring the aliens back to earth and use them as babysitters), and the ending (big groan from the audience; as one friend said: "Don't they do test screenings? Perhaps they should have different endings for Americans and Europeans"). Otherwise the suspense and effects and camera work bore the hallmarks of good Steven Spielberg films. And a bit like "Titanic", you want the destruction to start so you don't have to listen to the dialogue.

title: Overall entertaining, but unfortunately has to cater to all
review:
War of the Worlds. As with all "summer blockbusters" this movie is meant to pack'em in. The creators were trying to please every audience here. That is unfortunate for everyone. The problem is, you can't please all of the people all of the time, so they are trying to please all of us at least part of the time here.

The film, to start out, had a lot going for it. The effects were amazing, the action was great, and it was very suspenseful. The apathy of the invaders was frightening and it chills you to the bone. The movie even manages to feel nostalgic in remembering the older film and has a very vintage UFO feel.

So what's the problem? Well, with the necessity to cater to all, the creators felt they needed to have a sweet, cutsie, ending for the lead characters. I know there are those among us who can't stand to see a movie end on a downer, but come on. Aliens have just come a hairline away from conquering the entire planet, killing everyone, leveling towns, searching basements for any leftover survivors, obliterating everything, and we're supposed to watch Tom Cruise come walking down the street to his ex-parents-in-law's house, where the entire family welcomes him at the door without a scratch!?! They look as if they just sat down for Sunday dinner for God's sake! And if that wasn't enough, of course, the son lived, and made it home! Come on guys, would it have killed them to knock off at least one lead?!?

The conclusion is, this happy little ending is merely, in my mind an attempt to cater to that gum drop audience who probably used to be "full House" fans. I think if you're able to look past that, then you'll enjoy yourself. If these cookie cutter endings really get you down though, you may wait till you can rent it, so at least you can skip the mushy stuff.

title: When the explosions and effects end, there's emptiness.
review:
I love Spielberg's films and have enjoyed almost everything Cruise has done. Also, the novel "War of the Worlds" is probably my all-time favorite, and I read it at least once a year. Understandably, my expectations for this film were very high.

All the ingredients thrown into the pot should have created the final and definitive version of Wells' novel. Sadly, the soup is bitter and leaves one feeling empty.

I'll agree with the reviewers that say Cruise and Dakota Fanning give excellent performances. I agree that the CGI invaders and their tripod machines provide some of the most realistic and terrifying moments ever captured on film. I agree that the movie has all the elements of a Hollywood special effects blockbuster. But somehow, none of these qualities is enough to satisfy a true fan of the story this movie is based on.

In truth, this film has little to do with the original novel, other than that there are invaders from space who: (1) use tripod machines to try to conquer the world, (2) feed on human blood, and (3) are defeated in the end by germs.

The few elements of Wells' original story are quickly shoved into the background, as the movie focuses on the tensions between Cruise's blue-collar character and his two children, as they flee the invading aliens on their way from New York to Boston.

I left the theater shaking my head in disappointment. Wells' story is one of the greatest science fiction novels ever written, and this movie is but a pale shadow of it, when it could have been so much more. The movie is not about retelling Wells' story - it's about showcasing some "wow" special effects and providing a stage for Cruise to build up more of his star power.

Those of us who really care about this story are left feeling empty....

title: Suspenseful but illogical
review:
Why did the aliens bury machines over a million years ago? Why not take over the planet then? Why did the force fields lose their resistance when the aliens got sick? My car works fine when I'm not feeling well.

The entire episode with Tim Robbins added nothing to the movie. It should have been deleted.

How did the son survive? They should have killed him off.

Why were the aliens disintegrating the humans early in the movie, sucking their blood in the middle, and then capturing them at the end? But despite all the plot flaws, the movie was suspenseful and held your interest.

title: The aliens are not the scary things!
review: I thought this movie was terrible not because of all the aliens killing people, but the way that the characters were completely terrible. OK, I understand that the world is coming to an end and everybody needs to do something to stay alive, but stealing a car and not explaining that it is an emergency and killing a man with your daughter in the next room makes this movie terrible and makes me want Tom Cruise's Character to get eaten up by the aliens. I felt no sympathy for the family running away from the aliens. The only one I felt a little sorry for was the little girl, but the boy and Tom Cruise could be eaten by the aliens for all I cared!

title: War of the Worlds is Extremely disappointing
review:
The movie on a whole deviated from H.G. Wells story on a completely different tangent. The ending of the movie leaves too many questions in the viewers mind as it is very abrupt. Linking the movie to themes similar to Schindlers List and to those of the attacks during 9/11, simply point to the fact that Spielberg distorted such a great story according to his cultural and geographical background. Its a shame that such masterpieces written by notable authors such as Wells are allowed to be torn down by people such as Spielberg. The cast in the film seemed to be falling apart as Dakota Fanning has outgrown her cute childish state in life and now sounds like a broken record which has simply gone on for too long. I truly hope that she resumes life as a kid and takes on school on a full-time basis, so as to safe viewers from her irritating acting.

Spielberg's attempt to make Tom Cruise seem like your average American with a broken up family was also remarkably daft as the actor seemed like a complete hobo. On one side the character works in a shipping port moving containers, which in reality pays good money, but Tom Cruise in this role still could not manage to take a shower and wear clothes from this decade.

Anyhow, I have already wasted two hours of my life on this failure of a movie and would like to get on with my life. For God's sake if you have not seen this movie, do not waste your time and money to watch this movie. It should be shelved and locked for the rest of time, so as to safeguard the rest of the world.

title: A Travesty of a film
review:
First; this isn't a rethinking (a word I'm totally sick of) of the original film, nor is it a true adaptation (even updated) of the classic novel. What it is, honestly, is a post 9/11 mish-mosh that plays on peoples fears as well as lifting the best parts from the book and the 1953 film, while adding a silly and contrived sub-plot.

So where do we start? Like this:

The Good: The SFX was spectacular. The destruction was absolutely beautifully done. The War machines were awesome (and a bit of a nod to the old Classics Illustrated version); the aliens were somewhat original, but reminded me of the creatures from ID4 for some reason, and they had the hands of the Martians from the 1953 version. One of the end scenes is a homage to the end of the original film.

Other good: The lifting of the Ferry getting flipped by the Tripod as it crosses the Hudson was right out of the novel. Of course in the Novel the Steamram, Thunderchild destroys that Tripod by ramming it. Also earlier in the book a Martian capsule is destroyed by artillery fire. (See the bad for more on this).

The Bad: David Koepp and Steven Spielberg should be ashamed of themselves for allowing this crappy story to see daylight. The 9/11 references are way too

plentiful. As someone who watched in unfold from my home and had to wash the ash off my car, I found this irresponsible and unnecessary. Can't one simply make a great SF movie (see original War of the Worlds for an example) without beating the audience over the head with symbolism reminding us of a real event? Another thing, the whole Tom Cruise as divorced dad was so damned contrived as to be silly. What, a single person isn't going to want to survive this kind of horror as much as a married person? Also the kids had no personality. The son was a bland, anti-Dad kind of guy, all Dakota Fanning did was stare and scream. This whole aspect of the plot just bored me. If Koepp was adapting/updating the book, then why did the aliens have shields, ala the 1953 version? In the book the Tripods are tough, but two of them are brought down with 19th century weapons. Also the scene where Gene Barry chops off one of the aliens spy devices (on a long neck) is lifted for this film. Hey dudes, that didn't happen in the book, OK? Finally, if these aliens had been here for millions of years, having planted their war machines, why the hell didn't they think to test our air and water? Yes, the ending is right out of the book with the aliens dying of Terran bacteria, but it makes no sense. In the original film and book, there was no preparation time, the aliens landed and started blasting us out of existence. So these aliens, who have some kind of Transporter technology, didn't have the brains to check things out first? Were these cousins to the morons from Signs, who came to a planet 70 percent water so they

could die?

The Ugly; At the beginning, when the aliens are riding lightning down to Earth, all electrical power shuts off. How was this one guy able to freaking take pictures with his camcorder? Also, can someone explain the physics of a heat ray that dissolves human beings but doesn't destroy their clothing? This was a very heavy handed parallel to the deaths on 9/11, which was unnecessary. A

further point, Cruises son goes to watch the military take on the aliens, the entire brigade is wiped out - yet his son survives to make it to an untouched (mostly Boston). In fact at the very laughable end, Cruise and his daughter make it to Boston, see the machines start to topple and fall. Cruise notices birds sitting on the one machine (another homage to the book, where the

astronomer sees the birds feeding on the dead Martians), yet trained military men don't? He notices the shield is down? And when he gets to his ex-wife's parents home, the block is untouched. Looks like a Sunday morning. And his son is there, it looks like they've all been wakened from breakfast! This was just a silly excuse for a 'message' film, that failed to give me any message at all, other than Steven Spielberg shouldn't be allowed to do SF. A.I. stunk, Minority Report was a joke and if I never see this again, well I'll be pretty damn content. The original film was much better and probably had

1/100th of the budget. The difference is the original film and book both entertain without beating a reader/watcher over the head, while this ham-handed

mistake of a film doesn't.

Finally, save yourself some money and wait and rent this one out.

title: so so so disappointing!
review:
I thought this would be a nice film, for this I had a couple of reasons:

1. Steven Spielberg 2. The name: War of the Worlds 3. All the commotion and advertisement, even the trailer did it for me 4. Tom Cruise 5. See "1"

What a disappointment this was this afternoon.. The film starts basic, like all films they first introduce the main characters and give you a peak in their normal life, but as my friend quoted: "never change a winning team". The first action, the first storm, I liked this part because of the thrill it caused on the main character, at first no fear, only thrill. This shows some of the feeling that People have, "there cannot be major threads near me". So they just watched en got entertained. This was one of the parts I liked. Then you notice the special-effects, astonishing! But than, you see what comes from under the ground (what hes been there for million years... waiting for now), it is too earthly.. Humans could have, and can build something that looks like that: the "Tripods" (the name everybody suddenly knows and uses). They could and should have been more creative.

title: Makes "The Day After Tomorrow" look like an epic
review:
This movie was a letdown of the same epic proportion that "The Day After Tomorrow" was last year. Expecting to see an alien sci-fi thriller on the order of "Independence Day", this film was simply a vehicle to provide Tom Cruise some mug time on screen.

The film quickly focuses on an unlikeable character, played by Cruise and, to a much lesser extent, his estranged daughter, played by Dakota Fanning. Cruise's character is on-screen almost constantly and, unfortunately, displays his limited acting range. Dakota, who is otherwise an incredible actress - especially for an 11 year old (see "Sam I Am", "Man of Fire", "Taken")is given a character whose primary function is to shriek and scream. The son, played by unknown Justin Chatwin, is quickly swept under the rug.

The primary characters in this film are, at best, one-dimensional. Their emotions and interactions are too phony and contrived to capture the audience. All of the supporting characters are reduced to "wallpaper" status.

Spielberg squeezed out a lemon here. This is nowhere near the quality of "E.T.", "Taken", "AI" (The movie, not the steak sauce). Cruise was far better in his earlier films such as "Risky Business".

Save your money. Wait for this dog on cable. Rent the 1953 version for a good sci-fi thriller.

title: Not great by any stretch of the imagination
review:
Having been dubious of the fact that Steven Spielberg was producing this 'epic' remake, I went in thinking this is gonna be disappointing and boy, did it disappoint.

Don't get me wrong, I have nothing against Steven Spielberg's films but they all tend to have a nice and fluffy ending - all's well that ends well type of theme - but this film lays it on thick.

First of all casting Tom Cruise in a film like this was a bit of a shock. Did it really require a big name actor to carry out something like this ? not that I am a massive fan of Tom Cruise although he has done some great films. I felt it didn't....

The opening scene on how the martians are introduced to us is spectacular, breathtaking - but it is one of those films that starts on a high and spirals big time.

War of the Worlds as I understand it is about the battle of 2 worlds for supremacy ... which it is not - it's a stereotypical disaster movie.....

Seen Armageddon, Dante's Peak, Volcano, that film where the end of the world comes because of changing climate...name escapes me....

..Well congratulations - you have seen War of the Worlds too.

My preconceptions were something along the lines of Independence Day - but obviously not as bad .... over a period of 3 films to make this an epic. Where the first one we get our arses royally kicked, the 2nd we start to get a foothold and the 3rd where the martians finally die......This would be worth seeing...Where's Peter Jackson when you need him ???

There are however good points to this dire attempt:

1. Tom Cruise does play a half-decent role 2. Tim Robbins is as always, very believable and excellent. 3. The opening scenes were by all accounts awesome (although I never quite worked out why some electrical items - even the car worked within an electro-magnetic field which as I understand it fries anything electrical or mechanical whether it is plugged in or not)

Other than these points, I am struggling.

If you wanna go waste your money go for it, I would personally wait for DVD or for it to appear on Sky/Cable.

It is a watch, but that's about it.

If you wanna see a great film this year, go see Revenge of the Sith (if its your thing) or Batman.

title: A good start to a bad ending!!
review: The beginning of this movie was quite good! The action and suspense was Steven Spielberg at his best. I was fully impressed with the first half of the movie and I was intrigued! Than about half way through the movie it took a turn for the worst! First of all lets talk about the characters. Tom Cruise personified the arrogant and distant dad to the extent that it seemed way too contrived and rehearsed. His daughter was even more annoying and unlikeable with her constant forced screams and shrill voice! The daughter had too much face time in front of the camera and a lot less of her might have prompted a higher star review from me. Furthermore she was constantly condescending and spoke too much like an adult. Her constant questions to her father was getting quickly on my nerves. I would have been rather pleased if the Aliens had captured or evaporated her with those lasers shooting out from the spacecraft. Sadly everyone else met the same fate except for this annoying kid. Now to the son. In typical Hollywood drama there is always a son or daughter ( in this case a son) who is casted as the social misfit with angst and confusion about his life and his place in it. Of course the dad ( tom Cruise ) gets the brunt of this anger and of course a future resolution between the two is telegraphed, yawn! The son did some absurd things like running away from his dad so as to "fight" the aliens, absurd on its face! The script writer gave the worst lines to the kids. The movie became really bad especially when they were in the basement of that silly man. Why was he even in the movie? He served no essential purpose other than to waste about 40 minutes of an otherwise failing film. His character was confusing and not essential in my humble estimation. The most absurd moment was when we are to believe they actually were able to walk to Boston unharmed or even having the physical capacity to do so. GIVE ME A BREAK! If those aliens did exist there would be no realistic possibility they could have survived, none at all. Of course the son, who should have died, made it safe and sound. Better yet the whole family came away unharmed, LOL!!!!!! Truly wishful thinking in light of the human destruction abound in the film. It would have been more realistic if at least some of the family members died, also more dramatic. The worst part of the film is that we are treated to something of a really bad scenario only to discover in the end we are left thinking what is the big deal? It went from bad to good way to quick and it was kind of insulting to many viewers who wish not to suspend that much belief. The ending was terrible and so too the music that accompanied the credits. Overall a major loss of two hours.

title: Hmmmmmmmm!!!!!!!
review:
This may be considered to contain spoilers, but as this story is over 50 years old most of you will have some idea what happens anyway, but I do reveal the differences.

The 4 stars are only for the effects as the tripods are in the essence of the original drawings and move well (see the cover of Jeff Waynes album of the musical version narrated by Richard Burton), this was the only thing I had against the original film as they floated on 3 beams but it was probably technically impossible back then or at least too expensive. As for the story why change it to THIS!! This was a perfectly good story that has now been mullered. Spielberg has done to this story what an iceberg did to the Titanic.

At this point I should tell you I have read the book many years ago bought the vinyl mentioned above and seen the 1953 film (no, I'm not that old I saw it years after it came out) the same goes for the radio show. The 1975 film about the radio show 'The Night That Panicked America' showing how gullible you lot in the USA all were/are was most interesting. Sorry, I had to get you lot back for the "Europe fell in minutes" gag in the film. (Not Sorry really ;-) Well the USA were not making dent in them either.

If a race was so advanced 1 million years ago to create these tripods, why bury them in the Earth and wait for it to be populated? Surely they would know that in a thousand or even few hundred years later let alone a million years on they would develop much better craft that could take out/harvest humankind in one go and wouldn't be bothered with what would become 'that ancient junk tripod technology!' The original story has them coming from Mars (a million to one chance but still they come, as the story goes) landing, which made a crater from where the tripods were built and emerge.

There was no time given for investigation or explanation of many things that happened. For example in the 1953 film we had 'lets try this; oh, it didn't work lets try something else' etc. This film just had the troops throwing everything they had at them and we didn't see much of that happening.

In answer to comments about blunders I have read here. If you think about it you can get around some of the EMP knocking out everything electrical mistakes. As someone who has qualifications in electronics I know not everything would necessarily be affected depending on where it was at the time of the EMP and if it was shielded for example in a thick metal box or garage or even if it was underground in a basement or car park. But this aside when they emerged to find a plane had crashed on them it was very convenient for the car to have no damage and to have a path through the rubble to make their escape.

I had shown the original film of 1953 to my 11 and 8 year old a few weeks ago and they enjoyed it and even got a bit scared with it. The thing missing in this film is ambiance, no time given to get any real suspense, just burn baby burn. I will not be letting the kids see this one yet (it's a 12A in the UK) for this reason.

Not a good remake as so many aren't.

title: The negativity is ridiculous.
review:
Once again I find myself utterly confused as to why so many people want to tear apart such a breathtaking, visceral film such as "War of the Worlds." The one area I have seen repeatedly take a beating is the ending, which is not only faithful to the original book, but also makes sense (at least in the context of this type of story). This isn't the "gung-ho, let's ram our fighter jet into the alien ship while David Arnold's overpowering, triumphant, patriotic theme ushers rednecks across the world to cheer on their favorite drunk" of Independence Day. This film is about a family fighting to stay alive, using the alien "invasion" as a backdrop, but surely not as a second thought.

And even despite the family messages and what have you, the film is incredibly terrifying. It's not too long (barely scraping the 2 hour mark) and it seemed like an hour and fifty minutes of that runtime was dedicated to blowing up people, buildings, and just about everything else. Also, the acting is simply incredible, especially when Tom Cruise and Dakota Fanning are acting together during the many intense sequences throughout the film (which also happens to cover the majority of the running time). But instead of being "Independence Day II: Windows XP Edition," we get an adrenaline-filled horror/suspense title that recalls Spielberg's "Jaws" and "Jurassic Park" days, in which all he wants to do is provide a few hours of terror. With "War of the Worlds," he certainly accomplishes this task. Whatever happened to the idea of going to the movies for a fun time?

title: great moments, but a flat movie
review:
The book is always better, isn't it? H.G. Wells' "War of the Worlds" is a little soft on characterization, but it's still a fascinating showcase for Victorian scientific theory and anti-imperialist sentiments. Spielburg's ill-conceived adaptation leeches out all of Welles' science, speculation, and social commentary, replacing them with typical action-movie thrills and weirdly inappropriate 9/11 imagery. If Spielburg went further in transforming "War of the Worlds" into an exploration of terrorism's effect on modern American life, I might've liked his version more, but all he does is recreate moments of chaos and violence from 9/11 in a science fiction context, which seems superficial at best.

There are other problems with the film. Cruise gives his usual likable performance, but he simply doesn't convince as a grizzled working man. There are about a dozen "average Joe" supporting characters in the movie who would've made more appropriate heroes. The strained relationship between Cruise and his son is clichéd and annoying, and there's really no need for a screaming little girl character. Certain shots simply don't make sense - why is Boston deserted at the end, except for Cruise's family, who all seem to be dressed in their Sunday best? Why can a thin line of soldiers hold back an entire crowd that's trying to storm aboard a ferry? And why are all the refugees wearing dark clothes and wooly caps, like they're peasants from World War II?

The movie's entertaining enough anyway, of course. The war machines are impressive (if impractical - no doubt they would look even better in a Victorian setting), and the special effects are predictably spectacular. But the alien invasion kick is getting old now, and this seems like one sci-fi blockbuster too many. If Spielburg had set the action in the 1880s, or included some of the science from the book, this movie might seem more unique. As it stands, it's just another in a long string of summer action movies. It's better made than most, but no more intelligent.

title: A Disappointment for Those With High Expectations
review:
As one of the many poor slobs who have been waiting eagerly for the release of this film for (it seems like) years, I must say I was entertained but expected more from Spielberg.

Okay, the special effects are awe-inspiring, but everyone expects that. I'd go further, though, and recommend this movie simply on the strength of the effects. I was wondering how Spielberg would render the "fighting machines," and my jaw dropped when I finally laid eyes on one.

Despite what some other folks have written, the screenplay really DOES follow a good deal of the original H.G. Wells novel in basic structure, with the exception that there's not a gradual build-up of suspense while the aliens hide in their "cylinders" and prepare to attack. Here, they simply strike, and we're off to the races. The Tim Robbins character puzzled me until I realized that he was supposed to be a composite of the unbalanced curate and the tough artilleryman in the Wells novel, a combo which, if you've ever read the book, you'd know is doomed to fail in precisely the miserable way it did.

Other troublesome areas in this movie include the handling of the Red Weed, which was never really explained -- what was it, and what was its purpose? Who the hell were those people on the ferry crossing suddenly attached to Tom Cruise and his kids? And of course, the biggest problem of all, endemic to alien invasion movies, but which I expected some solution to here -- just how is it that super intelligent, super powerful aliens who can travel across light years of space seem to have no awareness of an obvious Achilles heel which will eventually destroy them? Independence Day -- oops, we've got no virus protection for our ships' computers; Signs -- hey, water is kryptonite to our species but we're invading a planet that's 70% water. War of the Worlds -- well, you know the routine by now, Wells used it too. But in the 1890s, it may have seemed a little less like "deus ex machina."

Tom Cruise, yeah, he can act. He's good in this role. Dakota Fanning I'd like to smack upside the head and get those vacant eyes of hers rattling around in her skull a bit. If there were an Oscar for screaming, she'd get it. They should have waited a few more years to remake King Kong, she'd grow right into the female lead. The kid who played Cruise's son should have been incinerated in the first carnage scene, he was absolutely useless. He's only there to keep reminding us what a crappy father Tom's been, yadda yadda yadda.

Overall, it's worth the price of a ticket. In fact, I'm gonna see it again, but only because these kinds of movies are my favorite kinds of movies. You know, the ones where civilization is destroyed and millions of people are indiscriminately slaughtered by some pitiless force, but everything is okay at the end because Joe Average and his family are safe and reunited.

title: Great action & suspense - mediocre acting, story and ending
review:
The special effects are great. The horror of mass death and devastation is powerfully rendered and there are some incredibly suspenseful moments. Spielberg is still better at this than his imitators.

But Cruise is miscast, and even though the film tries hard to build a credible family conflict, it just doesn't draw you in. Dakota Fanning is good, however, I don't think she overacted at all.

There's not much variation from scene to scene: The same basic "running & hiding from the tripods" scenario plays out in a few different ways, and there's just the faintest trace of character development.

The ending feels abrupt & the story incomplete. Probably because the defeat of the aliens and the family conflict are not truly integrated.

Still, it's not a bad movie.

title: On Cruise control as Mars attacks
review: Okay, so the headline is sort of deceiving, since in Steven Spielberg's newest effort, a remake of the 1953 classic, "The War of the Worlds," the invaders are not necessarily Martians. In fact, we don't know where the aliens are *from*, we just know they're *here*. And once here, they certainly do a number on the planet, rising from deep underground (after a series of lightening strikes) and wreaking havoc all over the world. In the midst of this catastrophe, enter Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise), a crane operator on the Brooklyn shipyards, divorced and irresponsible, who just happens to have his unenthusiastic kids, Robbie (Justin Chatwin, yes, Tom Cruise plays the father of a teenager!) and Rachel (Dakota Fanning, "Man On Fire," "Hide & Seek"). The kids don't want to be there, and when the earth comes under attack from huge, three-legged ships (think of those walkers on "Return of the Jedi" with whiplike tentacles), supposedly buried for a million years, they're kind of stuck with one another. Weak and indecisive, Ray clashes with his son, who is itching for action and wants to fight the aliens tooth and nail. Rachel, on the other hand, is claustrophobic and often acts much older than her age. When Robbie disappears while viewing a military attack on the creatures, Ray must fend for his daughter, not only against extra-terrestrial visitors, but also wild crowds of maddened humanity and a psycho ambulance driver (hiding in an abandoned farmhouse), Ogilvy (Tim Robbins, "Shawshank Redemption," "Mystic River"). Ray and his charges are put through the wringer by Spielberg  no stranger to working with aliens ("Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "E.T."). Like a James Bond film, they are forced to escape from almost impossible (and certainly improbable) situations time and time again. Those fans of the original film  starring Gene Barry and Ann Robinson  will notice immediately that this work is more faithful to the H.G. Wells novel (as well as the subsequent Orson Wells Mercury Theatre 1938 radio presentation). Instead of those cool, smooth, triangular ships flying about, these intruders walk on three legs, chasing and gathering up hapless humans for food and other needs. Never fear, however, the best scene in the 1953 version  Barry and Robinson trying to avoid the creepy, all-seeing alien eye at the farmhouse  is left intact here. Overall, Spielberg's work ranks right up there with some of his best recent action works, such as "Jurassic Park" and "Minority Report." The story is compelling (H.G. Wells buttressed by Josh Friedman and David Koepp), and the acting, especially Cruise and Robbins. As far as the CGI work, it's also top-notch. Sure, there are a few goofy scenes, but the special effects grab you almost immediately, fling you along for a few hours and throw you back in your seat  like a rag doll. It's a stunning, almost overwhelming sensory experience  for the eyes and the ears. Cinematographer Janusz Kaminski (who worked with Spielberg on "Schindler's List," "Amistad," "Saving Private Ryan," Catch Me If You Can and The Terminal) is a big reason for this, as well as FX work by Robert L. Anderson (the "Naked Gun" films) and Roy Augenstein ("Haunted Mansion," "Cellular," "Dragonfly"). What is nice about the picture is, while we see the aliens many times, Kaminski's camera does not dwell on them, preferring instead to capture the terrified faces of Ray, his family and those horrified masses retreating from the invading hordes. Scenes of stunned refugees crossing bridges ahead of the monsters are almost like films of terrified citizens fleeing the Red Army or Nazis in World War II. That's not to say the movie is perfect, by any means. I did not care too much for the pat ending (over and above what H.G. Wells had written at the beginning of the last century), Chatwin's poor acting or one particular scene. While hiding from the monsters in the basement of his ex-wife's home, Ray discovers that a huge jumbo jet (apparently blown out of the sky by the creatures) has fallen right there on the block. Strewn with wreckage and debris (but no bodies for some reason), the aircraft has conveniently avoided the family's minivan parked in the driveway  leaving nothing so much as a scratch or dent  plus there's a clear path for them to drive away on. It's silly, but does little to detract for the whole picture, which is certainly worth seeing.
