title: Despite holes, a fantastic flick
review:
I have finally seen this movie now that it has come onto the HBO heavy rotation, as was my plan.

In reading these reviews, I must say that I find the bulk of them to be fantastically petty and purposefully critical without good reason.

It's apparent to me that many of the reviewers are too young, or ignorant of the original War of the Worlds, to know that the endings of both versions are identical. This quibbling about the way the aliens so suddenly go down ignores this salient fact.

Second, many complain that Robbie re-appears at the end despite "being blown up in a fireball". Until I read these reviews, this never occurred to me; nothing in the film suggests that everyone in that short blaze of fire perished; who is to say that the son did? In addition, the fireball occurs minutes after the parting of father and son; the boy could be a hundred yards away at the point of the explosion.

The holes that do bother me include the sudden appearance of working camcorders and digital cameras where moments before no electronics, not even watches, were functional; this makes little sense. I also groaned when Cruise's stolen minivan is untouched by the nearby crashed airliner, and I groaned at the news crew who were desperately searching the crashed airliner for food despite being surrounded by thousands of abandoned houses... and why would they be so hungry after only a day or so of alien fleeing? The final groan was for the public bulletin boards plastered a'la 9/11 with "Missing" posters only a day or so after the invasion begins, as if the invasion had been going on for months.

All that aside, I thought that the evolution of Cruise's character was excellent, I thought that Dakota Fanning did a superb, REALISTIC job as an extremely whiny and needy 10-year-old girl in the crisis of her life. Many here call her performance "too screechy" and I believe that this is because in so many Hollywood pictures, kids under horrific pressure suddenly morph into heroic, thoughtful adults. No, they don't... they scream and cry and are needy, just as Spielberg directs Fanning to portray here. Excellent job by both.

I'm not a big special effects fan... they're great if they help the plot. The effects here are absolutely spectacular; the tripods are incredibly realistic, there's no "blue-screen" fuzzy outlines or perspective problems, and there's no reliance on effects to carry the action, thank you. Well, well done.

I'm very pleased that Spielberg stuck to the original ending, and didn't give in to the modern audience's desire to see Americans blow away every obstacle in their path. No, the aliens go down in a clever and realistic fashion that stays true to the original... no pandering to those who simply must see the US Army have its way by blowing up the latest threat (just to make us all feel good about how we can't get the job done in Iraq). Kudos, Mr. Spielberg, for staying true to the roots of the picture you so superbly honored.

Overall, character development made the movie; the eye of the film stays with the main characters and is realistic in that, unlike Hollywood standardization, they are determined to escape the invaders, NOT to cleverly figure out a way to sneak a computer virus and a nuke on board (as in the ridiculous "Independence Day" "We're American so we nuke everything while waving our flag" crap).

From the enthralling first appearance of the tripods to the superbly crafted characters to the sense of dread throughout and for the cinematic eye and faithful ending of this film, I give it a nine, holding back a point for the couple of plot-groans in the beginning of the picture.

title: Ulla again
review:
I'm not a fan of Hollywood blockbusters except as a piece of empty entertainment. I have no expectations about them; but I am irritated by people who complain that these films aren't 'Citizen Kane'. So 'War of the Worlds' had a lot to live up to. The book has some superior parts in it than others. The '53 film was a successful piece of commie bashing entertainment. To add to the challenge for Spielberg there is Jeff Wayne's musical version and a performance and recitation of that by a British actor, scientist and psychic called Stephen Armourae who is such a fan of the work and Richard Burton (who was on the album). Spielberg firstly remained fairly faithful to the book and paid homage to the 1953 film since it more successfully than almost any other of the anti- communist sci if films captured a sense of desperation and a strong style that was present in 1950s Hollywood productions.

The film is surprisingly dark and realistic and is prepared to hold to its convictions without pandering to the audience. Spielberg has been prepared to take risks of upsetting the audience since 'Schindler's List' demonstrated the importance of serious and mature film making to him. References to the Holocaust are present. In an essay by Stephen Armourae he points to Wells' prophecies: his description of the heat ray is similar to an atom bomb explosion and when the martians destroy London they concentrate the populace of the country into London before turning it into the martian's camp and exterminating them. Wells uses the word 'camp' too. All this 50 years before it happened. Having given the impression that this is a bleak and miserable film this is much like the 50's sci-if movies that it at times so successfully tributes and consequently is entertaining. Cruise being a Hollywood success has meant he is forever cast as an action hero. Here however he displays vulnerability as he breaks down over family pressures and the pressure of total annihilation.

A recurring problem for the sci if departments has been the fighting machines. Hence in 1953 they replaced by martian aircraft. Finally they have been able to manage the relentless and threatening movement as envisioned by Wells. The ending is hurried along as the the film has spent so much time developing the story More awareness of the invader's predicament would have been preferred. 'Dead London' in the novel and in the musical benefit from this. This film is worth seeing and to be surprised that this look back towards the 50's also contains the kind of old fashioned writing and craftsmanship that was blown away after the success of 'Jaws' created the Blockbuster for good and bad.

title: it was an entertaining movie, what movie about aliens wouldn't?
review: I have to say that this movie wasn't all it was said to have been. There was not enough action; the action doesn't include every every single scene in the movie, despite the intro, being aliens attacking humans and killing them and the humans seem helpless to prevent it. You have the big scene in the beginning where the first aliens arrive, and that is how the movie should have been situated. After that there should have been a solution to how to stop the invaders. It didn't even live up to the name of War of the Worlds. This whole thing was one sided. It was very entertaining, I'll grant that, but for a Spielberg movie, I was a little disappointed. In my opinion, Independence Day is beat WOTW by a long shot. Cruise was decent, Fanning was superb, and Robbins gave a nice side effect. All in all, I gave it a six out of ten.

title: No Wonder Tom Cruise Went Crazy...
review:
...After this, how could he not? Cruise's PR tour for "War of the Worlds" has been infamously disastrous. Cruise seemingly went crazier and crazier with each show he appeared on. No movie has had PR this bad since Bill Cosby publicly begged people not to see "Leonard Part Six", his own personal disasterpiece.

Well, there's a reason Cruise is acting the way he is. It's the movie. "War of the Worlds" is so vapid, shallow, redundant, and pointless that it becomes almost palindromic: it starts out dull, and it ends dull. The middle part isn't just dull, it's insipid too. This film is so full of plot holes, enormous leaps of faith, impossibilities, and continuity mistakes that I wonder if Spielberg even hired a script supervisor.

Here's the plot: Tom Cruise, Dakota Fanning, and some other kid I've never heard of (so far as I remember) run away from gigantic alien machines that have been buried under our feet for millions of years. I'm not sure how we never noticed them while laying pipelines and subway tunnels down, but this doesn't matter to Spielberg. Along the way the trio encounter crazed people running for their own lives, a plane crash with no bodies in sight, which is never explained, and other general destruction. This is "Armageddon" without the giant rock.

The movie carries on like this for two hours. I got so bored I was begging for a gun to magically appear in my hand so that I might shoot myself in the face and end the pain by the time Hour One was three-quarters over. You can imagine how desperate I became as the film progressed.

I've seen films with mistakes and plot holes, but "War of the Worlds" seems to be based on them rather than just having them. A plane crashes straight into a house where Cruise and company are hiding out, and yet it doesn't crush the van in the driveway, allowing them to drive away. Mind you, the entire neighborhood was flattened by this crash. The crash has no victims. Dakota Fanning's character remains clueless, despite looking the slimy martian bastards in the face, until the very end of the film. The rest of the time she asks why "the terrorists" are attacking. Does she think that people who had to steal jet planes to attack us only four years ago could possibly have ten-mile tall machines of mass-destruction, and just neglected to use them previously? Does this film have any right to draw comparisons between itself and the worst attack ever led on US soil? Spielberg apparently thinks he has that right, and for this he should be shunned, fired, and banned from all Hollywood studios. It's a disgusting thing to do. He knows it, and he doesn't care. Steven Spielberg is not only a hack director, but a sick freak as well. I will never ever regret saying that. I'll also never regret vowing to never ever see another of his films ever again. I may just throw out my as yet unwatched copy of "Schindler's List" in protest.

The only good thing about this movie is the special effects. Well, at least for a little bit. The first appearance of a martian machine climbing out of the ground is impressive. But once it started killing people just so Spielberg could use sights of genocide to jerk our tears, I became completely disgusted with the movie as a whole. "just so Spielberg can use sights of genocide to jerk our tears". Frankly, this sounds like a possible plot description for "Schindler's List", so maybe I'm not wrong to throw it out. Anyway, it's not like I can recommend the film based purely on the look of it's effects. That would be like giving Jennifer Lopez an Oscar for "Enough" just because she's attractive.

"War of the Worlds" is a shameful, vile film. Not only does it assault our senses, but it also insults our intelligence and uses allusions to a national tragedy to tug our heart strings. Steven Spielberg is a despicable person for making this, and the cast should be ashamed to have appeared in such a movie. The only people who can be proud are the special effects team, who made the creatures come to life beautifully. It's too bad they're used to progress such an evil plot.

title: Great story...... when it was first written !!!!
review: I sat down at the cinema and thought to myself "well I've read the book let's see how quickly Spielberg and Co destroy it", and right from the start typical bloody Americans have set the whole film in America (I know the earlier movie had been as well), why can't people just leave the locations alone, War of the Worlds is set in ENGLAND. So after the first disappointment I proceeded to forget to compare to the book as I would have probably walked out. Now, the special effects are what we come to expect nowadays and as this film heavily depends on them it's a good job too although the actual aliens where unnecessary as I believe not knowing what they look like helps to keep the audience guessing and allow them to use their own imagination. I would say that the first half of this film is actually very entertaining, but as soon as Tim Robbins enters the story I'm afraid the film just looses all credibility, I'm not having a go at Tim Robbins as I think he is a great actor, it's just the story telling was just none existent, it's as though the script writers had said "Hey let's show an intense build up to the Aliens starting the war, and then after that, sod it let's just wing it it's an old story anyway". I not going to go into too much depth of the story but I want to leave you with this thought, If a race of super intelligent beings had chosen Earth as it's feeding ground for it's future young, you would have thought because they are so much more advanced than us that they'd have checked for the only thing that could actually kill them, Bacteria. Now this ending is fine when it was first written, but seen as though Spielberg and Co had changed the story where they saw fit, you'd think that they could have incorporated the old idea with a new slant just so the 21st century audience could actually believe the reason for the Aliens demise.

title: Just one more thing...
review:
No need to add to the trouncing the film's already gotten here, but... I was astounded at how class-ridden the film's ending was. Here comes Tom, the yutz, grimy and beaten. Out comes Miranda from behind her intact 19th-century glass door, freshly-pressed and newly-showered. After scooping up her daughter, she won't even approach the guy, she just mouths "thank you" from a distance.

And up on the stoop: grandma and grandpa and -- my favorite character in the movie -- step dad Tim, well-heeled and ineffectual Tim. They're all smiling, but you can almost hear them discussing the tip: "What do you think for this guy, a twenty? Well done, son. Pick it up at the service entrance."

Absolutely ridiculous.

title: The minimal plot consists of characters too stupid to walk and chew gum at the same time experiencing an unending series of incredibly stupid moments.
review: This movie has just replaced Ishtar as the worst movie I've ever seen. At least with Ishtar, when Beatty and Hoffman weren't attempting to sing, there was almost a plot going on. I've never seen so many stupid characters gathered in one unending series of unbelievably stupid situations. Not only should these characters not be allowed to live, they shouldn't have bred. Going by how stupid these people were portrayed, it's a wonder any child reaches adulthood. They remind me of Douglas Adams' hairdressers and telephone sanitizers only not as smart. I finally left the movie when I realized I was rooting for the aliens to exterminate mankind. When you want the bad guys to win, you're either evil or really ticked off (mostly the latter for me - there's a little evil in all of us). I'm not sure any of this qualifies as a spoiler, however, there is one scene in the movie which is memorable because I almost liked it. Another major disaster occurs near Cruise's character, which he and his kids miraculously survive (they may not be smart but they sure are lucky), and he stumbles outside in his usual state of near comatose observation. He finds some reporters looting the disaster site. They're gathering water and food (something he has so far failed to successfully do). Now, I ask you, in a movie not about reporters, how bad is it when they are the smartest characters you've seen?

title: Best Human *** Kickery since Independence Day.
review:
It reminded me a lot of the "Oh...shit...we're screwed" feeling you get from Independence Day...

But yeah...it was pretty dang awesome.

It had a lot of the same mishaps as Signs did. I loved that you didn't see any of the Tripods in the previews or anything...instead you had to wait to see the movie. Revieling they they are tripods shouldn't be a spoiler..for it was based on the book...and the book described them as tripods.

Cruises character was a typical Tom Cruise performance... Cruise played himself in this movie...really. His children were the definition of annoying. There was the stereotypical scene/emo idiot who is so filled with stereotypical teenage angst...that you could tell he was going to do something stupid. The fact that he was still there... made me despise it as though he wanted to make it mushier for American audiences. If the Japanese made this movie... they would have killed him off... and show the family living on...well he was stereotypical anyway.

Cruises daughter in this... was a total brat...and I would have left her for the freaking aliens. If she were my kid. I would have given her the Brian Maddox. If she continued to yell... "sorry, you are alien food" but I'm a jerk anyway.

Special FX: Sweet I'm not a movie critic or a professional movie fan. I'm a guy who loved the movie...and was more than willing to overlook its bad parts.

The fiery train...was an omniscient mind-messer upper. It was a wonderful touch. It was on fire... And that was awesome.

The tripods looked cool...very much like Japanese fighting robots. I'm an avid audio synthesist and I loved the sounds they made. Lucckily my girlfriend is an audio junkie too...so we talked about the noises they made for a while.

The news broadcast showing all the tripods leveling a city was scary. The disturbing image factor was also pretty high in that the way they used humans for fertilizer.... It was quite nice. I also thought it was awesome that the Japanese were able to take a few down. I loved that part...because you know they know all about those Giant Robots. (I know I'm stereotyping here and sounding racist...I hope that whoever reads this is intelligent enough to know that I'm kidding).

The images paled in comparison to those in Asian horror..but they were still pretty gruesome. Just try and picture yourself as one of those people...any one of them..and note how well your day would suck if one day. All in all...I think you should see it. Just to see people get smeared across the board and go through yet another massive alien attack.

I'm going to see it again and get me a poster off of ebay. Good stuff here.

"as it did so a second glittering titan built itself from the earth" - Chapter 14.

title: Bore of the Worlds
review:
Disappointing. The one scene that could have really made it was only implied. Did Ray kill the Tim Robbins character, or did the Tim Robbins character kill himself when trapped in a room alone with Tom Cruise/Ray....is Ray a scientologist as well....did he take a moment to try to bring Robbins character into the light????

I cannot fault the filmmakers....well maybe I can, this scene or something like it in the H G Wells book, I get the wanting to create suspense with the outcome but, I really would have preferred Tim Robbins to get it from an Alien.

Dakota Fanning delivered a knock out performance. She may win best supporting actress. Spielberg has a gift for finding young talent and making them deliver performances that knock your socks off. You cared about her, and it was pretty funny when she turned to her brother for support rather than her father...dysfunctional family party of 3 all separate tables please.

The effects were good, but the other characters, who cares, let them get spun around in the alien salad shooter.

How did Ray's son escape the carnage, last time we saw him he was running into ambush land with the mean ET's.

If Ray is so smart, why isn't he a scientist....oops he is a Scientoligist....does that count? I found the images of the downed plane a little to close to home, in the post September 11 world, a little too real. Honestly I think the Tom Cruise has taken it too far and his antics over Katie Holmes have really soured me on his works.

If Tom Hanks had done this film it would be a masterpiece, but Cruise just doesn't have the acting chops for diverse roles. He is like a lot of Hollywood leading men, they have one delivery and thats what you get regardless of the role.

The ending with its neat and tidy :30 second wrap up was also contrived. The kids are safe home with Mom, and step dad in a completely undamaged part of Boston. Finally the last thing I wanted to see was not delivered. When Ray brings the kid home, the grandparents who HATE him just stand on the porch like it was the milk man delivering a half gallon of milk. No, gee Ray, you are not a total screw up you saved our grand daughter....but no closure....maybe that will be in War of the World 2 When the Grandparents sue Ray for child endangerment.........

title: had me at the edge of my seat
review:
I consider myself jaded where movies are concerned. I have seen so many that almost nothing elicits an emotional response out of me. This movie, for lack of better words, scared the crap out of me. For the first time since Signs, i was afraid for the main characters.

The movie starts out with Ray Farrier, a crappy dad, having his kids dropped off for the weekend. Soon a storm starts and a whole lot of very fantastically done and faithful to the book aliens start invading. Throughout the movie, we follow Ray,and we never see what he doesn't. This for me added to the realistic feel of the film.

The only gripe i have is that once the wow factor wears off, you are left with some glaring plot holes. But don't think about it too much and just enjoy the show.

title: Proof Steven S. hates you
review: As it was too hot to enjoy an afternoon outside the family decided to take in WOTW in the coolness of the theater. Unfotunately the air-conditioning was more enjoyable than this inane, disjointed, insult of a film. The best part was the trailer for the upcoming King Kong. I didn't expect the film to be on the scale of Close Encounters gone evil as many reviewers had implied but by 2005 every director, especially Speilburg, should realize even the least sophisticated audience can spot the massive continuity problems of this movie. Therefore it stands to reason he didn't care.Evidently there were tight scheduling constraints for Cruise & Speilburg & the film was shot & edited almost simultaneously (Speilburg's 1st all digital shoot evidently) in a third of the time he regularly takes. It shows.As Speilburg is a vocal advocate to preserve the use of film in movie making, perhaps this is his attempt to sabotage the all digital revolution. One can only wonder.

title: Original is way better
review:
You've seen plenty of movies featuring lots of action but little character development and dialogue. This is just the other side of the coin: plenty of focus on characters while the alien invasion is a background task. Great special effects are a diversion from a Spielbergian soap opera about a divorced part-time father and his kids, especially the son (who looks almost as old as dad) who rediscover their love for one another while giant metal alien guided machines emerge from the earth and sizzle people with death rays and poop out human blood. Despite a strong focus on the son and his apparent desperation to become a man by throwing himself into harms way, little is really served by the father-son angst, nor does the viewer care really at any level. Cruise's acting in this one goes from great, to mediocre to overacting and back to great, sometimes all within minutes.

The best part about this film, apart from its obviously expectations-met sfx, is Tim Robbins brief role as a mental case hiding out in his basement. Robbins is just great in anything he does, and this one is no exception. In fact, I wanted to see and learn more about Robbins character than the aliens outside, scooping up people and pooping out their blood.

The original film version had so much more character and heartfelt drama. I think Spielberg's come a long, long way in his career and unfortunately, I think I like his older stuff much better.

One last thing, I'm tired of today's generation of action movies where any scene using sfx features a gloomy, or dimly lit background, whether outdoors or inside.

title: worth seeing
review: This movie was very exciting, right from the get go. I was surprised that the entire film is shot from one persons view. Other alien movies shift between multiple people and their individual stories, but this movie stayed entirely with Mr. Cruise. great concept.I saw it at the drive-in and I'm looking forward to seeing it at home. The actors that play Tom Cruise's children are excellent. Other than Tom Cruise and Tim Robbins, their really weren't any other big stars in this movie. The special effects are great, but not over done as some movies tend to do. I can't wait till the DVD comes out so I can see the extras and making of and hopefully some deleted scenes.

title: Why is Tim Robbins an obligatory-cliché dirty old man in this sci-fi plot (flop)?
review: Steven; please do not make anymore remakes of good old sci-fi classics. Let other directors with energy and enthusiasms do the next movies in your company. Sit only as president of Dream Works. Get out of the directors chair! Why put Tim Robbins in this sci-fi "Disaster Movie" as an implied obligatory-cliché, of a dirty old man? Tim's a good actor. He did not need to do this weird character. Did H. G. have an implied dirty old man in his book? Maybe I missed it. What is Tim's "character" supposed to lend to this "Disaster Movie"? Shame on you Steven Spielberg! Go see the 1953 campy version - it's a lot more interesting and fun. Tom Cruse has lost "it" in more ways than one on screen and on TV. Dakota Fanning is good in anything. It is a shame she had to be in this dumb remake.

title: Better than expected
review: What is this movie reflecting about the American Society? The same thing that was being said at the time it was written in the late 1930's. The war was in Europe. The Americans were being criticized by the world powers for not getting involved. The enemy was too far away to be any threat (Mars). Hitler was causing chaos in Europe and was meticulously overthrowing each of the countries (like the tripods). And then there is the recent action in Iraq, only this time it is the other way around. It is the world army blowing up Iraq. Some people say it should never have happened, let's ignore it and let them get on with their repression. And some say lets get in their with the guns ablazing. Sort of like the conflict between the father and son characters. What is the world not acknowledging about itself that is being projected onto IRAQ. Who says that meritocracy is the way of the future - probably the rich! Anyway, the movie is to be seen by people to make their own minds up. It should not be up to others to say to someone "not to go and see it". Stop thinking just about the special effects and ask yourselves the deeper questions about what drove particular characters to do the things they did. Put your thinking caps on and still be entertained.

title: Very Entertaining Summer Flick
review:
Amazing visual effects and solid acting made this summer blockbuster work.

I am very surprised that Steven Spielberg met the deadline for this movie considering that he only started shooting 8 months ago, but the acting in this movie was fantastic and the Computer-Genertated images were flawless. But the abrupt storyline left many questions unanswered and it would be nice to know how the devastation of the Alien tripods affected other cultures.

But this movie really captured the drama of a worldwide catastrophe when we witnessed the hordes of people trying to escape the Alien Onslaught and eventually killing each other to get a single car.

Very well-done movie and it delivers what it promises. 9/10

title: Somewhat engaging but ultimately pointless remake with Evil E.T., P.C., and sci-fi horror for the modern dysfunctional family...
review:
Let's just break it down in simple terms. Steven Spielberg, with the rare exceptions of a few films like Schindler's List, Saving Private Ryan, Minority Report, and even AI, makes ephemeral thrill-ride movies with reasonably happy endings.

War of the Worlds is no different. This film is a throwback to the early Spielberg of Jaws, Close Encounters, and E.T., which were marvelously filmed, vacuous, and quasi-plot less masterpieces that were at least tolerable enough to sit through with a bag of popcorn. Spielberg, like his contemporary George Lucas, has taken the Dino De Laurentis model and just animated it more with computers. They can't provide, process, or direct a script, but man can they throw up a busy screen full of non-stop action. Josh Friedman, the screenplay writer, does nothing to improve Spielberg's track record this time either.

I am not going to recount either the H.G. Wells book, the Byron Haskin 1953 movie adaptation, or the dumb late-1980s syndicated show. You know the drill. The retelling of this version, however, involves watching the invasion through the eyes of a dysfunctional working class father, played by Tom Cruise, his married-up-from-her-first mistake ex-wife, played by Miranda Otto, his teen-son-on-the-verge-of-recklessness, played by Justin Chatwin, and the precocious-but-claustrophobic younger sister, played by Dakota Fanning. We are immersed quickly into the problems and interplay of the children of divorce with their parents, and quite frankly, that is the only redeeming feature of this film. Sadly for the viewer, the aliens arrive to screw up the interplay, and we quickly are immersed in the "Aliens-vs.-Earthings" gig that we have all seen countless times (particularly if one is over 35). This film could have been about how a disinterested father gradually grows to understand and appreciate his kids under the heat of adversity, but Spielberg never quite takes us there. Instead, Spielberg tries to make subtle statements against war and even self-defense with Cruise and Chatwin, and again with Tim Robbins and Cruise when trapped underneath an alien lair. I won't give away what happens, but clearly Spielberg takes the pacifist view (and the anti-patriot view in this reviewer's opinion with the outcome, which angered me quite frankly). Whether this was Spielberg's cut against the Iraq War or militia movements or something else in some subtle way is debatable, but it isn't particularly subtle or interesting in its conclusion. Perhaps Jimmy Carter was an uncredited script editor (and don't his eyes look a little alien?).

What really ticked me off about this film is that we are led to a battlefield scene between the aliens and the good 'ol U.S. Army, but we never get to see it! I think this is a cruel commercial manipulation by Mr. Spielberg to release a director's cut DVD with all the scenes in it, assuming this film flops at the box office. What he does not realize, if this is the case is that true sci-fi special effects junkies WANT TO SEE THAT ON THE BIG SCREEN, and not on the LCD at home, even if it's a big screen. I am not certain that I would rent the DVD if those scenes are included for that reason alone. Why cheat us out of what most alien invasion movie aficionados really want; a kick-butt battle between the good guys and the bad guys?

The special effects are dazzling, no doubt, but the only redeeming feature of the plot which never quite satisfies us is the masterful acting of Dakota Fanning. She plays to the camera and to her co-stars with a subtle brilliance that reminds of both of the ingénue of Drew Barrymore in E.T. and the early works of Jodie Foster. Her portrayal of the claustrophobic daughter is very believable and unforced, even when the script seems to take her off course a bit. If she matures in much the way that Jodie Foster has, she will have one heck of an acting career ahead of her.

At any rate, unless you just want to burn two hours and ten bucks in a syrup-coated seat, this is not worth going to see. If Spielberg still wants to buy his forty-one-thousandth Lamborghini and he decides to put the directors cut ON THE SCREEN and WITH ALL THE BATTLE SCENES, then one might be persuaded to see it there. Otherwise, I am not even certain that I would rent this thing. However, if you are bored or if you have a naïve (or surreptitiously naïve) date who wants to grab hold of you during all the scary scenes, then rent the DVD. Those kinds of cheap thrills are the only ones worth sitting though the entire length of Spielberg's War of the Worlds to actually experience.

I give this 3 out of 10 stars, but just barely 3.

title: Poor scriptwriting, Shallow Characters, Spielberg Not Up to Usual Standards
review:
Don't waste your money. Wait for the DVD if you must see it. Here's some observations:

  • Script is weak and unrealistic in parts. Streets caving in with people just standing around staring as asphalt splits beneath their feet. No screaming or running or panicking until too late. Excuse me, these New Jersey folks (where the movie begins) had just dealt with 9-11...they should be running at the first crack of the pavement!


  • Characters are two dimensional and stereotypical. Ex-wife is the nosy mom trooping and snooping through Cruise's house uninvited, complaining and moaning as her new rich husband says "I'm staying out of this" and slips out. Teenage son won't listen and won't talk, broods on bed with Walkman in his ears. Doesn't try to sooth his little sister even though he should realize dad isn't the best at doing this. Young daughter has constant panic attacks and screams throughout the whole movie, very irritating. Someone should slap her the side of the head or give her one of the medications that Tom Cruise badmouths on Scientology TV interviews!


  • The main characters get on a ferry boat to cross the Hudson River. The aliens are suddenly looming over them. Excuse me, when giant aliens are on top of you, it is impossible to flee or hide on a ferry boat compared to staying in town and finding a hiding place (basements and cellars seem to be the best places they stake out throughout the film).


  • They flee the city to visit the ex-wife's house looking for her (when they know that she and new rich hubby took a weekend trip). When they arrive, EVERY light in the 2-story semi-mansion is turned on! They begin looking for food to eat. They first go through the cardboard box they carried from home (filled with peanut butter, bread and condiments. Oh, by the way, the daughter is allergic to peanuts!) instead of immediately raiding (or at least checking out) the refrigerator and cupboards in the gourmet kitchen where they are seated.


  • Steven Spielberg borrows so much from past films: the weird storm clouds from the farm scene in Close Encounters of the Third Kind, the aliens from Independence Day, the gruesome music from Jaws, and predictable special effects and film angles that echo from several of his past films.


  • Hiding out in basements and cellars was like watching "Signs" with Mel Gibson all over again. In fact, I think Mel was more proactive in protecting his family and better at securing his "fortress" and finding hiding places. I would personally feel safer with Gibson on guard but certainly not with Cruise!


  • The ending fails to really explain why the aliens end up like they do. They made it very clear in the 1953 version of the movie.


  • There is an obvious lack of authority figures throughout the disasters - almost no police, firemen or ambulances, and even when the military turns up in scenes, they appear superficial and don't make you feel confident that they can do anything but look brave (and even that is highly questionable.)


  • There is no explanation for the stringy looking red "things" draped over everything and growing up walls and trees.


  • There are some bad special effects, like birds flying at night overhead. Obviously computer generated and not well done at all. I failed to see how it helped the storyline or what point Spielberg was trying to make.


I am a big science fiction fan and long time fan of Spielberg, but the movie lacks depth all around and people and scenes are just not believable for the most part. The saving grace is the special effects (even though so many of them seem like borrowings from all his other movies, not much new and exciting, makes you yawn because you have seen it all before.)

The movie is too violent and bloody for the under 13 year old and older people who tend to have nightmares. On the other hand, if Steven Spielberg was trying to terrorize people overall, I think he failed miserably except for a scene here or there. It seemed almost comical, like watching a bad "B" horror flick from the 1950s, only this was in color with all the computer-generated special effects added. Bottom line: I did not fear going home and having nightmares.

Spend your money on a different movie this summer. Or better yet, try reading the original H. G. Wells 1898 novel of "War of the Worlds". (If you are lucky, you might be able to round up a copy of the 1953 video too.)

title: Huge Disappointment
review: Easily put it was just plain bad. The acting, special effects, and film parts of it were all good, but the story line was absolutely horrible. It seemed like there was no story line actually. Started out, aliens came. And they ran. Seemed like that was the whole movie right there. Then the ending was a total bust. I thought of about 10 flaws before I even got to my car it was so bad. I don't understand how the director/writers didn't catch these obvious flaws in their story line when an average person like me can in under a few minutes. I would say to wait for this to come out on DVD before you pay to see it. It was pretty bad.

title: Weak, pointless effort
review:
As the film ground to its flat, unimaginative ending, and I and the rest of the audience rose stiffly from our seats, and walked down the long hallway through the multiplex to emerge into the bright sunlight of late afternoon New Mexico, I realized what a useless, pointless waste of money and effort this new War of the Worlds is.

Early in Spielberg's career I became an enormous fan of his work, eagerly anticipating every new effort he would involve himself in. I greedily ate up his television movie, Duel, and Jaws and Close Encounters and Sugerland Express were revelations. His promise seemed unlimited. The first Indiana Jones film is an unqualified classic.

Then, he seemed to begin to disappoint. Was he being given too much freedom? Was he too sure of himself? Too self-indulgent? While ET is considered his masterpiece, didn't it also show his increasing penchant to pander to his audience, indulging in sentimentality? After a while I really started disliking his films, especially when he tried to make 'serious' films like Empire of the Sun, which I walked out on halfway through. I particularly detested A.I. which I also walked out on in the last ten minutes. Did Spielberg really think he could take over from Stanley Kubrick and do him the honor of completing his lost project? How sad. Spielberg is to Kubrick as Margaret Mitchell is to Tolstoy.

How empty one feels after sitting through this War of the Worlds. How pointless; what a waste. I actually felt sorry for the crew of the film, spending days working on some absurd minor shot of alien destruction.

Please Mr. Spielberg, take a weekend off and rent DVD's of De Sica's Bicycle Thief, and Umberto D. Now that's real film-making. How do I know the difference? Your're moved afterwords, and you don't feel empty, that you've wasted two hours...

But I don't think he's going to change his style now. I can only imagine the sentimental mess he's going to make of the '72 Olympics tragedy.

title: Not since Pearl Harbor.....
review:
....has there been a bigger let down in regards to a big-budget movie. I wanted to like this movie, I really did. This movie has the actors (Cruise, Fanning, Robbins), it has the director (Spielberg) and it has an often emulated plot that has been around for decades. Sadly, these things are also its downfall. I will keep the spoilers to a minimum however there will be a few. Lets start with the actors... Cruise- Plays a completely unsympathetic character that I wouldn't

have minded seeing get killed in the first few minutes. Fanning-Scream(pre-teen) Queen. Oh yeah and she spouts out new age

healing (hints of Scientology) lines a few times. (They

must start 'em young) Robbins- The most interesting character with the most potential that

gets used the least. Too bad Robbins public anti-Iraqi views

crept into the script with the "Occupations never work' line

Next, Spielberg delivers one of the worst "surprises" that I've seen in years. It's an overly-done, tired, worn out "I'm a character you're supposed to care about that supposedly dies like everyone else around me but pop up at the end for a tearful family reunion". Come on Steven, you're the man who made E.T., Jaws, and 1941...how about some originality?

Lastly, we have the plot. Almost everyone knows the story and it hasn't changed much. But what has is that there's no feeling to it. The family is almost unbelievably dysfunctional. There's nothing shown where you should care about any of the characters. Also, while yes this is a science fiction movie, the suspension of disbelief can't be established. It tells you soon into the movie about electromagnetic pulse bursts that take out everything electronic. Yet, camcorders work....I may be nitpicking at this point but this is one example of a few glaring oversights.

As I said before, I wanted to like this movie but I have to tell everyone, save your money on this one and instead go to Batman Begins or Land of the Dead or even Herbie. That little bug was more likable than anyone in Spielbergs world....

Oh yeah, it gets a 2 for some decent special effect shots

title: Tom can run
review:
War of the Worlds I debated whether skipping this for a time just because it was a remake of an old classic I had seen and remakes rarely live up to, let alone surpass the originals. For those others not old enough to recall, the original was made in 1953 and starred Gene Barry, later to go on to greater fame as the star of TV's western series "Bat Masterson (1958)" and "Burke's Law (1963)". But boredom and a night wanting to escape reality won out, so I went on opening night, something I almost never do because of the crowds. As it was the theater was sold out all but the last showing, so guess how late I stayed up on a work night? Anyway... I digress... I was prepared to be disappointed.

Let's address the obvious first. Well, the script didn't exactly follow the book (which I read as a young boy along with the rest of Well's works) but it's likely better given the medium here. The screenplay did a rather great job of updating the old classic's story line to something that at least seemed plausible, given the theme. For that bit of slight-of-keyboard one must give thanks to Josh Friedman, who "consulted on the recently enjoyable "Sahara" but seems to have few other credits to boast of. His list should rightfully grow after this effort, all masterfully photographed by the stunningly talented cinematographer Janusz Kaminski (another Oscar for him perhaps?).

After the story, to build a good, never mind great, Sci Fi piece, we must have adequate sets, art direction and costuming. These were all top notch and also fit the film quite well. Some of the "looks" of the sets here are Oscar worthy in scale, scope and ambition so we should hear more in the future about this effort.

Next, one must mention the efforts of the director, the legendary Steven Spielberg. I think he elicited perhaps the best performance to date from Tom Cruise and excellent performances from Tim Robbins and the young Ms. Dakota Fanning. Their performances are somewhat limited by the type of story it is, but they all do extremely well in making it a great movie. Watch for Gene Barry, the star of the original film, making a cameo appearance near the end of the film (apparently Tom Cruise's character's ex-father-in-law). The one thing that is hard to do is introduce anything in this kind of a story, where all of humanity is so completely devastated by the invaders. The character Cruise plays would be very difficult for any actor as they made him a pretty unsympathetic blue collar/red-neck type of a shiftless ruffian; a failed ex-husband and what appears a joke as a father. Still, with all of that going against him, Cruise manages to make us root for his character. In the end I think they went a bit overboard in trying to make him look like just an ordinary guy who still manages to somehow survive the unthinkable against all the odds. The nuances in his performance will likely be missed or misunderstood by many, especially by his leagues of fluttering femme fans.

Last, but certainly not least in this genre, are the special effects. Here, all the stops are pulled and there are some great effects that contribute to the finished product in the best possible way. Sitting in the audience of a packed theater I could feel the audience react en-mass to many of them.

All-in-all, the producers delivered what is likely better than the original, thoroughly entertaining and definitely worth the price of admission. It is classic Science Fiction in it's rawest manifestation so it may not be favorite of general movie goers, but as I filed out of the theater with the pressing throng (I seemed to be one of the VERY few people in the theater OVER the age of 20) I heard many patrons speak positively of it. I can recommend it, especially to Sci Fi fans.

title: Some very interesting elements but overall disappointing
review:
I will warn before all spoilers, because there are very few and so those of you who don't want them could read most of this review without issue.

The Mercury Theater radio production of "War of the Worlds" makes a nearly impossible standard--its realism was so extreme as to famously induce panic that its events were truly unfolding--and Steven Spielberg, perhaps wisely, doesn't even attempt to match this level, instead opting to make a film with only the basic storyline and opening monologue in common with that production.

Instead, Spielberg's film follows a pattern used previously in George Romero's "Dawn of the Dead," Alfred Hitchcock's "The Birds," and the Stephen King novel "The Stand" by getting the catastrophe out of the way quickly, *SPOILER* destroying the world in about 20 minutes. *SPOILER OVER* This structure can lend itself to deep psychological drama, as in "The Birds," or social satire, as in Romero's films. Spielberg opts for something more akin to the latter, making a big deal of the feelings of anger and need for revenge that some feel while others do not and downplaying the (admittedly very tired) family dynamic and the mystery of what's going on or what the invaders want. We know from the opening monologue that the "storm" we see is an invasion--before Ray or anyone else knows--and it's never really explained why they do what they do. Even the ending is explained post-mortem in another Morgan Freeman monologue rather than in the film itself. Meanwhile, the family is the same as every other broken family we see on film--from the selfish father to the ever-frightened little girl to the kind and rich stepfather and so the fact that the drama of the family is only a minor subplot is perhaps a good thing.

Spielberg instead focuses on how people react to the events--with thoughtful confusion (Ray), with anger and a lust for revenge (Robbie), with panic (Rachel), or with a frightful mental collapse (Ogilvy). There's also a heavy war analogy played out throughout, culminating in a frighteningly beautiful scene *SPOILER* showing a man letting his son go off to fight a war he doesn't believe in because the son does believe in it only to watch the entire zone engulfed in flames. *SPOILER OVER* There's also a frightful element in the look of one of the tripods when it captures the Ferriers--*SPOILER* it resembles a female reproductive system to such a degree that its familiarity was disconcerting and yet there was seemingly no other reason for it *SPOILER OVER*. Still, the truth is that there's very little storyline and we can all predict that these would be the various reactions, so it's nothing too interesting.

The acting in the film is hampered by a lack of character, but in the meatiest role Tom Cruise is able to provide more depth than the character would otherwise have, providing one of his stronger performances in an almost note-for-note return to his previous role of Charlie Babbot in "Rain Man." Meanwhile, Dakota Fanning is appropriately annoying as the whiny, panicky daughter and Justin Chatwin is utterly unbelievable as the angry son who turns out to be more capable than anyone of handling the shock of the invasion. The only other performance of note is Tim Robbins, who is always brilliant and no exception here. Ogilvy may seem the most unbelievable character, but Robbins's performance turns him into the most real.

Overall, "War of the Worlds" is somewhat disappointing and yet it remains interesting enough to entertain. Spielberg provides some beautiful shots and some of the scenes are magic, but the dull, unimaginative characters, the plot holes, and the lack of storyline drag the film down from its possibilities. I personally would much rather have no visual and just listen to Orson Welles.

title: This film Kicks some serious Ass
review:
This is the reason i go to the Movies, To be enthralled, To be Entertained. "War Of The Worlds" does this, in the most gripping film i have seen since "Saving Private Ryan". Co-incidence or not.

I have just arrived home from a screening in Sydney and i was ready for anything. title: The 'Tom Cruise' of the Worlds
review: What a load of garbage. It is certainly NOT superior to the original movie. Even the lame television series was better. The only thing correct was the tripods from the original novel. Why did the aliens look like refugees from Independence Day? Why didn't someone just slap that annoying pre teen daughter of Tom Cruise's character? Can't we have a Spielberg movie WITHOUT the rebellious and often just plain STUPID teenage son who somehow, against all odds and tremendous alien weaponry, survive at the end of the movie? I'm so surprised that it wasn't called 'TOM CRUISE in the war of the worlds.' For crying out loud, people, the original movie had more character development than this. It even used NUCLEAR weapons. All this one had was Tom Cruise pontificating and posturing. Thank God I didn't pay for this crap. Read the book or see the classic movie. Maybe next time Spielberg will make a true WAR of the WORLDS (not TOM CRUISE's Personal TRAUMAS)

title: As entertaining as arguing with your family
review:
Half of the movie Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise) needs to drag his two kids around while they are either screaming, accusing him for being a bad dad or in all possible ways trying to sabotage his efforts in keeping them alive.

This becomes very annoying, and personally I lost all sympathy for the main characters. A great opportunity to remake a spectacular science fiction movie turns into some kind of half hearted soap opera about a dysfunctional family.

I actually eventually found myself hoping the machines would blast the kids away to get on with the action.

As you can expect from a movie who can afford paying Tom Cruise's ludricous salaries, the special effects are top notch. Any mediocre actor could have delivered the same acting performance though, and frankly Tom Cruise looks more like a sad middle aged man now, just a shadow of the sex symbol he once was.

All in all a disappointing movie, that could have been so great, but sadly is not...

title: Spielberg Screws Us Again
review: After the crap that was "A.I.", Spielberg takes another dump on the film-going audience with another SciFi extravaganza made up of annoying, unsympathetic characters; disjointed, pot-holed plot line; and a sappy ending that sucks the life out of this picture much as the aliens do of their hapless human victims. I must admit... some of the effects looked good... and that my dislike of this film is intensely fueled by my loathing of Tom Cruise, Dakota Fanning, and the other kid (I was rooting for the aliens). But it was in the discount bin and completed my collection of all 4 of the War of the Worlds films - of which only the George Pal version is worthy of more than one viewing!

title: Wow.. Just wow!
review:
Oh my freaking lord, wow!

This is one of the best film i have seen in the theatre since Sin City, now there are some odd quirks in this movie, but they are not too noticeable. title: An outstanding piece of cinema by Steven Spielberg!!!
review:
Wow!!! I am at a loss for words for this movie "War of the Worlds", Incredible!!! Stupendous!!

It quite possibly is one of the best sci fi movies ever, the audience I saw it with thought the same and gave the movie a standing ovation. Need I say more? Of course .

It's based on the H.G. wells classic originally brought to life in the 1950's by acclaimed sci fi director George Pal who brought us such hits as "The Time Machine".

Aliens have come to invade our planet and destroy us all. Their plans are simple as Tim Robbins character of Ogilvy says it's extermination!!!

The people at Industrial Light and Magic which worked on such hits as "Jurassic Park", "Willow" and "Terminator 2 Judgement Day" should really be commended for bringing more top notch and award worthy special effects to the screen once again!!!

Spielberg like other good directors knows how to input the human element and heart just like he's done in other Blockbusters like "ET" and "Close Encounters of the Third Kind".

In fact this felt a lot like "Close": for many times, When the strange alien ships emerge, there is a great deal of human curiosity and intrigue around them, then when we see the Aliens true intentions we are in disbelief as to the amount of destruction that can be inflicted by one ship.

Even the Aliens have a personality in this, they feed on us for food, and then conquer anything around them. They have no emotions , they're just carnivores.

Let's get to the acting shall we folks. Tom Cruise was great in this, like him or not.

As Ray Ferrier, Cruise for his time is able to capture the average working man once again, something he started in movies like "All the Right moves". He's not a perfect man, his wife left him, his kids hate him but deep down he loves them, and when the crisis occur there isn't a better father or guy than Ray.

Dakota Fanning you light up a room with your very presence. This girl is only 11 eleven years old ladies and gentleman, but in her short beginnings she has shown us the talents and skills of a veteran. She was utterly priceless and lovable as Rachel Ferrier.

In a time when former child actors go by the waste side and do nothing, Fanning has emerged as much more than just a kid with a pretty face, she can act with the best of them and she likewise needs to commended for her work.

Justin Chatwin as Robbie Ferrier is another memorable character. The rebel who steals his father's car to get away from him. The guy who still is at odds with his dad but when the time comes, the family comes together to get through this crisis and fight for survival!!!

You gotta love it how Spielberg, his writers like true master know how to put in the humanity into films like these while at the same delivering us with the big budge special effects we expect to see when we go to the theater, He gives us everything we asked for and then some.

Nicely done, Steven, once again, you've given us a classic memorable flick that not only we can enjoy as adults and remember it by but also a great flick that we can take our kids too and as a family we can be entertained once again by your greatness.

"WAR OF THE WORLDS" then will no doubt be remembered for another masterpiece by Spielberg and everyone involved in the production, making and release of the film should be EXTREMELY proud of themselves.

title: WotW is one heck of a movie
review: Watch this movie. You will not regret it. The suspense starts from the word go and keeps you on the edge right till the very end. Spielberg has worked his magic again and the cast is great. Spielberg and his team takes no prisoners. The effects complement the story and are out of this world. The Cruise-Spielberg collaboration is something movie-goers can look forward to and they do not disappoint. This is definitely as good as Minority Report and WotW appeals to a broader audience. In a summer devoid of good blockbusters, WotW takes you for a joyride that you do not want to come off. If there is a letdown and there are very few, the movie could have been longer and the ending appeared too snappy. If you're looking for entertainment and value in a movie this summer, you can't go wrong with WotW. This is definitely the best movie this summer.

title: Too rushed!
review:
Another comment said this is Spielberg's worst movie in 20 years, but I don't think that's fair because Hook came out in the last 20 years and aside from 1941 and The Sugarland Express that's probably his worst movie.

At the same time War of the Worlds does suck. The ending is ridiculously anti-climactic. The aliens just die? Come on, Steven, you're more creative than that. I know he wanted to stay true to the spirit of the book but he could have still made the ending a little more exciting. Maybe if he had spent a little more time on this picture it could have been better. Everything about it felt rushed. Ideas start to take shape but then don't develop. For instance, the red ivy and the human blood, there must have been some reason for that other than seeing Tom Cruise murder Tim Robbins, but I have no idea what because the movie ended 5 minutes later with no further development.

This isn't to say there was nothing good about it. But even the stuff that was good was all lifted straight from other movies. The crazy weather patterns preceding the alien invasion were cool but Independence Day did that 9 years ago. I liked the scene where the eye was searching for Tom and Dakota in the barn but it was almost identical to Spielberg's own raptor chase in the kitchen in the original Jurassic Park.

I would not recommend this movie. If you wanna watch a good alien invasion flick rent Signs or Independence Day. They are both far more satisfying.

title: Very good, scary in many ways!
review: I'll admit that usually I hate Spielberg and Cruise. Seriously. It took a lot for me to see past Mr. Corny and Mr. Nutty. But I got caught up in this movie right away. Why? (3) Similarly, there were many terrifying situations: not just running down the street while people get vaporized, but being trapped in a quiet basement with a questionable homeowner. All in all, a very entertaining movie only slightly marred by Spielberg's need to be sentimental. GREAT sound editing, too.

title: Turn a classic story of Alien invasion into family squabble drama
review:
Another Hollywood remake, why?

Actually I thought this should be a really good film.

I loved the 1953 War of the Worlds (and smiled at the special effects) I also remember listening spell bound to Richard Burton narrating the musical version.

You have older classics, from a classic book. Just take the 'classic aspects' and add modern technology it has to be an amazing film?

errr, No.

The film starts of well, Aliens invade, Cruise escaping with family etc.

Where it gets silly, is the script writers decide to make Cruise the focal point of the story.

Hint: The Alien invasion and mankinds fight is the 'focal point'. The clue is in the title "War of The Worlds" not "War between Father & Son"

Cruise's family squabbles with his teenage son and younger daughter become the 'main event' and the alien invasion relegated to a backdrop.

It gets really stupid when the son decides to run off and 'fight' the aliens. Duh !(unbelievable) as he has seen trained troops with latest equipment and technology anihalated with ease by the aliens.

However, it gives an excuse to focus on Cruise and his search for idiot son.

Tim robbins gives a passing nod to the original story but back to Cruise.

At the end we are shown the aliens have all died of Earth germs, almost as a 'by the way' offering so as not to detract from Cruise.

This should have been a great film. Instead another Hollywood mediocre remake on a par with 'The Magnificent 7'. 5/10

title: Entertaining, but disappointing
review:
In this film, directed by Steven Spielberg, Earth is attacked by aliens with giant mechanical tripods in a contemporary approach of the famous H.G. Wells sci-fi novel, and a remake of a homonym film by 1953. Has Tom Cruise in the lead role, Ray Ferrier, a father who seeks to put his daughter, Rachel (Dakota Fanning) in a safer place.

Although Steven Spielberg have used enough computer special effects and killed half of mankind, this film isn't only a human calamity, but the drama of a father trying to save his daughter from alien invasion, a theme who has been subject of several stories. In fact, most of them has been, directly or indirectly, influenced by the novel "War of the Worlds" ("Independence Day", just to quote one of them).

The tension follows all the film, where action and special effects scenes are mixed with suspense and expectation enlivened by scenes that remind us of the Holocaust or 9/11. The two main characters easily captivate the audience's sympathies and make us become more anxious and "clinging" to the film, which is always good. Tom Cruise managed to come out very well in his role, despite a certain ambiguity of his character, who only thinks about running away during the first half of the movie and spends the second half acting like the hero of "Mission Impossible", without we understand why exactly he changes his attitude. Another problem of this movie are the fairly obvious plot holes that we don't like to see in a Spielberg's film (I would even say that they aren't forgivable in a film directed by him).

For all this, this film leave some critics a bit disappointed, having just been nominated for Oscars in three technical categories (Sound Editing, Sound Mixing and Special Effects). Commercially, however, it was a success, largely due to the fame of Spielberg and Cruise, but also due to the special effects and the fact that is able to achieve its main goal: entertain who pays to see him.

title: Severely Underrated
review:
In 2002, Steven Spielberg and Tom Cruise paired up for the very first time on Minority Report. It turned out to be a huge success and so they decided to work again, this time on an adaptation of H.G. Wells' classic The War Of The Worlds.

This being a huge Hollywood blockbuster, there are a great number of fantastically epic sequences involving the huge mechanical aliens decimating the world's population. Spielberg gives us some great visuals ranging from the aliens' first attack, a capsized ferry, a flaming train and an ingenious use of a hand grenade.

Spielberg chooses to shoot the movie from the perspective of Ray, played by Tom Cruise, as he simply tries to survive the devastating onslaught. And it is an onslaught; once the aliens attack, the movie barely lets up for the remainder of its 2 hour runtime and you will no doubt be left breathless by the time the credits role. Credit must be given to Cruise as he resists the urge to play the action hero and instead comes off as a typical man trying to understand what is happening around him. Unfortunately, the same cannot be said for his children, as they make serious errors in judgement time and time again. In fact, the entire subplot of Ray's relationship with his children feels wholly unnecessary and only distracts from the main plot.

Thankfully, there is not too much time spent dwelling on Ray's parental failures, and for the most part you will be amazed at the spectacle on show. It doesn't quite reach the heights of Jurassic Park or Indiana Jones, but it is noticeably darker than any blockbuster Spielberg has previously made, with a distinct lack of humour and some really grisly imagery, War Of The Worlds is nevertheless a fantastically exciting blockbuster.

Aside from Spielberg's tendency to focus on parental issues, War Of The World's is quite a departure for the director but for anyone wanting a blockbuster movie with great effects and a real sense of danger, you could do a lot worse.

title: Convincing carnage...
review: Utterly believable fx buttress plausible performances all around and make Spielberg's WAR OF THE WORLDS one of the truly great invasion epics. Like GODZILLA (the 1998 version), WAR OF THE WORLDS depends greatly on its special effects- and, also like GODZILLA, the fx are very much up to the task. I've bemoaned the fact the most fx-heavy movies of the past several decades have left a great deal to be desired, but, when the DRAMA is this well integrated, even state-of-the-art fx are laudable and only ENHANCE the performances. (JAWS is still one of the scariest movies of all time, but the fx therein are all Practical Magic- and all the more remarkable because of it. Unfortunately, one need only sit through any one of the subsequent sharks-on-the-loose clunkers to see that cgi sharks are by no means as frightening as the faux "real thing.") With PACIFIC RIM looming on the horizon, it looks like we'll be treated to yet more convincing carnage. Keep 'em comin', I say.

title: Alien Invasion at its Best
review:
Steven Spielberg is well-known for his moderately-budgeted, box office hits and classics, but in 2005 he brought to the screen a new and different looking adaptation of H.G. Wells' classic novel that was truly an intense shocker; War of the Worlds. Starring Tom Cruise and Dakota Fanning, this sci-fi blockbuster revisited the alien invasion sub-genre with a vengeance; think 'Saving Private Ryan' but as a PG-13 movie with aliens as the enemy. The violence was not held back, the intensity was dialed all the way up and the performances of the two leads were spectacular. Tim Robbins' small but effective role was pleasing as well.

When it comes to the alien invasion sub-genre, there have been many films released to this day that have both been great and terrible (terrible being the recent Skyline and Darkest Hour films; they had great aliens and designs, but terrible scripts and direction). Happily, War of the Worlds was kind of a mix of Saving Private Ryan and Independence Day, having the intense close encounters with thousands of people being killed off, and an emotional human story at the center of it all; a father trying to bring his family to safety. The script was fantastic, having only a couple moments where it wasn't all believable. The visual effects, top-notch, even to this day; Steven Spielberg knew how to place their money on the sets and CG. The music was as classical as ever as well, with John Williams bringing us another suspense-filled masterpiece that's also loaded with emotion and trauma. For the film itself (in running time) there were plenty of unanswered questions, but some of those questions could be answered with a sequel (which i hope Steven sees), while some questions you have to answer yourself.

Overall, War of the Worlds was and is a fantastic alien invasion film that shows us that a sci-fi blockbuster can act like a powerful war drama loaded with heart and emotion. Transformers can be put to shame with this movie in mind

title: A hell of a lot better than many people say it is.
review: When the director of Jaws and Raiders Of The Lost Ark announces he's going to make an alien invasion film, there comes attached a certain buzz of excitement. For my money, Steven Spielberg is at his most effective as a film-maker when the subject matter is, for want a better expression, cheaper. That's not taking anything away from the likes of Saving Private Ryan, but it's hard to think of anyone who entertains so wildly, yet humanises what should be throwaway, low rent material. It's true testament to his talent that a film about a giant fish terrorising a beach community endures to be celebrated and revered as much today as it has ever been. So on to War of The Worlds, Spielberg's stab at reviving H.G Wells' seminal classic thriller. Modern day alien invasion films have screened the end of the world as a global catastrophe with vast military presence, presidents ordering "Go to DEFCON4″ , and an abundance of CGI critters. What we have here, and in keeping with the Spielberg style, is a more personal account of the invasion as told through the eyes of Tom Cruise's 'Ray Ferrier' as he and his two children flee the alien apocalypse. This keyhole view of the invasion is a daring but highly effective move. At times, we glimpse the unfolding disaster in the background as it envelops everything behind our escaping protagonists. That's not to say that there's aren't jaw dropping full on CGI moments, but these are done sparingly and without ever feeling like something's being jammed into your face until you submit (Transformers anyone?). Spielberg also understands the threat and suspense created by implication, as opposed to full on exposure. When it comes to use of sound, as with Jaws, Spielberg proved how much you can heighten that sense of impending danger with a few notes. In War Of The Worlds, the alien invaders have machines that omit a low sonic boom that immediately sends shivers down the spine and recalls the ominous sound of the air raid siren used during World War II. It's another master stroke, a simple idea executed for maximum impact. Jumping and leaping around like an energiser bunny, Tom Cruise brings great verve to the film and instead of playing the all American hero, his character is presented as a failing father who's relationship with his children borders on mutual apathy. Once all hell breaks loose, that dysfunction allows the film a pleasing dramatic scope which helps drive the film forward on two fronts. If i have any criticism, it'd be that the film isn't long enough. In some ways that's a back handed compliment, such was my enjoyment that i was disappointed when the end came so abruptly. All things considered though, another fine addition to an impressive catalogue of films from the true king of the summer blockbuster. 4/5

title: what makes this "War of the Worlds" stand out is not its story or its characters, but the overall harrowing atmosphere that would be natural if invaders should attack earth
review:
I am familiar with four adaptations of the H.G. Wells novel "The War of the Worlds," which to my mind is one of the best books ever written. I liked three and had a rather strong disdain for the fourth. The two most popular are film adaptations, one in 1953 by George Pal which has gone on to be come a classic and one in 2005 by the always creative and trustworthy Steven Spielberg. Spielberg's version of "War of the Worlds" is not one of his best films, nor is it one of the best science-fiction films, but it is, I say, a very noteworthy take on the science-fiction alien invasion genre for this reason. Spielberg shows us what a real alien invasion would be like: scary with a capital S.

Although I do enjoy the old light-hearted classics like the original "The War of the Worlds" and their modern-day followers this "War of the Worlds" tackles the subject of an invasion with a surprising amount of realism. I am not only talking about the special effects, which are very plausible, but the way Spielberg has his characters react to them. This is not "Independence Day" with Will Smith punching an alien's lights out, smoking a cigar and saying "Now that's what I call a close encounter." When the alien tripods arrive (it's refreshing to see the filmmakers choose Wells' original idea instead of the usual flying saucers), the characters don't stand up, but turn tail and run for their lives. The whole movie is about Rey Ferrier (Tom Cruise) and his children simply trying to survive through the invasion while hundreds and hundreds of less fortunate people die around them. Although there is nothing wrong with a lighthearted action film like "Independence Day," this take is ultimately more plausible and more visceral. I tell you, if aliens did invade the planet, I would not be running out to fight. I would duck down and run for my dear life.

Spielberg once again uses the scare tactics that he used before in films such as "Jurassic Park" and my personal favorite of his', "Jaws" and he does them with sheer brilliance. The alien tripods are very well-realized: scary, unnatural-looking, unresembling anything on this planet (the use of three legs instead of four is brilliant) and what they have inside of them is also quite scary. But what's also great is the way Spielberg keeps the tension on the rise when there is no immediate danger. The movie's about Ray and his family trying to stay out of the invaders' path. It's also refreshing to have it follow Ray's perspective, like in the original book, and not cut away to government officials and scientists. We are left to wonder and guess just as much as he.

This "War of the Worlds" is a flawed film with some weak characters and a few unnecessary scenes, but it is saved by director Spielberg's genius and the way he manipulates our minds to ignore those flaws and keep in the atmosphere of the story. This I admired about "War of the Worlds." I saw it twice when it was in theaters and I have seen it several times since. I do enjoy the 1953 film as well. I enjoy both movies for different reasons. The original is in the always welcome, nostalgic tradition of lighthearted adventure and the fight of science; this adaptation gives us a very authentic feeling of what it would be like if aliens did come to earth.
