title: A very disappointing depiction of an overkilled and aged cliché
review:
I walked into the cinema theatre not really knowing what to expect; the trailer certainly doesn't give much away. I'm a big lover of computer graphics, so in theory I should have been enthralled by the movie's awesome visuals, but even they couldn't save it. As soon as I saw the huge alien robot armed with laser beams rise from the ground, I actually found myself begging for the movie to not be like that. I couldn't believe that in the 21st century Hollywood was still trying to cash in on that cliché. I didn't know that the movie was a re-make of a 50s film so unlike 'c-horse', who also posted a review on this film, I have no way of appreciating the movie on that level. I am probably not too wrong though in saying that the target demographic of the movie was not the generation which was around to watch the first one. Consequentially, MANY viewers will have missed out on that, myself amongst them. All I saw was a mindless, shallow, unenlightening and time-wasting presentation of a cliché which I had hoped movie producers had given up 40-50 years ago. Even though I try to remove all the extreme negativity I have towards this movie, I find myself unable to. It was little more than the standard, boring Hollywood formula of: something with family ==> action ==> more of same action ==> even more of same action ==> wonderful happy ending for main characters

The only thing I found interesting were the scenes depicting the animality of humans when it comes to ensuring one's own survival. Beyond that, not much left anything resembling a positive impression.

2 out of 10; the marks I give for the graphics

title: Oh so disappointed
review: Excited expectations to see it, should have waited for it to get on T.V, but you never have hindsight when you need it. Complete twaddle and I love this genre. It seems to me that the incredible Mr Spielberg has lost his touch with this one, I've seen the the original and I remember being far more engrossed in that one, and with the talent that is available it should have been more, much more, it's as if it was the first part of a 10 part series. But hey, what do I know, it's just my opinion. I think that to get one of these comments passed you have to have ten lines of text which in the case of war of the Worlds is hard to do when there is so little to comment on, apart from what,s already been said.

title: Waste of a potentially brilliant movie
review: I wanted the aliens to win, or at least to destroy some of the most irritating, pathetic characters, and put them and me out of my misery. Parts of this movie are brilliant, but I found it hard to enjoy any of it. How many times is this theme to be used in a movie - I'm not talking about the alien invasion. I'm talking about the dysfunctional family. Father doesn't have good relationship with his children, disaster happens, then he proves what a wonderful father he is and abracadara happy families. The main annoyance was the teenage son. I cannot believe anyone would behave like that, not even a teenager. Everyone is being vapourised with ease - people stand no chance - and he wants to run towards them (unarmed no less ha ha ha) to fight them. How totally ridiculous. Worth seeing if you love sci fi and are immune to shallow characters and usual underlying storyline.

title: Absolutely unnecessary
review: Better watch the movie from the 50s. Another example of a absolutely unnecessary remake. Boring script and Tom Cruise, stupid conclusion. Spielberg avoided definite nonsense like in "Independence Day" (upload virus), but there is nothing that makes it absorbing to watch that movie in relation to the origin picture. Less tension, stupid explanations (they came within that lightnings, the machines have been there for millions of years). A life form considerably more intelligent that humans start an invasion and do not think of the threat of microorganisms. OK, that was the conclusion in the first movie, but I do not accept this in a movie produced in the early 21th century. Even my 6 year old girl would declare this nonsense.

title: Not worth watching at all
review:
So, lemme see what vote this move deserves:

* 10 is for excellent movies, movies one wants to see again and again. Well, this wasn't it: -1

* Parent and kids have to run from something really, really bad - what an original storyline: -1

* We learn nothing whatever about this really, really bad thing, despite being given a few quite interesting clues. No back-story at all: -2

* I usually like kids in such movies, but this one was annoying: -1

* Ending that was at the same time utterly predictable (and I am not talking about what is already in the book, but about the movie storyline) and yet utterly unbelievable: -2

* Plot holes the size of the Grand Canyon: -1

* Annoyingly pathetic moments, several of them: -2

... Errrr ... can I please have a new rating system here? I am down to 0 and not even finished! No? OK, then let's try something else:

* There are worse movies than that one - not many, but some. +1

* The tricks are reasonably decent: +1

* Miranda Otto: Uh, well, can't really call that a part, can you? 0

* Tim Robbins: Would get this movie one point if his end hadn't been so pathetic: 0

* Tom Cruise: Has been a lot better in other movies: 0

I guess I can only recommend ID4 then - same subject, much better movie. Even if that one has a bit too much pathos, at least it isn't so pathetic.

title: Crap.
review:
Zero creativity. It placed the original radio broadcast from a newsworthy description into the perspective of a substandard father - who shows little growth by the end of the film.

There has never been a movie that I have walked out on... but this came extremely close.

The acting was decent, but every twist and turn was more unrealistic than the last.

I can live in a world where aliens attack - I am a big fan of "Independence Day," "Mars Attacks," "Alien," etc.... But give me a break. You're telling me that aliens planted giant robots under the soil millions of years ago so that it could take it over later? Why not take it over then? Before people had guns and missiles and nuclear weapons.

And at the end when that Robbie kid magically appears at his mother's house? Come on. You mean that billions of people were killed and special soldiers were all taken out - but one kid, who ran toward the exploding tripod lived to tell the tale?

And then there was the germ thing.... when Welles did it in his broadcast, it was creative. But when Spielberg just flat out copies it in some monster "blockbuster," I believe they call that plagiarism. I think they should've spent a little less on the fancy effects (which weren't all that impressive) and a little more on writing a decent script.

This film was almost as bad as that M. Night Shamma-lamma-ding-dong movie "Signs." "Hey guys, let's take over a planet where 75% of its surface can kill us instantly."

Shame on you, Andy Dufrain. I expect this from Cole Trickle, but never you.

title: Not impressive
review:
I don't know why I watched it for more than an hour. No points for guessing the end of a film with alien tripod robots. Yes, the hero survives and the alien dies.

In between you will hear people screaming and not answering the questions they were asked. At one point, this erratic behavior of the mob and screams started getting on the nerves. Specially Dakota Fanning screams in a pitch that you really need ear plugs.

The specials effects were good in the start of the film. But overall not an impressive film as we all have seen such stories over and over again.

title: What an utterly moronic collection of rubbish.
review:
Wow.

Coming into this movie with no expectations of greatness I was drawn into the plot. I was impressed by the destruction and the portrayal of the rampage of the aliens on the earth. Some plot twists were gnawing at me, however I dismissed them as minor and forgivable.

Then came the ending. The ending which took around 2 minutes to unfold and did not do what endings are designed for. Completing the plot. The story basically ended with a rubbish explanation that seemed to have been shot in 1 afternoon as an afterthought.

So what does that leave? Nothing. No plot = no movie in my book. I have in fact lost my will to live and function when movies like this get made and people in their millions spend their hard earned cash to see.

Shame on yee Spillberg, you have unleashed this on the world. I hope you can not sleep at night.

title: Highly implausible sci-fi melodrama
review: The plot of the movie is extremely weak. Movies starring Tom Cruise sometimes tend to exaggerate his potential as an action star. Sadly, the apocalyptic atmosphere of this story is tainted by the completely unbelievable scenes in which Mr. Cruise miraculously escapes from the dead while everybody else dies. The last scene (which I won't describe but if you watched the movie you know what I'm talking about) is one of the most implausible endings for a movie that I have seen in a really long time. With a theme so rich and profound as the one that is the background for this story, Spielberg disappointed me by sticking to the most simplistic Hollywood recipe for a movie: cheesy scenes with boring melodrama which are supposed to be touching (the type of style that you can find in Titanic, only less effective). One last comment: the ending is totally anti-climatic. We all know what the ending is from the book, but it seems like Mr. Spielberg ran out of time to film the movie and just wrapped up the last 10 minutes on the last shooting day. A shame, really. I think Tom Cruise had a better chance to show that he can act on Collateral. As for Spielberg... man, not a single decent adventure movie since the early 80s. He should really stick to drama, which is what nowadays he seems to do... at least, better.

title: Great effects but rather shocking disappointment
review:
I honestly thought that this would be a great film. I have been a big fan of big special effects films for a long time. So naturally I had been pretty hyped by what I had seen in the trailers.

While the actors in it gave great performances and the effects blew me away, these where the only good things about it at the end of the day.

The first thing that came to mind about what was wrong about this film was the fact that I was told mostly from Tom Cruises POV. I would have thought it may have worked better from a Third Person POV instead. I am aware it work for some films but not the kind of film this was meant to be.

But one problem that comes to mind that some of the special effects during that invasion scenes was that it looked well dated.

One good thing I could think of it from what I had seen from DVD or album covers is that they managed to do a good job of bringing the book to life. Which was helpful to know considering not everyone knew it was a book.

At the end of the day I would suggest that see it for the effects or besides that don't bother.

3/10

title: Questions
review: Couple of things that came to mind while watching (and being somewhat disappointed by WoW): -Wouldn't harvesting blood from individual humans be a rather cumbersome, inefficient task? Wouldn't throwing a few thousand at a time make more sense? -If they need our blood, why were they vaporizing so many people? -So, were the aliens here for our planet or our blood? Is the blood used to run their machines or is it more like food for the alien beings themselves? -What in god's name were the red roots all about? You've got all these mechanical tripods running around and then all of a sudden weird root systems sprout everywhere. What the hell? Thanks in advance for any assistance.

title: Hmm...How Familiar The Aliens Seem...
review:
I saw this movie, just Sunday, and I'm here to comment on it. Don't get me wrong it's a good movie, but it seems the budget was so low that the 'aliens' looked sorta like the ones from "Independence Day". Another thing, yet, Tom Cruise looked like he could've choked his children in this film! Especially Robbie, his son in the movie. Mr. Cruise was a little too, um, psycho in this film. And that little girl screamed and cried way too much, I mean I understand she was 10 and scared(probably of her "dad", too...) But there is a line there and she crossed it... Back on the subject of the 'aliens', I found them to have the same wide head as the ones in "Independence Day" and some of them even look like the ones from "Alien". Now that's totally my opinion, maybe I wasn't paying that much attention, but they did seem familiar...

Now please, don't get me wrong, I liked the movie, but I want to see some different 'aliens' or different shaped head 'aliens'.

~*~*~*~G.F.~*~*~*~

title: If this were a meal, it would be a happy meal from Mc.D. It doesn't leave you full, looks like it were done in a hurry - and doesn't taste very well.
review:
The general idea of the movie is very good and could be a giant hit. The idea however isn't anything new. War of the worlds doesn't manage to deliver anything new to the genre. It leans far too much towards movies like Independence day, in fact if you have seen Independence day you will be very disappointed by War of the worlds.

The movie doesn't give any reason for the majority of elements. It assumes you are a big fan of the science-fiction genre and wont question anything. An example of this could be, a guy filming with a digital-camera right after an EMP strike. Furthermore, as seen in the trailers, the aliens almost defeats the US military in 3 days. In the movie we see how the US are attacking the aliens. This leaves us with the thoughts "If you are doing it like that - no wonder you aren't defeating them, THEY HAVE FORCE SHIELDS." One would think that a mighty military power as the US military would reconsider sending wave after wave of tanks, planes, helicopters after a target that doesn't even get a small dent when fired upon. But apparently Spielberg doesn't think that the US military would re-consider their approach after loosing everything attacking a target without giving this target as much as a scratch.

We aren't given any legit reason for the end of the movie either. All of a sudden the movie ends, and a dark voice tells us what happened.

On the acting side. Cruise delivers a very good performance, if it wasn't for him the movie would get a 1/10. Rachel, Dakota Fanning, is a very good kid actress but I suspect she were directed very bad. In almost all scenes where she appearers the only "sound" coming out of her is a very loud "kid scream". After 15-20 with this I know for a fact that I will never have children. It truly started to hurt my ears.

The image composition also lack the "Spielberg feel" in some scenes. Sometimes faces are too close to the edge of the screen, for my taste, whilst they are speaking.

title: Damn this movie sucked
review: I had high expectation for this movie. Went in to watch Spielberg get this H.G. Wells literary genius out through his special effects. Well i guess the special effects were good but the story, oh my god the story line sucked worse then Sharkboy and Lava girl which I happened to watch purely on accident. Well anyways if you miss this movie in the theaters please do not feel the need to rent or buy it on DVD. The story was very similar to the Independence Day (Will Smith and Jeff Goldblum) but the way it was carried out proved to be a huge let down. It almost felt like Spielberg got tired of making this movie and put it together in a last ditch effort.

title: I am sad
review: This movie looked wonder full, the special effects were awesome(except for the fact the ships had headlights, that was weird) and the acting was awesome, I mean Dikota Fanning and Tom Cruise were awesome...but it was so boring, the story was dull it could have been so much better, but it reminded me of Indendence Day...and I hated that movie, and the whole movie was running and screaming that it nothing else, and why were there clothes flying around, also they should have had more aliens, there were like four aliens in this movie, We need more Aliens Speilburg!!!! This move was a disappointment and it made me cry, Spielburg you let me down, how could you? *sobs*

title: The most banal stupid movie ever!!!
review: Seriously,,no one can think that this garbage was anything more than a catalogue to sell the coming toys and video game. Starts out well ,,like a very good movie and then just gets more unbelievable as it goes on. Truly this was utter garbage . Worst movie I've ever seen. A joke! A real shame and a rip off. You need 10 lines ,,it will be hard to write 10 more words never mind 7 more lines,,the stormy clouds were good,the story line was ridiculous,the outcome was just plain stupid and not credible in any way. To say that this was a great movie makes me realise that some people just never get out. To think that T C and DS could make something this bad,,,it made Ishtar look great, Real Oscar material.

title: The master lets us down one more time
review: An unfortunate day in movie history. I was excited to see how Spielberg would handle the literary classic and to his credit, there's much to like visually, but the story is trite, weakly directed, and takes on no measure of import or excitement. Some scenes are dry and drawn out, others have such glaringly pointless plot devices that it hardly supports its own gigantic weight. Tom Cruise is exactly as he should be, a decent actor playing the role given to him, but the things he says, the feelings he's asked to emote, simply childish. There was more believability to Independence Day. If that doesn't draw a parallel, I don't know what will. The explanations are weak, the meandering script shows none of the tautness of Close Encounters, and on the whole I was left tired of watching after a half hour and wishing a tripod would stomp into the theater and end my suffering.

title: Expect more from Spielberg and Cruise
review: I expected way more from Spielberg and Cruise. This oh-so-familiar alien-invades-and-destroys-earth movie is so predictable that I had to have someone wake me up a couple of times during the movie. Cruise's familiar take on the "I'm the leading man, so watch me beat my chest" scenario grows tiresome. Thank goodness for Dakota Fanning's honest and believable portrayal. One scene almost derails the movie (a guest star's preachy and solemn sermon halfway through), and another ruins it completely. I won't give it away but if you manage to sit through this until the end you'll see what I mean - it is so typical of Spielberg's overly-sentimental direction. I am so tired of the big Hollywood movies with all the flashy technology and over-hyped stars that can't even tell a decent story, but of course there's always a happy ending, right? Schlocky!

title: Retarded!
review: I know it's not PC to use that 'R' word, but I can't think of a better way to describe this movie. So many holes in the plot I can see cartoon Jerry devouring this monster chunk of Swiss cheese. These holes have already been eloquently revealed to you dear reader by better IMDb critics who precede me. Just felt compelled to add my harsh review of this stupid movie. What a waste of talent and special effects! I entertained myself by noting every oh-so-unrealistic plot factor during it. So, in that respect, yes, War of the Worlds is an entertaining way to pass the time. I think Spielberg is in the early stages of senility. I never saw so many people run toward danger rather than away from it.

title: a true waste of a great story
review: Had anyone involved with the story and its history read the book??? why did we need a screaming girl a surely boy and a wooden Tom Cruise? Speilburg too one of the great alien story's and turned it in to a not quite making it B grade film. H G Wells must be turning in his grave along with Orson Wells. While the aliens were well done and the creeping red plant was there they seemed to be in the background as just something for the girl to scream at and to fill in pauses when Tom Cruise was having a break.The work of done of the aliens in the basement was very well done and a few of the scenes of them stalking across the landscape were really the highlights of the movie. When will Hollywood learn that theses great stories should not be made to fit their scheme of how the public want to them to be seen bit follow the book as this is what the writers intended.Please someone stop them using Tom Cruise in movies!!!!

title: How does this movie keep getting good reviews?
review:
Let me start off saying that i was excited as anyone about this movie. I'm a huge scifi fan, and even badly directed and poorly acted (any feature on the SciFi channel) movies i enjoy.

This movie was so bad, as to completely eclipse the worst giant snake movie the scifi channel has ever decided to force on the public. Yea sure, the special effects were great, but thats expected of any big budget film.

Everyone is raving about Dakota fanning, and i spent the whole movie hoping she would die in a terrific fireball, or at least be strangle to death by Tom Cruise. Constant questions, hysterical outbreaks, and generally the most annoying character in a movie. Think Jar Jar Binks, without being remotely funny.

Justin Chatwins character is only moderately believable as well. Wanting revenge, he keeps trying to join the army. Why is it though, that every teenage boy has to be a complete punk, disrespecting parents, loud headphones, and just a general reject? So the ideal TV family might not exist, but that doesn't mean it has to be completely dysfunctional.

The reactions in the movie are either slow, or completely wrong. When the earth quake around the hole starts, no one tries to run. Even as the monster is coming up, barely anyone tries to run. Tom Cruise makes a point, early in the movie, of placing a gun in the back of his pants. Yet when his family and wellbeing are threatened, he takes a full 5 minutes to even pull the gun out, then promptly loses it. Later, for some reason a crowd of hundreds, even thousands, is held off a boat by maybe a dozen army guys. Facing certain death if they stay where they are, these people aren't gonna force there way over the army guys? Come on. I've seen bigger riots over Pokemon.

I was glad to see the army realistically portrayed. Being a soldier myself, little things like the speech each Javalin gunner gets before firing, really strike home. But why is there no escalation of force? Brigade after brigade march to their doom, and the tactics never change. Throughout the entire movie, there is no mention of nuclear weapons, the Navy is sadly missing, and air assets seem to be the only step in the right direction. Still, the artillery fire sounded scarily realistic, even if the special effects team still likes to make explosions full of fire instead of debris.

Now, i can see the film maker, at the end of the movie, wanting a happy ending. But how does the entire family survive, and Boston as a whole, remain untouched? And when you get to the end of the movie, shouldn't there be some kind of explanation for some the the things that happened? Why were these machines buried? Why didn't these creatures take the planet when the machines were buried? Whats with the red blood vine stuff? Why do the shields go down? Why did i pay to see this movie? WTF? Thats almost exactly what went though my mind, and anyone after watching this movie, doesn't say out loud, WTF? I think needs professional help.

title: Is there ANY logic to this film?
review: OK, it's Spielberg and the effects are fantastic. Add the wonderful screams of Dakota Fanning and you can see why I gave it a 3 out of ten. But suspension of disbelief only goes so far even in sci-fi. Surely the auto mechanic saw hundreds of people running in absolute terror, yet he engages in chit-chat about the broken solenoid while TC is stealing the car he worked on? It gets worse from there: - All the cars' electrical systems were fried by the invaders, but, conveniently, TC is able to drive through all the disabled cars on the highway (Did the writer ever get near city traffic? There would be absolute gridlock!) - Why did the kids think mom & step-dad were home when they were dropped off at TC so the mom & step-dad could visit Grandma in Boston? - TC and kids arrive at mom's home and TC looks in the box they took from home for something to eat - DUH, you've got refrigerator and a whole kitchen of FOOD in the house you just arrived at! - Again, TC is able to drive his stolen minivan through the debris of a jetliner crash site without so much as a flat tire or the need to make a 3-point turn! - These "superior" beings haven't the simplest technology we have, such as infra-red imaging to locate humans, and they are using MASSIVE machines to kill humans ONE-BY-ONE! HUMANS COULD (AND HAVE) KILL HUMANS MORE EFFICIENTLY. I could go on and on: Why was the Boston neighborhood in pristine condition while the aliens were destroying (and hunting for humans) in rural farmland? Sorry, I just had to vent. This movie was terrible.

title: Read the book instead
review:
Had I written this last night, when I came back from the screening, it would have gotten a '1' - but the visuals were OK, I guess. And I don't hate SF, Tom Cruise, Steven Spielberg or H.G. Wells.

The reason why I think this movie is such brainless crap is because Spielberg seems to have made it on autopilot. He handed it over the SFX department with the request to leave him 5 meters of celluloid to include some acting - which then got cut as I didn't see any in the entire movie.

There is no suspense at all after the initial rise of the first tripod. We are given no reason to care for any of the characters beside little Rachel - who is the only one who comes across as somewhat believable, although her part seems to be limited for a large part to screaming.

You don't see real fear, honestly, just attempts at shock. Just hordes of running people getting zapped. You don't see love, affection, sorrow.. name an emotion and it's sure to not be there. Yes, Cruise attempts to show them, but the man's emotional range is limited to what he must believe is emotional but can't really feel.

The story has little to do with the original War of the Worlds, really, it's no more than 'based upon' it and I suggest you all read the book and listen to Jeff Wayne's unforgettable musical version instead. What a waste of money.

title: Another story not told
review:
How disappointing! What a beautiful movie wasted. Why is Spielberg bothering to base his movies on novel if he can't tell the story? None of the storyline is told during the movie. It is like telling the story of someone accidentally being there during the Independence Day invasion and not telling anything about the actual invasion.

Why does Spielberg think that we need to hear a little scream in order to understand that the characters are scared?

It makes me think on how he missed the story in Jurassic Park in the same manner. This is a repeating theme for this director.

I hope somebody will tell this story with that kind of magnificence one day.

Jean-Michel

title: Movie stickler digs in
review: I watched this film in the theatres, and it's a good thing that I did. The visuals were fantastic, but I felt that it carried the movie. The alien crafts and the aliens themselves looked very real. In most scenes, you would be hard pressed to find out if they were electronic puppets or computer animated... As far as the aliens of this film go in a writing and story sense, I thought the individual scenes were written well, but some of the plot concepts regarding the aliens were terrible. Let's start with their technology: Death rays that vaporize people and leave their clothes behind, but no infra-red or heat tracking systems. Shields to block bullets and missiles, but no water-purification (or at least not implemented). While watching this movie, I thought the aliens weren't given enough credit. For a species that had been monitoring our planet for thousands of years, they seemed to have forgotten to test the water (which is ultimately their undoing). I did, though, have some problems with this film. First of all, there were several continuity errors that I won't actually specify so as not to give the movie away. But I will say that Cam-corders require electricity, Mr. Spielberg. Along the same lines as continuity problems; there were several convenient story devices in this film. For instance: when the characters come out from hiding in the basement, they discover the street in utter shambles... except the house they were in... which seems to be in tact for the most part. This kind of thing happens more than once. The character development felt like a good attempt, but I found myself not caring whether most the characters live or die. As much as I like Miranada Otto and Dakota Fanning in this film, I didn't care if they died. As for the ending... I thought it was abrupt and slightly silly. But those endings never really bothered me, and so I'll just say that I smiled and nodded when the movie was over.

title: A good entertaining movie! *beware of minor spoilers*
review: I liked it! There I've said it! You wanna know why? Well first and foremost it was everything Independence Day was NOT. This movie succeeded in showing the downfall of Earth from an ordinary family perspective. You almost never got to see anything that cruise and his family didn't see which made you feel that you were on the ground with them, fighting for your life. Of all "Hello we are aliens and have come to beat the living crap out of y'all (literally speaking!) and not to forget ALL YOUR BASES ARE BELONG TO US!"-movies I've seen, this one tops them all. Especially the ending! It showed me how utterly defenseless I would be if something like this would happen in reality. Which it will!!! Just wait and see!

title: nothing new
review: Just another action movie, in my opinion its Spielberg's worst job. No history line, terrible ending, predictable.... If you like to see an action movie its OK, but if you are looking for something more don't waste your money with this movie. Tom Cruise isn't doing a great job, very similar with MI. Maybe the difference is that this time he isn't a cool and lovable person, now he is coward, full of fear and a little bit stupid. The girl did an excellent job, quite e solid performance. The "out of the world" part of the movie could have been done a lot better, its similar to older jobs... this movie should have had Close Encounters of the Third Kind spirit.... buy that didn't happen. I almost forgot, in this movie you'll see sentimentalism just as every other movie from Steven Spielberg....

title: Sound and Fury Signifying A Summer Movie
review:
With all due respect to the Bard, Spielberg's WAR OF THE WORLDS was certainly jammed full of the requisite sound and fury. Whether it be the lightning blasts the alien hordes road in on, their reigning devastation as humans were vaporized by the hundreds (that's one solution to Earth's over-population) or the fury  the outright horror  that human actors Tom Cruise, Dakota Fanning and Tim Robbins, nearly mimicking his award-worthy role from MYSTIC RIVER, experienced, WAR OF THE WORLDS was a great summertime amusement-park ride.

Spielberg provided many of the elements fans of his films come to expect, and provided them dead-on. The alien invaders were as creepy and menacing as the news coverage on Tom and Katie's engagement as Dennis Muren and the ILM team set out to create a very menacing, and ultimately very cool, threat. Spielberg once again allowed the everyday man, a member of the post-nuclear now-acceptably dysfunctional family, to play witness to the fantastic with Dakota Fanning picking up the 21st Century role of cute, screaming blonde kid once held by Drew Barrymore.

The signification? Other than summertime action, not much else. Perhaps Spielberg has done his "everyman" story format once too often as not only does Tom Cruise fail to live up to this Spielberg-ian status, but the story does tend to become slightly ridiculous as this superman tends to be the only human that not only survives every encounter with the invaders but also becomes one of Earth's saviors as well. Perhaps Cruise's superhuman ego could not simply disguise itself with eyeglasses and a fedora.

As the movie lumbers forward like the Tripods, the alien tech just does not make sense. Would not space-faring aliens have better ways of tracking these insect-like humans other than line-of-sight targeting? Even the mighty Tom Cruise must have some form of kryptonite  other than bad q-ratings.

The end result is that the film satisfies the need for a summer action hit as well as giving humanity a nice positive ending in this pc-world we are specimens in. It's well known that Spielberg can be highly sentimental  just look at SCHINDLER'S LIST  so it should come as no surprise that the aliens meet their ultimate end, as fans of Wells' story were already aware of, in the city of the world champion Patriots and Red Sox. This ride has it all: plenty of dips and loops, but also high-speed action that can take your breath away.

title: Apocalypse Porn That Fails To Satisfy
review:
War of the Worlds, the only summer movie to have received anything close to the usual level of hype and attention, satisfies tradition by failing to deliver on almost all counts. Conceptual artists, software engineers, production designers, code writers and CGI modelers are once again doing the job of the director, writer and actors. The Academy should retire its Oscars for anything but technical achievement for a while.

War of the Worlds has the benefit of some of the best technicians in the industry. The CGI is flawless; the exploding streets, flying debris and panicked hoards all created with utmost realism. The production design, from Ray's cluttered townhouse to Ogilvy's ruined basement, is original and surprising with a fine attention to details, and the sound design is Oscar worthy. The tripods are the real stars of the show. They are beautiful creations - sinuous, domineering and malevolent - and in a better movie would become iconic images. There are several scenes in which the tripods appear over a hilltop, backlit by moonlight, that take the breath away.

The technical aspects of the movie could not be bettered, and the Academy Awards will, in these categories, be a battle between War of the Worlds and Revenge of the Sith. The 'above the line' talent, however, as is so often the case, does not deserve such quality work.

From Jurassic Park to Mission Impossible to Spiderman, Koepp has proved his ability to write a tautly structured screenplay, successfully finding a satisfying balance between action and character. War of the Worlds has the feeling of a filler project, something thrown together in a few spare weekends. The plot consists of nothing more than having characters running from aliens until they die. Note 'until they die', for the characters do nothing to bring about their demise. The lack of even rudimentary character development makes many actions confusing and unbelievable, Ray's son sudden disappearance half way through the movie to join the army being only the most obvious. The climax, if it can be called such leaves the viewer feeling deflated. The audience I saw it with audibly groaned and filed from the cinema asking a unanimous, 'Was that it?' The lack of ANY tension, suspense, dramatic development, surprise or real character study is unforgivable. And don't blame the book. Books are changed all the time for the sake of film narrative, why make an exception now, when a change is so badly needed.

Spielberg, who can direct this stuff in his sleep, does what you would expect of him, but is happy to do no more, though we are thankfully spared the usual Spielbergian mawkish sentimentality. The performances are routine and generic, but lack anything approaching even the shallow depth of action characterization.

As an example of Apocalypse Porn, the movie works very well. Everything is blown up and incinerated with gleeful abandon, and the screaming crowds and violent mobs will satisfy any fan of the genre. The technical team should be well paid and awarded, but overall, the movie is a dud and another example of the recent trend for style over substance. Spielberg, Koepp and Cruise are all capable of far better. Let's hope they deliver soon.

title: A bit dodgy

The story was supposed to be an explanation of Cruise and his kids bonding as the journey progressed, however none of this happened - he never really got closer to either of them. And the payoff at the end when he 'triumphantly' arrived at his ex wife's parents' immaculately untouched doorstep was extremely poor! ...Another thing that bugged me as well, the aliens planted the machines under the earth even before mankind evolved. And as numerous characters throughout the film said, "They've been planning this extermination all along". But why would they plant the machines here to exterminate us later on when they didn't know we were going to be here in the first place...because the human race didn't exist yet!!! You see?? Stupid! Excellent special effects though!

title: Imperfect, but it has a lot of good moments
review:
I mention some spoilers here in my review. I enjoyed Spielberg's War of the Worlds, but I have problems with it. The movie from the start till the first tripod's rise was quite good.

Then when the Martian tripod started firing on people I experienced my first discontinuity. The people were turning to ash but their clothes were being left behind. It may seem to be a quibble, but it distracts from what should have been a thrilling moment. Maybe the idea was invented so that it could pay off in a scene several nights later, when the clothes of incinerated people would flutter down from the sky, but why make something complicated or a mystery for no significant reason?

Then the next portion of the film depicted moments that are horrendous, not because of the Martians themselves, who seem to serve as a plot device to drive humans into panic, but because of desperate people doing unto each other what they would never imagine doing under saner circumstances. These are the moments neither Orson Welles in his famous radio broadcast nor George Pal in his beloved film version had imagined. The Martians are the herders, causing masses of people to panic, which leads to holocaust-like moments from "Schindler's List". This is my favorite part of the movie.

Shortly before this portion ends, I'm rewarded by a glorious image, of a tripod engulfed in flames, then rising above the flames, impervious to it, invincible, implacable.

Then the film goes underground and the story focuses on a group of three people. It has a nice symmetry to it- tripods, three-legged Martians, three people in a closed-room drama like in Sartre's "No Exit". However, this is a threesome with one wobbly leg: Tim Robbins. I imagine Spielberg had cast him because he would be a helpful, decent fellow at first who later descends into craziness because of the pressure of being cooped up while hiding from Martians. Robbins the actor bothers me in this part. He seems to have mistaken unhinged with goofy. At times, he still thinks he's "Nuke" Laloosh in Bull Durham, especially with that bug-eyed doofus look he gives when he's "acting".

When they go above ground, there is a nice tense moment in the alien "basket", but it seems a little abbreviated. We spent a long time during the set-up, some time on masses of people acting in panic, and an almost interminable time with Tim Robbins, but the basket seems like a sketch more than a scene. Tom Cruise's means of escape, well, it's not exactly a cliché, but once he grabbed those grenades, I could see that shot of pull rings in his fingers immediately.

Now for some complaints. There's that ending, which is faithful to the George Pal Movie, the radio broadcast and the original novel. I think the ending suits Welles' novel which was written at a time when it was discovered germs were causing diseases. Today, such an error on the Martians' part would be unbelievable. We go to our moon taking every possible precaution to make sure our explorers survive, it's hard to imagine the Martians wouldn't do the same.

Two more minor nitpicks: first, the aliens have binocular vision, making them cute and E.T.-like. Having two eyes seems unlikely when the Martian tripods have three legs. The Martians themselves have three legs. They have this obsession with doing everything in threes, and their bodies have trilateral symmetry. So why suddenly have only two eyes?

Lastly, I don't like Morgan Freeman's voice to read from the novel, starting the movie and ending it. His voice has too much dignity, like God was reading it. However, in the movie's trailers, I think the actor Peter Coyote (or someone who sounds like him) read the lines from H. G. Welles, and the results are much better. I think the difference between Coyote and Freeman is Coyote can (and truly does) read like it's a documentary.

title: Nice effects, ruined by bad decisions
review:
First, let me get the awesome things about the movie into the review: The Fighting Machines are amazing. They mostly fit the book's description concerning tentacle appendages, the baskets on their back (although they're technically below them now) and the barely-visible heat ray are well done and just feel right. Also, in the scene where the aliens enter a human shed, they seem fascinated by a bike wheel, which fits the book's description of martian technology, which does not have any wheel-like components.

But this is not enough to overshadow the huge weaknesses of the full movie.

It starts right at the beginning: For some reason, digital cameras and camcorders are completely immune to EMP blasts, as opposed to car engines and radios. The whole city shuts down because of the Martians' arrival on earth, yet still people are filming the first machine with clearly electronic devices.

Apparently for some reason, the machines were underground for billions of years (not arriving in pods like the book said). Seems like the martians didn't expect to make any technological advances during the time mankind developed from single cells to city-dwelling humans of today, and obviously human cities have no underground components that required digging more than a few metres, since the machine did not emerge from a huge pile of debris.

Another really bad adaptation change, that pretty much every War Of The Worlds movie made, was shifting the plot from 19th-century England to present-day America. Doing so made other changes necessary that made the whole premise of the movie completely ridiculous. In the book, the greatest weapon of mankind was horse-drawn artillery. Since these guns are really difficult to arm, and it's nearly impossible to hit a target that's not on ground level (since there you can hope for the blast to do some damage). Now, there are pretty devastating and easily-aimed weapons, so the machines need an impermeable energy shield to remain a threat. Now, the previous Vernes-Wells-era aliens got a jump to a technological level comparable to Star Trek, which makes it completely unbelievable that none of them thought about the possibility that a completely foreign ecosystem might contain bacteria which they are not naturally immune to and thought of some kind of countermeasures (air filters are standard equipment in hospitals now, and we don't even have developed energy shield technology).

Speaking of the aliens: It's a Steven Spielberg movie, so, while the martians in the book were completely different from humans, and genuinely frightening, in the movie they are inappropriately cute. They look like three-legged versions of ET, and absolutely not like leathery balls with lipless, beak-like mouths and lots of tentacles. While the machines are quite threatening and their awesomeness excuse any artistic freedom in their appearance, the aliens themselves are just too familiar to be adequately scary. The Pendragon aliens looked a lot better despite the inferior rendering.

Also, the harvesting of humans, which was a big story point in the book, was horribly executed (OK, it's supposed to be horrible, but this is the bad kind of it). In this movie, the martians catch humans, grind them down and spray them all across the land, probably to fertilize the red weed (which, in the book, was mostly scary because it grew fast from spores brought in the pods, and conquered the land WITHOUT any fertilizer, just because it had lots more nutrients available than on Mars), instead of feed on their blood (which, also in the book, was a major carrier of the bacteria that brought them down later).

Multiple characters in the book (the artilleryman, the parson and for some reason also Ogilvy) were fused into one single deranged redneck with an impressively shallow characterisation, reducing the actual cast of the movie to one air raid siren (the little girl who seemed incapable of coherent speech), a stereotypical slacker-turned-hero (the son) and Tom Cruise, who apparently was supposed to be the protagonist. Not counting thousands of Red Shirts.

Add to this a lot of cliché panic stampede scenes, and you pretty much got the whole movie.

Some suspense still gets built up nicely towards the end, until you can almost hear someone shout "Hey guys, the movie is already longer than we planned, wrap it up!", and within what felt like twenty seconds the perceived climax of the movie stops and we see a stumbling fighting machine, a flash of a malfunctioning energy shield, a heroic missile (after all, we can't just let the aliens die from their own stupidity, their technology needs to be broken too, so no one can try to analyse it later, because that would be too close to the book) and a family reunion.

The End.

It's not a really bad movie, it's just so riddled with bad decisions and mistakes that even the Pendragon Pictures version is a lot better (at least for people who care for story more than for effects and want to get a book adaptation when they are promised one)

title: Spielberg's Disturbing Apocalyptic Saga Sports a Mastery of the Long Take
review:
Steven Spielberg's up-to-date rendition of H.G. Wells's relentless nightmare is a lot better than it is given credit for being. It follows a real family with real complications, none of which Hollywood screenwriters were to be expected to create when enlisted to construct a formula visual effects extravaganza, and because writers David Koepp and Josh Friedman took that expository time to make us care about the friction between self-centered New Jersey dock worker Tom Cruise, his 10-year-old daughter Dakota Fanning, who suffers from a panic disorder and his teenage son Justin Chatwin, who outright resents him, the cataclysmal disaster that comes down just like the wall clouds and electromagnetic pulses that unleash it is all the more harrowing.

I was glued to Spielberg's Morgan Freeman-narrated blockbuster. The fears it stimulates create an unrelenting mood of hopeless, helpless fright which we share with the people in the movie. Spielberg's mastery of marrying spectacle with tension, working with nine-figure budgets and hundreds of thousands of people, none of which deter his strength of vision, generates a dark realization in us, rather than a simple escapist entertainment. He presents strange cloud formations associated with thunder strikes, an arresting amount lower than the rain-free base of the sky. It starts to let loose poundings in the in close proximity to Tom Cruise's everyday Newark neighborhood, immobilizing all of the functioning electronic mechanisms nearby, including cars, leaving everyone trapped. A huge Tripod android surfaces from underground and commences in vaporizing people and buildings in its ample path.

There is truly a disturbing feeling of tragedy whenever there is a casualty of the least significant bystander. There is something very freaky about red weed, the ever-growing plant that, according to H.G. Wells's story, gives Mars its fuzzy blood red color. Ships sink. Cities are destroyed. Children are in peril. Blood is everywhere. Tentacles. A magnificent plane wreck. And a treacherous expedition from New York to Boston with these devastating obstacles exploding in the way.

This sci-fi action chase picture certainly has its glaring clichés here and there, but it is very observed, as films should be, especially spectacle films. The standpoint of the story is very personal. Any given human being can feel connected with the point of view, because it's about a family struggling unremittingly to survive and survive together, and they're contained by the most ambitiously dire and staggering events one could envision.

Not being particularly partial to monster-budgeted special effects blockbusters, I much prefer a director like Spielberg, whose knowledge of film language can be seen in extensive concept shots rather than in heaps of coverage. Spielberg's disturbing apocalyptic saga sports a mastery of the long take, not to mention the logistically impossible several-minute- long tracking and dollying. Many of the film's biggest effects shots are unbroken, where the audience studies its magnitude and absorbs its impact. Michael Bay, or even a fairly talented director like Tony or Ridley Scott, would create artifice with a dozen camera angles, where no shot lasts longer than a brief moment before the film cuts to another. Spielberg, no matter how layman the majority of his film's audiences are likely to be, refuses to talk down to his audience. What makes this $132 million disaster movie above average is that there is fluency, ominous pace and a sense of realistic style, all of which put us within the actual events.

Cruise's character is the worst father I have ever seen -- and he doesn't even play this convincingly.

The son runs into a wall of fire 100 feet high (obviously perishes), and then he shows up at the end of the movie, unscathed and very much alive. What kind of cheesy, ridiculous ending was that? Also, when I saw the movie, the theater I was in was packed full, and the moment Tim Robbins' face showed up on the screen, the ENTIRE audience in the theater started laughing uncontrollably. Didn't they test this scene out before releasing it? When you have a "thriller" and the whole theater laughs at a scene that has no humor at all, you realize that the movie is doomed; it will not end up being good or engaging.

Stupid, lame, unrealistic -- there are not enough negative adjectives to properly describe this waste of film. Spielberg was never any good at "serious" movies; this incomprehensible mess of a movie proves it.

title: Near flawless, terrifying, and awe-inspiring
review: One of the scariest blockbusters in years, and definitely one of the most awe-inspiring. From the get-go, this is not a typical alien invasion film, as there are no wide shots of famous landmarks, nor scenes of government figures discussing counter-attacks. By focusing on just one family, Spielberg makes this a very human and emotional invasion flick. The first hour or so is fantastic film-making, as the suspense gradually builds up to the action scenes, the interaction of the characters is quite well-developed, and the special effects are top-notch. However, as soon as Tim Robbins enters the flick, there is an definite shift from wide open, general horror to claustrophobic terror. While taken individually, each scene is fantastic, they don't flow together at all. Put together with Robbins' manic, deranged, over-the-top performance, and a too-happy ending (not Wells' original, but Spielberg's family reunion), this film falls just short of being another Spielbergian classic. Still, it's a near flawless film, and a roller-coaster ride of thrills.

title: Great effects, no plot, glaring logical errors
review:
War of the Worlds just might be the most disappointing movie Spielberg has ever released. There is a lot of good material here, mostly due to Spielberg's undeniable skill and the phenomenal special effects. However, the story is illogical and poorly thought out. I would say there are plot holes, but you need to have a plot first in order for there to be a hole in it. Maybe that was Spielberg's strategy - wow them with special effects to cover up for the lack of a coherent plot or character development. Reminds me of Michael Bay or Roland Emmerich, to be honest. This movie was just as flashy and pointless as Bad Boys II or Godzilla, without the feel good payoff.

There simply is no plot, and only bare bones character development, all at the beginning of the film. Basically, Cruise and family try and escape from aliens who are killing everyone. Then the movie ends. I couldn't believe it. Why even have a script? This should have been a silent movie, except for the dreaded horn that the tripods blow before they start slayin'.

For people looking for logical errors, I submit to you the following: (i) the camcorder that works after all electrical and mechanical devices have been knocked out, simply because Spielberg thought it created a nifty shot, (ii) the idea that Cruise could drive New Jersey's last automobile for miles on roads full of stopped cars, (iii) a plane crashing on top of a house that Cruise is hiding in - it manages to destroy an entire neighborhood, but not his car, (iv) the entire concept of tripods being hidden for a million years about 10 feet below a city street, and (v) if the aliens are powerful enough to ride lightning bolts and create unstoppable killing machines a million years ago, how come that couldn't pack some Sudafed or control the tripods from space?

One big question for someone out there - what was the deal with the birds? Near the end, Cruise is shouting something about birds, but his voice is covered up by noise, and the soldiers respond with some shouting that was unintelligible. Maybe they had the bird flu. Who knows. The screenwriter sure doesn't.

title: The So-So movie of the summer! *spoilers*
review:
Despite all the makings of a great film here (beautiful effects, a big name actor & director, john williams on the score, etc), this film embodies mediocrity.

The acting in this film is painful to watch. The writers best attempts to make us feel something for these characters are futile, and none of them really feel fully developed, even at the end of the film. Cruise alters his typical role just slightly here but doesn't try anything dramatically different. The children are either a: screaming too frequently (flanning) or b: trying to embody every teen angst stereotype simultaneously (chatwin). But on to my favorite part, the plot holes.

As noted in other reviews, the movie begins with a tripod landing somewhere in Queens, NY, following an electromagnetic pulse. Despite this fact, this scene is photographed and tape recorded by pedestrians. In every scene involving a car, conveniently a path exists for it to drive through (you would think Cruise would have to plow through dead vehicles or debris, but no). This especially gets on my nerves during the scene at his wifes house, where there is a convenient route straight through the wreckage. Speaking of which, how the hell does a car survive when a 747 hits the house it is parked at?

The scene where Flanning and Cruise hide from the eye is Spielburg reusing his shots from the velocirapter/kitchen scene in Jurassic Park. In fact, I found myself repeatedly comparing this to Jurassic Park: mediocre everything, cutting edge effects. Somehow it was cooler when I was younger, though.

My final, biggest gripe with the film is this: If the aliens been plotting the invasion of earth for millions of years, HOW DID THEY FAIL TO REALIZE THAT PARTS OF THE PLANET HAVE FRIGID WEATHER? Couldn't THEY HAVE MAYBE FOUND A WAY, WITH ALL THEIR ADVANCED TECHNOLOGY, TO KEEP FROM FREEZING TO DEATH? They manage to find ways to shield themselves against every weapon known to man, but get the temperature to freezing or below, and its game over.

This is not a bad a film by any means, but its certainly not the blockbuster some of the reviews here are portraying it as.

Sigh.

title: One of Spielberg's worst films
review: I saw it at the cinema yesterday after having watched the 1953 version on TV the day before. The real story seems to be about a jerk of a father who during the course of the film learns how to be a good father and the aliens are a sub plot. War of the Worlds? or war between LA and Boston? The US Military are making more of an effort against Iraqi insurgents than they do in this film. Ordinary people from street-cleaners to weirdo's in basements seem to have all the scientific data and despite a number of direct references to the 1953 version, the earlier version has a much better story. As for the effects - Independence Day was better and I'm sure that I've seen the Aliens from this one before - I wonder where? Having said that Tom Cruise is excellent but Tim Robbins is wasted and the sound, as well as some of the camera work is good. I had such high expectations, having visited the sets in LA, but it was never going to top the Richard Burton CD. One to wait for on DVD I think.

title: An Invasion Worth Looking Forward To
review:
Okay. So this movie may have a few unexplained points and figures, but they're simply more unnerving ends to the already 'unmoved from the edge of your seat from start to finish' plot. Granted, the idea of the suction cup feet were a bit odd, but the tripods and their mechanical bodies and legs, not to mention the deathly blue rays, were a fascinating enclosure to the idea of an alien invasion. I resent Ebert's criticisms. He pushes the question of alien intelligence being that of an extraordinary great power. But how do we know if the aliens aren't as smart as we take them to be? Just because they didn't evolve with our world, doesn't mean they have double or triple the brain expansion as we humans do. So why do we always enforce the idea of hovering spacecraft, world-ending weapons and such? They could be as simple as us, with machines we haven't seemed to think of, at least for world destruction.

Granted, the ending was a bit sudden, but the idea was really fascinating in my point of view. Our world has gone through billions of deaths just to find one of our means of survival - immunity. And because of our adaptations, we have guaranteed our survival amongst such ideal situations.

Now, for the truthful action sequences, just-right special effects, and dramatic familial viewpoints, Spielberg has brought up an amazing experience for us to bite our nails over, forget the world around us, and find ourselves remaining on the edges of our seats while wishes for the family's good fortune. He adds the right touch of humor, and the perfect moments of special effects. Not too much, not too little. Yet just enough to get the point across, and didn't focus the movie on the great things we are capable of doing in this 21st century. It focuses on real life and a true family, which led us into our own lives and put us in the movie with the Ferriers as they fought, or rather ran, their way to live. It didn't follow a government in its troublesome journey of finding a way to stop the invasion and a heroic savior, but the idea of every man for himself in such tragedies.

The aliens who revealed themselves in the basement of a determined survivor seemed as if they were young, and human-minded. Playing with a bike, forced to jump back in reflex, and looking at pictures with what seemed interest, in a way describes my idea of alien simplicity. My brother, after we left the theater, was explaining how some of the moments in the movie reminded him of other movies. Sure, how could they not add in a few other ideas of worldly invasion? But it did seem a bit like Titanic, with the ferry, though it didn't bother me. I was too into the mind-wrenching drama. That's another thing. Even with the few goofs, odd moments, and criticized ideas, Spielberg continued grievously through the action, thrill, and drama, leaving no room for scowls or disappointed thoughts. It continued on, in, once again, realistic situations.

Spielberg knew just how to put in sorrowful moments, and the acting put such emphasis no one knew what to think during the film's length. Tom Cruise performed what was, in my opinion, one of his best performances, following off of my last view of him from 'The Last Samurai' (which I loved also). I really resent the people who offer rude criticism towards the movie, without seeing it, just because of Cruise's personal life. I don't take such things into account. I see the movie for what the movie is, and for whatever I like in the idea. The actors aren't actors to me; they're characters, characters who are on a screen or all around me, depending on how well-rounded the movie comes out to be. Dakota Fanning shows skills beyond her other movies, in my opinion. I enjoyed her shrieks, her desperate need for comfort. And while others scowl at it, who wouldn't need the comfort in such a situation? She also seems to hold her own being, not always playing off of Cruise's role. I enjoyed her much. And Tim Robbin's performance added the right touch as well.

Personally, I loved such scenes as the first appearance of the tripods, the lightning storm, the plane crash, the incredibly realistic mobbing of Ray and his family in the blue van, the ferry boat, the countryside invasion of fires and destroyed armies, the searching of the basement, Boston's destroyed tripods, and more. The bright eye coming from below the water in front of the ferry was predictable, but as I said, Spielberg put such drama, thrill, and suspense to it I completely forgot my comment once the tripod showed itself.

All in all, I loved it, and have seen it twice in a few days. It was worth the money, and it was worth the time on Spielberg and the cast and crew's part. I give it a 8 and a half. Fantastic job to all the cast and crew! But ignore others' comments. See it for yourself and decide on your own terms whether it is a good movie or not. Have fun!

title: Disappointed
review:
I had high hopes for this movie after being a fan of the original radio play and the 1953 movie. I was sorely disappointed.

Tom Cruise was disappointing, some of the plot is predictable, the effects are not bad, but not worth the reported $160 million.

The final was the normal predictable ending that we have seen from many alien blockbuster movies in recent years.

It would have been nice to see the aliens finally win something. Some parts of the movie, especially parts with the aliens in, reminded me of ET.

Too much style over substance, in general I was bored. Give me the original anytime.

title: Horrible ending, Spielberg must think we'r stupid
review:
Terrible movie with too many flaws, and the ending was atrocious, I wont spoil it for you by telling you what it was, but it was so disappointing to see Spielberg such a lousy and crappy flick. The movie started out well enough, there were some places where i found loopholes but most movies have at least a couple so I kinda ignored those. But OMG he ruined the movie by making the ending so lame and silly. Remind me not to watch any more Spielberg flicks, I came out of the theater furious and annoyed at myself for having gone spent good money on the ticket. Not even worth watching this movie once.

Was this the very same guy who made ET, JP, jaws and independence day? What in heaven's name was he thinking when you came up with that ending ?

title: Seven Ulaaahs Out of Ten!
review:
This film isn't perfect but it's well worth seeing.

It's worth seeing for the tripods alone. They are extremely well realised and fairly scary given the limits of the 12A certificate. The first time appearance is particularly breath-taking. They were so good I could almost say we didn't see enough of them despite their prominent role.

Overall the special effects are great. The film leans heavily on them of course, but they are always to used to advance the story or wind up the tension - they never completely overwhelm (Are you taking notes Mr George Lucas?)

I also loved the nods to the 1970's musical version. I was about the age of Dakota Fanning's character when that first came out and it scared me witless!! There was the brilliantly done heat ray, the hiding from the alien appendage in the basement, the character who was a mix of the parson and the artilleryman. Looking back I'm surprised that the parson character wasn't included in this version - a man who believed the Martians were sent from Satan would have fitted nicely into an American version of War of the Worlds. Maybe Spielberg is just a bit too Establishment to have a poke at the Bible Belt ... never mind.

Some people seem to have given this film a hard time. Maybe they're the lucky ones who haven't seen Revenge of the Sith!

I did say this film wasn't perfect though and it lost points with me for these reasons -: 1) The ending was a bit sappy and pathetic. Why wasn't Boston wrecked like everywhere else? 2) Tom Cruise doesn't really convince as a tough labouring guy - he's way out of touch with that way of life. The acting all round seemed a touch wooden to me (But compared to Revenge of the Sith it's Oscar calibre) 3) Seeing the aliens out of their machines was rather unnecessary and slightly diminished them in my eyes. I wish they'd stayed in their scary tripods. 4) Lack of ulaaah's (but that's a personal thing!)

When I left the cinema I wondered if anyone round George Lucas would have the courage to tell him that War of the Worlds was a thousand times better than Sith.

title: It's all praise for Spielberg's perspective.
review:
Steven Spielberg. Tom Cruise. An H. G. Wells classic. Do we need more names? Do we need more hype? But that's where the problem is. We tend to expect too much. We expected it would be another masterpiece by the director. No, "War of the Worlds" is not Spielberg's masterpiece. His "Minority Report" with Cruise was even better. But what I dislike is how we thrash everything that doesn't meet our rising demands. Some critics described it as "major disappointment of the year" or "worst Spielberg film"! Excuse me?! What more can you possibly want of this story that you've read a hundred times since childhood? I'm glad that Spielberg didn't change any basic structure or ideas of the story and ruin it. What he added are touches of his genius.

Forget about special visual or sound effects. When Spielberg makes a blockbuster sci-fi, they are always top-notch. What I want to discuss is his perspective in storytelling. I confess, it's really hard to make a film about hostile alien invasion in serious mood after all these years (especially after Mr. Burton's "Mars Attacks"). Technologically advanced fierce-looking aliens destroying cities and killing humans without any apparent reason -- this is now comedy element. Serious movie aliens are now either friendly as in Spielberg's own "E.T." or if they are hostile, they're sinister and mysterious enough. And they find no reason to declare war on Earth in a mass scale. So I think Spielberg took a major risk on making this film, because it doesn't fit in the modern alien trend (I know how I disliked "Independence Day").

So what can he do to fit this thing in the trend? Tell the story not from a well-educated telescope-wise guys point of view as Wells did, but from a common middle-class worker with social problems. Enter Tom Cruise as Ray: dock worker, divorced, with two children. He's got enough problems before he thinks of alien invasion. What we see in this film is what he sees. He's the representative of a part of mankind and the movie deals with how that part is affected. It's a wise decision by Spielberg not to include everybody in action. So he didn't show how the politicians react, how the scientists react or how religious leaders react. The greatest thing about this film is this is first-person and that person is not a hero to mankind by fighting the aliens. All he does is to save himself and his kids. And how Spielberg built his experiences! His magical visions and excellent cinematography aided him to make some classic shots like, the radiation massacre on the running crowd by the aliens or the 'hide-and-seek' in Ogilvy's cellar.

But is there nothing really in this film that deserves criticism? Take the characters: Robbie, the son, is an extremely two-dimensional character and the guy who played him is equally pathetic. There was no need to bring this character. Rachel's character also appeared a little bit conflicting. The grenade trick that Ray did is just very cheap and entirely unexpected from Spielberg or Koepp. And for the ending, I wish it was more dramatic. It entirely lacked the surprise element.

Tom Cruise may be nuts off-screen, but once again he shows why he is the highest paid actor and the most wanted movie star now. He develops the character of Ray nicely, any other actor would overact and ruin it. Dakota Fanning is just awesome. She successfully brings out the inner mentality of a girl of her age and thus gives the character a serious importance. And Tim Robbins delivers yet another impressive character performance as Ogilvy.

There are plenty of moments in this film that reflects Spielberg's originality. Most of them one would appreciate (I won't spoil it by mentioning them) and some one would disapprove. It's really stupid to say things like "It's the best invasion movie ever" or "best take on Wells classic" about this film. Because that depends on time. The more the cinema technology would develop, the better these films would be. But Mr. Spielberg once again showed there are other things to praise besides CGI in a sci-fi film. Yes, he could do better, but it is the best we could get.

title: Spielberg... where are you taking us?
review:
I think it may have been wise for Spielberg to stop making alien movies after ET.

Apart from the entertaining special effects, the movie was a real let down. But this is the problem with creating a movie that deals with some sort of global apocalypse or end of the world situation, too many plot holes are created, and the audience is simply expected to swallow whatever crap the director is trying to feed you.

As soon as the aliens begin to attack, the movie gives the viewer a feeling of hopelessness, which can be good or bad, depending on where the plot takes you. But in the case of WOTW, this is bad... really bad. Here you have these 200 ft tripod aliens sweeping the earth of people while protected by some sort of invisible shield, thereby eliminating any form of human defense. For 90 minutes, the characters are hiding and running, then hiding and running some more. The audience never understands why the aliens are attacking, what they want, where they came from etc. Instead, humans choose not to survive or defend, but to rather outrun the thousands of giant laser armed alien tripod things. However these attacking aliens, as intelligent and superior as they are, somehow fail to escape the awesome forces of microscopic earth bacteria, which takes them by surprise and kills them all on the spot, but not before they vomit some sort of tomato soup looking stuff. I guess the aliens never thought to check that stuff before investing millions of years in planning an attack on Earth, but hey, aliens can make mistakes sometimes too. I mean, E.T. missed his ship home, didn't he? Morgan Freeman's 30 second speech at the end leaves the viewer with a pretty bad taste in the mouth, not to mention Tom manages to get to Boston somehow on no food or bathroom breaks to deliver his screaming child to her mother and family. And how perfect was it to see them all walk out of their beautiful brownstone city home, looking like they just finished eating brunch, completely oblivious and unscathed by the crap that is going on outside. Also, the runaway son also appears from out of the house after abandoning his family because he wanted to see all of army/alien spectacle first hand. But of course, Spielberg could never allow one of his main characters die... he has to come back in the end and satisfy the audience.

But hey, I guess you cant blame Spielberg for all of this. This is just the stuff that annoys movie buffs when doing a movie about the end of the world. Too many holes, too little explanation and development, too much guessing for the audience.

I am surprised to see that the film is only rated PG-13, although when people are killed by alien lasers they just sort of turn to dust, rather than spew blood and guts... which might have made the movie a little more entertaining. The movie could have used a little more Tim Robbins, and A LOT less Tom Cruise... realistically, Jerry Maguire isn't going to save anyone from anything.

War of the Worlds will definitely be considered a flop in Spielberg's catalog. The special effects and Tim Robbins give it enough juice for a 3/10.

title: A hit in the first week
review: I imagine this film will make a killing in the first week of release, especially the first weekend, then the word of mouth will get around and the box office will plunge. Which is okay by me. Granted there are some impressive visual moments in the film such as the ferry attack, the plane crash, and similar ones which are due to special effects, and then there are sort of interesting parts where due to editing and Spielberg's "I'm a director" you might pause at, say the murder in the cellar, or all the shots of reflections. But humanwise, characterwise, I frequently found myself saying, "This sucks." Why would I be interested in these people, they are unpleasant to be around. The hunting for goofs may be a trivial pursuit but it can be more satisfying than this film was in total. So...I could sort of overlook that Tom Cruise's character doesn't know his daughter has been allergic to peanuts, "since birth". It goes with the unappealing nature of his character, but why would the home where the mother and daughter now live even have a jar of peanut butter around? It's like having a loaded gun lying around in a home with small children and about as dangerous.

title: At least the trailer wasn't bad
review:
Spielberg and Cruise reunite for this summer blockbuster which one would expect to be entertaining but not necessarily awe-inspiring. In fact the end product is a massive disappointment with a plot that would struggle to gain any fans were it not for the big names involved.

The central acting performances are OK, although Dakota Fanning is far too mechanical in her delivery of what should have been a very human character. The effects and backdrop is excellent as one would expect and there is some genuine tension created by Spielberg but this is surprisingly lacking in punch and the viewer is more mildly interested than engrossed as they would hope to be. Perhaps a few more viewings of the film will enable me to spot some of the other positives in this remake (the original was no masterclass either it must be said) but I, along with many others left the cinema feeling let down by a man who has failed to produce in recent years (no doubt many will disagree with me on that point).

title: Missed things about mil-gov-sci
review:
I saw the first version of this story when i was a child. And I remember the news (cinema style) about the invasion. There was initial strike with conventional weapons and another with a nuke from a flying wing (YB-49 i think). I think there was little detail about military, government/presidential effort.

And the scientist? Really wasn't a better argument to defeat the ETs with something less unbelievable that just microorganisms? (in the XIX century -H.G. Welles century- it was OK for the knowledge of that time, but now in the XXI the script could have based the solution upon nanomachines or other top invention or knowledge)

title: A disappointing melting pot of previous alien films
review:
I went into the newest of Spielberg's blockbusters hoping for as rewarding a film as last summer's "The Terminal". In reading the magazine articles about the film I was told that they were going to do the sci-fi genre well by not reverting to the usual stereotypes and catches involved with a action packed, CGI carnival type film. Upon watching a quarter of the film, I was solely disappointed by these aspirations. "War of the Worlds" displayed flat characters usually not found in Spielberg's more successful films. The movie made you sincerely dislike the main characters and as a result of this lack of relation to the characters, there was a painful lack of respite in the intensity and gore of the film. Normally I am not one to shy away from violence and gore in films but "War of the Worlds" spent the entire film on a very high intensity level with unnecessary violence. I began to wonder to myself how many times and how many ways the audience had to see people killed. Spielberg needs to take a lesson from the much higher quality alien invasion type movies like "Signs" and learn that if you want such high intensity you have to relieve the audience of that intensity once in a while otherwise, the audience, like me, will be so sick to their stomachs by the end that your effects will be lost to them.

The film was extremely disappointing and audiences considering the film are better served going to a much higher quality action film like "Batman Begins" this summer.

title: Rent the original and bypass this piece of garbage
review:
In a war of the worlds movie, I expect to see a war, i.e. the armed forces against the aliens. This was basically Tom Cruise vs the aliens. There was one flyby of some jets, and one scene with some tanks. Otherwise, just Cruise, nothing but Cruise. There was not one freaking scene in this entire movie that did not have Tom Cruise in it. Then there is Dakota Fanning. She is a cute little girl. So put her in a cute little girl movie. She certainly brought nothing to this movie. I suppose she was supposed to be the reason Tom Cruise cared, (although, basically he just wanted to hide so what was the point) but if we were really being attacked by indestructible aliens, wouldn't you care even if you didn't have a cute little daughter. Not to mention that the movie spent an inordinate amount of time showing us that Tom was an uncaring father. Okay, I got it after the first 30 minutes.

Independence Day was closer to War of the Worlds than this was. My advice is See the original War of the Worlds. Sure it only had 1950's special effects, but it had story and characters you cared about. And battles between the aliens and the army!

title: a bad surprise!
review: I was so excited when I first saw the trailers. Today me and a good friend of mine went to this movie and after the first 30 minutes our opinions to this movie was changing from awesome to awful step by step. I thought Spielberg would come up with something like a more serious and threatening version of independence day. Okay this movie is kept serious, but it's story has too many illogical points and you don't see much of the fight between the human soldiers (actually you only see the Americans) and the Alien "walkers". Most annoying element of this movie was the girl Rachel. Me and my friend were wishing that she would be.... by the Aliens.
