Spielberg started the first zapping through the eyes of the camcorder specifically to convey this message, that we are desensitized to such images or so we think, because most us in the modern world now at the beginning of the 21st Century are seeing events through the TV, or movies, or photos, and not seeing these sorts of horrors first hand as we may have once done, only a couple hundred years ago, when such nastiness as hanging, lynching, beheading, torture and humiliation were presented and shown in public spaces, at the village square for example.

Personally I would like to have seen more people running around without a leg (bad pun, sorry) or an arm, and more people running around burned or disfigured would have also helped in making us feel more disgusted. Seeing the field of red tentacle-roots and red liquid flowing just doesn't cut if for most of us to make us feel frightened. The one man who we are allowed to see as his blood is sucked out of him was rather too deliberately hidden from our view. Censored, in a sense, to make this movie PG-13 was to bring in a bigger audience to pay for its hefty production budget which ended up making the filmmaker ease up on the violence factor.

In fact, we were supposed to be terrified as we went on the run with the 3 of them, but somehow the tunnel-vision effect worked so well to encase the viewer into Ray's perspective that we became just as detached and emotionally exhausted as Ray is, in his life - his methods of trying to control his own children are put to test here, even though the trying circumstances end up actually showing us how pathetic and meaningless he is as a father. Even when he attempts to protect his daughter from the horror he is about to bring upon Ogilvy, he is somewhat reckless - even though he put blindfolds around his daughter's eyes and she sings to tune-out any supposedly horrific noises, the scene indicates that the young ones in our modern society are pretty savvy to what's going on around them, as she knows the exact moment that the deed had been done; and I think Dakota Fanning was picked especially and precisely for her "awareness" which is, in fact, the prelude to her character's (and possibly the actress') future as a desensitized human being. And she ends up simply being annoying. And Robbie: He is just one generally confused kid, isn't he? I didn't quite understand what brought on his sudden madness to want to SEE it all happening, besides the fact that he wanted to get away from his dumb father who actually happened to have saved him up to this point, no matter whether his father had been a wastoid until the aliens arrived. We never really got to know Robbie much except for the fact that he was going to turn out to be a fool in life like his father is, his disrespect for authority shown in his behavior at the beginning of the film where he "borrowed" the car. OK he seems to get along mightily with his mother and sister and his mother's new husband, but his desire to see the battle was not motivated enough because his character was never fully fleshed out. So when he came out of his mother's apartment to let us know he survived, we actually felt that it would have been better if he had been dead - the message for the audience then, could have been that there is a lesson to be learned here not to be a wastoid father!

At first glance, it's an OK movie at the higher levels of Hollywood mega-budget film-making. The effects are about what we would expect, the production design is on par with that, and so is the cinematography. And those things are all pretty, alright. The acting could have been better to keep us suspended in disbelief, but once again, Star Power did get in the way and more often than not we were taken out of the film's reality. All that is glossed over with the story moving along as fast as the plots would let it, but unfortunately, there are far too many questions left unanswered and though it was a valiant effort to make something of an homage to the book, they could have done a lot better about controlling the plot lines and certain fake-out edits that made some audience members groan because they knew the filmmakers did some things in this film in haste and the intentions did not pay off in the end.

title: Spectacular, but flawed.
review:
SOME SLIGHT SPOILERS This film had great special effects and very good sound effects. The screenplay seemed non existent to me, and the dialogue was certainly nothing to be proud of. All i can really say for this film is that the interpretation of the aliens was well done: they looked cool in a sci-fi sort of way and some good damage was done (all in America i should add).

None of the violence shocked me because i've seen worse, but (SPOILERS!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!) dead bodies in a river, and people being blown to pieces by alien weaponry is a bit too much for a 12. It could maybe even be classed as a sci-fi horror movie.

MORE SPOILERS: anyway, the lack of a structured plot lets this film down, and a classic unexplained Hollywood ending ruins what could have been a half decent film. Its good to watch in the cinema, because the effects are worth it, but anyone who knows about films can see that this film is severely flawed.

It needs a screenplay, it needs a dialogue, and it needs a structure which explains whats going on. I mean, (SPOILERS!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!) when the aliens keep searching for cruise in the basement: whats the point in that!!??!! They don't look for anyone else and the rest of the time they just destroyed everything - so why spend ages looking for a human?? Anyway, you guys have your opinions, but i'm right.

I still like Spielberg and cruise though, this film was just plain weird.

title: Very confused
review:
Just saw the movie. Disappointed like the rest of you who saw it, but I have a question for the ones who did see it. How did the Aliens lose their force field around their ships? and why did the tripods start acting crazy and falling over? I didn't understand how all of a sudden they began to die and fall over. Is it because they were drinking the water? Can someone clear this up for me, because I was terribly disappointed in the ending.

All in all though, I thought the movie had great potential. Tom Cruise was very good and I did enjoy watching the movie up until the end where it seemed the just cut it short and didn't really explain anything. Usually I really enjoy Spielberg's films but this one was nowhere near what he usually produces. Some of the things I really enjoyed was how it jumped right into the action, but then again that took a bit away from the plot.

title: Spielberg launches you in the midst of a Martian invasion
review: This is a great movie based on the famed HG Wells novel of the same name. A list actor teams up with A list director to make a good entertaining film that needs to be appreciated. The effects of the alien tripods are amazing especially the sound design- they evoke fear. The plotting and pacing is efficient which should be expected from Spielberg and the acting is good. You know how the film ends and yet this film keeps you engrossed. If you haven't read the famous novel I suggest you read it before seeing this film.

title: A Bastardized Version of H.G. Wells Classic
review: This is not a sci-fi thriller. This is not even a bad story. This is a muddled mashup of disjointed series of events involving mindless action, mayhem, explosions, running with no apparent purpose. In other words, a typical Spielberg horse-manure. It is true that if an alien force struck the earth, confusion, chaos and disorder would prevail but that that doesn't mean that its story must be scattered all over the place. The chaotic narrative leaves the impression that the aliens rather hit the movie set. The movie has no plot, no acting, no dialogue, no character development and offers nothing to engage the viewer. When you don't feel connected to the main characters you also become indifferent to their ordeal and struggle for survival. The suspense and tension that a thriller is supposed to build hangs in the vacuum. The movie starts with no promises and delivers nothing in the end, which makes it consistent at least in one thing. After seeing his prominent movies, this one erased all the doubts in my mind that Spielberg can't tell a coherent story.

title: Americanizing a British Classic Using Tom Cruise?!?
review: Ugh. I've read the book a number of times. Seen the original flick a couple times. This? This is painful to watch. Just painful. I don't know what else to say. The whole thing was just set on cruise control. Ugh.

title: One of Spielbergs more forgettable films
review:
This is the sort of film that critics over-rate, on the basis it visually "looks good" (which it does) and has a big star in Tom Cruise. But that's about the films only positive traits.

There's only one battle scene, and you don't even get to see that because the film is too busy focusing focusing on Cruises character Ray (whose an a hole) his son Robby (also an a-hole) and his daughter Rachael (an annoying, know it all, whiny kid.) The whole film primarily focuses on them but they're so unlikable you don't root for them at all. When you wish the aliens would vaporize the three main characters, you know the film has failed.

There's no real ending, Ray reunites with Robby who supposedly died halfway through the film, no explanation as to how he survived. Robbys character arc alternates between being a teenage a hole and wanting to join the army and fight the aliens. This behaviour makes no sense, it's just there for the sake of "coolness."

The aliens are completely generic, aliens with impenetrable shields has been done as far back as 1953's "war of the worlds" film. The formula was repeated in Star wars, Independance day etc. Not that it's supposed to matter, since the film only wants us to care about this family of a-holes. No real creativity was put into this film, it just exists as a easy cash grab. It bears similarities to "The lost world" which had similar problems.

Even people who liked this film probably wouldn't watch it again, it has no replay value.

title: War of the Worlds
review:
Short and Simple Review by WubsTheFadger

Gangbusters effects and terrific camerawork propel Steven Spielberg's film well into its last act, when it runs out of energy and ideas. This collapse is especially disappointing because War of the Worlds begins as a provocative look at how terror affects family and community, that is, something more complicated than an explosion movie. If the first part of the film offers an absorbingly detailed look at the family's dysfunction, the ride in the minivan tightens the focus, as they struggle to make sense of the disaster unfolding around them. "Is it terrorists?" asks Rob. No, says Dad, this "came from someplace else." Rob tries again: "What do you mean, like Europe?" This brief comedy only sharpens the scares that follow, not all caused by aliens. Indeed, two of the most awful scenes involve people fighting each other.

This and other particulars -- a monstrous surveillance eye on a sinuous, seemingly endless arm invades Harlan's basement; clothes from disintegrated victims float through tree branches; a peanut butter sandwich Ray has thrown at the kitchen window slides almost imperceptibly down the glass as he wonders what to do next; Ray asks a man who appears to have survived a plane crash, "Are you a passenger?" -- create a potent mix of recognizable and fantastic moments. The film's last minute breakdown is really the loss of such clever details.

Overall Rating: 6.4

title: Aliens invade an American populace suddenly reduced to two handguns and a shotgun
review:
and one of the handguns belongs to Tom Cruise who, although just an average schmoe, seems to have a better handle on the situation than anyone else.

I didn't dislike this movie, but it wasn't as good as the previews made it out to be. The special effects were good and the aliens believable, although I'd have thought a civilization that advanced would have figured out a more effective way to eliminate people than giant walking tripods, and maybe would have done a few air and water samples before deciding to move here, but that's just me.

Gore is kept to a minimum, good if you've got kids. I never did figure out what the blood vessel network was all about, and like the poster above, I did wonder how the camcorder was working when nothing else was.

title: Ridiculous... This movie made me laugh loudly!!!
review:
The only reason I rented this title was because I really like Tom Cruise's acting. As usual I enjoyed him but the whole movie was terrible disappointing! I was expecting something really scary from the aliens but all I could do during this movie was to laugh.

I did not watch the original from the 50's so I cannot compare. Anyway, I didn't find these aliens threatening at all!!! Those tripods (and their pilots) looked so stupid even killing people!

I admit there are very good sequences, mostly because of the SFX. The stormy sky, the earthquake, the ferry part were amazing and I also liked the suspense when they were in the crazy man's basement.

I cannot forget something: Dakota Fanning is a lovely child and very good actress but... what a terrible role and behavior these writers gave her. Why did they take this lovely child and turn her into such a bitch??? She was so annoying, restless, obnoxious, uptight... that I would have LOVED to see her killed!!! But well, both parents were stupid in this movie, so what can I expect? Obviously a stupid kid! I cannot blame Dakota. Her acting was great. What I did not like was her character.

title: Nice Special Effects  Pity About The Rest of It..
review:
Nice Special Effects  Pity About The Rest of It..

This attempt by Steven Spielberg to bring us a 21st Century interpretation of the classic H.G. Wells was certainly a brave project so what did we get? In the end we had a very well made film but with some notable low points that just did not seem to gel properly. The special effects were impressive as was the photography and direction whilst for the most part, the cast did their bit.

However we can only speculate as to how good this film really could have been were it not for a number of major failings.

Characters  There was not really a single memorable character amongst the cast, with the exception of Cruise's battling divorced father (and even he had a number of faults), their was an awful lot of cardboard cut outs, cannon fodder and plot device carriers with no depth or even names for the most part.

The Kids  Any movie with clichéd 'irritating yet cute' characters grates with me. Once again instead of a couple of ordinary reasonably intelligent children, we got the delinquent teenager with the attitude problem and the irritating little girl with the health issues (allergic to peanut butter, back problems and claustrophobic). If this is representative of the majority of the youth of today then quick frankly its time to pull the plug on the entire human race!

The Nutter  Tim Robbins is a great if underused character actor but his role in this as the nutter in the cellar was utterly pointless and should have been jettisoned at the first script review.

The Plot Holes  You could see the car being repaired just in time plot line coming a mile off. Meanwhile there was no apparent explanation of how on earth the teenage delinquent son managed to escape certain death to appear once more at the end although yet again I suspected this was what was going to happen.

The Alien Defeat  Yes I am fully aware that the way the alien's just roll over and die in mid battle because of bugs in the air is indeed in the original story but it still smacks of a lack of imagination Star Trek style end of episode reset switch that brings the story to a juddering halt.

The Sound Track  What has happened to John Williams of late? There was a time when the musical genius could do no wrong but yet his recent work, notably the totally out of character (in comparison with the rest of the series) soundtrack for Star Wars Episode III plus this have been very weak and lacking the classic punch and glory of his earlier work

With a bit better script, some attention to the obvious weaknesses and maybe even some different casting, this could have been excellent but as it is, it is watchable but disappointingly average.

title: Not bad, but no classic
review:
I was disappointed with this film for several reasons. First of all, if you haven't seen the film, don't read any more since I'm most likely spoiling it for you.

I never bought into the notion that aliens could successfully bury hundreds of tripods and have them go undetected by human kind over the course of what had to have been thousands of years. This of course did make for a spectacular entrance, seeing one burst forth, but come on! Logic flew out the window for the sake of just being spectacular. Which is something that tends to spoil man of Spielberg's films, at least for me. It's his tendency to impress using unjustified gimmicks. Remember "The Sugarland Express" where the sheriff played by Ben Johnson decides to stop a news van by shooting out its tires causing it to tumble into a ravine? Now I ask you; what officer of the law could do such a thing and get away with it? I know people distrust the media and that was the case back in 1974, but it smelled of a contrivance used to shock. There's much of this in "War of the Worlds." Too much. I'd mention more examples of it, but since there are those reading this who haven't yet seen the film and I don't want to spoil it too much for them, I'll remain quiet.

Another thing about the film that bother me were all the various mistakes. Mistakes in continuity, mistakes in the visuals, mistake after mistake after mistake. Much of the CGI is quite good, but there are times when the tripods dramatically change size. As the film progresses, they get bigger until by the end they're at least three-times as large as the first one we see. The movements of the tripods seem a bit odd as if the animators took liberties with where they touched the ground. As Tom Cruise is running away from the very first one leading up to him ducking behind a building, in the background we see the legs of the tripod moving backwards. As Cruise settles in the shot the legs begin to move forward, all the while we're hearing the mechanized beat as the machine advances. There are other scenes like this where the joining of the CG material over actual locations doesn't quite work.

Would I recommend the film? that depends on what you're looking for in entertainment. "Independence Day" was awful, but it had a sense of fun about it which made it somewhat bearable. And its visual effects were on par with "War of the Worlds" and in some ways even better. It's aliens tended to look somewhat like the aliens in Spielberg's film. I still prefer the shrimp-pink, pulsating vein-covered cyclops of Pal's version of "War of the Worlds." The classic scene where it placed its three spindly fingers on Ann Robinson's shoulder left a lasting impression with just about all who saw the film for the first time. Nothing like it in this version. The aliens are shown in a cut and dry fashion.

For me Spielberg's "War of the Worlds" lacked imagination. It's rather dark and brooding. Where George Pal's version instilled a sense of wonder as well as fright, this film only succeeds in brining out the feeling of dread mixed with a sense of futility.

I give it a 6 out of ten. I'd have given it a 7 had Tom Cruise not been in it.

title: Great action, annoying characters
review: The special effects were spectacular, and the action sequences mostly riveting. But the characters of the two Ferrier kids were so annoying that it pretty much ruined the movie for me. Dakota Fanning may be an adorable little girl visually, but Rachel Ferrier was probably the first little girl in a movie I actually hoped would get captured and eaten by the aliens. She's a screamer and tantrum-thrower, and intellectually incapable of learning what the children of Baghdad, Beirut and Bosnia figured out like lightning: in a war zone, you become a mouse - neither seen nor heard. And son Robbie is little more than a collection of every single emotional hangup possible in a child of divorce (especially when the custodial parent is blue-collar and the non-custodial stepparent isn't). Tom's really trying to reach his ex just to get rid of these two brats.

title: Pass the clichés
review:
The best thing about this film is that, though transferred from 19th century London to the US East Coast in the 21st century, it does otherwise at least try to follow H.G. Wells' original fairly closely. For example, the invading aliens use tripods as their fighting machines and there is a fairly lengthy scene in which the lead character (not named in the story but called Ray Ferrier here) is trapped in a cellar with a madman (played, with obvious relish, by Tim Robbins).

Unfortunately, in his attempt to inject human interest into the story, Steven Spielberg opts for a set of main characters so clichéd that even Lifetime would be embarrassed to portray them. Ray (Tom Cruise) is our hero, a flawed man and neglectful father whom his wife (Mirando Otto) has renounced in favor of Tim (David Alan Basche), a clean-cut, responsible sort who takes care of her and the two children she has by Ray. Tim, effete rich guy that he is, virtually disappears (of course) when the crisis hits while Ray emerges as strong, loving and caring, taking calamity as an opportunity to redeem himself with his children. Can anyone say "soap opera"? The special effects, particularly early on, are pretty good, but the music is absolutely forgettable. Meanwhile, the attacking aliens are never actually stated to be Martians, a fact obvious in the original story and that the 1953 film made a point of right from the start, and their reasons for attacking are never identified ("envy" is mentioned, but why do they feel envious?) leaving the film seriously adrift.

Dakota Fanning, as Ray's daughter Rachel, is an irritating, glib brat who screams too much! Meanwhile, Morgan Freeman, as the narrator at the beginning and end of the action, sounds half-asleep - perhaps understandably.

In all, this is a pretty unsatisfactory movie experience, inferior to the 1953 version and something of a step back for Spielberg. Except financially, of course.

Rating: 4/10.

title: A big blundering mechanical mess
review:
Here we have a well-milked premise of a dysfunctional family disguised as a sci-fi adventure. So there are two struggles - one father's (Tom Cruise) struggle to reconnect with his kids, and one struggle to escape the alien invasion that is simultaneously taking place.

Because War of the Worlds is a first person narrative, from Cruise's character's perspective, we do not find out a whole lot about what is actually happening outside of his own personal struggles. That is a clever device because then the film never needs to explain what leads to the course of events (like aliens coming down his basement) or WHY ALIENS SUDDENLY INVADE THE EARTH at all. After all, Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise) does not know, so why should we? I found this device mostly frustrating because I wanted more knowledge of what was going on and why it was happening.

Although the narrow perspective through which things were seen did sometimes work to the film's advantage. Some sequences were extremely intense and absorbing, like the basement sequence. The good aspects end there however, because War of the Worlds is a not a good movie. Very little of the content is actually believable and all (I mean ALL) Hallmark family clichés are present at one point or another

The worst part is the stupid cop-out at the end, as narrated by Morgon Freeman. Basically, what destroyed the alien invaders were tiny earth-borne microorganisms that we humans had suffered for millions of years, i.e. evolved into being resistant to. Sure, I'll buy that. Then, in practically the same sentence, Freeman says "the microorganisms that God put upon this earth..." Really, huh? God did that? What's it gonna be, Spielberg? Evolution or Creationism? You just contradicted yourself. It was just such a transparent cop-out to satisfy both scientists and believers. It really bothered me for some reason.

This whole film really bothered me, to be honest. It is not subtle or intelligent, but a big clunky mechanical mess with no good ideas or remotely interesting approaches to save it. 4/10.

title: Great movie ruined by a stupid ending
review:
Up until the last two minutes of the movie, this was one of the best science fiction movies I'd seen in a long time. The ending was absolutely horrible, and I'm not talking about the fact that the aliens were wiped out by viruses/bacteria. That's in the original, and is exactly what I expected. I'm talking about the fact that Tom Cruise's character makes it to Boston and finds his entire extended family alive and looking as if they just got done with tea, despite the overwhelming improbability of ANY of them making it through alive. I felt like this was an insult to my intelligence, but when his kid, who absolutely COULD NOT have survived running unarmed towards a bunch of alien ships that were killing people by the thousands, mysteriously showed up alive and in Boston. It completely ruined the gravitas that was so well established by the rest of the movie. This ending felt like a personal insult. I felt like Spielberg must have a pretty damn low opinion of his audience to tack on an improbable, stupid happy ending that makes no sense.

This movie would have gone down as one of my favorite science fiction movies of recent years, had the ending not ruined it all.

title: War of the Worlds
review: I've seen this movie twice now, so I believe I have formed an opinion about it. Fortunately and unfortunately the director is Steven Spielberg. Why am I saying this? Fortunately, because he can raise a big budget, so the special effects will be of excellent quality. Unfortunately, because he doesn't seem to get over his ET-period, except when it involves Jews as victims. The movie starts at a good pace with a little insight in the family, the subsequent scenes with the alien machine rising from the ground is also good, but could have been more horrifying. Still, it gives an in look in things to come. People seem to want to be killed by the machine because they start running only, when it's too late. Maybe this is the normal reaction of the average American under a Bush-government. I however would have run away at the sign of the earthquake, which starts when the machine wants to crawl out of the ground. Then eventually, starts the runaway with the only working car???. Just change the starter and it will work,.. yeah right like this is a car from the pre-electronic age. Let me explain what disturbed me in the movie. The son. He acts like a real asshole and moron, and seeing him alive at the end of the movie seems to be very contradicting with his actions, like.. wanting to see how the army fights the aliens, while it was a massive fire-sea he went into. How the hell did he escape from that and get before the main character and his daughter to Boston at his mother family-home. If I was his father I would kicked his moron butt. The daughter: She really started to an annoy me from the start. She seems to be intelligent, but on the other hand acts like a scream-queen. another contradicting element. I really hoped she would be killed bloodily by the aliens when she was stupid enough to leave the house. But there's no blood in this movie.., except the one used as fertilizer for the alien's favorite plant, which is also red. Tsk, tsk Spielberg, when a plant is red, it doesn't mean you have to spray it with blood, water will do just fine. Hell, spraying it with human-blood will probably kill the plant. Ah, now I get it. the aliens where out of fertilizer, that's why they planted the machines ages ago, to wait until there where enough humans to use them as fertilizer. And in all those years nobody seems to have digged deep enough to uncover one of these machines. Even HG. Wells would have found this a stupid idea. One of the end-scenes with the unshielded alien machine who eventually gets shot down but the military looks forced and at this point I completely lost interest in the movie. Having seen the original movie with the hand falling out the machine, I'm quite disappointed. I'm not going to speak more about the last scene, that was a real turnoff. Typically ET-Spielberg. The book for this film was probably quite acceptable for the movies from the 50's, but having the same plot again, that a super-intelligent race gets beaten by bacteria can't cut it in the 21th century. It would be like an astronaut going in space with his T-shirt on. Totally unacceptable for a plot. I would at least suspect Spielberg would have changed this in another more intelligent defeat of the aliens. Although on second thought, based on his other SF-movies, that's just what I expected Spielberg to do. So, I gather, this is a movie for the masses an not for the intelligent viewer. I didn't expect much more from Spielberg. He'd better stick with holocaust movies in the future.

title: Should have been called 'Massacre of Earth Cliché Fest'
review:
I had high hopes for War of the Worlds, especially with such an advancement of CGI technology the potential of such a blockbuster was there. Instead the CGI became the only good thing about the film. The films suffers from everything that can go wrong in a film. Even people back in the 50's would laugh if they saw this. War of the World is perhaps the biggest collection of disaster movie clichés ever made.

The characters- The focal point of most movies and the anchor of us, (the audience) into the film's world. The characters in the film wouldn't seem to be able to pass a grade 2 math exam. All of whom seem to do their best to be as hateable as possible, Armageddon has arrived on earth and people bicker and fight among each other about such trivial matters like a cheap sit-com. We're also treated to a 10 year old girl who's presence there is merely as a screaming machine. Also after a street is torn from under their feet, and behold a giant mechanized alien device towers before everyone, suddenly brains fade out of existence to stare up at the behemoth before them dumbfounded. I mean come on, especially when the teen makes an emotional scene just to have a better view of the futile military engagement. The characters manage to make themselves so unsympathetic that you're hoping the aliens succeeds in killing them.

The plot- The plot is simple enough, aliens exterminating humanity, And we follow a certain blue collar worker's hard path of survival from the ultra-advanced alien invaders. All the while he has to show how bad of a father he is along the way with a child and a teenager deciding now was the time to be rebellious. Oh by the way the rest of the world has been destroyed. I don't know how they managed to green light that gem...

The Aliens- Ah yes, the great antagonists of the film. They are killing people on sight, Why? The film never bothers to explore that. As far as we know, it's just a zoo gone mad. Where did they come from? The film also never bothers to explore that either. They're just around, in big machines, zapping people one at a time in the most inefficient extermination methods possible. Of course they are totally invincible for the sake of making our character's plight even more hopeless. I don't know about you but it seems to me something is more scary when the odds are against us rather then when it's totally hopeless. The aliens are just there cause the movie has nothing better to do, so they'll kill off a whole species one at a time for the hell of it.

Cliché upon Cliché upon Cliché- could the film be even more predictable and clichéd? Even Roland Emmerich couldn't top the cliché list higher then this. Father just woke up, Big mechanized Alien zapping everyone. Father escapes in a car, idiot killed, Big mechanized alien zapping everyone. Father and kids make it onto a boat, Big mechanized alien zapping everyone. Military engages, energy shields deflect everything. Sudden weakness discovered, Aliens don't stand a chance anymore. Main characters survive. This list of clichés is just from the plot alone, There's a whole bunch more during the finer points of the film.

I mean there's nostalgia I understand but there's a limit to that too, A film called 'War of the Worlds' consists of 3 people running and running and running. A foe which is impossible to to defeat but all miraculously die from something you'd think with all their advanced technology would be able to counter. This makes even sci fi films from the 50's look bad.

title: War of the Bores
review:
I'm sorry, I was't going to make a comment regarding this until I saw the high but unworthy praise drizzled over this charade of a movie. Yes, we may have the worlds supposedly greatest director directing one of Hollywood's top stars, but Spielberg seems to be film-making by numbers these days. Pick a topic, gather stock crew together (John Williams music again. Janus Kamnski DP again ILM Effects bunch etc etc) Pick nice safe box office dead certs for cast. Rattle the thing off and get working on the next job before even finishing the last one. I'm not saying War of the Worlds is a turkey, but it should have been on my Christmas dinner table with an onion stuffed up it's backside.

It is truly abysmal. Take an age-old English classic, move it both in time and space to New York (WHY!!?) Screw around with the plot and bury the story deeper than the spaceships, (What was wrong with meteorites?). Set the "hero" as a miserable, obnoxious idiot with a dysfunctional family of a separated wife, car-stealing son and a precocious daughter that never stops squealing. She is one good reason to keep the pro-spanking bill. Most leads, you want to follow them, empathise with them, worry for them. Personally I wish Tom Cruise's character had been made toast in the first reel and put us all out of our misery. He was totally unlikeable, as were most of the cast. The only redeeming feature were the effects, but we still spent far too much time running around dark cellars with little green men.

The recent remake of "The Time Machine" was not great, but it had the atmosphere and joi d'vivres of H.G.Wells, The fact that Victorians would have reacted so much differently to this technology. Shifting it both historically and geographically so that Americans could understand it just makes me wince. Why do filmmakers SO underestimate their audiences intelligence?

I despise Hollywood for messing with other peoples work. Maybe we should take an American Classic like "Gone with the Wind" and transpose it to 1980's Guy Ritchie's London. I think there would be a riot.

"Frankly my dear, I don't give a rat's arse."

title: Fascinating Jim but not as we know it ?
review:
Captain's log stardate 2548. We appear to have hit a time portal and are viewing the Earth in the year 2005. Spock is observing some film making from his magnification consul.

"Captain they seem to be making a film about alien invasion. The aliens have already been on earth for eons and yet are dying of disease. Quite illogical as they would have acclimatised during that time, also illogical is the selective way some of the earth electronics have ceased to function. Cars have stopped working but the ancient cam-corders operate?

The plot seems to revolve around a dysfunctional family. The father quite illogically seems to be trying to deal with family personal issues whilst the rest of humanity are blasted to pieces! It seems more of what they used to term 'Soap-Opera' than an adventure Science Fiction picture."

Sounds like an amateurish 'B' film Mr Spock what about the original references?

"Captain the story is based on a book from the early 20th Century Science Fiction writer H.G. Wells. There was a film made in the early 1950's. Then the invaders came from Mars and their Spaceships embedded themselves in the land. This version has the Space ships in the Earth for eons, ready to be activated."

So why then Spock did they not plan the invasion a hundred years earlier when there would have been less people and science?

"Good question Captain. I might add that the director of the film has been trying to educate the masses as to the existence of 'Alien' life forms over a number of years prior to 2005."

Fortunately or unfortunately he doesn't seem to be aware of Vulcans, only the 'greys' and other 'bug-like' creatures?

"Precisely Captain."

Tell me Spock what is the 2005 state of the Hollywood film industry?

"My computers indicate it is full of remakes of earlier films and film versions of popular TV series a few years before. The actors lack charisma and the industry is run by agents, lawyers and accountants. There appears to be no indication of creative activity. There is however quite an active 'old-boys' network."

Your prognosis Spock what is your prognosis?

"The future does not look good as the industry appears mired in has-beens and 'B' class wannabees."

Interesting Spock, interesting. I always wondered why that successful industry instead of going the 'Way of the West' went 'East'.

title: childish, inconsistent....but great special effects
review:
jvc2....I really appreciated your comments...and agreed.

A few more negative's you didn't mention.

Do you suppose Dakota Fanning might have been totally confused with her role?

She alternated between the insightful & clever sister/daughter, and the idiot that screamed & ran away at the worst possible moment, during the entire movie.

Didn't ANYONE wonder why a father with even a half-a-brain-cell in his body, would, during an alien attack on earth, would run the gauntlet between New York & Boston...just so his daughter & ex-wife could cry on each others shoulders ?

Yup, I must admit I was entertained, but not by the great script/directing/realism.....it was a pathetic comedy.

George Williams

title: Not HG Welles, Not Orson Wells, not even Kitty Wells
review:
This movie is far inferior to the original 1953 SiFi thriller, or even the 30s radio play.

First of all, it puts the emphasis on the personal troubles of Cruise and his kids, rather than the alien invasion. What is the bigger story here?! Secondly, it substitutes special effects for a decent script. Third, We are told nothing about who is invading -- Martians, Venusians, ET? Fourth, I guess the moral is to run and hide, and not fight back -- evidently the lord will provide. No that's not right, God isn't even mentioned until the very end. No one even prays during the entire destructive sequence. The one person who gets the idea to fight back is portrayed as a right-wing wacko. Liberal Hollywood at its best!!

title: I am going to demand my money back from the video store
review: I rented this stinker and shut it off after about 45 minutes. From the moment Tom Cruise makes his appearance as some blue collar jerk, they had lost me. Like Paul Newman trying to play a wiseguy in Road to Perdition, Tom just can't pull it off. The dialogue was so annoying I just couldn't stand it: the phony animosity between Cruise and his ex's new husband; the smart-alexy kids who say the stupidest implausible things in the midst of this world crisis; the idea that every vehicle in the world is shut down except a minivan Cruise decides to commandeer; the idea that all freeways are clogged but Cruise manages to sail down the road; the notion that only Cruise knows when something is about to explode; and that despite the ferocity of the attacks, good 'ol Tom always manages to stay one step ahead of collapsing buildings, etc. In fact when the destruction first starts and there is a kind of earthquake effect wherein the street starts to separate, why is it that all the spectators just stand around without even pretending to be in shock? Why should the cops have to tell them to "move back"? I was told by a co-worker that this film was shown as their in-flight movie and the entire planeload of passengers asked to have it shut off. The last straw for me was when Tom encounters a news crew near a crashed airplane whose entire mobile station works just fine. Oh, I forgot, at this time Tom had only traveled about a block from his ex's home where he had stashed his kids but when he gets back there they don't have a clue what's going on outside! With 747's crashing and burning and everything! Who needs syrup of ipecac when this garbage is around. At least the 1950's version was hokey without trying to be so darned cinematic. Special effects are not enough to save this crock.

title: What is this movie about?
review:
Extremely disappointing. What was Spielberg thinking of when he decided to make "another" aliens movie? "Close Encounters..." didn't have enough violence? "ET" had too much of a soap opera? Nowadays, if you plan to make a new action/drama picture based on aliens stuff, you need to make sure that you are not going to deceive your audience with a naive argument. Specially if your country is able to wipe off more than once every trace of life on earth without any need of goofy tripods.

If Spielberg would've put the movie in the thirties, maybe it would've had a chance to lose some of its goofiness. Because, whether he wanted to speak on peoples' chance to become heroes, he didn't succeed; whether he wanted to establish a milestone in digital effects, he didn't succeed. WOTW in this sense is completely forgettable.

Not everything is that bad anyway. Dakota Fanning's had a remarkable chance to demonstrate what the cool child actress she is.

review:
Great computer work. Crap story. Takes to long to get there and when they have a chance to save the story the machines turn out to be stupid. What, no heat sensors on the machines? we have them here? They rely on sound? Granted no sound in space but these were left here, on earth, unknown years ago, and there was heat. An advanced being would have known that.

They were killed by our diseases?! Iwont even go into the fact that they would have seen that before the 'beemed' there men down.

Sorry but I give it a 9 on CGI but a 4 on movie itself and the CGI can't save this piece. 4.2 overall.

title: A real disappointment from Spielberg...
review:
"War of the Worlds" has some brilliant sequences, and the long middle section of the film is alternately thrilling, suspenseful and even funny. But the beginning drags and the end is completely ludicrous, a concession to test audiences and an exercise in defeat for true fans of science fiction. Tom Cruise plays a character very much like...Tom Cruise, an abrasive, hyperactive man who behaves like a child. Charged with guarding his own children in the midst of an alien invasion, Cruise's character observes the goings-on from what is strictly an Everyman's point-of-view, and it was interesting to see a disaster film from this perspective. Cruise's character is no governmental leader or military figure; he does not pilot a ship into the belly of the alien beast, nor does he do anything of great significance during the movie apart from thinking quickly and acting decisively to save his family. The film takes a rather dim (and highly realistic) view of humanity as it shows people behaving in the worst way out of a sense of panic and impending doom. The sequence in which Cruise's character and his family is carjacked in the midst of a surging crowd is terrifying, more disturbing in its way than any sequence involving the alien invaders.

This film was shot on a film stock that echoes the grainy realism of a digital handy-cam. This has a twofold benefit: first, it helps blend the CGI aliens and their machines better into the "real" landscape around them. This film is virtually free of awkward green-screen edges and the effects look much more realistic than they do in similar films with a lot of computer-animated creatures. Secondly, the film's grainy stock echoes the footage captured during 9/11, and I think it was Spielberg's intent for that great tragedy to infiltrate this film so completely. Terrorist attacks are feared more than the aliens in the film, and sequences involving mass panic, jet crashes and the terror of ordinary life suddenly upended all invoke the events of September 11th. Moreover, the aliens shoot rays which incinerate their victims, transforming them into dust. As Cruise runs to escape the first alien onslaught, he becomes covered in ash and, upon arriving back at home, looks exactly like those who made it out of Ground Zero in New York. It serves as an interesting parable and helps make this update of H.G. Wells' classic sci-fiction story relevant to life in 2005.

As I said earlier, this film is flawed by a completely unnecessary ending. The middle sections of this film were executed with great technical mastery and interesting storytelling choices, but all that collapses during the final five minutes with an ending that feels so tacked-on, so unbelievable and shallow that it serves only to betray the audience in an effort to make sure everyone leaves the theater in a good mood. This is a flawed film, and it is very far from Spielberg's best.

title: almost there
review:
Although thanks to so many alien films spielberg manages to get the human side completely spot on (or at least the way one would imagine human reactions when faced with alien invasion) this film has one major drawback..

It's been holywoodified.. from the start it appeared as if the main character was more concerned with calming his daughter rather than, as in the novel, surviving..

the screaming kids don't really make me wan't to watch a film, and the whole "i'm 16, faced with vastly superior technology, and yet wan't to go to certain death to kill aliens.." is the last straw..

or rather would have been had the death been as certain as it was supposed to be.

more tragedy and less miracles and it would've been a very good film and fitting to both book and 1953 original film, ad it is it's just an overblown 9/11 homage in times where that need should be fading

title: If they gave an Oscar for biggest plot holes...
review:
this would be a front-runner. Also a contender for Worst Pacing. But it ends up with a four, since the action sequences did keep me tense and interested. I just lost a couple of minutes of concentration every time one of those staggeringly huge holes popped up.

I won't bother trying to list them, since so many others here have already done such a fine job.

I wish they'd skipped the whole "blood, cage and grenades" subplot and put that time into properly developing the ending. It didn't do a thing to advance the story, such as it was. That whole sequence was just empty meaningless horror-filler.

I'm not sorry I watched it, but am REALLY glad I got it from NetFlix!

title: Stylish, but too nihilistic
review:
From Jerry Bruckheimer, I would have thought this to be an inferior film. From Spielberg, its an outright disaster.

War of the Worlds is on par with Independence Day and that ludicrous Bruce Willis movie with the flying rock - big, ungainly loud moves that are still a financial success. It was easily the worst, and most disappointing film I saw in 2005.

As goes with Spielberg, it is expertly made and has flashes of brilliance all over. Some of its best moments are in the few quiet ones. But for 90 nearly endless minutes, it is simply Tom Cruise and company yelling, running and watching everything around them get destroyed. I have never experienced the onslaught of senseless, plot less death from a Spielberg film that I got from this one.

The ending has to be seen to be believed, and it is what elevates it from disappointing to downright bad. The script entirely forgets about the character of Tom Cruise's son, who seems to miraculously appear for the final scene. And miracle of miracle, the whole of the US eastern seaboard is annihilated, save for the block on which the mother of Cruise's children live.

War of the Worlds received a lot a press for being made in a short time span and it feels rushed and unfinished. It is purely and exercise in special effects, a not a very good one. *1/2 out of ****.

title: Not worth seeing not worth buying
review: This is without a dought the worst movie that has been based off the book "The War of the Worlds" that I have ever seen. Not only dose it betray the book but also the original movie made in the 50's which I think is much better dew to its plausible relationship with the book than this 2 hours worth of rubbish called a movie. The plot of the story is terrible the only thing that it has incomen with the book is that it has aliens in it and even they don't look like the ones described in the book also where the heck is the dialogue all the actors do is stare blankly at some one or at the floor and when there is dialogue it's simply a scream or 'Dad what's going on what are you doing' its like watching grass grow which seems to me far more enjoyable then this bag of air which by the end you find your self hating the characters especially the nagging no dialog character Dakota Fanning plays but also the characters father(played by Tom Cruise)who is to weak gutted to kill the people who tried to kill his kids. I understand that it can be hard to make a movie but they could have followed the book more closely then this lose fitting and a shamble of a movie they could of at least had the part where the war ship Thunderchild was destroyed while holding off the alien's so a boat full of people could escape to safety but no they just through together 2 hours of rubbish and called it The war of the worlds. The producers, writers and the director should team up and kick each other because they would have to be daffy to leave out such good material what the heck where they thinking. But hey I'm going to giving the movie the good end of the stick and will say see it for your self and make up your own mind but I think you will think after watching this movie that itis not worth seeing and not worth buying.

title: So where's the story?
review: This looked like $200 million spent on excellent special effects and 35 cents spent on a sad screenplay by a five-year-old. A terrible waste of so much talent but indicative of what drives Hollywood. It also very much reflects the obsession of Hollywood producers with relationships between divorced parents, young children and teenagers at the expense of other genres. HG Wells wrote an enduring sci-fi story that was exciting, with a plot, structure and battles, leading to a war and its conclusion. Spielberg treated us to psychotherapy angst and a series of dramatic explosions and scenes of destruction. If Wells had written the original in such a manner, it would have been forgotten decades ago.

title: Mostly Naff
review:
Dear god, when will Holly(crap)Wood stop making AMERICANISED versions of this story!! Why is this film called "WAR OF THE WORLDS" when a: it doesn't involve more than ONE WORLD, and b: bears NO resemblance to the original story? Spielberg, you are an ass. Though I commend you for taking a break from your crappy Holocaust movies.

Next, it's high time someone made a decent version of Well's classic, set in London in the 1800's, I realise producers think this would be commercial suicide in the U.S but I know for a fact a lot of people would love to see this.

*deep breaths* This film is deeply flawed, yes, but at it's heart is an OK no-brainer popcorn action movie. The action starts no less than 20 minutes in (why?) and basically the rest of the film revolves around Tom Cruise being an idiot, Dakota Fanning does nothing but scream and be annoying (WHAT is the fuss about with her?) and "Robbie" who is a grade A JERK.

The rest is predictable fare and certain little parts remind me of "Land Of The Dead" and a bunch of other Apocalyptic movies.

One good thing, the special effects, the tripods are great, as is the way they process the human bodies and spray offal and blood from their exhausts, I liked that.

title: Could Have Done Better!
review: I won't lie, the beginning of the movie shocked me! It was full of moments that made my jaw drop, there was non stop adventure & just from watching the beginning I knew I'd want to continue watching the rest of the film. Don't get me wrong, Tom Cruise is an incredible actor, he's talented, but his role did not quite fit his actual character too well. The movie did not do such a good job of establishing the overall point by the ending. I felt betrayed when the ending came because the beginning was so good that I felt the end had to be twice as good. I felt like the movie did not do a good job pulling all of the stunts and special effects together. When the movie was over, I was still sitting there expecting for the screen to show that jokingly the movie wasn't actually over yet, but that moment never came; just a list of credits flashed on the screen. This was one of those movies I would have watched even if it were 3 hours long because the plot was so complex, there was no way to get the whole point across in just an hour and a half. There better be a sequel.

title: cruel and angry
review: Tom Cruise usually lights up the screen for me (Last Samurai, The Firm, Far and Away) and his choice of characters is usually sympathetic. But his character in Spielberg's War of the Worlds was simply unappealing and even repugnant at times. It's too bad because the Spielberg/Cruise machine has the money and the man power to do just about anything they want to on screen. Even thought this made a heck of a lot of money it was far less successful than the original black and white version of the book, or even the 2005 version by David Latt, "HG Wells War of the Worlds". The main character in that had more heart and held more sympathy than Cruise even came close to in the Spielberg epic.

title: Tom Cruise is nutty off screen and now on screen
review:
So quickly this character is built, Ray Ferrier. There is no way you can be expected to respect him or even pity him. Hes wrong in all the ways a person can be wrong, not exactly leading role stuff and hardly the calibre for this sort of movie.

It is beyond belief that the plot manages to maintain itself with the senseless mentality Cruise's character has been designed with, pushing the rule that says the lead character cannot die. I wanted to reach into the movie and pull the trigger myself.

After enduring this, and being fed delicious samples of what was quite an exciting and well put alien invasion we are then supposed to go along with the idea that this guy is both lucky and when he needs to be, a contradiction of himself - suddenly a hero with all the right tricks. If there was to be a perceived development or thawing of relations between Ray and his son - then it was so poorly developed they need not have bothered.

Such an irony it seems that the character design reflects so much of what Tom Cruise has become offset (ie the man beyond the movies). Did Spielberg take a back seat and let Mr Cruise run things?

title: Where's the plot?
review:
The special effects were very good, but there's hardly any plot. The ending is abrupt and it almost seems like someone ran out of ideas and just decided to end the movie quickly because they'd reached the allotted elapsed time.

In my opinion, there should have been a lot more initial character and plot development prior to the aliens appearing. I don't think I've ever seen an apocalyptic movie such as this where the disaster occurs so soon after the start of the movie. Movie makers of "blockbusters" such as this should try to put as much effort into story telling, plot, and quality acting & screenplays as they do into special effects. Stories should be able to exist on their own without special effects and be just as entertaining. I will say, however, that this movie had a better screenplay, plot, and acting than the newest Star Wars movies. To me, the new Star Wars movies are classic examples of movies that suffered from too much special effects and not enough attention to story and acting quality.

title: No lessons learned from War of The Worlds.
review:
• No lessons learned from War of The Worlds.-


A million years ago, a far-more-intelligent & superior alien race buried thousands of death machines (huge Tripods) underground, which have remained undiscovered because they were apparently cleverly hidden "in-between" where all municipalities on Earth would ever lay water and sewer lines. Anyway, in 2005, members of this non-specific alien race return in the form of lightning-bolts to pilot the Tripods out of the ground. First, the Tripod monsters announce their presence with an unimaginative, steamboat-like "HOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOONK!" Then, they proceed to terrorize curious onlookers who must all be thinking, "Wow, a 900-foot gigantic, scary-thing just erupted out of the ground. I think I will get much closer and see if I can read the Industrial-Light-&-Magic copyright on its leg."

There are attempts to parallel the attacks from these gigantic-force-field-protected-alien-machines to terrorism, providing our first indication that Steven Spielberg REALLY needs a vacation.

The alien machines spend a good part of the movie disintegrating people, and conversely, another part of the movie harvesting people (to use as fuel?). I guess the aliens had no more idea of their purpose than then we, other than one obvious objective, which was to prevent Tom Cruise from getting his loudmouth daughter to Boston to reunite with her Mommy. Luckily, Mommy happens to be vacationing in the only neighborhood in the entire movie that remains protected from the alien's widespread destruction. Maybe it is an Historic district.

Of course, the movie looks and sounds great (except for the steamboat honk). The DVD's optional DTS (Digital Theater Systems) encoded soundtrack was crisp and powerful, providing deep, tight bass, clear voices, and provides a more accurate surround-sound experience than the standard Dolby Surround encoding. But, the impressive DTS surround-sound experience could not cure the film.

Do they make it to Mommy? Do they escape a thousand alien machines? Well, at a point seemingly chosen to help provide a profitable running time, the alien machines suddenly begin to die for no explained reason, but it is implied that the "far-more-intelligent, superior alien race" caught a cold. This allows Cruise to get his daughter to Mommy's. It also allows him to reunite with his angst-ridden teenage son, who somehow arrives there first, even though we saw him intentionally walk directly into a cataclysmic explosion an hour earlier.

So, the aliens die from a cold...like in the film "Independence Day." Oh, but wait, those were different aliens, and that was a "computer" virus. But why didn't THESE aliens learn any lessons from when they were here back in 1953? More importantly, why didn't Hollywood?

PK

title: Big Spoiler!
review:
This has to be the worst movie I have seen in a long time. So much is left to conjecture and speculation as witnessed by the responses to detractors of this waste of everything.

A lot of scenes are so terribly hacked together, it's either the result of pathetic editing, or because of a continuity supervisor intern. Many are so incongruent, they leave a, "Huh?" way too many times

title: No Thanks.
review: When this came out, I looked forward to seeing it, despite having Tom Cruise in it. But, I was pretty disappointed after watching it. What I expected was an updated version of the '53 movie. This was far from what I saw, and there were only a few things they had in common. I was disappointed with the added gore, the idea that the aliens already had killing machines buried in the earth, which had never been detected. And the machines were doing some kind of processing of the captured humans, then flooding the ground below with blood. was this necessary? And Tom Cruise? title: Good, True to Novel but Flawed Adaptation
review:
I always had a special place for "War of the Worlds" from when I read the novel in 5th grade and stayed up late to watch 1953 "The War of the Worlds". Recently, I re-read the novel, set in Edwardian pre-WWl England. The 1953 movie had it's flaws and tried to be upbeat in that noxious 1950's way where the novel was pessimistic about England and man in general. The 1953 film even had words of praise for the doomed British and their fighting spirit when the book had them melt into mass panic and selfishness after the first string of disasters.

What tripped up the movie was not Spielberg's pretensions or Tom Cruise's eternal pretty boy act but the actual plot and characters. Spielberg was trying to work a modern split family-stupid dad theme to it. You just couldn't respect the hero, Ray Ferrier crane operator(like a modern Fred Flintstone) He wouldn't even use some force to knock his two bratty, smart ass kids in line during the flight from NJ or intelligently stock up on necessities in flight. He was too common to admire; he was rebuilding his 69 Mustang's V-8 in his kitchen and his kids were like 30 points higher IQ and years ahead in sophistication. He was almost a serious Homer Simpson. Then, his great plan for the attack onm earthj, go from NJ across from Manhattan to BOSTON, MASSACHUSSETS! Why Boston, why would anyone want to get boxed in in Boston, as well as travelling a dangerous corridor to get there? Well, there is the plot line. His only concern, besides running to Boston, was to protect his daughter from any ugly sites by blindfolding her. His one heroic scene was accidental. What about the rest of humanity, Ray? Like your friends and the people you saved? Why not team up for survival and resistance like a man, instead of running like a mouse? The efx and the Martians were good and it was truer to the novel than the 1953 version. Obviously, Ebert never read the novel, with his ignorant comment on tripods. But the character in the novel was an intellectual who had no real plans, fled alone and was no great hero. In this flick, he was a blue collar scheisskopf. That is what really hurt it. Dakota Fanning needs to be phased out, her precocious little brat routine is getting stale, as she carried quite a bit of the movie. His son, Justin Chatwin, did better but he was another modern brat, but didn't suck up space like his stage sister. I gave it a seven due to good concept, efx, camera work, great scenes of the destruction of the Pulaski Skyway and I love WotW.

title: Fairly good, but some bad casting....
review: For the past hour about, I have been watching The War of the Worlds. Now I just can't get this off my chest... Tom Cruise does a fairly good job on this film, and is able to pull off a regular father caught in a crisis. The son does a good job too, pulling off just the right amount of teenage angst and acting into one. What makes this movie entirely unwatchable for me is Dakotah Fanning. Many of you that have watched the movie already know what I am talking about. Dakotah Fanning was the worst choice for the girl part in the movie. The only thing she seems talented at in this film is screaming at the top of her lungs about nothing. Now, this part was made to be kind of like that. But she doesn't pull off anything endearing, or something that would let viewers see the merit in her cries. All she manages to pull off is crying and screaming and, to be truthful, just being a little pain in the... Compare her to Drew Barrymore in E.T. and her other childhood movies. Drew carries a charisma makes her more likable for us. Dakotah can't seem to find that feeling anywhere, in any of her movies. I can't even watch the rest of this movie, because she ruins it so terribly. Do yourself a favor and go buy another movie besides this one.

title: Scary but ultimately unsatisfying
review:
I stumbled across a showing of this movie at a hotel, late at night, after the kids were in bed. Good thing--despite the PG-13 rating, this is NOT a movie you want your kids to see. Lots of scary special effects, and a relentless mood of despair that would give all but the hardiest thirteen-year-old nightmares for weeks.

For those who like to see neat CGI effects, this movie has lots of them--flying trucks, collapsing bridges, retro looking Martian walkers--this movie has got enough stuff to keep special effects fans happy. And for those who like to be scared, this movie will not disappoint either. Not a lot of explicit goo and gore, but bad stuff happening all over all the time.

Unfortunately, this film doesn't have much else to recommend it. Dakota Fanning, with little opportunity to be charming, spends most of this movie shrieking at the top of her lungs. Tom Cruise, as her deadbeat dad, is unconvincing and entirely unlikeable. His son, who wants to run off and see the aliens slaughtering the army--well, I would have let him go and told him not to come back even if he did live. Spielberg seems so intent on throwing together short set pieces that he has given up on trying to maintain a believable story line.

The worst flaw in this movie, however, is the utterly horrible ending. In H.G. Wells' original story, and in Orson Welles' radio broadcast, the death of the martians by lowly earthbound bacteria is an ironic but satisfying ending. In Spielberg's hands, however, it becomes a ridiculous deus ex machina that abruptly changes the tone of the movie from doom and gloom to "It's a beautiful morning." Cruise is suddenly reunited with his ex-wife (played by Miranda Otto, who mercifully gets to skip most of this movie), her family, and the son who ran off an hour ago to watch the martians splat New Jersey. You half expect to see Mr. Bluebird land on Tom's shoulder while a rainbow appears above the miraculously untouched brownstone where Miranda was hanging out.

All in all, not worth staying up to see.

title: Disappointing state-of-the-art cinema!
review:
I have always liked Spielberg's movies because they have always been hi quality productions, mostly. But I think he's lost the feeling... Spielberg has become a lazy director who make movies for a non-thinking audience. What he lacks is the details and depth in his stories and good acting performances.

I think the special effects were nicely made and I also felt that some of the scenes were quite strong for a Spielberg movie. I think of the fleeing people who get caught in the heat beams and vanishes. That was pretty strong I think. But the strongest scene in the whole movie in my opinion was when Rachel see the dead floating people in the river. That shot was not like Spielberg, that was brilliant stuff. Scary..

Otherwise this movie is way too short and it would have been better if it was half an hour longer. It felt way too rushed, too many questions left unanswered by the end of the movie. And do we need this laughable happy ending too? The world is burning up with millions of people been slaughtered and blood spurting all over the places, and what do we see at the end? Clean, well dressed-up grand-parents welcoming the hero and son-in-law. And the son can look at his father with great respect, he has proved that he's a real man. Outrageously bad!!! This movie is really not worth its price and I'm glad I downloaded it!

title: Very unoriginal.
review: There is no doubt that Steven Spielberg has given us some of the most important movies in history. Schindlers List, Jaws, Saving Private Ryan etc. But his movie only falls into what really is the Spielberg cookie cutter formula. His last movies fell in this trap and this one is no exception. Stupid father doesn't know how to take care of his kids, treats them like junk, trouble comes, then the father realizes how much he loves his kids and everyone smiles little rainbows of happiness. Now in this movie, the visuals are totally unoriginal compared to movies like ID4, or Men in Black, so nothing new here. There was no reason to include the character Tim Robbins plays. ( A rare flop for Robbins) and the ending, ( do not read if you have not seen it spoiler spoiler spoiler) is stupid. The aliens essentially die for no apparent reason, the son, whom we believe is dead turns out to be alive, (gosh how did I see that coming a thousand miles away?) and the whole family is reunited, THE END. Do not waste your time with this. Tom Cruise is not at his pinnacle of acting, (he rarely is, with the exceptions of Last Samurai and Born on the Fourth of July) and if you have watched even one Spielberg movie in the last two decades, you will be able to see everything coming a mile away. So don't waste your time with this.

title: Thank goodness for DVD and Fast Forward
review:
The War of the Worlds is a great book. For its time it was a tremendous leap in imagination; the story of humankind brought to its knees by a technologically superior alien invader told through the eyes of an unnamed observer.

The War of the Worlds (1953) was an interesting adaptation, re-locating the story to the USA and providing a slightly more human backdrop to the futility with which the human race battles the invaders.

The War of the Worlds (2005) is a great piece of commercial film making. It's the story of a dysfunctional family incidentally set against the backdrop of some sort of conflict. It allows the stars to show off their huge acting skills with lots and lots of close ups, oh and there are some special effects as well. It contains all the necessary commercial ingredients, two major box office stars, kids, and a heart-warming ending. Unfortunately it seems to have nothing whatsoever to do with telling the story of the War of the Worlds.

Please! I thought we'd stopped making star vehicles but obviously not. Fortunately I rented it on DVD and could skip the bits which were boring, mainly any time Cruise was on the screen, oops, that's 99% of the film!

Not even worth the rental.

It might sound naive ..but there are some questions about the whole story, such as..how come those Aliens devastate the whole planet in a few days..and then one simple morning their shields fail..and they suddenly lose their "war" against us? or, several events happen by magic, ( Ray's Son appears at the end of the movie out of nowhere-probably 'cause this way it the filmmakers would achieve the "happy ending" purpose of that film). The only thing that this film, achieves is to create this whole terror-panic-desperation atmosphere though it lacks of originality (plz remember those Panic Films back in the 70's). So we have a film that focus to the main characters (Ray and his children) leaving this whole Alien-invasion event work as the factor to their family issues they may have offering a family-conflict film than the movie that most of us expected to see. War Of The Worlds?? Don't Think so...

review: Yes well as summaries go, that wasn't overly helpful, I know. But let me expand a little. review:
That Hollywood can make pretty pictures is a given.

The Cruise flick is very much what it is supposed to be, visuals wise. And the cellar scene was suspenseful enough, while it lasted.

That said, Cruise is playing Cruise, and the only movie that he was bearable in recent times, was Magnolia, when he was basically parodying himself.

review:

title: intergalactic road show of antique clichés
review:
A few years ago, Stephen King's alien-takeover novel "Dreamcatcher" was transformed into a feature film, meeting with as much success as a 900-page novel condensed to a 2-hour run time could. As a whole, it was uneven, but not without ambition, a brisk pace, and well-drawn characters. This kind of low expectation is quite unusual for a filmmaker of Steven Spielberg's caliber and a screenwriter of David Koepp's skill (ironically, he gave us last year's underrated King adaptation, "Secret Window"); to combine these two talents for a summer-ready adaptation of H.G. Welles' "War of the Worlds" must have sounded ideal on paper, and with Tom Cruise leading the cast, how could it possibly fail? I don't know what's more bothersome--that the summer movie season has passed with very few memorable entries (save for "Land of the Dead" and "Charlie and the Chocolate Factory"), or that a film as hollow as "War of the Worlds" is still playing after all this time. Though I suppose its success is no mystery as far as escapist fantasy is concerned--Spielberg's and Cruise's name recognition aside, it is a film that delivers exactly what audiences want--big, fantastic spectacle pixellated with elastic-looking CGI effects. But that's not the problem--I have voluntarily put my brain on the shelf for many summer senses-obliterators (I even enjoyed "The Rock," for Christ's sake) that jettisoned plot and character in favor of rapid-fire action and thrills..."War of the Worlds," however, is such a stilted, empty experience that even the sight of tripods towering over cities and reducing scampering earthlings to ash loses its bite well before the film is over.

In a bit of opening narration that seems lifted from a '50s B movie, it is revealed that "unsympathetic" aliens are gearing up for an attack on our planet because they're so darned jealous of our "advanced" ways (though watching this movie in advance might have saved them the trouble). This setup is about all the 'plot' we get, thus allowing Spielberg free reign to indulge special effects for the remainder of the film. We are introduced to Ray (Tom Cruise), a divorced, blue-collar dock worker who is given the kids for the weekend--Robbie, the ersatz-rebellious son, and Rachel (Dakota Fanning), the endlessly screeching, wild-eyed daughter. His ex-wife is pregnant with #3 and married to a well-dressed, clean-shaven #2. Cruise's house, intended to reflect his 'neglectful father' persona, is messy and cluttered, with a refrigerator full of spoiled food. After some teeth-gnashingly clichéd 'bonding time' with his children, we witness a bizarre electrical storm that stops all magnetic devices (but has no effect on digital cameras!), followed by an introduction to the tripods that is admittedly awe-inspiring.

Unlike "Signs," where a martian invasion didn't overwhelm the human story, and in a way became an extension of it, "War of the Worlds" insists on cramming 'family values' down our throat. Sure, those aliens are nasty buggers, but the story is really about a Father Trying To Better Himself In The Face Of Impending Doom, and the triteness of this is not helped by an unconvincing Tom Cruise (who is driven to murder at one point) or Dakota Fanning's shrill daughter (she serves as a great argument against procreation, however). Tim Robbins shows up halfway through in a pointless role that echoes his "Mystic River" shtick, but gives Cruise an opportunity to show some Fatherly Courage. When son Robbie inexplicably heads into the military mêlée on a hillside, only to show up without a scratch at film's end, is an infuriating, cheap (and illogical) attempt to milk some feel-good tears. In a film where we're left staring at the increasingly uninteresting tripods or the sappy familial drama, we quickly run out of things to hold our interest (when, in the best-case scenario, all aspects of a movie should envelop the audience completely) and devolve into a chorus of "Is it over yet? Is it over yet...?" At least in "Mars Attacks!" the badness of the overall product was part of the fun. In "War of the Worlds," we are asked to suspend disbelief as the tripods descend a hillside toward a farmhouse where Robbins, Cruise, and Fanning are hiding. Why it seems to take days for the tripods to arrive is anyone's guess. More questionable is why the martians, who level cities without a second thought, inspect the farmhouse with a tentacled 'eye' and snoop around the basement where our heroes are hiding--in addition to them looking for antiques to sell on the intergalactic market, the answer is obvious: the scene kills some time, and allows our handsome protagonist to keep living (this can also be applied to Cruise's uncanny skill in avoiding the path of lasers during the opening attack). After all, nobody--the producers most of all--wants a bankable star like Tom Cruise to be felled by martians, unless it's in a softly-lit, dramatic sequence that might earn a nod from The Academy.

To his credit, Spielberg busily dresses scenes with lots of visual flair, as if to compensate for the clunky script, but his efforts aren't enough (the film looks grimy and unappealing). Also, the constant references to 9/11 and terrorism come off as a cheap attempt to lend the story some modern-day relevance (it worked a lot better in "Land of the Dead," man). Though "War of the Worlds" has moseyed toward a generous box office take, it's a hollow ride, with thrills that aren't thrilling, characters that inspire no sympathy, and visual ingenuity that inspires more yawns than gasps. By the end, I was nostalgic for the cinematic junk food of "Dreamcatcher," "Signs," "Mars Attacks!" and "Independence Day"... Okay, maybe not "Independence Day," but you get the idea...
