title: A cliché ridden disasterpice, but surprisingly entertaining
review:
I decided that I would not go to the cinema to see this film (I use the term 'film' in its loosest possible sense) based on my principles as a lover of the novel. However, I was not going to pass up the opportunity to see it when a free ticket was given to me by a friend.

In order to salvage any kind of enjoyment from this trashy flick, one must first get over the initial shock of how Spielberg has raped Wells' visionary classic.

The logic-less plot wrestles with the bizarre idea that the Martian war machines have been buried under the earth since the dawn of man. Which begs the question that if man has advanced so much technologically since the time we were throwing rocks at one another to prove masculinity, why have the Martians not invented more efficient ways of laying waste our planet and destroying our way of life?

When the movie begins, we are 'treated' to several scenes of Tom Cruise's home life, we find out that the protagonist is not a writer, nor is he middle class, he and his wife are separated and they have children together. Cruise's character swaps the quill for the hard hat; one can only assume this is to make the philistines that the movie is aimed at feel as though they can relate to the hero in some kind of pathetic way.

Once the Martians land however, the film starts to look up, first they eliminate our technology with E.M.P then they attack us. A tripod raises itself from under the earth and emits its death cry, this is the first time you hear "the voice of the Martians." This scene, although impressive, is fatally flawed. We learn quickly that all battery operated erm. Things, have been wiped out (even Cruise's watch) yet when the first of the fighting machines appears we see someone standing around filming it on his video camera. Silly enough for you yet? You would think so, but sadly it's about to get a whole lot sillier. The genius Martians, who (as we later are told) have been planning this invasion for centuries, decide to use the most inefficient method of extermination ever put to film. They unleash their heat ray on individual humans fleeing the scene. Hats off to the screenplay writer for that little gem. However, there are many positive thing about this scene and subsequent others. As much as I did not wish to enjoy the film, one cannot deny that it is an awesome visual spectacle. The special effects are truly stunning; they may well be the best I have ever seen. I must also confess; that the first time the Martians 'spoke' from within their machines, I was amazed, so amazed in fact, that I came shockingly close to soiling myself.

I enjoyed every action scene in this film. I especially like the part where a huge crowd of people trying to board a boat in order to escape the carnage are suddenly thrown into massive panic when a fighting machine appears in the distance. True Spielberg suspense reminiscent of 'Jaws!'

One aspect where Spielberg has failed to live up to his previous films was the pitiful attempt at adding a human angle to the film, luckily, this is ended quickly with some killing and lots more explosions lovely.

The verdict

Pros

Martian Voice.

Amazing Special Effects.

Suspenseful.

No Cheesy Destruction of Famous Landmarks.

Red Weed.

Homage To The Original. (Hand Crawling Out Of The Craft After Death.)

Cons

Dreadful Script.

The Martians Looked Like Pocket Dragons.

Badly Edited. Martians Were Suddenly Dying After A Handling Machine Scene.

Tom Cruise.

The Ending, You Must Be F***ing Joking!

Script 7/20  Some very good lines like "there's no more of a war between us than there is a war between men and maggots" but largely poorly structured.

Visual Effects 19/20  almost flawless, but the Martians themselves were very CGI looking.

Character Development 1/20  Cruise became a better father, that's it! It wasn't handled well either.

Thought Provocation 2/20  completely stripped the story of all social and political comments.

Entertainment value 17/20  annoying scenes with Tim Robbins nearly ruin the movie, other than that, I was massively entertained.

I enjoyed this Movie. It is important that I refer to it as a movie and not a film, as it was a piece of entertaining garbage and had nothing to say. The special effects were wonderful and the action scenes were so entertaining that I no longer cared about how terrible this movie was when compared to the novel.

7 out of 10 Great Movie. Rubbish Film.

title: Motive vague or absent.
review: Overall I must say WOW ranks high on the special effects. I wasn't disappointed with the machines. I must confess, the first WOW, starring Gene Berry(circa early 60's), ranks higher on plot and character development. The machines in the older version (considering the time period) looked more menacing. My big question ... "Why did they invade?" I either slept through it or they simply forgot to put it in. Second question ... "Why wait until mankind had technology (neuclear)that might come close to defeating them?". The older version clearly establishes this early in the film. The older one establishes a sense of urgency to their invasion. The newer one seems to say they were in no hurry. I would recommend getting the older version from someone to better understand the newer's weakness in this respect. On the upside, I am elated the script wasn't 'sanitize'. Seems as though any references to God these days are 'verboten'(forbidden).

title: Average
review:
OK, I'm no film buff, just a normal person who went to go see the movie. I have not seen the old movie nor read the book .I love my Sci-Fi's, so when a big budget movie hits the screen I was licking my lips.

This movie is a tale of two halves. The First half was very good, the special effects of the aliens arriving and bursting through the ground was excellent. There were some questions floating around in my head but the special effects were keeping me going. I kept out certain flaws in my mind because I was trying to stay in the moment.

The second half, I'm afraid to say, that, as the pace died down I had burning questions in my head that were never answered. The special effects were not carrying me anymore. I needed more information; I needed to know why the aliens were there etc etc..

The ending, I was hoping for a whopper, but was left with a complete flop! I'm the type that likes a movie to climax and you can reach a sense of finality. Sadly, you are left with more questions than answers, and a cheesy ending to boot.

In summary, if you like your sci-fi to end with an epic battle, a triumph of good over evil. Nope you are not going to get it. The special effects are great in the beginning, but there are no new effects that come into play, so that become a bit stagnant too. Plot, No. Heroic Characters, No. An average sci-fi watch that will be filed as 'Not the best I've ever seen'

title: Justice for Wells.
review:
Spielberg has finally done it. He's corrected the mistakes of the 1953 cinematic disappointment of HG Wells' vision. Granted the film does break from the novel in a number of places and updates the timeline for today. Months ago, I was disappointed from the teaser trailers that the film would not take place in the same era as the novel, and it bothered me up until the breathtaking moment when I watched the tripod rise out of the devastated cityscape in all its three-legged glory. Awe struck by the spectacular visuals, my fears were quickly laid to rest. Whether in the late 1800s or early 2005  it doesn't matter.

War of the Worlds is timeless.

It's a testament to the genius of Wells how well (no pun) the tripod designs stand up to modern era alien-invasion ships. The city-sized frisbies in Independence Day could cast ominous shadows as it hovers. "Yay." The martian War Machines, by contrast, had a dynamic movement that was interesting to watch as it defied the laws of physics with its surprisingly graceful steps. The ever-moving tentacles and the deadly heat ray had me on the edge of my seat longing to see them in action again and again, but Spielberg wisely refrained from going into overkill. Top it off by associating a mechanical "roar" with the walking death machines to play with the power of suggestion later on, and you have yourself a recipe for suspense.

Hitch would be proud.

Moving on to the characters: strangely, I didn't like the characters (any of them) at first. By the end of the film, I still didn't really like them all that much, and yet I still cared for them. The characters weren't idealistic, they weren't heroic, they didn't have very many redeeming traits, and it created this sense of reality around it. Spielberg presents a family with problems, depicting the family life behind closed doors - the arguments and behavior that the outside world, the neighbors, and friends never hear about. The family life we never lead in the presence of company, and the film never really takes time to try and resolve the family issues either (Thank you Spielberg.) This creates some interesting paradoxes. For one, when I don't like a character I typically can't connect with them yet here I did. And two, while I didn't like the characters, I adored the details about their relationship to one another such as children who would rather get the weekend visit out of the way then spend time and connect with their parent, children who really don't want to resolve their issues, a father who frustrated that he's losing his kids and his feeble and selfish attempts to win their love. So bitter, and so true. The family portrayed by Cruise, Fanning, and Chatwin is of genuine human beings with dark sides.

We get to explore the characters flaws, their dark sides, and we really don't get a chance to see life outside their darkest moments. These people don't have time to be epic tale archetypes or change the world, they're just trying to survive.

Spoiler - Unfortunately, War of the Worlds has a finale that screams "screen tested with a G-rated Disney audience." It has an ending that leaves a serious stain on the overall viewing experience. It must be nice knowing that if you're the main character in a movie, nothing bad will happen to you or your family despite the alien invasion that threatens to wipe out humanity  that no matter how bad things look, there'll be a reunion at the end of the movie and even the little dog fluffy will show up safe and sound, and the birds will chirp, and we'll pan up to a blue sky, and the world will sing "Kumbaya." Martians just decimated the earth's population, is it really too much to ask for one character to stay dead? Why not have 3 billion people rise up out of their ashes and be okay too? Why discriminate?  End Spoiler.

While flawed, War of the Worlds is still an epic experience with very human characters, and special effects that possess more wonder, more scale, and more excitement than Revenge of the Sith. If history has taught us anything, it's that the imagination of HG Wells not only can transcend mediums with maximum potency, but it will forever awe the audiences of each new generation. It was true of the novel, it was true of the Orson Welles radio broadcast, it was true with the Invisible Man and the Time Machine novels, and now it's true of Spielberg's film.

title: Horrible continuity errors
review:
They've messed with H.G. Wells, and have thus messed with the best. I, for one, am incredibly surprised Spielberg signed on to a project with this many continuity errors.

1) The EMP knocks out every electronic device, from car ignitions to watches, yet a bystander is recording it all ON VIDEO CAMERA! Also, the sink works when Ray washes all the people dust off of him? Hmm, water pumps and the mainframe for the water system would be COMPUTERIZED. And when he and Rachel finally arrive in Boston, the city lays in ruins, yet his ex-wife and her parents have had showers recently? 2) These aliens are advanced enough to bury machines ahead of 21st century technology millions of years ago, but can't rely on anything more than a camera to find people? No biosensors? C'mon! 3) There are United States soldiers in the basket thingies under the machines. One of the primary objectives for American POWs is to attempt escape. These men are sent up fully armed, yet it takes a dock worker to realize that grenades can go up that anus thing?

The special effects are quite good, as is the editing. It's a toss-up: pay the $9 to see the FX on a big screen, or wait until it's on DVD. Either way, the errors will bug you.

title: The end of the Worlds
review:
Three things particularly puzzled me about *War of the Worlds*.

One is the strange chronology of events. As the film opens, the first inkling of anything amiss are a few reports on the news of power outages in Ukraine. When the tripod emerges in New Jersey, there is no reason for us to think that any have yet struck elsewhere. And yet within just a few hours, we hear people talking about battles around the world as if they have been going on for weeks: and this when all sources of communication are supposedly down.

The second puzzle is what the purpose of Tim Robbins is. This is a larger philosophical issue, not a casting query.

The third is how Spielberg and the scriptwriters ever thought they could get away with the ending. Why does the boy need to survive when all plot logic dictates that he should be dead or missing? It shows such total contempt for the audience that I'm staggered Spielberg ever let it cross his mind, let alone film it and put it in the final cut.

title: Definitely not a classic.
review:
Steven Spielberg's War of the Worlds remake can only be described as a letdown. After all the hype there is nothing but a flawed endeavor in which the dazzling ILM special effects dominate. There is a cast of hundreds, but they're all technicians unseen by the camera.

According to the plot, the Martians buried their war machines on Earth about a million years ago in preparation for it's conquest. Why not take the world then, before man even existed rather than wait a million years?

This film also reinforced my belief that just because Tom Cruise is in a movie, doesn't mean it will be enjoyable or well made. Most of his on screen time is spent yelling at his family members. We're stuck in one long domestic disturbance.

Josh Friedman's and David Koepp's screenplay is so weak and unoriginal they borrowed lines from the original 1953 release. Anyone remember "Once they begin moving, no more news comes out of that area"? If you think you've heard it before, you have. Cute, but hardly original.

Viewing the 2005 remake only makes the 1953 original seem all that much better. Byron Haskins iron fisted directorial style kept one on the edge of their seat throughout. Despite half century old technology and flawed science the 1953 version is more frightening, entertaining and riveting. The war machines are more original, futuristic and high tech compared to Spielbergs clumsy, clanky, stumbling tin cans, which signal each other with foghorns.

Spielbergs heart simply wasn't in it. He's admitted to almost abandoning the project after the release of Independence Day, which more mirrors the 1953 original. Maybe he should stick to dinosaurs. However, credit where credit is due. Dakota Fanning's performance was probably the best of all involved. The special effects are unbeatable. I've never seen buildings collapse, highways cave in or freeway overpasses turn to rubble more realistically. Unfortunately special effects do not a movie make.

title: Terrible acting, characters are absurd
review: Two words "Gar bage". It's as though each seen was shot a month apart with no reflection of the last. I found that even my 9 year old daughter was pleading out loud for the actors to recollect 5 minutes ago. Justin Chatwin may be the worst actor in Hollywood. If this kid ever gets another role the director should be ostracized. The whole relationship IE father/ son and father/daughter was so forced even Tom came out looking like a B movie actor. As for the daughter, well by no fault of her own the script wasn't sure if she was an old sole and could give advice to her father or a whiny little baby. Oh yeah, Crane operators at a ship yard make very good money, yet Cruise can't afford tivo or his sons school, come on! This movie was the biggest disappointment this summer. The only reason I gave it a 3/10 is because the special effects were decent, thats it.

title: Weathered and Unimpressive
review:
The movie came with two big names: Spielberg and Cruise, which usually means the much deserved title of BLOCKBUSTER. Not in this case. The movie was nothing short of a waste of money.

While there were certain limitations with the creative aspect to the storyline - due to its predecessors, there were areas that could have been drastically improved upon. The technology used in the film is akin to that of the 70's. Nothing spectacular, yet unsurprisingly similar to many past SCI-FI movies, like Close Encounters of the Third Kind. It leaves the movie-goer with the cheated feeling of having seen it all before. Additionally, the manner in which the movie ended was rushed and cramped. There were many elements left unexplained that were shoved down the movie-goer's throat within the last 5 minutes of the movie.

In regards to the acting, Tom Cruise was once able to provide stellar performances, but seems to have lost his touch. His performance was abysmal, and thus he takes on the role of Supporting Actor - at best. His acting job is flawed and flat, leaving MUCH to be desired. Dakota Fanning, on the other hand is the only redeeming quality of the movie. She presents a riveting performance that gives the movie some credit... if only temporary, as it is not enough to carry the heavy weight of this movie.

Had Spielberg and Cruise improved their performances, the movie may have moved closer to a BLOCKBUSTER instead of the dregs of filmography. The only reason why the movie made so much money, is due to the preceding popularity of Spielberg and Cruise. It just proves that anyone with a popular name can produce poor quality movies and still make millions.

title: Godd movie with some bad spots
review: While this invention of WOW is more along the lines of HG Wells's book and the tripods along with the red weed and the use of human blood as fertilizer for the weed which is their food (while in the book blood was their food, and the weed was just that an alien weed). The Short lived T.V. series also touched on the aliens need for blood (but for different reasons) and the fact that they were not actually martians but only used Mars as a staging area. The idea that they had buried their tri-pods on earth millions of years ago is a bit of a stretch and would have done better if they had followed the book and the 53 movie in that they came to Earth via a meteor storm. It also failed in the scientific area as not attempt was made to address the aliens as was done in the book and the 53 movie. This movie would have been better if it was maybe 45 min longer and added more of the elements of either the book or the 53 movie. But over all the special effects were good and just about the only good thing from this movie. The acting by Mr. Cruise was so flat I was wondering if he was even trying to act or was sleep walking. (maybe his Scientology has depriving him of his humanity). He seems to do less acting and relies more on FXs. The acting was well done by Dakota. The story could have been well done except that there were far to many missing elements.

title: My Two Cents on War Of the Worlds...
review:
...ended up costing me $8! Ugh -- despair! A monumental failure masquerading as a top grossing film, W-O-W is far from WOW-ing anybody. Talk about begging the word "contrived". A true fall-de-grace, if there ever was a word -- Seriously, did Tom Cruise really have to LIVE? For the love of Christ, if a movie ever had to create every opportunity for a dead-beat character to survive every possible life-threatening situation without having to really DO anything to merit his survival, the script writers of this film have demonstrated just that. Does the weird basket of captured people, including Tom and Dakota, really have to fall into a conveniently placed tree softening the blow of perhaps a fractured arm or leg? Surely the writers couldn't afford to excite me with a broken neck. I would do anything for Tom Cruise's foot to be vaporized and have him limp across the streets, scurrying away from a bunch of overgrown tripodal metal eyeballs. Ahh... a LAMAO moment.

True, we can all agree that a story originally written for a Victorian audience cannot incite the same reaction of surprise and awe from a more scientifically advance generation of viewers. Perhaps it would have done me some good to don a bonnet and corset and throw comments at the screen with my refined, but fake nonetheless, British accent. Would that have helped? Probably not. For the sake of keeping true to form, I will give the movie a C-.

I will not say I did not find a few moments that excited me. To watch a mass herd of humans running like wildebeast, getting zapped left and right, disintegrating into poofs of dried carbon did bring some good old fashioned comedy to the screen. Oops! Was I supposed to be scared? Sorry. OK, lets say the sheer magnanimity of the damage did concern me. Where do we put all the dead people now? Oh I forgot, they were poofed.

Obviously, I will not spend a penny on renting the DVD. Neither will I exhaust a single brain cell in containing this movie in my memory banks. It will be a another thing I conveniently forget -- Which is why I documented this online, just to prove to myself that it did suck.

Alfred Hitchcock (love of my life) where are you when we need you???

title: Big Budget waste of time and talent
review:
Just because something is "only a movie" doesn't mean that the filmmaker gets a free ride in terms of making the not conceptually and logically believable. It also means that every film needs a real plot. This took H.G. Wells classic and turned it into a series of horror incidents, cute shots, and cool but unemotionally grabbing special effects. There was no real terror, no at the edge of your seat wondering what was happening, no people trying to combat the aliens (or find away to keep people safe from them). It wasn't even clear how many actual alien breeds there were -- I thought only one while my companion was convince there were "biguns'" and "littleuns'." The only thing this film really had going for it was Morgan Freeman's wonderfully spelling binding narrative ability.

THE SPOILER of the thing that completely and irrevocably spoiled it for me:

Just like in the original (and the earlier film and Orson Welles radio classic) the aliens die because they are allergic to the microbes (bacteria) that are found everywhere on earth especially in the water that covers over 75% of this planet. In the earlier versions this made sense because the aliens came from outer space and had never interacted with any of the life on this planet. But Spielberg decided it would be cool to put the destroying tripods below the ground so they could tear up city streets as they ascended. To do this means that the aliens must have sent at the very least some sort of probes to earth at least tens of thousands of year before. Maybe even tens of millions. No species with a shred of intelligence is not going to verify down to the last detail that the planet that they covet can, in fact, sustain their life forms. It's like not checking the thermometer and putting on a windbreaker to take a stroll in the middle of winter in Alaska! The microbes that these aliens were allergic to have existed on earth since the beginning of life.

It boils down to a bunch of technologically advanced species who are idiots in real life. Maybe this film was meant as a commentary on the world today. Maybe they just wanted to have fun with cool effects and spooky stuff. Maybe the only thing this film has proved is that Dakota Fanning is in the same league as Shelley Duvall as someone who can continually be terrified throughout an entire film and not annoy you very much.

Wait for the DVD  but only if someone else lends it to you and you have absolutely nothing better to do.

title: Not As Good As The Book or The 50's Original Film
review:
Having read H.G. Wells novel and seen the 50's version, I was initially thrilled about watching this movie. The trailers for the film looked quite good, though I was not excited about Tom Cruise as the lead. I am still not content with his part in the movie. After the movie, I was very disappointed. The movie is mostly heavy in the special effects department and cinematography, but lacks emotional impact and character development. Tom Cruise as deadbeat dad Ray (he doesn't know his daughter is allergic to peanut butter since birth and doesn't have food in his home, always insisting they order food instead). Dakota Fanning as his daughter. The text from the novel is narrated by, and this is a guess, Morgan Freeman. The plot of the original 50's version is taken to our present time. Some things were changed. The aliens have buried their tripod destroyers underground millions of years ago and now are landing on earth via lightning storms and driving the tripods to exterminate humanity. But bacteria and the earth's environment proves to be too much for them to handle and failing to adapt, they die. Nevertheless, unlike the book or 50's version, which contains messages of hope, this movie in its length attempts to suggest the aliens have won and all is lost, there is no hope for mankind. Tom Cruise despairs along with the rest of us as we see a world driven by fear and panic. It may also appear that the aliens are substitutes for the new threat: terrorism. At one point the little girl Dakota Fanning plays asks "is it the terrorists ?". Memories of 9/11 and terrorist attacks worldwide are present in the film. Yet, there is no mention of God or religion. A church is blown up early in the film. But for all the gloom and doom, no one prays or even mentions God. I thought this was because of Tom Cruise's Scientology background or perhaps some of the other actors or because it was not Steven Spieldberg's thing. In the original 50's version, much of the last portion of the film takes place in a Church as people shelter themselves there hoping God will save them. It's a very disturbing and frightening film that will send chills down your spine. I thought it was OK for what it was, but War of the Worlds as it ought to be.

Special effects is the true draw to this film. The aliens look a lot like the typically sci-fi aliens we expect to see. There is no parallel to 1995's Independece Day at all, as humanity cowers in fear and doesn't fight with such patriotism for mankind as they did in ID4. Some of the film is confusing. Why do the aliens spray blood all around the ground as if it were fertilizer ? Why do they want human blood ? Is it because they hope that by consuming human blood or DNA they will be able to live on earth, an alien planet to them, successfully ? Why was it necessary to deceive the audience into believing Ray's oldest son had died only to see him alive and well at the end of the film. Also, his wife, whom he is separated or divorced with, comes back after only a little intro to her at the beginning of the film. One would think she died too. It has very little development. It's not that bad in the long run but I'm very particular and picky about what makes a movie great. This one is only so-so. Read the novel or see the original 50's version, which is a cult classic of sci fi and a sample of 50's film nostalgia- at that time the aliens were substitutes for Communists. Now the threat is terrorism.

title: Closer to Independence Day than HG Well's vision
review:
OK I was persuaded to go and see this movie, even though I'm not much of a Spielberg fan (I always find him a bit juvenile, ever seen a young kid die in one of his films??). I also studied Wells at University and know the original text pretty well, as well as the climate under which it was written.

Now, my first obvious gripe was, like a lot of Hollywood movies, something English is misappropriated and transplanted to America. It is also updated to the present day. Having said that, if you throw god knows how many millions of dollars at something maybe you have the right to do whatever you like...

Don't get me wrong, there's nothing that sucks too much about this movie, what I didn't like was the bastardization of Wellsian ideas. Tim Robbin's character is a mish-mash of The Artilleryman, The Curate (wearing a wedding ring around his neck rather than a cross though!!!) yet is called Ogilvy, who is the astronomer at the beginning of the story.

The War Of The Worlds is in amazing novella written in the 1890's (very short - so no excuses) that predicts the massive destruction and urban desolation of the First World War, the fall of the British Empire, biological warfare, extraterrestrial life and space travel, the decline of orthodox religion, light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation (laser to you and me) etc etc (I could go on) and of course, most notably, taps into the new Darwinist ideas of the time concerning evolution (martians described as evolved humans, just heads and hands). Women and children die horribly, it's dark, scary, adult; all the things which ultimately this movie were not.

Yet I gave it a chance, treating it as a modern and very loose rendering of the story - the machines didn't quite look right but the height of them was spot-on and the heat-ray fairly accurate. Then the martians themselves appeared, and any suspense that had been generated up to that point disappeared. In a lot of ways Wells' vision is a satire, the martians (as evolved humans) are disgusting loathsome blobs with flailing tentacles who are sluggish under the Earth's atmosphere (somehow Wells worked out that the Martian atmosphere is considerably lighter than that of Earth), relying on their machines (Wells anticipating couch potatoes of today?).

What does Spielberg come up with? Something too humanoid, too lithe, too small, malevolent e.t.'s perhaps but a million miles away from what Wells was saying - they are just as agile on this planet and just not repugant enough, not terrifying at all.

So I left the theatre predictably disappointed that the name of Herbert George Wells had been attached to something significantly less than the sum of its parts, whereas the original novella is so much more. Do yourself a favour - instead of paying a few quid or dollars to go and see this film, buy the book.

title: H.G. Wells, a century ago
review: But Aye me, no more in the 21st Century. What was once a major piece of Sci-Fi achievement is no longer working. It is neither a great nor an entertaining movie. A girl in the theater said that "even Deep Impact was better" I might not go that far, but without a doubt, better rend ID4 and delight with entertainment rather than spend your 8 bucks on his badly aged story. Tom Cruise as a Byronic hero? maybe, but not here, and now. He's getting back his wife's esteem, his kids' love, and where everybody died he and his kids survive (ah, it's good to be the hero...) so no, not even Byronic. Has he learned something, except that anti-heroism pays?? And what about this pro American anti terrorist ridiculous voice over ending... well I'm speechless. Please, go and watch the first hour and a half. Once they lose the car, lose your seat, go home and watch ID4.

title: Very average
review:

The first three quarters of the movie were great but then the movie just seemed to end. I know they were trying to stay true to the original but I would have thought they could have made a bit more of an attempt at and ending rather than it just end.

I left feeling incredibly disappointed and certainly won't be buying it on DVD.

One other thing - the young girl is THE most annoying thing I've ever encountered in a movie

title: Spielberg needs a producer
review: SPOILERS AHEAD After a very promising first act, with a well written and well played family situation, pix shows a constant disrespect of the audience : it is just a succession of scenes which were, in all likelihood, imagined long before a script was written. Then, writing it was just a matter of splicing these scenes one after the other, with no effort whatsoever for payoffs, drama, character logic nor character development. Tom Cruise sees the earth cracking and opening under his very feet ? Good scene, except that he has two kids waiting anxiously for him at home, and instead of spending his lunch hour hoping to see whatever monster comes out, he should already be running for their lives. Tom and kids end up in ex-wife's house where Tom shows that he doesn't even know how to spread peanut butter on a slice of bread Good scene, except that they're starving, and forget that there's certainly a fridge in there with goodies in it! (has the thunderstorm turned off their brains as well ?) Incidentally, they don't know what's going on around the country, but don't even think about turning on the TV set! Still incidentally, an airplane crashes on the lot, destroys everything BUT Tom's car! Tom torn between getting to his son and reaching for his daughter good scene, but what does it reveal ? What are the consequences ? None, as he doesn't make any choice : his son makes the choice, and survives it anyway (how ? God knows ; do you, Spielberg ?). Tom and family in their car, caught in a mob frenzy good scene, but what does it reveal ? How does it enhance or develop the character ? And what are the consequences ? None, as they reach the ferry in time anyway, like all the others, and the ferry capsizes anyway with the cars that made it on board. Tom meets a woman he knows in the crowd as they're about to board the ferry Not even a scene, but a happening. This encounter reveals nothing of Tom's character, nothing of the woman's character except that she has a daughter Nora and that they're written to die, something we don't care about as they're not " alive " anyway. Tom feels that Tim (Robbins) is a danger as he may draw the aliens attention, so he decides to kill him Promising situation, except that he's not thinking for an instant that he could be the one to get killed, leaving his daughter all by herself! So he kills Tim, but it's to absolutely no avail anyway as, a few minutes later, the alien's snake eye is back and this time catches them ! Good thing Tom knows how to use a grenade, which means that someone who doesn't know how to spread peanut butter knows how to spill guts. What a character revelation. So the guy probably spent time in Irak or Mogadiscio. And Tom finally makes it to Boston where ex-wife and ex-in laws look like they were having a nice Sunday lunch while the whole world was collapsing  and where Tom sees that his long lost son is safe and sound, and made it (how ? God knows Spielberg doesn't) to the Sunday lunch despite having been caught in the middle of a gigantic blaze. Well, maybe Spielberg thought that the lightning and thunderstorm would also turn off the audience's brains

title: The dumbing down of America reaches Spielberg -
review:
I never thought I would be this disappointed in a Spielberg film - but this film is a bloody mess -

Visuals - yes Spielberg is a master there - but in this high tech world we expect more and more of "special effects" and I just didn't think most of this was that special. Some great scenes technically and visually yes - but most of it became mundane and underwhelming.

If it weren't for Dakota Fanning, I would want the invaders to win by the end of this film, or at least to make her their new queen. So many heavy handed moments of processing "family stuff" albeit minus an "On Golden Pond" soundtrack were just too much for me. Style sans substance?

speaking of audio - maybe thats one of the missing elements here - the lack of scary sounds from the aliens made it much less terrifying than the film's predecessors - a little death ray or juicy chomping now and then would have made it much more suspenseful as well -

Two lamest parts of the film (NOTE SPOILER WARNING)for me were: A)with most of the world being sans power and with your neighbors being harvested or blown away at any given moment, some folks still had time to fire up their scanners and printers (and generators?)to make all those nice 9/11-esque missing person flyers - all neatly displayed for those similarly less than panicked masses to stop and notice? B)for the final dose of "family values" and class warfare, the blue collar hero brings the girl child back to the Bostonians (oblivious to their impending demise as they stand around in cashmere and khakis - almost like a merlot commercial or something), and miracle two - the other child survived too and actually hugs teary Tom and calls him DAD - but it's still not enuf to get him an invite into the townhouse, alas.

title: had potential
review: This movie had excellent visuals, and the acting between the two main characters Tom Cruze and Dakota Fanning superb as usual. However the lack of solid plots and the fizzeling out of the entire movie itself is what made me give this movie such a low rating. I read the original story a while back and have to say that it isn't one of my favorites for that very same reason. I expected that since the director added a lot of things that weren't in the book he would revise the way the story ended as well. If he had focused more on the issue that actually decided the outcome of the "war" it would have been one of the best movies of the year. Alas he stuck true to form and it was a very drawn out disappointing film. WHAT POTENTIAL!!!

title: Shock and awe
review:
Dakota is as charming as ET ever was. However, her humanism does not settle the major hangups I had watching this, the most expensive movie ever made. I haven't written many of these, but I feel that instead of telling people I didn't like the movie, I will write here why and lie and tell everyone I loved it. Cause I know everyone else will.

It's Dakotas movie. I truly hope she can retire on royalties from this one. Being that this is the most expensive movie ever made, it's strange that the most price worthy asset is a little kid with a strange name. I absolutely can not avoid smiling when she does and this lifts the movie from a 2 to a 3.

This brings me to my problem with the movie: It's playing on my feelings, or lack thereof, of fear of war and the chaos around it. However, as a movie, it just draws lines to the real world (as I understand both the book, the radio"show" and the previous movie all did, 1st, 2nd and cold war... at least I have been told), but it does not do anything else than terrify. Much like a cheap Koraen horror movie, where it horrifies just to horrify, I sit there, with my War Of The World popcorn and feel nothing. If anything I look slightly disconcerted up at the sky and wonder what the point of the latter two hours was. Was it so that you could impress me with special effects, was it to let us watch Tom jog with tight pants, was it to make some kind of weak political protest (casting Tim Robbins as a depraved redneck/lonely man certainly did the trick of that) or was it just to entertain? Well, for me, and who else can I speak for, it did neither of the above. It was the porn of the alien movies, the soapopera of the big budget movies. It had no purpose or answer, just some cop-outs to justify the idea of having big, bad aliens and let everyone leave with a sigh of relief.

Give me the open ending of Cube or Dawn of the Dead. Give me the humanity of Randy... er..Dennis Quaid from The Day After Tomorrow. Give me a breather. Don't try to R-Kelly impress me with your blingbling-special effects. Don't be a war benefactor.

Just make something that makes me feel something. You have to work for my 6 euros.

And the only one who did that, was Dakota.

And from now on, I will tell anyone who wants to know; "I liked it. It was cool"

title: War of the Worlds or War of the Blended Family?
review: I expected a bit more from the Cruise/Spielberg camp, but all in all a worthy effort. I spent a lot of time wanting to see more interactions between the humans and aliens and a lot less of Ray (Tom Cruise) arguing with his kids. OK, Ray is a bad father, we get it!!! Can we get back to the aliens please? I kept waiting for the big BAM! moment and it never really came. What happened? Yes, Ray is developing that natural human instinct to protect his offspring, congrats, but umm, the aliens? Where are they? The movie does a great job regarding human character/behavior in a crisis situation. The scene with the car is a great example. Like I said, a worthy effort, but they didn't knock it out of the park this time.

title: worst Spielberg in 20 years
review: OK, so I haven't gotten soft. This is easily Spielburg's worst film in 20 years, if not his weakest work ever (1941 not included, I think everyone let that one slide). What little interest the film creates in the viewers in the first ¼ of the film, mostly by sight and sound, quickly disintegrates into a complete mess of failed characters, character arcs, and writing. The special effects and camera work were OK, but nothing compared to Minority Report. Tom Cruise is terribly miscast as a dock worker and the world's worst father, Tim Robbins character has no reason to be in the movie, and Dakota fanning just screams for and hour and a half. The ending, which was pushing it when it was originally read in 1896 just comes up lamer here, with a sappy Hollywood touch that doesn't even try to mean anything but make you feel good. There are three signs that this was a sub-par movie. 1) is that it was boring, I saw people look at their watches a number of times, and a couple even went out to take a cell phone call. 2) The biggest, is making you miss other movies that are better. Signs still is the best alien invasion movie, any of the "Dead" movies are better end of the world films. This made me even want to watch Independence Day, or the 1950's version of War of the World's, both pretty mediocre films. 3) I noticed flubs as the film went. If all of the electronic devices won't work how is a guy tape recording it? As well as just some stupid logic that somehow no one seemed to think twice about

title: fantastic film
review:
Awesome, fantastic effects and shocking in places. For all those people who say that Spielberg borrowed from films such as abyss, Jurassic park etc think about this. War of the Worlds is the grand daddy of all science fiction, every science fiction story every told has some elements of war of the worlds in it. By keeping in with the HG Wells storyline people are going to make these abserd asuptions. Cruise was fantastic in it. If you are a good actor you have to be believable in a role. This is the case with cruise being (de-cruised) in this movie being an average guy who is trying to save himself and his family from becoming a martian snack.

This is probably the best film I have ever seen and I recommend it to everyone.

title: In simple words: Best movie ever made. Spielberg and Cruise shine in this magnificent, heart-pounding and emotional epic.
review:
This is the most profound movie ever made in the history of great sci-fi movies that has been produced in Hollywood. Spielberg directs Tom Cruise. Imagine the blast of combustion produced by these two mega-explosive talents. This film has everything you will ever want; adventure, horror, action and even drama which is very rare that the drama section is perfectly dissolved in this sci-fi masterpiece, but this movie succeeds in it.

I have never doubted about Tom Cruise's actor talent, but this just removes any doubt about having any doubt. He is utterly amazing and in the same time very believable in many various scenes of the movie. Spielberg in a sophisticating and suspenseful way brings this movie into a domestic scene that touches us in every way.

Spielberg's craft is confirmed in this movie of how he handles the camera and the special effects. He does not use it in a way of showing off like most other directors but he smoothly blends it in a flow with addition of tension in the movie.

I congratulate also the down-to-earth screenplay, which is outstanding if you ask me. In addition to this, an applause to the supporting actors, Dakota Fanning, Justin Chatwin and also Tim Robbins.

To summon up, this breathtaking movie will stun you in every scene, in which the story is magnificently told, with every kind of colour, movement and greatness.

In simple words: Best movie ever made. Spielberg and Cruise shine in this magnificent, heart-pounding and emotional epic.

Believe me when i say this: You will want to see it again, the second u step out of the theatres. THIS FILM IS TRULY A MASTERPIECE IN ALL PROSPECTIVES AND ANGLES U CHOOSE TO SEE IT IN.

A true 11/10 (It is that good)

title: WoW, a summer blockbuster
review: I saw War of the Worlds last night on a midnight session here in Australia, I have to say that i was very exited to see this film and could not hold my excitement for the first 20 minutes. In this first act Spielberg sets the story well, his shots represent perfection, you can see from the very first shot of the film how well constructed it is. Then we start seeing how a dysfunctional family (a Spielberg classic mode) deals with each other until a "storm" comes in. An alien invasion !!! OK I really wanted to see the tripods, and yes they look cool, yes I wanted to see mayhem and I got a little of that, yes I knew what the story was all about so I knew at the end humanity prevails, but ... I know a film must not try to recreate reality, but represent a reality, I know that there must be suspension of disbelief and that we should all relate to the hero of the story and see it unveil trough his eyes, but it all seemed to fake for me, too staged, the hero finds answers to his choices too easily, the director made it too easy, I do not think they let us time to think. And there are scenes, like the one with that other famous actor that seems out of tune. Overall, I did not like it, I'll wait for the DVD for the special features and try to understand it with the commentaries, perhaps ...

title: Disappointed
review: After a summer of slight movie disappointments, War of the Worlds is a major disappointment. I feel about the same as I did when I saw "Sphere" -- this is another great book turned into an expensive, predictable, mediocre science fiction movie. Except this one has lame plot twists like "the Village" did. The special effects fail to impress. I truly think that "House of Wax" is a better movie. I would give War of the Worlds one star, but am adding one extra in support of Mr. Cruise, a good actor who does the best he can with the bad hand he is dealt. I am old enough to remember when Mr. Spielberg never disappointed. It was apparent that other people in the theater, like me, felt ripped off. What a waste of a great idea this thing is.

title: Did anyone even screen this movie?
review: Did anyone even screen this movie? Because if they did, they should have had some comments for Stephen Spielberg. I knew it was a disaster movie, but didn't think the movie was going to be a disaster. I was really looking forward to this one, and was highly disappointed. *SPOILERS* - Tom Cruise wasn't nice to his kids at the beginning. I thought that events would mold him into a great dad by the end of the movie. No, i didn't like him any more at the end, than the beginning. Where was the ingenious plan by the human race that brought down the aliens? Oh, there wasn't any. They just started "acting erratically" and then we could shoot them. That was totally lame. There was no dramatic conclusion, no resolution, nothing except a feeling of being ripped off at having sat through that movie for no point at all. Dakota Fanning was awesome. I liked the "cameo" by Tim Robbins. Oh, yeah, and the effects were great. If you like effects with no storyline, or character development, then this one is for you. Otherwise, don't waste your time.

title: Makes Rollerball look good.
review: Have I seen this movie before only done better? I swear I have. Surely one of the worst 'big release' movies of the last 10 years and without a doubt Spielbergs' worst film (and that includes A.I) Obvious mistakes (all electronics not working but a guy films it with a digital camcorder), tired old broken family clichés and repulsive references to 'is it terrorists'. The lamest jokes I have heard in a cinema for years (well I guess Spielberg has to keep the jokes to a level where a 8 year old can find them funny. A rushed ending as predictable as anything and lacking imagination and detail (yes it's worse then Independence Day's computer virus ending). Overall an uninspiring 'seen it all before' special effects romp with no humor or long standing cinematography. Believe me if you have seen it once that's enough, whilst it wasn't the worst film I have ever seen in my life (Bad Boys 2 takes the cake) i can't imagine ANYONE paying to see this film twice.

title: Don't bother, Spielberg's worst.......
review:
OK, so everyone's a critic. I do not know exactly what was wrong with this film, but from the beginning it just didn't work. It could be just my expectations were to high. I was expecting Top Gun, Minority Report meets H.G. WELLS, a sort of Independence Day (a War of the Worlds copy-cat)....... What I got was a major let-down. The plot was very lack-luster Cruise and Fanning just drifted along no real plot line that I could find. Don't get me wrong the acting was first rate but the script and dialog, wouldn't even make it in a "B" movie. The special effects though well done are just not that believable (the alien tripods), although the "death-ray" was very cool.

Dakota Fanning seemed to spend a great deal of the movie screaming her head off (annoying), Cruise whispered a lot. In (many) parts, the film got so slow, that the audience I was in, got so very restless (board out of their sculls) you had a hard time hearing all the whispering.

It seemed to me the film was all about Cruise and not about the Martians. Their was far to little action, to little of the aliens and the difficulty in stopping them. In all the 1953 film "War of the Worlds" is far superior in every way even the special effect hold up even today, but the 50's "death ray" is a bit cheesy, but the ships/tripods are a lot cooler and more believable than Speilbergs version. I'm a fan of Steven's but this is the worst movie of his I've ever seen. He should have dusted off the 50's script, updated it a little, keep the characters, add Dakota, updated the effects, and you would have had great film.

Enough ranting to be fair (to the film) this is sort of an every-man's version, it is from the perspective of just an ordinary man caught up in all the chaos of an alien invasion. He clueless (obvious from the film) and is just struggling to survive. Its all about his struggle to keep himself and his kids alive, from that perspective I suppose the film works, but I wanted more, much more from a Spielberg film.... He has done many fine works (ET, Shindlers List, Close Encounters, And many more, so I'm disappointed)........... Beyond all doubt James Cameron or Ron Howard should have directed this one. I think they could have done what Steven couldn't this time, Do Justice to the story... And especially the audience.....

title: Keep the simple stuff real
review:
I was very excited about WoW, but reality puts this movie as one to avoid.

The movie gets rolling quickly, and the point up to the aliens appearing makes you think that this could be really good. Tense, exciting, and a little spooky.

Then the special effects take over and the simple things get completely lost in the shuffle.

We know that the lightning first hit in the Ukraine about a day prior, but just 20 minutes after it hits in New York, the aliens appear. OKAY. The multiple paths for the Miracle Mini-Van are comical. Where is everybody going? Sure, Cruise wants to get his kids to their Mom, but why is everyone else walking somewhere. The food scene in the kitchen. Nobody thinks to look in the fridge? Everyone getting onto a ferry that is lit up so bright you could see it from the moon. Not to mention they have it loaded with cars that don't start with people sitting in them (must be an advanced auto parts store on the other side of the water with a special on solenoids). Starts making you think that the human race is to dumb to live. The battle scene where his son needs to see. Why is everyone walking towards the battle in the first place. They get there, and then realize maybe this isn't the best place to be. The list could go on for quite some time, but I will finish with the ludicrous ending, in which his wife and her family are fine, not to mention the entire block, as well as his son. Joke.

I realize that movies are made for entertainment, but make it intelligent. Special effects are good, but that does not save this movie. Watch 'Independance Day' for a much better invasion flick.

Last note. Morgan Freeman narrates the beginning & the end. Why not use him for narrative updates throughout the movie.

title: the ending
review: I'm not going to give specifics of the ending, but for someone who has read the book, they might infer what the ending is, so if you do not want to know, stop reading. Many critics and moviegoers have complained of the ending, that it is too unlikely, a bit on the cheesy side and that you should walk out just before it ends. First of all, that is exactly how the aliens are defeated in H.G. Wells brilliant novel, and that is exactly the same reunion atmosphere that is presented at the end. So, please read the book and then you will see how faithful Spielberg and his cast and crew were to the essence of Wells' masterpiece.

title: A disaster of Epic Porportions.
review:
In a summer season of grand blockbusters, "War of the Worlds" is perhaps the biggest dud in years, and is a failure of epic proportions. The film is a remake of the classic 1953 film of the same name which like the new one is inspired from the H.G. Wells novel of 1898.

The new version is directed by Steven Spielberg, and stars Tom Cruise as Ray Ferrier, a divorced dockworker who is spending some time with his estranged children, Robbie (Justin Chatwin), and Rachael (Dakota Fanning), while his ex-wife and her new husband take a trip.

The children are very cold to Ray as they feel they were dumped on their mother as Ray only cares about himself. When a series of freak electrical storms hits various cities around the world, Ray attempts to comfort his children who are disturbed by the storm as well as the fact that all electronic devices have ceased to function.

Ray leaves the children at home and ventures into the neighborhood and is soon facing a waking nightmare as giant machines burst from the ground laying waste to everything in their paths.

Ray gathers his family and flees in a working vehicle trying to stay one step ahead of the alien machines in an attempt to find safety and reunite the children with their mother in Boston.

As basic as the above plot outline is, it is pretty much the entire plot of the film. There is little else to it aside from a few interruptions such as the family seeking shelter in a couple of houses or facing an angry mob as they attempt to reach a ferry.

While a thin plot can be excused for many action films, what cannot be excused are the painfully bad lack of any excitement in the film and the lack of any compelling action or suspense.

We are supposed to believe that the world is being destroyed by the alien's but aside from a few blasted bridges, and small buildings, we see a surprising lack of carnage. There are no sequences of classic landmarks being reduced to rubble, there are no scenes of vast armies locked in a desperate struggle against the invaders. Instead, we get a sequence of helicopters firing, and a line of soldiers firing, but they never show us what they are shooting at, nor do we see the alien retaliation behind a bright explosion and a few vehicles emerging on fire. This is particularly frustrating when you consider that the 1954 version at least showed a few tanks being blasted outright.

Another issue I had with the film was the painfully obvious superimposed backdrops as during the films limited action scenes; the background was clearly inserted into the shot as it was so fuzzy that it did not fit in with the events in the foreground.

While I am willing to dismiss this as stylistic nitpicking what cannot be ignored is that for most of the films running length, the cast does little more than stand around waiting for something to happen. There are no great segments of character development, no insight into why the aliens waited all this time to attack when they could have done so centuries earlier, why they want the planet, and numerous other plot holes, some of which are so glaring. One of my favorites was the guy who was able to use a video camera to record the opening attacks when it was clearly shown that all electronic devices were rendered useless.

Much has been made of Cruise's recent off screen actions and I must say that those have been far more interesting and engaging than his performance here. Cruise spends the majority of the film in a wide-eyed gaze or frantically moving and yelling. His character like his annoyingly bratty daughter are so unsympathetic, I found myself hoping that the aliens would take them out and end our suffering.

I hate stated prior that I thought this film may have problems as in light of films such as "ID4", the story would seem bland to modern audiences unless the action was increased and there was a dynamic story with interesting characters. Sadly all of those are missing from a film that also has one of the worst endings in recent history. There is no build up, no final confrontation, no moment of high tension to get to the payoff; it just ends with a whimper. One would think that a grand battle or an FX royale is in store instead, it plays out in a very matter of fact fashion with shockingly little action or suspense.

I could go on and on, but suffice it to say that between the weak acting, tired, thin plot, and infrequent and underwhelming action and FX, this is a film that exists only due to the talents of Cruise and Spielberg., That being said, I have to wonder how and why they could not have picked a better product than this stale offering.

1 stars out of 5 Gareth Von Kallenbach www.sknr.net International Association of Film Critics.

title: Cliché ridden nonsense
review:
I'll start off the way I mean to go on: I *HATED* this film. The ending couldn't come too soon for me and I can honestly say the only thing I liked about this film was Tom Cruise's jacket. We're supposed to believe that hidden underneath the surface of THE ENTIRE PLANET there were hulking great big metallic tripods just waiting to conquer the earth. Would we have not noticed these things before while excavating cities to build subways and tunnels? Would they not have been picked up by science and technology as we strive to learn more about our planet? Apparently not. Believable over 100 years ago when the story was written, not now.

Another problem with changing around the time period is that the storms supposedly knock out EVERYTHING electrical - even analogue watches. So how is it possible that pictures of invading tripods were transmitted to a TV news van? And how was it possible that they were able to pick them up? And why does the van work? And why does Tom Cruise's car work? And the radio in the car? And do all cars run for 24 hours without needing to be filled up? And why didn't the storm knock out the ferry? Then there's the problem of the characters. Naturally, being a Spielberg film, it involves a dysfunctional family. After the parents divorce, naturally the little screeching girl and the sullen teen boy have "issues". Don't remember them cropping up in the HG Wells version, but that could just be my memory playing tricks with me. Dakota Fanning as the daughter is excellent at portraying a screaming brat who needs to be told to SHUT UP on more than one occasion. She alone is perhaps the reason why I disliked this film so much. I would gladly have sent her to her "safe place" and abandoned her there.

The despondent son never uses the word "dad" until one of those cloying moments when it's necessary to show that he has changed. And why does the son who has no opinion on anything, and who doesn't care about anything, SUDDENLY decide that he simply MUST fight for his country? When did he grow a conscience? And will he turn up safe and sound at the end? Oh, if only it wasn't a Spielberg film then perhaps we might actually bother to guess.

Like the most recent Star Wars film, the special effects are decidedly unspectacular. It's not that there's anything wrong with them as such, but a train with flaming carriages was frankly the only stand-out moment (and I've seen better on TV). The 'evil' tripods were obviously designed with a 1950s pen in hand and the operators seem to be design rejects from Men in Black (a cross between a gremlin and a penis head)  wholly unconvincing as a sign of menace. And that is the greatest problem with the film, there's no sense of danger  just a feeling of irritation with the characters. There's no sense of foreboding when the first tripods appear, just the question "what are they going to blow up?" There's no drama when Tom Cruise decides to reunite his kids with their mother and grandparents, just the feeling that it's a pointless exercise given that THE WHOLE PLANET is under attack. When Tim Robbins appears, it's not a feeling of disquiet that he brings to the screen, only a few more kilos.

After watching our planet for a million years, why did the aliens decide to invade NOW when the world is in such a bad state and when we finally do have the artillery to retaliate. Would they not, having noticed we had started to build powerful weapons, decide to attack then, before we got too powerful? And having observed us for a million years (apparently) would they not have learned even a little about the way we have evolved, how we react to different things, what makes us ill etc. And why do they kill us when it's our blood that they need?

title: Excellent
review: Ray is a typical man living on his own just making it in this world. Many families experience the estranged relationship with their kids when there is a separation. This is nothing new, however, Tom plays the role perfectly with a lot of deep emotion to discover about himself and his children along with some humbling. He tries to do the best he can with what he has to work with; a separation, another man taking his place,an ex-wife that finds fault, basic wage earner. Remember the point Raymade at the outset when his boss said to the effect, "Ray do you know what is wrong with you?" and Ray's response was something to the effect,there are 2 other women that could make a list....He is already working with a vulnerable situation and feels it. This is not the issue....the issue is; he really does have a deep loyalty to his kids and it takes tragedy to bring it out, as in most of us. This show should make anyone stand up to attention. The possibility of war, terrorism, etc. could be inflicted upon us in an instant. Hopefully we come through it with as much dedication as Ray did and concern for not only his own but others. Linda Buchanan

title: What the...?
review:
Could this have been any greater of a waste of my time? This was little more than yet another vehicle for Cruise to be ... Cruise. No acting involved (as usual), just Tom being the usual "Tom character".

* Characters whom I didn't care if they lived or died. Whining, screaming Dakota Fanning; hateful son whose name I never did care enough to learn; bad father Cruise; bitchy ex-wife and limp step-father.

* The flag waves at the start, ribbons unfurled, the statue of The Patriot in Boston, Robbins denying that Japan could ever solve a problem before the US ... all we were missing was the apple pie.

* The aliens start disintegrating people by the hundreds, and we can assume from what we are told to be the magnitude of the attack, by the millions. Yet, halfway through the film, they start to harvest them for their blood?!? What the hell is the point of that? What's more, the red-vein-vine that they cover the Earth with has the exact same vulnerability to our bacteria as the aliens themselves? Come on. And they harvest them only a handful at a time? Sheesh.

I have to stop here. Mentally regurgitating this film is upsetting my stomach.

If you don't get the ending, or don't like it, read the book; again, this is a nice nod to an ingenious ending devised well over 100 years ago. title: Compelling Concept Undermined By Flawed Script
review:
The screenplay is easily the weakest aspect of this movie. It is essentially Independence Day with scarier aliens. The ruthlessness with which the aliens consume humanity is shocking but in practically every other important element, War of the Worlds is a remake of Independence Day, where Will Smith is replaced with Tom Cruise.

Tom Cruise adds a new twist to his typical roles. In many of his movies, Cruise plays a hyper-talented cocky man who is haunted by unresolved father issues. In WotW, he plays the father who is creating issues between him and his son. He plays the distant father rather than play the son whose distant father left him empty and aching for approval.

The screenplay's dialog is average and it adequately conveys the contempt between Ray, his ex-wife and children. He has no credibility with them and there is so little affection that both children refer to him not as Dad but as Ray.

The plot line is initially creative and fascinating. The New York-Jersey Metro area is visited by incredibly powerful lightening storms that end up being instrumental in how the aliens distribute themselves around the world. As the aliens break cover and begin destroying the world, however, the movie begins its spiral down into inconsistency and frankly, utter stupidity.

For example, as the first alien in Jersey (or maybe it was Brooklyn) starts vaporizing people and buildings Cruise manages to avoid ray beams multiple times, discerns flawlessly how to bypass the exploding and collapsing buildings around him and consequently, emerges unwounded.

In one scene that insipidly borrowed from the bathtub scene in Minority Report, an alien probe snoops around a basement looking for hapless humans. And yet for all their interplanetary travel and ostensibly vast intelligence, they couldn't detect three noisy people. What? These guys don't have the ability to sense thermo differences between humans and brick? They can't detect breathing and heart beats? They are cosmic versions of Larry, Curly and Moe who are easily snookered by humans? Come on! (And seriously: at one point, three aliens are scouting out the basement of Tim Robbins and one of the aliens actually spins a bicycle wheel playfully. This speaks to many logical breakdowns in the movie: it seems highly improbable that a creature with interplanetary travel technology would be distracted by something as arcane as a wheel).

Just as the aliens have the world firmly by the balls and are squeezing quite hard, their dominance inexplicably begins to rapidly crumble. Just like in Independence Day, there is a crucial weakness that the aliens have. It is at the point where this begins to be evident that the movie utterly collapses. After Morgan Freeman's opening voice over asserted the staggering intelligence of these creatures, we find that their due diligence was inadequate and failed to take a simple biological reality into consideration. The movie doesn't explain how they could have made such a mistake when clearly they are technologically advanced and capable of decimating an entire globe.

Which leads me to their method. What bothered me was how analog the aliens were in their approach to annihilation: very mechanical, very time and resource intensive. It seemed blunt, coarse and brutal. It lacked sophistication in its approach. I thought the brutality of their consumption of humans (hey wait a minute... consumption of humans. Wasn't that in Matrix?) was well-portrayed but the means by which humans were being destroyed was awfully inefficient for such an advanced species.

The character development was adequate. There wasn't much complexity to the pathos between the father/son/daughter triad so the tension was quickly developed. The children are aware of their father's lack of meaningful involvement in their lives but as the movie progresses and they see that he is not quite the man they thought he was, the loci of trust gradually shifts toward Cruise with each of the kids. With this shift comes a change to calling him Dad instead of Ray.

The acting was okay. You don't expect much from a space aliens disaster movie. The characters are believable. The only character I really believed was the daughter. Cruise was passably believable but not authentic.

The cinematography and production were disappointing. I have higher expectations of Spielberg. His vision for Minority Report was superb as was the composition of his shots, the lighting and the clarity of the image. Similarly, Spielberg went off the scale with Schindler's List in terms of vision, composition, style and clarity. WotW lacks the polished Spielberg production quality. Last week, we saw Batman Begins and its production and cinematography were outstanding. So, between my expectations of Spielberg and my most recent movie experience, WotW was a big let down.

There really was no soundtrack and there was one sole sound effect that stands out: the foreboding rumble of an approaching tripod. The theater shakes viscerally with this sound. It is felt in your body and that brings a sense of reality to the experience.

Finally, the special effects are impressive. This is definitely a movie that needs to be experienced in a high quality theater. Don't wait for the DVD on this one.

It is ultimately the screenplay that undermines this movie. It's still a worthy movie to watch, but don't expect a compelling plot line. Expect a remake of Independence Day with exactly the same viral ending to the invading species.

title: I would rather have preferred watching something else
review:
I had high hopes for this movie. With the tremendous amount of media attention this movie has been receiving and the amount of advertising, I thought this movie would certainly deliver (that and I'm a fan of Steven Spielberg and yes, even Tom Cruise)... Alas, I was sorely mistaken. At the end, I tried to convince myself that the film was a good one, only because I thought it was me who felt something lacking in it. But hearing the responses of my friend and other movie-goers around me, I think the feeling was mutual: you're just not satisfied by the end of the movie. It's not that you're upset with a lack of resolution or anything, you just feel cheated when the hype was promising so much more. It's a simple plot, and while the acting and special effects were very good, there's nothing much this movie offers that you haven't already seen in other alien movies. For entertainment value, I would far more recommend INDEPENDENCE DAY without hesitation. I'm glad I didn't have to spend more than $4.50 - otherwise I would have been really upset.

Without giving away any particular elements in the movie, I have to say that, frankly, for such intelligent aliens, they did some pretty stupid things.

If you're trying to convince yourself that the movie you just saw was good, stop trying to convince yourself. It probably wasn't, and that's how we felt about this. Sorry for you die-hard Spielberg/Cruise fans.

title: Aw, c'mon folks!
review:
This movie is really taking a beating. Now I confess that, because my mom read sci-fi (Galaxy and Science Fiction, Fantasy, etc.) while she was pregnant with me, that I have an unnatural love of a great spaceship or alien critter up on the big screen. Especially embarrassing in that I am a woman, and we're not supposed to love that sort of thing. So I liked the tripods. They looked cool. And I'm one of those suckers that directors and producers love. The kind of person who willingly suspends her disbelief, drops the price of a matinée, and goes into the theater to be entertained. I spent the dough. I want the experience, and I'm willing to give the picture a break. In short, I'm easy.

But the lint I'm picking that makes me mark this movie down does not have to do with the premise. Spielberg respects the source material. It doesn't have to do with Cruise's performance. Compare his performance to any other space opera you've seen in the last few years. 'Star Wars'? Please. Independence Day? Someone shoot Bill Pullman.

Nope. I'm a little peeved about telegraphing. There just weren't enough surprises. There were some good ones. But in this flick, we all know the story. So Spielberg needs to find more places to surprise us in the script with minor things.

However, having said this, I really liked the film. It engaged me. Great eye candy. Good effort, a la Stephen King, at making us care about characters, and then scaring the bejeezus out of them, which scare us, too. And Spielberg put every penny of his budget up on the screen.

So, if you're a sci-fi sucker looking for a great summer treat, this is a good film. If you're a jaded punk who likes to pick things apart just so you won't look like a dork, stay home, and let us dorks be happy idiots.

title: Stupidity At Its Worst
review:
It was really disappointing. It's overtly dramatic and tries to play on sympathies that they just don't set up. I find it very hard to believe that any intelligent critic truly liked this film. Character driven? That is the most overused term, thrown around by those who don't know any better. If a character strings together more then four coherent lines people love to label the movie as "Character driven." The fact is, the characters aren't developed during this film. Sure, they are scared but the movie is presented in such a over-the-top fashion that you just want to cringe.

title: brilliant up until the horrendous anti-climax
review:
SPOILERS In recent years, Hollywood and the rest of the movie making world has suffered from a creative disorder. For many film makers, this illness has ruined some of their finest works, whilst for others, it has simply been the nail in an already sealed coffin. This plight is that of the anti-climax. In films like "Artificial Intelligence", "28 Days Later" and "The Hitchhikers Guide To The Galaxy", films which have ranged from acceptable to amazing have been ruined by an ending which a two year old would write down and then throw up on. "Artificial Intelligence" in particular was a dirge of a film which never really got going, but which would have finished brilliantly if it had finished thirty minutes earlier. Unfortunately though Steven Spielberg, a man seemingly obsessed with happy endings and should probably see a psychologist about this, took over the film and stuck a woeful conclusion onto it.

Spielberg, perhaps unfairly handed the title of greatest director ever (personal preference lies with Hitchcock), has made some amazing films over the years, but he has also made some absolute stinkers. Teaming up with actor Tom Cruise for this 2005 remake of the HG Wells classic "War of the Worlds", it seems with five minutes to go that Spielberg has created another classic. Unfortunately though, it is at this point where he experiences a relapse of the ill-fated disease and produces a dire conclusion to a previously amazing film.

Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise) is a dockworker in New Jersey having his children from his now deceased marriage over to stay. Unable to connect with son Robbie (Justin Chatwin) and abandoning his daughter Rachel (Dakota Fanning), Ray's life is not one to shout about. As tensions raise in the house however, a mysterious cloud forms and machines break out of the ground. Now, travelling across America with children in tow, Ray must fight for survival as the human raise is systematically exterminated.

From Morgan Freeman's opening narration, "War of the Worlds" is a clever and well shot film. With amazing special effects and some truly awesome acting (most notably, and scarily, from young Dakota Fanning), it leaps out of the screen and leaves you clutching to the edge of your seat throughout.

Steven Spielberg is a director who knows how to tell a story, and that is increasingly evident here as he pits Ray not only against alien invaders, but against other panicking humans. The fact that Ray survives for so long is a miracle in itself, but to have so many characters vaporised or shot or stood on or eaten, Spielberg knows how to get our nerves shaking.

Yes there are flaws in the story, Tim Robbins eccentric slowly deranged Ogilvy is an annoying role which we probably could have done without, but ultimately when you witness scenes of beautiful choreography like the red vines in the field, it's acceptable to forgive Robbins' character.

We also can forgive some of Spielberg's slow moments in exchange for one or two amazing criticisms of America. At one point Ray is driving a car and explaining events to his son. The boy goes "Is it terrorists" only to then say "Is it Europe then?". Insulting the American ignorance and this constant terror that something new might happen, this little conversation is a joyous moment in the film. A reminder that Spielberg is aware of the real world and that he is more than willing to criticise it.

Unfortunately, Spielberg is also a man with anti-climax syndrome and for that we can not forgive him. Ironically sticking with the one major point of HG Wells' story that he shouldn't have, Spielberg creates a dire resolution to the invasion and rushes his ending. Adding salt into the wound, he also manages to present us with the one conclusion to Ray's journey that we wished would not happen. We can argue whether this is a joyous ending or not (one person posting a message on the notice board is spot on in regards to whether the ending is tragic), but ultimately it is an ending which just should not have happened.

Steven Spielberg can be an amazing director. Creating some of the most well known and well loved films of the last twenty years, he is easily one of the finest directors ever. In recent years though he has suffered from a debilitating decease called anti-climax syndrome. Taking films which range from average to amazing, he successfully destroys them without batting an eyelid. In the future whenever you watch a Spielberg film, make sure you leave before the ending, it'll make you appreciate the film more.

title: Should be War of the Stupid Children
review: Tom Cruise singing a lullaby. Get real. This story can be told so many interesting ways and from so many angles. I do not understand why essentially Spielberg told a story about a rotten father dealing with really stupid children trying to get to of all places Boston, after leaving a destroyed New York.
