title: Coulda Been Worse... Coulda Been Better...
review: WAR OF THE WORLDS (3 outta 5 stars) Not one of the best Spielberg movies (not even the best Spielberg/Tom Cruise collaboration) but the movie has a lot of good stuff in it and is a lot better than the average "summer action" movie. The movie starts out pretty well... with some very believable and well-directed bits of suspense (the lightning, the wind, the cracks slowly opening up the ground). The alien tripods (and their accompanying sound effects) are a pretty scary sight for the most part. I found the death rays a little silly (uh, why are the martians blasting humans to atoms anyway when it is discovered later that they are harvesting their blood?) but the depiction of the panic and the widespread devastation get top marks. The problems with this movie are mostly apparent after the scene on the ferry. It seems that after that scene the filmmakers can't decide what to do next.. so Spielberg retreads old suspense "gimmicks" from previous movies. There is a ridiculous scene with three humans hiding out in a wide-open, bombed-out basement and remain UNSEEN (!!!) while a bunch of aliens walk around them (for no real reason, really... uh, sightseeing?). Firstly, it is very reminiscent of the kitchen scene in "Jurassic Park"... and seems like a too-desperate attempt at hooking the audience. Secondly, why do they have to show us the aliens anyway? (Dull, unimaginative aliens at that!) I think it would have been much more effective to not show them at all until the final scenes. Did Spielberg forget about a great, little movie called "Duel" where the identity of the driver of the killer truck was NEVER revealed? Did he forget how effective that was? How it added to the suspense? Spielberg's worst movie crime comes in the last 5 minutes of the movie... I won't say too much about it... just that it's totally uncalled for and it brings to mind Hooper's "miraculous" escape at the end of "Jaws". It seems like Spielberg is staying firm with all his bad habits and slowly shedding all his GOOD ones. Not much to say about the acting. It's standard disaster movie emoting... Tom Cruise plays a "bad" father (but in a kinda cute, lovable way, Dakota Fanning gets to scream and be annoying and Tim Robbins gets to play a possibly psychotic survivalist (more of that Final Act desperation I spoke of earlier). The movie's not all bad... it could have been a lot worse in less capable hands... unfortunately it also could have been a lot BETTER!

title: Definitely not Jaws
review: Spielberg has lost his touch. Not only has he proved himself to be a master of the irrelevant, blotting his movie with dialog and scenes that have absolutely no place in it, but he also inhibits the much anticipated fear by allowing us to see too much of what at least in part should remain veiled in mystery. Why do you suppose Ridley Scott's 'Alien' was so terrifying? In any case, you can't improve on a masterpiece. For all its age and lack of computer sophistication, the 1953 film version of WOTW still holds the title for best adaptation of H. G. Wells's classic sci-fi novel. That one's articulated script, imaginative soundtrack and cold-war inspired montage make Spielberg look as though he has reverted to a pre-'Duel' stage of creative development.

title: Spielberg's Alien Fright-Flick
review:
Steven Spielberg has the talent and command to do pretty much whatever he wants with an audience. If he wants to move you he can move you, if he wants to make you laugh he can make you laugh, if he wants to wring sloppy sentiments out of you, well, he can do that too. All through his career he's demonstrated this facility for supreme manipulation, and with it the willingness to deploy said talent in the name of projects both noble (Schindler's List) and not-so-noble (Jurassic Park). He has shown himself to be shameless in the best way possible: shameless in that he allows no thought of offending anyone's sensibilities to get in the way of his objectives. Is there a moment in the whole history of cinema more brazen than the one in Jaws where the boy is slaughtered by the shark, his blood gushing like a crimson fountain? Such a scene would seem profoundly tasteless, even amoral, if executed by a director of lesser skill than Spielberg, but the master gets away with it because the master knows just how far to go (how close to put the camera, how quick to cut away). With War of the Worlds Spielberg shows that his talent for pushing audiences to the edge of their tolerance is as sharp as it's ever been, maybe sharper. With this movie he proves that when he wants to scare the pants off you he can scare the pants off you, even if the story he's working from is a bit on the wobbly side.

The story is well-known to anyone who's read H.G. Wells or seen the serviceable old George Pal movie: a blissfully heedless earth is attacked by Martians driving indestructible, death-ray-shooting machines; human beings race around like helpless ants until the seemingly invincible aliens are ironically done-in by the microbes they neglected to inoculate themselves against (Who planned the invasion? Donald Rumsfeld?). The earlier incarnations of the story were characterized by, in the case of the Wells novel, a Victorian floweriness and sense of dread; and in the Pal version a vague Cold War paranoia suffusing the general '50s sci-fi quaintness. In Spielberg's version there is only cold terror, accomplished not only through cinematic virtuosity but deliberate referencing of modern-day catastrophe. It should be no surprise to see the man who turned the Holocaust and D-Day into box-office gold openly calling forth the ghosts of 9/11 to help add extra zing to his melodrama. There are moments that are staged to recall the chaos of that day - people running down streets to escape the carnage; improvised bulletin boards plastered with Polaroids of lost loved-ones; dazed survivors coated in dust. Spielberg calls forth these horrible memories in direct service of his narrative, and there's no doubt that it works. The cinematic carnage is lent an extra layer of emotional resonance by its awful familiarity. Whether this is tasteful or not is a matter of little concern to Spielberg, who knows his job and isn't afraid to do it.

The film is often stunning in its you-are-there shiveriness. Spielberg does a great job keeping us always in the shoes of his heroes, determined Tom Cruise and plucky Dakota Fanning, the alien machines being seen always as they see them, as towering monstrosities. The initial invasion is one of the better set-pieces in recent memory, a brilliantly executed progression from wonderment to fear to stark raving horror, and there are other scenes so chock-full of detail that they become physically overwhelming (the aftermath of a plane crash has never before been rendered with such a staggering volume of debris; one hopes the set-dressers got paid overtime). The movie is at its best when it's overpowering us, when the details of the plot fall away and all that's left is the spectacle of the alien machines vaporizing people, laying waste to whole cities. Unfortunately the details of the plot are not always so readily ignored. The problem with this story is simple: the aliens seem so ridiculously powerful that you have a hard time believing anyone could survive their onslaught even for a few hours. In order to achieve a dimension worthy of a summer blockbuster, Spielberg has taken Wells' powerful-but-vulnerable invaders and turned them into such mighty beings that the only way his protagonist can remain living long enough to see the end of the story is by sheer luck. Predictably, the human-sized elements of the story are the ones that let-down. There's so much straining for dynamic between Cruise's character, Ray, and his rebellious son Robbie that it's almost a relief when Robbie finally tells the old man to shove it and rushes blindly into the fray. Maybe it's the sheer power of the images that does it, but the human conflict, both inner and inter-personal, that plays out in front of the action seems hopelessly dopey.

It's a measure of Spielberg's virtuosity as a pure player of the audience that we so readily suspend, if not quite overlook, whatever objections we might have to his story both logically and character-wise, and simply let ourselves be carried along. What the movie demonstrates above all else is that beautifully-mounted, highly-detailed action can cover up for a lot of inadequacies in the writing department. And it shows too that Spielberg at the top of his game is still the best since Hitchcock at making us squirm in our seats.

title: Excellent, excellent movie
review:
This version of War of the Worlds manages to keep much of the book intact while grafting on a modern sensibility. Spielberg also manages to put his stamp on the story while retaining the feel of the original. In brief Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise) is a father in a split family where mom is doing much better. Ray, pretty much a teenager all grown up physically, has the kids for the weekend when, wouldn't you know it, the Martians invade.

As usual, Spielberg is a master of building suspense. This film reminded me in spots of Jaws, still in my opinion his masterpiece, with its gradual build-up of horror and its ability to impart upon you the vague feeling that something is wrong without actually telling you what it is. The slow unraveling of the Martian threat, coupled with the terrifying visual when you first see the tripods, is startling; the visual of the heat ray is monstrously effective, and the Martian calling noise  described as 'ul-la' in the book but sounding more like an evil foghorn here  is frightening.

Spielberg blends the family stuff  strongly played by Cruise and Dakota Fanning  and the terror very well; one scene where Ray loses his cool because he doesn't know what to do is excellent. The man-child has to grow up suddenly, and Cruise conveys his frustration well. Toward the middle of the film the horror takes over completely as civilization succumbs to the onslaught, and we are treated to ghastly scenes of the sinister tripods striding above us, towering overlords bent on destroying us. Every ounce of the horror Wells was trying to invoke is preserved on screen.

But there is another level that makes War an effective film, and that is the analogy to 9/11. We are living our lives as ordinary citizens when a monstrous event happens; an enemy we did not foresee and cannot understand strikes at our very way of life; we are powerless to fight back (indeed one of the strongest scenes in the film is the doomed attempt by the military to stop the tripods); and we never truly understand what they want or why they have chosen to attack us. Images that mirror that awful day pop up in the film; a dust-encrusted Ray stumbles like a zombie into his house; people run pell mell, not knowing what to do, as the city falls all around them; hordes of people run across the bridge, an almost perfect reflection of what we saw on the news that Tuesday night. While Spielberg is perfectly capable of creating horror all on his own, his skillful tapping into our collective psyche notches up the fear factor even higher. For much of the film there's so much tension that you're on the edge of your seat.

The acting is all excellent  from Cruise to Fanning to Tim Robbins playing the composite character of the parson/the tunneler (two scenes from the book are merged, but it works fine, even if the Martians come off as a tad dim). Everyone reacts to these horrifying events in a completely believable fashion (again, sadly, we have a real-life precedent), and aside from a little Spielberg treacle at the end, they achieve a consistent emotional state of teetering on the edge of panic  not easy to maintain.

This is a very strong picture. Spielberg is clearly at home in this piece, able to flex muscles he hasn't used in a while. The film entertains and frightens on a number of levels and is wholly satisfying. The only weak part comes at the end, where Spielberg gives a little too much of an up-beat, and the plot lets us down a tad - but that's Wells' fault, not Spielberg's, and far better to adhere to the original than have the hero take out the alien armada in a clumsy ham-handed fashion (ala ID4). War would be best seen on the big screen  the terror would not be as effective and pervasive on your TV. Do yourself a favor and see this in the movies; it'll probably end up being the best movies of the summer, and it's well worth your $7.50 to see.

title: War of the Worlds: more like Apocalypse Now than Independence Day- COLONIZATION.
review:
"...French colonization of Algeria..."

These four simple words spoken at the beginning of the movie gave away the meaning of this film and the tension between devising a blockbuster movie from a sci-fi novel with a political message.

This message is: COLONIZATION IS BAD. Thank you Britain, France, Germany, Belgium, Spain, among them, for showing us this through history, and thank you the United States for not learning from this history ("Those who don't learn from history are doomed to repeat it." - George Santayana).

This movie was NOT about finding the tricky way to defeat the aliens (a la Independence Day and most other alien invasion films). So please don't compare it to Independence Day! These movies aren't trying to accomplish the same goals.

This movie is an allegory to colonization in general. What happened when European nations and Japan colonized/attempted to colonize Africa, India, China, Korea, etc.? Similar things as happened when the Aliens tried to colonize our world. Mass murder of the native population in the service of gaining control (i.e. what first happened when the Aliens started invading), followed by slavery of the native population as a resource (i.e. when the Alien vessels would hold the people captive in cages to feed their ships), followed by the difficulties of colonization that are not a direct consequence of the native population (i.e. not being acclimated to the native environment: bacterial evolution).

Of course, all of these aspects do not map on to every case of colonization. In some cases, the people ousted the colonizers (South Africa, India for instance). In other cases, it may have been disease and hardship. Let's not sweat the details on the allegory because it's sure to bottom out at point (this is Sci-Fi after all).

What I appreciated was setting up the allegory with some degree of accuracy to actual colonization, and then showing how an ordinary guy (should have been someone more ordinary-looking than Tom Cruise, but that's where you draw the line I suppose in making a blockbuster film) would go about trying to keep his children alive.

The brilliance is in seeing what colonization does to a population. We end up having to kill each other over resources and self/familial-protection. We have to endure the lack of food, electricity, safety, sleep, walking for miles on end, and the horrible uncertainty of not knowing whether you will ever, as a parent, be able to provide for your children. The trauma makes us emotional wrecks. This is all crucially important because to those aliens who are colonizing us, we become "unreasonable" and "uncivilized" barbarians which justifies their superiority (an sad but useful irony to the colonizers). This point, that the process of colonization MAKES the native population barbaric (rather than the native population being barbaric) is made clearer in books like Heart of Darkness and the related movie Apocalypse Now.

I loved the movie overall- but there is a compromise in trying to make a blockbuster movie out of a political Sci-Fi novel. Basically, some of the aforementioned aspects of colonization have to be ignored in order to promote flashy scenes and cheap thrills that make it blockbuster worthy. I don't mean that with disdain though- I loved the special effects- though I wish they didn't water down the horrors of colonization so much.

A few things that could have made this film stronger politically:

1. Expose the irony of people becoming barbaric as a consequence of colonization more, and how this fuels the motive of colonization (a contemporary example of this would be our invasion of Iraq).

2. The whole scene with Harlan Ogilvy (the crazy guy Ray and Rachel have to share the house with)- perhaps make him a little less menacing so killing him is harder on a humanistic level, but still necessary.

3. Cast Ray's character as someone more ordinary-looking such that we have the that-could- be-me feel. Tom Cruise is too superhuman in this film from how he looks to how he drives. His consequent breakdown in the coffee shop after losing the van seems fake. A more everyday Joe kinda guy would have brought this home more- but then loses out on the blockbuster potential.

Overall, probably about the best you can do with the book to make it have blockbuster appeal in our time. Three cheers to Spielberg and Friedman!

title: Spielberg raises the sci fi / horror / blockbuster genre by injecting what is usually left out - personal drama and fragile heroes.
review:
Steven Spielberg, Tom Cruise, Dakota Fanning and screenwriters Josh Friedman and David Koep are at the top of their respective games in this version of H.G. Well's War of the Worlds. Special kudos to director of photography and two time Academy award winner Janusz Kaminski who gave the movie the dark, gritty look that only heightened the already tense script.

Unless you have lived in a cave for your entire life, I do not need to explain the gist of the "War of the Worlds". Whether it is the original book or the Orson Welles 1938 radio broadcast or the 1953 George Pal version (I loved that one)- the basic awful attraction are all the same: Aliens invade, possessing unbelievable military superiority and they, without warning, without explanation, without mercy, start committing mass killings of killings, extermination of "earthlings". That simple tone and set up are beautifully arresting. The alien invaders are both a metaphor for any invading force that we want to pin the "evil moniker on" whether it be Nazis or terrorists or whatever and the fact that they are mainly faceless and they kill indiscriminately of our race or geographical location make them something else. An evil force that unifies all races, all nations, all religious and political factions together to fight them.

And in a certain sense, that is the rosy picture presented in this usual genre. People unite against an outside, evil force but Spielberg turns this sentiment on it's head. In his vision, told through the eyes of Tom Cruise's character, a very flawed but real portrayal of a man who seems to have lost most of his emotional ties in his life, in this vision we do not see people pull together but we see mass pandemonium and panic and Americans, earthlings, turn on ourselves.

This is one of the true horrors depicted in this movie that makes it so riveting, depressing and scary at the same time. In one particular scene, (ATTENTION: MAJOR SPOILER AHEAD)- When confronted with the possibility that the recklessness of one of the survivors might result in the death of his daughter, the Tom Cruises character takes matters into his own hands and kills this character. This actually shocked me in a way that I haven't been shocked in a movie in a long time. In depicting this, not only did Spielberg and writers Friedman and Koep take a daring step in making the fallen hero incredible fallible but they also pulled the moral rug out from under him and the viewing audience.

This movie is full of nightmares, of chilling images rendered in a horrible and beautiful way. It is a story, really, of survival during incredible violence and most of all, it is a story about consequence. We see the main character, Tom Cruise make choices during the entire movie, many that we, the audience, may argue are the incorrect ones but they are made under the shadow of survival and love for his children.

title: 1-Star to all those that didn't get it and 10-stars to me !
review:
If you're going to watch this movie, please leave halfway through, around the time Cruise is resisting the tripods efforts to take him inside. Watch until that point, go home, think about the movie, go to the theatre the next day and watch the movie in full.

What we have here is a deeply subversive movie few people will "get". The clues are clear at the beginning, the clue is the reaction of Ferriers kids on him arriving home somewhat distressed after evading plasma-death-ray. Children who have not seen death with their own eyes do not understand death. One expects even science fiction movies, whose scenarios are usually wholly unreal, to have characters who behave like they're experiencing reality(as disturbing and as unreal as it appears to the viewer).

And thus even though an extremely noisy incineration of the local populace takes place on their doorstep, Ferriers daughter and son are oblivious and perplexed by their dads deeply shocked state. Incidentally, Ray Ferriers daughter(Sophia) is always telling her dad what to do, until she Experiences true fear.

OK, what follows is the theme of judgement day, collective judgement day is a dramatic device designed to make one aware of ones own mortality(and even better - others). The other theme is love perverted into attachment. Such love knows anger, giving commands and orders, and not generosity or even ethics.

It is notable that come judgement day, those who have been deprived of their possessions will vent fury on those who adamantly keep hold of theirs(this would be Ferrier driving his car into a crowd oblivious of the plight of others, absorbed in the fate of his own possessions, those kids of his). By the way, Ferrier doesn't even own the car he's driving, do we truly own anything other than our deeds?

The allusion to a beating heartbeat that is the noise of the footsteps of a tripod heightens the existential message of this film, when ones appointed time with the lord of death is near, you'll hear your heartbeat.

Of course Hollywood is incapable of telling it as it is, although it isn't the fault of Steven Spielberg and Josh Friedman in this case(both of whom combine to turn out an excellent movie for those who have the seeing eye). Because the conditioned public can't handle the truth, this, one of the best of movies (science-fiction or otherwise) makes a mockery of its audience. Cruise escapes from the clutches of tripod death, saves his daughter, and is reunited with all his loved ones(make that - attachments)....and all thanks to his own will and the humblest of creatures - bacteria.

Evading death just isn't possible, and it goes without saying your children are neither immune to the inevitable or in fact "yours". And so the film culminates with man paying homage to micro-organism, if anyone bought that, this is the final insult to mans stupidity.

END WORLD POVERTY NOW

title: I was unsure about this film. Then I was sold!
review:
Having read the original H G Wells book and have always been a huge fan of Jeff Waynes musical adaptation, I have always thought this would make a brilliant film. I have questioned for years "Why haven't they done War of the Worlds yet?" So when I finally heard that Spielberg had got his mitts on it, I awaited it's release with baited breath.

But then I saw the trailer. No! How could they do this? I couldn't believe my eyes when I realised that they'd taken the story out of the 1800's when it was originally set AND taken it out of London where it was originally set.

Notwithstanding my foreboding that it was not going to be worth seeing, I went along with serious doubts to see it (after all they ruined Hitch Hikers Guide to the Galaxy).

To say I was pleasantly surprised was an understatement! The transformation from journalist to caring family man was brilliant, not least because of the added angle of strained family relationships coming good under extreme pressure. Most of the threads of the original story are there. They even managed to role two of the original characters into one and make it look as if it had always been that way.

My vote? Go and see it, even if a fan of the original story. I think you too will be pleasantly surprised!

title: Spielberg does it again!
review:
Make a blockbuster hit that has no reason to be one, I mean.

When I heard that War of the Worlds was being made into a movie, I was sincerely happy. Of course, then I hear that Tommy Cruise is going to be in it and it will be directed by Steven Spielberg. Hoh boy. Bad gets worse.

Out of sheer boredom, I drag myself to the theater and plop down seven bucks to see something that I really could have done without. The movie was decent, in a general sense, when you average all of the terrible scenes with all of the really good scenes. The film had plot holes, but that's not anything to base an argument on. What we're looking for is good writing, which this movie lacked.

Through the entire hour and fifty minutes it played, I felt as if I was going to have a heart attack from all of the tension that was running through my body. "Oh noes! The Walker just came out of the ground! Where are they going to go? Oh noes! The aliens are attacking the ferry! Oh noes! The arm's coming around the doorway and it's twofeetinfrontofthegirl! Aaa!" Give me a break. If keeping the audience so absolutely afraid of everything going on is reason enough to make a good movie, then this one was fabulous.

I actually underestimated Tom Cruise, but not by much. He matured as an actor, and was certainly better than when he was in 'Minority Report', yet another superbly amazing Spielberg hit. Tom didn't have time to flash his grin much when he's supposed to be running in terror and keeping after two kids who are incredibly disobedient in a crisis situation. Tim Robbins I expected to be much better than just some random crazy that Tom Cruise kills to save his daughter from being exposed to such awful things as "We're being exterminated!" The only truly good actor was, in fact, an actress: Miranda Otto. Boy, can she carry a scene! So underused, though, sadly.

After the initial craziness of the Walker coming out of the ground, the action literally doesn't stop there. It goes on and on, but with little breaks, and then back again, so the audience can't forget that this is a scary movie. The truly underrated actors were the aliens themselves. I kept hoping for more of the scene in the basement when the aliens are looking at the pictures, giving us a glimpse into the alien psyche for just a fleeting moment. The movie plods along after that: Tom and Dakota get kidnapped, escape, and make it to Boston, somehow. There, Tom looks at a statue and decides, out of nowhere it seems, that the aliens are dying. How'd you reach that decision, Tommy? No, really. The fact that the aliens are allergic to our planet doesn't really get explained entirely until the very, very end when the Narrator busts in to unconfuse the audience. Until that time we have to sit and wonder why in the world the Walkers keep wobbling around.

All in all, the movie was a decent try for an adaptation of the novel by H. G. Wells, but fell short very early on. Too much action, too little aliens . . . hmm, sounds familiar. Independence Day, anyone? No, not to that extent, but it got close. Close enough for the movie not to be much of anything, despite how much a lot of people tried.
