title: Disappointing sci-fi dross - 53%
review:
I like to think that most film audiences receive some sort of idea about whether they're likely to enjoy a film or not. In this regard, it is perhaps understandable that although I got the DVD for Christmas, I only felt the urge to watch this updated version of H.G. Wells' classic yesterday. Alien invasion films have been around for donkeys of years but "War Of The Worlds" has that extra something, a deep-rooted sense of apocalyptic menace and hopelessness in the face of a superior enemy. I'm still traumatised by Jeff Wayne's musical version, which my Dad played for me as a kid and which may also play part of my reluctance to watch this film. But once you're used to the prevailing sense of doom, this is little more than a special effects-laden science-fiction horror but one with all the usual Spielberg sugar.

Tom Cruise plays Ray, a New York dock worker with an estranged wife (Miranda Otto) and two kids who don't really get on with him (Dakota Fanning and Justin Chatwin). After his wife drops the kids off before heading off to Boston, a strange storm captures everyone's attention. Before long, huge alien Tripods emerge from the ground and begin laying waste to everything and everyone, forcing Ray and the kids to flee in terror. As they join the large number of refugees, Ray struggles to keep his family together as the aliens continue their extermination of mankind.

I always thought Spielberg was an odd choice for director for something like this. The material is too dark for him as this is as far from "ET" as you can get. Personally, I would have liked to see David Cronenberg have a go but there you are. As it is, "War Of The Worlds" is little more than the standard familial drama but set at the end of the world. And there is no doubt that the effects are spectacular as America is (yet again) witness to destruction on a massive scale. Imagine "Twister" mixed with "Independence Day" and you're not far off. But after the initial burst of the aliens arriving, the film sags badly as they rest in the basement of trigger-happy Tim Robbins and doesn't really pick up again until the final reel. As far as acting goes, nobody really has a great deal to do but the cast scream and feign fear well enough.

It's a shame that despite the high production values and effort, there isn't really a great deal to enjoy. We've all seen endless films where mass-scale destruction is the order of the day, from "Godzilla" to "Independence Day" so watching New York getting torn up once more, there is a feeling of déjà vu. Something else that seems critically damaged was the script as there are massive gaps in logic and credibility, such as Ray finding the only car in the state that not only worked but also had the keys in the ignition and the horribly predictable ending which is so ridiculous that I immediately took a mark away on the score for that alone! "War Of The Worlds" deserved to be much better than it actually is, although there are plenty of scares and the novel's famous sense of dread is thankfully intact. But the pacing and script needed much more work and the sheer amount of effects means you find yourself wondering how much of it is simply computer graphics and how much of it is "real". It's more of a technical showpiece than a movie classic and that's a real shame, given the strength of the story.

title: Excellent Remake Of A 50's Classic
review:
With the glut of remakes currently being released nowadays, I was somewhat sceptical of seeing this new version of a film which I have loved since my early childhood. I remember also very well Jeff Wayne's Musical version and loved that as well and didn't want anything to spoil my fond memories.

I was very surprised by this film in the fact that, in a lot of ways it did stick to the original version (especially from half way through) but it also offered some great differences as well. There were also elements in the film that were apparent in the Musical version but not in the original film. All in all it was a lovely mixture of the old, new and the musical (I never read the book.) Now, most remakes I have seen I have despised, but this is the one exception. It is absolutely outstanding in many, many ways. Firstly there is the special effects - the tripods looked excellent crushing everything in their path, the death ray worked wonderfully (I just loved how the clothes from the people destroyed by the ray just fluttered down to Earth in the wind, totally unblemished - what a very novel idea I thought.) The electric storm effects were great too but the crowning glory had to be the aliens themselves - fantastic creations that looked every bit alien from the way they moved and behaved - their faces were totally obscene! One part of the movie had me in stitches, I won't say what it was but it happens about 35 minutes into this movie, it's just indicative of my type of humour.

The whole thing grabbed my intention from start to finish, quickly getting into the action which was practically non-stop all the way through.

The only thing which was a bit of a let down for me was the ending - the last scene. A little too mushy for me and a bit fairytailish.

I highly recommend this film to anyone, in my opinion it is much better than the original and I thought that the original was fantastic.

A typical Spielberg blockbuster!! 8 and half out of 10!

title: Very underrated
review: When you see a movie that is basically an effects movie you don't expect anything other then the effects with other things like plot and acting relegated to the deep, deep background. And so it would seem with this movie. However, this is far from the case. The story is the driving force with the special effects taking a second place. So as not to contain any spoilers, I will refrain from running through the various encounters that Mr. Cruise go through but when faced with some difficult decisions the easy route was not taken. To compare this movie with the awful Independence Day is like comparing The Godfather with Married to the mob but if you want just the Special effects with nothing to bother your brain then ID is the movie for you. And having said that, the effects in the movie were okay but we have seen them all before.

title: You know it's a bad film when all you want is for the aliens to kill off one of the leading characters
review:
In the film "Ed Wood", producer George Weiss admits he is not interested in making classy films, just cheap crap. Ed Wood tells him that he can get him a real star for one of his pictures to which George Weiss replies "So, you've got crap with a star".

The remake of "War of the Worlds" falls pretty much into this category, but as well as stars it has tens of millions of dollars worth of CGI effects.

Perhaps it is supposed to reflect the times with divorce rates going through the roof and one parent families mushrooming, but I am at a loss to see the relevance of this to the story. All I can say is that, in Tom Cruise's shoes, I certainly would have fought tooth and nail NOT to have custody of Dakota Fanning. Within a couple of minutes of her first opening her mouth, I was hoping against hope that this whining petulant brat would fall victim to the Martians' heat ray - and I mean Dakota Fanning, not the character she plays.

And when will film makers realise that, no matter how seamless the special effects, it's the story that counts? Only when suckers like me stop spending good money going to see their limp offerings, I suppose.

I saw the film at the cinema and was later given the DVD as a Christmas present. I haven't bothered to watch it yet. Life's too short.

title: Absolutely great movie
review:
I haven't read Wells' book. This was anyway happening in contemporary world, and some changes must have been made to the original story.

As in the other "dark" scifi films of Spielberg: "Minority Report" and "A.I.", the visuals are very beautiful and well made, just like everything else in this movie also. Spielberg must be the biggest film maker today in many ways, and in some way also the most important. He's the real mainstream voice of the world. Cruise is very good, of course, has he ever been anything else? Also Dakota Fanning, although I had some suspicions towards her, because of the "child-actor" thing. This must be her best role this far.

What was surprising to me, considering the story of the film, was that it wasn't in any way made to represent some "problems of today": The aliens aren't symbolizing anything, they're just aliens, and the horror comes from the story itself. That's a great and brave choice.

I think Spielberg has really become a movie director in the last years. His newer movies are deep, thought and important. Deep respect to him.

title: Struck By Lightning
review:
I think the only word to describe this film is: Wow. Personally I'm not a fan of Spielbergs alien-crap like E.T., A.I. and Taken, but I'm willing to make an exception for this extraterrestrial masterpiece. It all looks so realistic even though my common sense tells me it's not. The special effects are amazing of course but in my opinion they're not the reason why this movie looks so real. I expected some stupid romantic scene somewhere in the middle of the film and lots of emotional conversations, but they are very limited. There is constant action to highlight the immense cruelty and mercilessness of those Tripods (which is a ridiculous name, no wonder Scary Movie 4 makes fun of it). This movie is definitely less boring then the previously mentioned Spielberg-movies/series. And the acting is outstanding. We all know Tom Cruise and Tim Robbins are high class-actors, but even though she has an impressive filmography I'm still struck by Dakota Fanning. Someone so young acting so good, that's amazing.

War of the Worlds is definitely one to remember.

title: Frightening but great movie.
review:
I viewed this firstly on the big screen, and was on the edge of my seat! And that doesn't happen often, although it did during the heavy horse charge in Braveheart, and during Forest Gump when he was caught in the artillery bombardment.

I think it lost a bit of impact on DVD, but I found it great entertainment again, nevertheless.

The overall visual effects made this film, but that is all part of great movie making, that Steven Spielburg is - as always - brilliant. Yet the screenplay was also a unique interpretation and I think it improved on the original novel and the 1953 film. It modernised it really.

I felt Tom's character was interesting. Because it seemed to highlight his parenting ability developing during an alien catastrophe, that struck a cord with me a parent. I thought that was admirable actually and added a deeper human dimension to the screenplay and Tom's character.

Overall, I have given it no higher than 8 because I thought it was a bit gory in parts. But I loved the philosophical ending, that has a sound scientific basis. 'What hasn't evolved naturally on this planet, wasn't meant to exist or survive here'. So I hope any ET out there with an appetite for humans, sees and digests this film's message before they come and sample for themselves.

Pat

title: Some Other Flaws
review:
I'm not sure if this is a "spoiler", but be warned that it describes the ending.

These are H.G. Wells' fault, really. If the Martians buried their machines millennia ago, why didn't they just populate the earth then, when resistance-- indeed humans-- would be weak or non-existent? How could they have studied us "coldly" for, what, millions of years and been unaware of microorganisms and their possible deleterious effects? Why not activate just one of the machines, destroy, say, Washington DC, and wait a few weeks to see if things went well. You'd lose the element of surprise, but so what?

They must have been pretty confident in their superior technology. Still, to go exploring on an alien planet, in the midst of an invasion, without body armor or hand-held weapons seems foolhardy.

title: I want to hurt Steven Spielberg
review: I know people have already bashed this ending over and over, but it was so bad that I don't think the bashing should ever stop. As people have pointed out, the idea that it was a good decision by Spielberg to stay true to the ending is absurd due to the fact that there were plenty of parts of the film that were entirely Spielberg's creation. Anyway, if he had to keep the ending the same, he could have made it work and brought some resolution to the film instead of just having Morgan Freeman come on and provide us with a cheesy, pseudo-philosophical anecdote about life. I like Spielberg in general, but this film leaves you feeling about as satisfied as 45 minutes of fornication with no... you know, ending. I'm not an angry person, but this movie left me bewildered and wishing I hadn't watched it in the first place. For that, I want Steven Spielberg to sustain some type of injury, preferably from me. Thanks for your time.

title: Entertaining, yet some parts are confusing
review: I love sci-fi films, and 'War of the Worlds' is one of the best I've seen. The special effects (very important!) are great, and the scenes are finely directed. Although it's quite a wonder how the family manages to be so lucky, in the midst of all that is happening- they find a working car, a hideout, ray is saved from the suction, etc...... Anyway, the only problem I have is some of the parts are confusing..How was Robbie saved? How come Ray's ex-wife's family wasn't even hurt? How did the alien's die (I think their mothership was killed, although it didn't say so in the movie)? But all-in-all, I recommend every to watch it..:)

title: Better On a Big Screen
review:
War Of the Worlds is probably the best alien invasion film since ID4. Steven Spielberg gives you a film about RAY who is a divorced father and his ex-wife drops off her kids who don't really have a good relation ship with Ray. Then the aliens show up and Ray takes his two kids and struggles to survive the alien attack.

The special effects are the best. It was better than star wars 3 (My Opinion). The acting is great so don't see just because Tom Cruise is in it. His performance is great in this movie. Dakotoa's screaming.

IT"S THE BEST ALIEN MOVIE EVER (100/100)

title: not QUITE as bad as Independence Day
review:
But otherwise a top contender for worst movies of all time. Unlike many of you, I don't allow low-budget movies in the running. The 'worst movies of all time' contenders must be major motion-pictures, notable cast, notable director, etc. In other words, they need to have EVERYTHING going for them, and still be stupifying bleak nauseating depressing incredible failures. title: A confused retelling of a great story
review:
Filmmakers have tried to tell this story before, with limited success, and it has also been brought to musical life by Jeff Wayne's iconic musical of the 1970s. This film rates well compared to the other celluloid efforts, but it pales next to the original book and the album.

Spielberg's turgid, sloppy interpretation attempts to gain impact by associating the story more closely with the familiar world of the viewer, but lacking either the vision of the book or the grandeur and unsettling tones of the musical it falls well short of either of them.

I'd rate it as the third best of the various WOTW incarnations, slipping in ahead of the other two films (which are awful). Spielberg tries to spin the story into one of human interest, stripping it of any of it's social commentary on the nature of war and imperialism, something which could have had real resonance coming from an American filmmaker in 2005, and the result is that what we end up with is not really War of the Worlds. Instead we get a hammed-up family hug time intercut with big-budget special effects.

Basically, this story is one that could have considerable impact on the big screen, but Spielberg wussed out and gave us "WOTW lite". Notable was the absence of any US servicemen being killed or injured on screen, which was apparently a conscious decision. HG Wells wrote about a war, and a brutal one at that, in which mankind is ruthlessly slaughtered and subjugated. He wrote it to shock the ruling military power at the time, the British Empire. The sense of catastrophe and helplessness was palpable, and would have been shocking to an audience used to winning wars, as it could have been in this case. Spielberg's tripods are very cool, and moderately menacing but the aliens themselves, although they appear, serve no actual role in the story other than an excuse to squeeze in another couple of effects shots. Yawn. Again, themes and substance lose out to eye-candy, as if the two have to be mutually exclusive.

Overall, fairly disappointing. Do yourselves a favour and read the book. It's short, and maybe someone one day will finally makes a WOTW movie that lives up to it.

title: Ruined by schmaltz and bad casting
review:
The problem with making a film of 'War of the Worlds' is that your source material - H G Wells' classic sci-fi novel - is over 100 years old. Many of the concepts in the book are standard children's science fiction fare these days and have been for decades, so they lose their impact. Also, in Wells' book, the narrator is primarily an observer and diarist. He is neither a protagonist in any Hollywood sense, nor does he experience the kind of dramatic tension or conflict that a hit movie requires.

So, instead of Victorian suburban London we have modern day suburban New Jersey (or somewhere like that). This means that the invaders can't come from Mars, as Wells imagined; instead, we get an even less plausible, less fully thought-through explanation that the tripods had been buried underground for millions of years, with the aliens arriving on lightning bolts. (I'd have preferred Victorian-era Woking and huge missiles from Mars with screw-top lids, personally).

And, in addition to the simple struggle for survival that Wells describes, we have an intensely annoying plot line about Tom Cruise being a lousy parent. It makes for an unconvincing Hollywood action drama, and yet also a feeble adaptation of the original book.

Primary responsibility for destroying a project that otherwise had potential falls with Cruise himself. Acting has never been Cruise's strong suit, and his talents remain firmly within the wet paper bag from which they have been fighting to escape. We see just one of the three facial expressions he is capable of, and you are left wondering why Spielberg never explained to him that 'shouting' isn't an emotion.

With better writers, a different cast and no annoying children, this is a movie that might still be worth remaking again.

title: Spielberg's Bad ETs
review:
Steven Spielberg has always been known for his optimistic sci-fi flicks, such as Close Encounters and E.T., where nice aliens befriend humans and develop very special connections. In War of the Worlds, there's no such thing: this time, mankind has to run for its survival, as they're followed by tripods ready to incinerate them. It's like Mars Attacks!, only a lot more serious and much, much darker.

At the center of the story is Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise), a single dad who's trying to be friends with his kids (Dakota Fanning and Justin Chatwin). Too bad Earth is being attacked at the same time, which means he has to postpone the "I love you, guys" speeches and go for a more traditional, but efficient, "Let's get the hell outta here!". It's all a long escape, with visual references to other Spielberg movies like Jaws, Jurassic Park and Saving Private Ryan.

War of the Worlds is unusually dark to come from the director of Indiana Jones, and it's certainly his scariest opus since a certain water-related shocker from 1975. Like Alfred Hitchcock did with The Birds, Spielberg refuses to explain why the ETs are invading our planet. It's our reaction to that apparently pointless event and our excessive fear (the 9/11 parallels are quite obvious) that interests him. Okay, so not telling us why the war is about to begin is a wise choice when it comes to adding suspense, but it also leads to a serious plot hole towards the end of the movie, albeit one you might not notice immediately because of Spielberg's ability to keep you amazed the whole time.

Alongside the dread, another remarkable thing about War of the Worlds is the performances that two actors give: Fanning is the usual child wonder, Chatwin and Miranda Otto (who plays Ray's ex-wife) are OK and Tim Robbins is perfectly creepy and creepily perfect as the paranoid Ogilvy, who appears briefly halfway through the film. But it's Tom Cruise who deserves more attention for his very convincing portrayal of a Normal Guy: Ray Ferrier is probably as far from Ethan Hunt as he will ever get.

So, apart from a few weaknesses in the plot, War of the Worlds is a riveting blockbuster, another great Spielberg/Cruise collaboration after the superb Minority Report. Rumor has it they're planning to make a couple of other movies together (a Western would be one of the options). If they're gonna be as good as the two they've already done, it looks like a very promising cinematic future.

title: Interesting Special Effects, No Story
review:
War of the Worlds is not only Spielberg's worst movie, but the worst movie I have seen in some time. It is right up there in the running for the worst movie I have seen in the last ten years.

Wells' story has never translated well into a visual medium. The story, inherently, lacks any of the elements necessary for a movie. There is no real conflict resolution, the story just ends. While that might work with a book, where pages and pages can be spent developing the back story, it doesn't work in a movie. In this particular treatment of the story, about ten minutes is spent on character development, resulting in characters that I didn't understand and could have cared less about. After that, the movie set out to try to "wow" the audience with special effects. Unfortunately, not even those where very good.

The appearance of the "tentacles" of the alien tripods were a poor imitation of the effect first developed for the water tentacle of the alien in James Cameron's 1989 thriller, "The Abyss." The same effect was resurrected, with somewhat less success, for Luis Llosa's 1997 stinker "Anaconda." Aside from the tentacles, the alien craft - and the aliens themselves - looked more than a little like the aliens from Roland Emmerich's 1996 classic, "Independence Day."

The story is,basically, the same story as was told in "Independence Day" and Tim Burton's 1996 tongue-in-cheek "Mars Attacks." In those movies, though, the story consisted of more than just a series of almost totally unrelated and entirely contrived scenes of the heroes, (in this case, Tom Cruise and Dakota Fanning, who, hopefully, will recover from this film and go on to make more movies with actual plots, characters and stories), running from the monsters. There was, essentially, nothing that connected any of the scenes in "War" to each other. Most of the scenes didn't even make sense - If the monsters are attacking cities, why would you run towards New York City? The monsters are flattening everything in their wake, why hide in a basement? - and seemed to be contrived to show off some novel special effect.

There were more plot holes than I care to count - If the electromagnetic pulse destroyed the electrical circuits, it is unlikely any car could ever be made operative, yet they find one car that they can drive off in. If the aliens were smart enough to plant the tripods millions of years ago, how come they weren't smart enough to figure out how to protect themselves from earth bound viruses? How come, at the end, when the ex-wife and the parents walk out of their charred house in Boston, they look like they just stepped out of a GQ spread when the rest of the world around them is in ruins? For that matter, how did the Cruise and Fanning characters even make it to Boston, not to mention the Chatwin character? And, finally, why is the reason the aliens died only explained by the narrator after the end of the movie?

I was not particularly impressed with the special effects, as a whole. There were some good ones, like the bridge exploding at the beginning of the film. However, because their was no story, no plot and no characters that anyone could care about, the special effects were left to carry the film. Given the film, it is hard to imagine that any special effects could have carried it. If I had been Industrial Light and Magic or Stan Winston, I would have been embarrassed to have my name associated this movie. Both ILM and Stan Winston have done much better and, in nearly all cases, their effects could have been used in movies that were much better.

For Spielberg's sake, I hope "Munich" is much better. But, then, it would be hard for it to be worse.

title: An excellent action-packed adaptation.
review:
After a rather disappointing year of movies, War of the Worlds seemed to make everything better again.

Having expected an OK action film I was quite surprised how good WoTW was. Not only worth the price of admission but the kind of film an action movie junkie would want on DVD.

Starting at a slow pace the action soon picks up as a worldwide catastrophic storm hits America causing mass blackouts and panic. However the EMP damage was soon to be the least of everyone's concerns. Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise) finds himself in the middle of the carnage when he goes to inspect the site of which lightning struck many times. What he didn't know is that what lurks underground is about to let hell break loose.

War of the Worlds is a very 'personalised' film. The action is focused entirely around Ray's point of view as he and his children Robbie (Justin Chatwin) and Rachel (Dakota Fanning)escape the city and venture into the countryside (or sub-urban surroundings).

After the first sighting of the tripods (the alien war machines) the action is fluent and very regular ranging from masses of people running for their lives to the military effort against the machines.

However be advised; if you want a film which challenges intellectually then look elsewhere. WoTW is a 'no-brainer' type of movie in which all you need to do is turn off and enjoy.

One thing I'd definitely recommend is try and see this in the cinema (although all showings have probably stopped now). War of the Worlds works best with a giant screen and digital surround sound - having these two things really makes you feel you're right there beside Ray in the middle of the action. TV just doesn't work as nicely.

8/10

title: Questions
review:
This film was worse than WaterWorld and worse than my Ukrainian grandmother singing in the shower. Yes, worse.

There is not much more I can add that many, many people have already commented upon, but there are a few questions I pose about the continuity:

1) A jumbo jet crashes on a house, does anyone care? No really, if a jet goes down, it make a pretty big mark on the ground. Dirt gets pushed around, fuel spilled, lots of flames and dead bodies everywhere. None of this is seen, why? Even the seats of the plane are uncharred and... empty! The whole plane?

2)What sane person would board a slow moving ferry when 200 meter tall alien war machines are walking (each step more than a city block is covered) towards you firing death rays?

3)And speaking of which... death rays? And why bury an attack vessel on the planet? Wanna take out a planet; you pitch one mile-wide asteroid at it and stand back and wait. Heck, history shows what it did to the dinosaurs. Much more efficient... and practical... and logical.

4)Why would any first rate writer, director, or actor (if there was one on this set - sorry Tom, you can't act or emote) place a the main plot (I've got to get to Boston.... for what?) above the the obvious plot (I have to survive)? Moreover, why elevate the "family dynamics" plot even higher? You've got to be kidding?! My two year old wouldn't believe that.

5)What the heck was that farmhouse scene about? No really, Tim Robbins holding up a shotgun and shouting to Tom "This way, this way", with thousands of people running around in terror, in the middle of the night? And he catches Tom's attention? Wow.....

6)The Original WOTW scared a generation and set the standard for movies to startle and challenge generations of movie-goers to come. Uhhhhh, I cannot even fathom where to begin with comparing that with WOTW 2005.

7)The whole EMP thing has been beaten to death and though I'd love to add a few whips, I really can't add more than a guffaw or two.

8)Tom driving along the highway.... and doesn't hit anybody or anything? Thousands of aimlessly wandering people (oops, that's right, they are going to.... Boston) on the highways, cars scattered, inoperable everywhere and he still manages to avoid everything? And doing so without any of the drama of his Mission Impossible motor bike stunts. More like he was driving the kids to Sunday school (or, say, Boston).

9)Ok, the gun scene where the crowd takes his mini-van. Like Tom and one other person are the only citizens to carrying firearms 'as the world is being invaded by aliens'. As a Canadian, even I laughed out loud at the thought of American citizens running around during an alien invasions, well, like a bunch of unarmed Canadians.

10)I am also amazed at how stupid the crowd is. There was an earlier comment, with kudo's to the original poster, which stated 'even a herd of sheep would have better survival instincts'. That said, and I agree, it is amazing that the crowd was organized well enough to.... post "missing" notices all over the city... like the invasion started months or years ago. In "Stalingrad" ("Enemy at the Gates") the "missing" posters were believable. In WOTW, well...., apparently an EMP will not disrupt the local Kinko's or Business Depots and everyone will be able to run off a few copies of "missing posters".

11)Lastly (only because I lack the time to go on), how is it that some people thoroughly liked this film? Including my brother, who is 39, and encouraged me to see it? I would sooner press an icecube into my eye than watch this film again - even for a laugh factor, it's not worth it.

title: Bored of the World
review:
Thanks goodness I didn't go to the movies to see this shallow horror of a film. From the ridiculous arrival of the Martians (They buried these huge honking war machines underground and no one found them? Not bloody likely) to the casting of Tom "Gee, don't I look good in every scene" Cruise as the protagonist this movie has nothing to recommend it. In the extras one of the screenwriters tells us that it was Spielberg's idea to have the Martian war machines buried, to give it a new twist. Apparently Spielberg doesn't remember classic sci-fi like "5 Millions Years to Earth." The science in the film was laughable. An example is the EM pulse that knocks out everything except for one camera right next to where the first Martian machine comes out of the ground. Can you say "Plot Hole?" Character wise we found ourselves cheering for the Martians to come. There was nothing likable about Cruise's character. As much as I hate to pick on a kid who was probably following some very misguided direction, Dakota Fanning's impression of a 10 year old going on 5 was a scream - I mean her screaming every five minutes about the Martians, lightning, finding some lint on her sweater got old very quickly and made us want to scream.

You could also see the points in the film where Tom probably went to Spielberg and said "I'm not doing that, this is what I want." One example is how incredibly clean his face and hair are all through the film, despite the destruction of everything around him. Another was his destruction of the Martian war machine - thousands of soldiers all over the place and the only one who thinks of packing a grenade is a loser with a good hairdo. Right.

I have to say though that the same scene also was the movie's only redeeming point. I wonder if Tom and/or Spielberg realize just how much fun it was on many levels to see Tom struggling to get out of the rectum of the Martian war machine. Intended satire or incredible short sightedness? You make the call.

This film is right down there with another sci-fi gem - "Battlefield Earth" and threatens to push "Plan Nine From Outer Space" out of the worst sci-fi movie ever if you take budget into account.

title: Unrealistic plot; disappointing of Spielberg
review:
OK... without giving too much away, I want to say right off: Why is this movie based on the Orwell novel? It has no real relation to the novel in that the novel occurred completely on the radio with no actual 'alien' attack, but a perceived attack by the American public. This movie depicted an actual fictional alien attack on the world.

Next, why did Tom Cruise drive home form work in a '67 Mustang (which, by the way would not have been affected by what the Earthlings thought were sunspots (because it has no electronic ignition)), yet the vehicle he chose to rescue his family in was a Plymouth Voyager van which is renowned for electronics for everything on board and has significant electronic problems to this day on REAL Earth?! i.e.- Why did HIS car work, when he was driving past all of these vehicles on the road that had failed electronically?

Also, there was no explanation as to why the 'wierdo guy' living in his basement, who motioned for Cruise and his daughter to come and stay with him did so. Was it just by chance that they happened (out of the twelve million or so people passing by) to catch his attention?

Additionally, the military (with all their faults) DID HAVE weaponry apparently capable of taking down these 'things'. Why not take out their legs so as to make them immobile? An immobile threat is a threat that can be easily contained. Instead, they kept shooting at the body of the creatures (which eventually DID work) but not nearly as effectively (Bush must have been in charge in the background).

Last, a technologically advanced race such as the one that attacked, surely must have been prepared for some sort of warfare, especially if they had been watching for so long (as one actor put it, "for hundreds of years"). Two simple grenades lodged in just the right place puts the entire pod out of operation? Surely, these beings, intelligent enough to hide pods underground for centuries, travel through eons of time/space, and use what is apparently microwave beams to destroy everything in their path would have a 'safe room' in their ship in which to examine and/or dissect humans, that would not be susceptible to explosion or resistance.

OK, finally, Spielberg made ET many years ago and even then the graphics were great. Only ONE alien was actually shown, which was the one who came out of the downed ship and it was a poor excuse for a Spielberg alien. Come on already! It didn't even put up a fight!

Then at the end of the movie, the voice (which I believe was Lawrence Fishburn's (a great choice, much like James Earl Jones was for Star Trek and other fantastic movies)), sums everything up in an instant, telling the viewer how the invaders were ultimately killed by, apparently the smallest of organisms, which humans had become immune to over the centuries, indicating that the aliens begun dying from 'the moment they set foot on the planet and began partaking of our food and water'. Again, if these beings were intelligent enough to do all that they did, why would they eat and drink of Earth substances that they surely would have know were deadly to them. Come on!

Sorry to spoil your fun. Great movie and great idea. Poor planning and research. Tom Cruise, although I did not find him the actor for the part, performed well. The little girl (his daughter) was fantastic for her age. The son, well, his whole behavior was a mystery.

review:
Usually i enjoy the work of Spielberg,but not this time. I totally agree with tieman64's review about Spielbergs new "eye",but it doesn't save this one. The story is wafer thin,and doesn't carry a feature film. It's much more suited for TV,as the "Tales of the Unexpected" by Roald Dahl in the late 70's. I still don't get the purpose of the alien invasion.

Often enough with Hollywoodfilms,a couple of big names ie Spielberg,Cruise and Tim Robbins guarantees money back.And then some. It's all about the hype! I saw "The Day of the Triffids" on TV in the mid 80's,and it made a lot more sense.

title: A waste of time and money.
review: I was surprised to find that this film was incredibly ill-made. I would expect much more from a seasoned director like Steven Spielberg and a well-known lead actor like Tom Cruise. The four actors with the most screen time (Tom Cruise, Dakota Fanning, Justin Chatwin and Tim Robbins) all delivered half-hearted displays of acting. The plot was neither solid nor very true to the book. The writing was mediocre. The characters were shallow and poorly imagined. The film was also filled with inconsistencies and plot holes. For example, the 3-legged alien walkers were supposedly buried underground for a million years. Anything, even something made of mysterious "alien metal" would decay to the point of being unusable, if not non-existent, over the course of a million years. It was the many small mistakes and inaccuracies that made this film unbearable. The only thing that made me give this anything better than a 1 were the special effects, which were rather nice to look at. DO NOT BOTHER.

title: Great CGI, but weak story and acting
review:
There are scenes in the movie that would surely leave a lasting impression: e.g., a barren landscape filled with gloom and blood, giant tripods destroying whatever in sight. The CGI-induced atmosphere is often fantastic.

But characters are either underdeveloped or too conveniently stereotyped in the movie. What's with the son's ridiculously immature attitude? The constant screaming of Fanning Dakota's character is almost cartoonish.

Moreover, Fanning Dakota seems to be over-acting. And Tom Cruise in this movie is more reminiscent of his character in Minority Report or Mission Impossible than a redeeming father.

The family subplot in the movie is clichéd, which is actually okay given the focus of the movie. But I had expected more story-telling about the aliens' plans and the governments' responses, which of course are conspicuously absent in the movie. In the end, the movie feels like a uni-dimension bad dream, which is remembered far more for the fear it strikes in the visual sense than for most other things one would expect a good movie should deliver.

title: Worst movie EVER!!!!!
review: I absolutely hated this film and cannot believe that I wasted my time watching it. For one, I despise Cruise, I wanted to smack the little girl for all that screaming and what the heck was the boy thinking when he took off, did he think he could save the world?? This movie made no sense at all, the part where Cruise was being pulled into the thing and the people were able to pull him out w/o dislocating his arm was just plain dumb. If I could rate this film a minus something, I would. Whatever was Spielberg trying to do when he decided to make this film, and why was the "alien" just in one location and wasn't it just brilliant that the soldiers could eradicate all of them just like that???

title: What A Waste!
review: I was as angry after watching this film as I was after watching Spielberg's other big blunder,The Lost World.There is absolutely nothing in this movie to suggest that it has been made by arguably the greatest film director of all time (and someone who I hold in high esteem,regardless of this misfire).After the first half hour of spectacular pyrotechnics,the film completely runs out of steam.A lot of it is based indoors - in rooms,basements and cellars and whenever we do go outside,its just more of what we've already been served earlier.All characters are strictly cardboard and the running time is stretched at least a half hour too long.Knowing the production history of the film(it was greenlit in an emergency when Spielberg suddenly had nothing on his platter and Cruise had delayed filming MI:3 due to the non-availability of his first choice director J.J.Abrams),I guess one shouldn't really be surprised with the lack of content.Its just sad to see talent as mighty as this deliver a product of such mediocrity.

title: possibly one of the worst movies I have ever seen
review:
*likely to contain a spoiler* If this movie weren't so over-rated I would almost feel sorry for it. It is one of those movies that seems to earnestly try to be exciting, dramatic, and entertaining...and fails to be any of them.

The "excitement" comes from the impending threat of aliens invading the town of Tom Cruise and his two estranged children. "Drama" abounds as they steal a car, have it stolen from them, ride on a really crowded boat, have the brooding son leave them (for virtually no reason), hide in a hole and on and on.... "Entertainment" comes from, well...

"War of the Worlds" does not prove to be that entertaining of a movie. The closest thing coming to viewing pleasure is pointing out the ASTONISHING lack of plot and character development (a woman named Carol and her daughter Nora are "introduced" when getting on the boat. There is no room for Carol to get on the boat. Carol is never seen or mentioned again...); the poor pacing, the amateurish lighting choice, the fact that the "aliens roaming the basement" scene was right out of "Jurassic Park (only it was kind of scary then); the fact that the aliens are not frightening in the absolute LEAST (the little silver eye..thing that scanned the basement practically looked like a happy face, and the "sick" alien could almost be described as cute)and on and on...

In short: there is nothing about this movie I found well-done. The grade-Z sci fi channel movies are literal MASTERPIECES in comparison... and yet, those remain relegated as kitschy grade-Z films, while this so-called blockbuster bizarrely gets fawned over, for reasons absolutely...alien to me.

title: Four stars for the special effects, zero for everything else
review:
Well, what can you say about a movie like this? The special effects were great. The whole beginning of the movie is quite suspenseful and exciting, due entirely to the effects.

As far as everything else, like acting, story, etc., there's just nothing there. Cruise hardly gives a performance at all, he's just Joe Anybody, not having the least bit of personality other than what we're supposed to intuit from the fact that he drives (surprise!) a hot car. But I guess that basically is the limit of his personality in anything he's ever been in. His ex-wife is the stereotypical shrew, his son is obnoxious and utterly undisciplined, and his daughter, well, his daughter screams into the camera in a manner that should be enough to empty every theater in the country. She's also extremely dumb for her age - her dialogue seems more suited to a toddler than a pre-teen.

The story doesn't really exist. Aliens invade, everybody runs away and hides, eventually the aliens just drop dead on their own. If you're renting this on DVD, feel free to fast forward through any part that doesn't involve special effects - I guarantee you won't miss a thing. It's unfortunate that since this is a remake, they didn't come up with some way of foreshadowing the death of the aliens, so as to give some forward momentum to the story leading up to the conclusion, but that would of course take a combination of creativity and cleverness. Perhaps they should have given the job to the people at the special effects house, since they seem to be the only folks involved in the picture who had either of those two qualities..

Overall, a somewhat below average "big dumb summer blockbuster". Lots of cool special effects, characters that exist solely to run around and give the aliens something to shoot at, and...well, there you have it.

title: does spielberg think we're idiots?
review: i was absolutely disappointed with this movie... special effects were cool, dakota fanning is irritating & an awful actress in this film, & i am soooooooooooo tired of tom cruise... i have a huge problem with the movie, can anyone explain this for me?... maybe i am an idiot... but, after the aliens blow out everything running on batteries or electricity w/ emp's (electric magnetic pulses), one guy is taking pictures with a digital camera (ran on batteries), another is filming it with a digital camcorder (ran on a battery), then miraculously, tom cruise's escape minivan (also uses battery power) is up & running w/ a new solenoid (just in time)... obviously steven spielberg thinks we're idiots... that first 15 minutes of the movie ruined the rest of it for me... not even rental worthy... glad i didn't see it at the theater, i only wasted $3 renting it.

title: In like an injured lion; out like a lamb.
review:
War of the Worlds: **

War of the Worlds, adapted from HG Wells classic novel of the same name, starts out as an interesting semi original take on the alien attack genre with a few flaws. Dakota Fanning(Rachael) shows up for what seems like her millionth movie in about 3 days, playing Tom Cruise(Ray)'s daughter. Both Fanning and her on screen brother Robbie (Justin Chatwin)are extremely annoying in their characters which may or may not be on purpose, but either way, both come across as scripted and I never once felt involved enough to care about them because it was impossible to even pretend that they were real their dialog was so wooden. This, and a few other flaws (why the hell did that camera still work?) are relatively minor and I was still able to enjoy what was on screen. I thought the concept used, the migrations and evacuee scenes or confusion and disorder were very interesting. It's display of panic and chaos serves as a perfect companion to 'Signs' (which was a much better film overall) which took the micro approach of one family isolated in their basement over the macro approach here.

Thats about as far as I can go with praise. The first 2/3s were OK, and at least interesting, the last third was utter rubbish. Spielberg has made some pretty good films, though I wouldn't consider many of them at all to be overly intelligent rather than Hollywood extravaganzas, with some exceptions of course (my personal Spielberg favorite is Empire of the Sun). I consider him a good director...but I think he is overrated. Some filmmakers you know are going to deliver something at the very least good to you every time: Terrence Malick, Werner Herzog, Robert Altman, Scorcese, Wenders, etc)unfortunately Spielberg is, to me, not one of those directors. I initially had high hopes after seeing the teaser trailer, but the more i learned about the direction the film would go the less my expectations were. Unfortunately, the film wasn't able to even meet with my lowered expectations. We're given nothing more than a summer blockbuster filled with stupidity, ambiguity, tons of plot holes, and such unrealistic situations and reactions that we should be able to ignore, because it is after all a movie, but are unable to overcome. There is the seemingly pointless death of Tim Robbins' character (Cruise and Fanning are making a lot of noise throughout these scenes as well. Robbins has quieted down by this point) and the clichéd 'I thought you died in that massive explosion/inescapable situation but here you are at the finishing line anyway without any explanation of how you defied physics and all logic' cop out. The son, Robbie, and his actions and motives are clear, yet unclear at the same time- not to mention overly clichéd as well. So many things in this movie so obviously don't make sense that it was impossible for me to look back at it and say that it was worth it. If you want to pay, watch the first 2/3's, then hit the road you'll be satisfied with your transaction. It won't matter that you didn't' see the ending, because if you did you would not be satisfied. You're better off reading the last half of Wells' novel (infact you're much better off reading the book and avoiding the movie altogether).

'War of the Worlds' comes in like an lion (an injured one-still has some bite in him) but closes out like a lamb- the final product is weak and very, very flawed- but if you're out there just looking for some dumb action and fun, you'll enjoy it. Myself, I'm not just looking for such films: If i want to see dumb, mindless action, I'll turn on my TV and see it for free. The only thing that saves this movie from getting a failing grade is the decent first two thirds. Nonetheless, it gets a thumbs down.

5/10.

title: Aliens invade earth for the umpteenth time etc., etc...
review:
Entertainment is supposed to be entertaining. One imagines that Spielberg and Company had some free time in their busy schedule and decided to quickly remake a perfectly good film. The original movie, made in 1953, diverges from the book by H.G. Wells but is still a great movie with a great script, filmed in beautiful color and populated with interesting characters who act out the story in an unpredictable fashion. Even the special effects are superb.

The new version is closer to the book but lacks color and the ending is not only predictable but dull. I kept hoping that the aliens would win because the earthlings behaved so stupidly. Every time Cruise tells his son or daughter not to wander off, I knew that they would wander off and cause him great grief, which they continually did.

The music score by John Williams is forgettable. The casting is uninspired, the acting is wooden, the characters poorly written and the over-all tone of the movie is dark and dirty and depressing, not entertaining in the least.

The story is not completely thought out, the special effects are disappointing and the aliens do not get adequate screen time. Many aspects of this film appear to be borrowed from a number of other sci-fi movies.

I think that a lot of women really like Cruise because they find him physically attractive, but as an actor he lacks the ability to project emotion. Dakota Fanning is equally over rated and cries throughout the film until eventually I just wished she'd be eaten by the aliens, who may or may not be from Mars. Justin Chatwin, who plays Cruise's son, does not integrate well into the cast, vanishes a little over half way through the film, and is assumed to have been killed only to miraculously reappear at the end of the film, no explanations offered.

In my humble opinion the only indication that Spielberg had a hand in making this movie is his name in the credits.

title: Worst Movie Of The Year
review: Okay, the kid's acting wasn't bad, but other than that, there's nothing to like about this movie. I laughed out loud when Cruise's character placed a mirror in front of the creature and it actually fooled the creature into leaving. Come on! These are supposed to be brilliant aliens? And they don't know the mirror trick? And we didn't see it coming? And oh gosh, the ending? I thought for a second I'd dozed off, because all of a sudden it was simply over, without any resolution other than the kid being reunited with her mother. I am tired of these cheesy movies and I cannot believe that the viewing audiences don't see through all this crap.

title: Well done Mr. Spielberg. Another enormous budget movie, well made, but for children
review:
The movie is good entertainment.

Contains spoiler!

Although it begins very interesting, the effects are great, the revealed secret is not such a big deal.

Am I the only one who wondered how come a superior race, which planned the extermination of the human race 1 million years ago and buried their destruction machines underground, on Earth, "forgot" to test the environment on Earth so they would be able to survive when attacking? And with such superior machines, untouchable by man, while in middle of annihilation the bad guys (the aliens) suddenly get ill and die because they couldn't adapt to the environment on Earth?!

It might have been believable in 1930 but today it's at least silly...

I was expecting something else from this movie, considering the beginning, the story.

title: this movie sucked out loud
review: the only thing that this movie had going for it were the computer graphics. I swear to god tom cruise spent most of the movie running around with his screaming child. this experience can be replicated by either going to day care center and watching the kids run around at recess or going to the special Olympics. No amount of special effects is going to change that HG Wells is not a good author. he just isn't and nothing is going to change that. this story is particularly bad because it is anti-climatic the aliens get the sniffles and die. it is like he got wrote himself into a corner towards the end of the book and needed a way out. which may be fine for a book but it is amplified in the movie. I tell ya I am damn glad that I did not waste money to go see this in the theater.

title: Terrible tribute to the story
review:
Where as this film had good cgi (duh that's all Spielberg cares about anymore), its choice of actors and little flaws in the film made this movie terrible, but because it's Spielberg nobody notices yet because he's always been so good.

first of all, TOM CRUISE???!?! he's a terrible actor! horrible father portrayer. secondly, what was with that camera? i thought all electronics were not supposed to be working. and i love how the debris that surrounded the untouched house they crashed at the first night, had a neatly laid path for them to drive down as they went into the next scene.

even funnier, is how the aliens looked like rip-offs of the aliens from independence day, which ID4 is actually a rip-off of War of the worlds to begin with! what a tangled web we weave...

Dakota fanning was good, of course, and the cgi was great, like i said, but nothing more. even john williams' score was rushed through, no emotion or effort put in it. someday people will realize that spielberg is getting too old to know how to make movies. he was my idol, but his movies just aren't the same anymore. i think it all started with AI...what was with that one? ~Leo

title: War of the Wrolds or Dumb and Dumber?
review:
I had high hopes for this movie directed by Steven Spielberg. I thought a genius like him would bring some intelligence and credibility to the Science Fiction genre. To my dismay, War of the Worlds was worse than the 1953 version. Tom Cruise does a fair job at acting and the special effects are nice but that is all there is. There is one scene with an alien probe inside a basement that was done very well but that's about it.

Nothing is explained in this movie. After the action there is only a little information on what the aliens want and why they're attacking us to get it. They want human blood to fertilize their plants they brought with them. It would seem that an alien race with enough intelligence to build force fields and space ships would be able to do a few more things. Things like examine what in the blood makes the plants grow and create it, hell if we stupid humans can do this, why can't an advanced space faring race?

Oh and the humans in the movie are pretty stupid too. Well all except for Tim Robins character, a loony survivalist that utters the smartest line in the movie. "They must have weaknesses and we need to find them." Anyone with a lick of sense would see that those things are walking on very long legs and they're hitting the ground. Common sense would tell you the legs aren't protected by shields so shoot them with the tanks and missiles. If they couldn't figure that out at least they could have tried tactical nuclear weapons. But no they were too dumb.

Watch this movie only if you like special effects. Oh, and check your brain at the door.

Rayvyn

title: Craptacular! (SPOILERS)
review:
(SPOILERS)

All good things about this movie:

The visual effects and imagery. The bookend narrations by Morgan Freeman

A few of the bad things about this movie:

Tripods underground. Awful dialog. Annoying Rachael. Moron Robbie. In-laws and their home completely unharmed. Robbie survives.

Rampant stupidity: Who goes to a major population center like Boston when the world is being destroyed? Who drives into a mob when you have the only functioning vehicle for miles around? Who gets ON a ferry when the tripods are bearing down on the landing? Who walks TOWARDS the sounds and flashes of a large battle?

Volumes could be written about the two brats, but I'll just leave it at Annoying Rachael and Moron Robbie.

Why does the tripod shield go down when the crew gets sick?

The Dolby Digital sound track on the DVD sounds thin and muted and/or range-compressed.

title: Disappointing
review:
I was really hoping that Spielberg had done justice to the classic book by HG Wells and brought it up to date, but unfortunately this is just a shambles of a film that you will be wishing was over about half way through. The book has been mangled beyond recognition into something that is typical big budget Hollywood cinema fodder. Once the ending comes you just feel relieved that it's over.

So what's wrong with it? Well there's a number of things...

First of all the kids. I know it's one of Spielberg's trademarks, but really, this film would have been so much better without them. The youngest (Dakota Fanning) is a screaming little brat of a girl who you wish would just be atomised by the aliens at the very beginning. She screams and shouts her way through the film and it's difficult to feel anything but annoyance at the amount of screen time she's given.

The older child is just as annoying. He fulfils the obligatory part of male moody teenager. Not only does this moron go off driving his father's car in the middle of the night he also does possibly one of the most stupid things possible. He wanders, unarmed, into the centre of a gigantic fight between the army and the alien invaders because "it's his destiny". Tom Cruise, ever the useless father figure, lets his son go, and by now you will be hoping that the useless kid has gone for good, but no, he miraculously survives everything and reappears at the end. Can I just mention that there were no kids in the original film.

What else, well the special effects are completely overused, the film stalls at a scene in the middle in an underground house for what feels like a month (yes, it's painfully long) and the ending is abrupt and unsatisfactory. I could go on but you get the idea. Do yourself a big favour and go and read the book instead.

title: awful
review:
i sat down yesterday to watch a couple of dvds since i had the day to myself and was bored!the two movies in question were, its a wonderful life and war of the worlds. the first of these movies being a truly great masterpiece did not help my first impressions of the second!

from the first moment we get to meet the characters, tom cruise plays a typical cruise character, supposedly humorous and laid back, the daughter who is played by dakota someone who plays the same role that she plays in every movie, a little girl who is too intelligent for her age, and finally the stupidest character in the movie, the son!the son who is just so annoying and adds nothing but hate and anger to this movie!

the aliens come, blow up the place as aliens always seem to do in these movies, and then die!nobody knows why they are dying but good old morgan takes about 20 seconds at the end to explain to us!

so many scenes were annoying for me, the scenes as they escaped in the car, the words "this is your space, you own it" will annoy me for a long time! the scene in the basement where they really did milk the alien interest in that house!why were two of those machines sent down to look for anyone living in that house?why were 4 aliens then sent down to look?after finding nothing both times why was another machine sent in to look?i suppose they knew that there was a good chance for a high profile kidnapping down there, i mean its not every day that you get the chance to kidnap tom cruise! what about the ending too?how come the whole family survived this?i would say that 90% of the population were killed but both kids, tom, the wife and hubby and the grandparents all survive?and unharmed?haha and just what was the son trying to do by chasing the army?he wasn't going to get involved with the fighting so why was he so eager?he was the most annoying character, always being a petulant bore and then to add insult he survives! then when the boat capsizes, this little girl survives being thrown into the ocean, waves over her head, ice cold water etc and she is fine?

terrible terrible terrible!

title: quick comment
review: I'm currently writing a paper comparing this movie to the 1953 version, and while I could list all the reasons why this one is SO unoriginal and so TEXTBOOK Spielberg, I'd like to quietly point out that this version is ruined from the get-go. Does anyone recall Tim Robbins saying something like "they've been here a million years... we're done." So the aliens were in parts of the world before humans were huh? Aliens been preparing for this and studying us and the earth for millenia? Funny how they completely missed the microbiology on this planet. Guess a million years wasn't long enough to figure that one out.

title: H.G. Wells and Orsen Wells turn over in their graves with this one
review:
This is one movie out of principal should be avoided. If you have not seen this movie yet, please do not bother to rent, buy or even tune in on cable or sat TV. If you have to see how bad it is or more so insulting, download it from the internet for free.

Between the two mega egos they ruined a good novel's story line, and the various adaptations of the novel for radio and screen, this is a sad representation. Cruise's and Spielberg's self centered ego's have come together in to a massive effort to ruin a great story/plot line.

Cruise has done to this story what he did to the Mission Impossible story line. As time goes on I wonder if there will be a screen wide enough to fit his head on.

If you have seen the 1953 version or even listened to the original radio broadcast, if not I suggest you make a effort to do so, you will understand what I mean. This attempt of a remake in no way portrays people at their best nor even attempts to portray what people should strive for. It is an insult to the previous efforts and the original authors efforts.

This type of movie I swear is one of the problems with our modern world as it does not give us strong images to look up too as we had in the movies prior to the 1970's. Even the propaganda films of WWII where better.

If you have seen this film was there any portrayal by any of the cast that made you feel better or want to strive for or want your kids to strive for in later year? There are no heros in this movie. well maybe the bacteria.

I had to watch this movie 5 times to finally get thru it, because I was bored or just plain disgusted. Cruise is far from a hero in this movie, don't expect anyone else in the movie to even have a chance at being one either. The closest scene is when his son wants to join a military column and Cruise tries to stop him. Cruise's dialog with his pleas and excuses sounded as though Jane Fonda wrote it and the son was wanting to go off to Vietnan, not wanting to fight back at a threat, defending hearth and home. The logical dialog for this scene should have been the argument he was needed more to save his sister and get her to Boston then he could go off and fight. Gee but loyality and commitment to family first is a not a PC idea anymore. All Cruises dialog did was to show him as weak and not worth respect or leadership status.

The son in this film showed the only courage and backbone in the whole film. If Cruise was my dad in the movie and I was his son, think I would have decked him took my sister and made for Boston leaving him behind.

As for the daughter played by Dakota, well she was just plain annoying, based upon Cruise's performance it was a understandable performance. Of course a child will loose it in a situation like this when the adult in her life is weak, selfcentered, and a failed role model who even fails to rise to the situation.

All she did thru the whole movies was act like a spoiled brat, screaming (easy dialog) to the point even if I was her father I would have at the least backhanded her, or dumped her out the door and let the aliens have her. I sure found myself cheering on the aliens in this aspect, just to shut her up. I can understand panic in a young child but not being strong willed and showing strength doesn't give a child something to draw strength from to deal with the danger around them.

Again, a good movie should inspire strength, leadership, and hope. All this move inspired was weakness, hesitation, panic and despair. Every film with conflict or strife should have it's John Wayne, Clint Eastwood, or William Holden.

If this movie is to portray human beings in a good light it failed, if this movie is to do justice to earlier efforts of the story it failed. If this is the best that can be done and this is what we are, then maybe we deserve aliens to come and dine on us.

Avoid this flick and don't add to Spielberg's and Cruise's ego nor their bank accounts until they have produced something of worth and inspiration.

If your into weak willed, poltical correctness, lack of inspiration and seeing people at their worst, then it is the film for you.

title: Aliens that have been living underground before humans ruled the earth. Now they have come up to rule planet earth.
review: The mean idea of the movie isn't that bad. But the part that i didn't like at all was the ending. All the special effects and all the obstacles Tom goes through make the viewer think that the ending is going to be incredible. But the ending was horrible. I felt like asking for my money back. The aliens that are tons of years more advanced than us in technology don't think of checking out what our atmosphere is like?? What kind of invading army doesn't think about how they are going to breathe in the planet they are invading??? The ending seemed to me as if they were tired and thought of a quick way to end the movie. I really respect Spielberg for all his work and he is the only reason why i payed to watch this movie but the ending really disappointed me.

title: Like having sex with a turkey

title: Sound and fury
review:
"War of the Worlds" is largely a reversion to a Fifties Sci-Fi scare movie, with far more splendid and real-looking effects but less of a world-view or point than those earlier things had. These silly pod creatures, with their various pod-offspring or excrescences, that all wither away like the aliens at the end of Shyamalan's "Signs" -- allergic to terrestrial microorganisms instead of H2O -- if they're such superior beings, how come they have to go out and mow down humans one by one? To scare us in an old-fashioned way, must be the answer. But there is no time allowed to speculate as to their purpose (other than extermination) since all Tom Cruise and his two children do is flee -- to mama. But to get back to the creatures on vast spindly stilts: if they're so menacing and powerful, why can't they find three people in a basement (where Tim Robbins helps provide the movie's most tedious minutes)? The screenplay of War of the Worlds is contemptible; but the effects, especially in the big crowd scenes and when some New Jersey streets are crumbling, are terrific. Some of the simple desperation of cheaper, but more human end-of-the-world movies like Michael Haneke's recent "Hour of the Wolf" is evoked as Cruise's son Robbie (Justin Chatwin) and daughter Rachel (Dakota Fanning) are almost whisked away in a darkened field and a crowd struggles to get onto a ferryboat. The end is as lame as that of Roland Emmerich's "The Day After Tomorrow," whose trajectory it much resembles: going home to mama resolves the problem of a wrecked planet.

Spielberg has always used children, sometimes in heartrending, sometimes in purely manipulative ways. This time he begins with a divorced couple with shared custody and a contrast of class and attitude. Ray Ferrier (Cruise) is a surly construction worker, macho and uncooperative on the job, unable to bother with his little girl and young teenage son who're deposited with him on weekends by his ex-wife Mary Ann (Miranda Otto), who's off to her parents' in Boston. The world erupts when freak electric storms herald an invasion of monsters out of the earth which destroy much -- but not all! -- around the holes they emerge from with horrific blasts of sound. So Ray and the two kids don't have to decide how to spend the weekend. They go on an expedition -- in (wonder of wonders) the only car for miles around that runs after the storms (it was the solenoids--smart Ray to think of it!) -- first to the big McMansion Mary Ann occupies with her new husband in a posh suburb, then when that turns into a war zone over night, on to grandpa and grandma's place in Boston. Heroically inclined Robbie runs off in a field -- presumably to join the army at fourteen -- but is at the grandparents when Ray gets there: wonder of wonders! Little Rachel (perhaps the braver of the two) stays to weather Tim Robbins' dialogue in that dank basement.

Tom Cruise hasn't had a good role other than "Collateral's" nihilist hit man -- which was a very good one, in a beautifully crafted movie -- in years. In "War of the Worlds," he's been accused of sentimentalizing his character, playing for our sympathy when he began as a prick. This is a misreading of the screenplay, which has this quite natural progress toward caring for his kids built into it; this isn't Cruise's betrayal of his role. He's okay, but he has nothing to deal with. He hardly deserves credit for not hamming it up. It's not a sure thing that he knows how to ham it up. Dakota Fanning is excellent. She takes us through a lot of emotions the action calls for that the movie would lack without her. The kitsch pseudo-ecological thinking behind "The Day After Tomorrow" looks like Newton and Einstein next to Spielberg's "War of the Worlds."

Still, Spielberg provides entertainment and some thrills with his awesome effects, not so much the monsters and their reaching tentacles and insect bodies and faces, which we have seen before, as with the cracking up of streets and falling down of buildings, and some splendid devastation, notably the wreckage of houses and cars and airplanes outside Miranda Otto's McMansion, and for the manipulation of crowds, especially around the ferry landing.

title: Epic, Exciting, Modern-Day Version Of H.G. Wells' Classic Alien Invaders Yarn
review:
Ray Ferrier is a docker in New York City. Following a freak storm which causes a power blackout, his neighbourhood is suddenly attacked by a monstrous alien war-machine. He steals a car and flees the city with his children, only to discover that a global invasion is taking place and mankind is powerless to resist.

Despite changing the setting and characters completely, this is - like the fifties version - a surprisingly faithful adaptation of the classic H.G. Wells novel. What it does best are the tripod war-machines, which are a triumph of sinister visual effects at their best, wading through the population, incinerating people and buildings with their deadly heat ray and booming their mechanical victory cry. All the big mass panic scenes are sensational; riveting, full of action and brilliantly shot. This movie has some nods to its predecessor; the sequence where the characters are snooped on in the basement by the alien camera is a spiffy souped-up remake of the eerily effective scene from the older movie, and the stars of that film, Barry and Robinson, have a cameo at the end. It also has a lot of stuff from the book though - the red weed appears and the vampiristic habits of the invaders are shown in great grand-guignol style. The cast are not bad, if not great. Cruise does a good job portraying Ray as a simple man, albeit not a very bright one, and his moments of genuine terror at the hopelessness of the situation are very affecting. I have one gripe with this movie however; I don't mind the changes to the setting and the story, or the strange amalgams of character (Robbins, for example, has the name of the astronomer from the book, but the character of the curate, with a bit of the artilleryman thrown in). What I cannot forgive however is the removal of the word Martian. The book is about invaders from Mars; to make a movie of the book and neglect to specify where they come from for whatever reason is like adapting Moby Dick and changing the whale to an octopus. That aside though, this is a first-rate sf movie. Kudos to the great stuntwork by Vic Armstrong and the dazzling visual effects by Dennis Muren and Pablo Helman, and especially to Spielberg, for proving he can still make terrific science-fiction films.

title: Contrived: Too many coincidences
review:
Despite all the reviews which criticized focusing the H.G. Wells story through the eyes of a deadbeat Dad desperate to protect his children, I liked that element of the film. The simple story of a man trying to win over and protect his two children was just enough humanity to bring the pathos of the story to the forefront. But in the final analysis, neither this heart-wrenching humanity nor the very good SFX are enough to make this film a masterpiece. I don't think this is the kind of film that will stick with me, about which I will keep thinking.

Today's audiences seem more interested in spectacle than depth, more interested in the next gag than something of meaning, that is, until given something of meaning. Perhaps this is the nature of consumerism. Audiences become blasé, inured to visuals, sounds, and sensations that are "in their faces." And they grow weary of something that doesn't delight either immediately or doesn't generate a new and better delight every four seconds. But not to sell audiences short because when they are given something of real value, they know it, they recognize it, and often, it establishes a new standard by which they will judge everything else.

War of the Worlds is the flavor-of-the-week, but it's neither powerful enough to last nor engaging enough to elicit further thought. It does not stick to the bones.

Thankfully, Spielberg may have realized this mediocrity and moves quickly from establishing Ray (Tom Cruise) as hard-working crane operator (a skill he should have used later in the film against the aliens), who must care for his kids for a weekend when his now pregnant ex-wife and her new hubbie are off to Boston, to a father in full protection mode as the tripods emerge from the ground and begin to vaporize everyone and everything.

The children Rachel (Dakota Fanning) and Robbie (Justin Chatwin) are interesting characters with whom we don't get to spend nearly enough time. Rachel is a high-strung, worry-wort, though we don't know why or much about how she functions aside from how she deals with splinters and defines her personal space for safety. Robbie is easier to understand. He's the typical disgruntled teen who hates or pretends to hate his Dad. He's best defined by his strong bond with his sister, which makes it all the more puzzling when the boy insists on watching the army try to stop the tripods, leaving Ray to choose between his son, who wants to walk into certain death, and his daughter being carted away by two well meaning adults who think she's been abandoned.

Robbie's insistence that his father let him go seems too contrived and convenient, as if Spielberg couldn't figure out what to do with the character after his sister chides him for trying to go off with the army the first time. And it is hard to see how Robbie would fit in the scenes in which Tim Robbins shows up in a brilliant cameo as Harlan Oglivy. The dynamic in which Ray must kill Harlan to avoid being detected by the aliens, a hiding tactic which doesn't work anyway (again, too conveniently), would be a completely different scenario with his son there. Also, the story needed a goal. The trek to Boston to reunite with ex-wife and mommy Mary Ann (Miranda Otto) is made all the more important and thus poignant because "Robbie is going to meet us there," even though Ray watched as the tripods blasted the hill where he left his son into a rolling fireball, and so we really have little hope for Robbie's survival. How Robbie survives is another of the film's many unanswered questions. At least, The Day After Tomorrow (another father saves son epic) had the dual story lines of the father's trek and the son's survival.

Here, Spielberg seems handcuffed by Ray's story, which may be from where the criticisms of the story came. By telling the tale through the father's eyes, he gets the human element, the heart-tweaks and teary eyes, but it's not Independence Day. Much of what is going on with the aliens is not explained and their eventual defeat must be dealt with, much like Wells did, with a postscript. Still, it's intriguing to see an invasion like this from the perspective of an uninformed character, who would not have the benefit of exposition to explain what's happening to him and to the world. Though Ray does meet a news crew early on who show him some tape footage before high-tailing away. But other directors would make the news people into characters.

There's also many laughable convenient coincidences. Like when a jet plane crashes into the house where he and his kids are hiding, the wreckage somehow destroys everything around it except the van Ray stole. Likewise, basement doors do not become blocked with wreckage, and the cage that blows off the tripod conveniently breaks apart like an egg so everyone can get free instead of remaining intact and keeping all hopelessly imprisoned. At least, Ray's and Rachel's survival (Robbie really shouldn't have survived) is not too coincidental to be believable. After all this is a story about those who survived, not those who died.

The SFX are definitely worth another look. It's a great re-imagining of the classic SF story and the 1950s film. But it's not the greatest alien invasion film ever made, not even the best one Spielberg's ever done.
