title: H.G. Wells' Novel for the 21st Century.
review:
I was originally reluctant to see this film. My first assumption being that it would totally tarnish the essence of H.G. Wells' novel, perhaps modify and create a happy ending that tied up all loose ends, waved a few flags around at the climax for added patriotism, and to top it all off, fixed up that long lost broken relationship with two ex-lovers, reunited due to the catastrophic events of the story. My second reluctance was Dakota Fanning being cast in the film, and I envisaged her glaring out to the audience with her usual 'know everything about everything' pose, or as Denzel Washington once put it on 'Parkinson', "..ten going on forty."

Both of these assumptions were quickly diminished within the first 20 minutes of the film.

Instead, I was almost glued to my seat in what has to be a highly suspenseful yet surprisingly faithful modern adaptation of H.G Wells' Sci-Fi classic. Some reviewers have been making references to the CBS Radio Show dramatization, plus the 1953 classic film. Both were masterpieces in their own right, yes, but I never felt that either of these stayed faithful to the original story. The CBS radio program seemed much like the novel transformed into a public news broadcast, which was admirably done, so much so that it scared a number of American people into believing it was all too real. George Pal's 1953 version just seemed to me to be an average 1950's glamorized Sci-Fi horror flick. I do believe it did follow the book on some counts, but swung away from it on many other occasions, too. Kudos goes to Spielberg for his slight reference to the film, including some cameos from the 1953 classic.

**SPOILERS FROM THIS POINT**

With some regard, I suppose you could also judge this film as your typical CGI-Boosted-Aliens-Attack flick, and for those who haven't read H.G. Wells' book, it may seem to fit perfectly into that genre. Many might be disappointed with the film's abrupt ending - there's no grand-scale, climatic, good triumphs over evil conclusion in this film. Like the original story, the chaos ends as abruptly as it begins.

And just like the original H.G. Wells' tale, I was left stunned at the amount of correlations and similarities between the characters of the film, and those of the book. I saw shadows of the artilleryman in the female CBS news reporter, her cold overtones emphasizing the futility of man's weapons against the invaders, but also her determination in continuing with her duties, despite all the hopelessness that surrounds her and her colleagues. There was the rather obsessive (and slightly crazed) recluse who'd lost his family, digging his makeshift 'tunnel' to start mankind all over again, a crazed dream that Ray (Cruise) knows is hopeless. There's the classic ferry exodus too, and the frightening realization that the tripods are just as deadly over sea as they are land. (No 'ThunderChild' remake though. Re-commissioning of the USS Missouri, anyone?) And although we (thankfully) don't see some ridiculous premise about Ray running about on-screen to save his estranged ex-wife, we do see a slightly similar lost and found story from the original book with Ray and his son Robbie.

Usually, I'm not easily stirred by suspenseful films, but my hat goes off to the creators of this contemporary remake of the science fiction classic, as this film had many moments where I was either glued to the back or sitting on the edge of my seat. I never thought it would have been possible to recreate the alien death-ray to appear so terrifying, yet ILM has pulled another hat trick with that one. Nail-biting stuff.

If you're going to see this film, you're familiar with the original book and looking for a not-so-dissected Hollywood remake, or if you're looking for a suspenseful alien invasion film and you're not too concerned about continuity gripes like camcorders filming after a massive electromagnetic pulse, then I highly recommend that you give Spielberg a shot, and watch this film on what it was meant for: the big screen.

title: Thrilling, gripping - high stakes action and soft tender moments.
review:
I actually just signed up for this board so I could write a review of this movie.

It is a wonderful example of the craft of Spielberg and the surprising restraint of Tom Cruse.

Being introduced to our main character first as a person, then getting introduced into his lousy life - you really hate him in the beginning -then getting introduced to the bad guys - they aren't even formed yet, just storms and bad things happening, ominous really scary from the inside out.

The way he does his transitions from one moment to the next just pulls you along. Each moment sets up the next and invites you deeper until you are so involved there is no escaping.

You get moved, step by step into the movie - invited, your guard is down and then BAM! The action is intense. The way people talk, their accents  the way they move - the small moments it all works and makes this one believable tableau for the story.

I was just grabbed by the lapels and thrown around emotionally and visually. I was scared most of the time. You feel the sense of extermination of being powerless and yet hating those creatures and wanting to do something.

There was one moment that was a little schmaltzy  that was during the scene where the army was making a last stand the officer told his men it didn't matter if their rounds didn't stop the things, they were just buying time for the refugees. I would not have used that word, it made people sound like they were not Americans. I don't know what word I would have used, but it seemed out of place. During the scenes where people were displaced and walking about in the country side  somehow it felt like the American Revolution  don't ask me why.

It rained a lot, and people were wet and vulnerable  you felt that.

Then, there was the big surprise  no Tom Cruse moment. It is usually there somewhere in his films where he just lets his emotions rip and he screams and jumps around. It is kind of overdone, and I usually just sit there during his films and wait for it. This time around, his moment was one of real depth, tenderness and anguish  transmitted through stillness and tears as he his hugging Dakota Fanning. This was very poignant moment and very disciplined and focused. BRAVO! There were some reviews that slammed the way Tim Robbins came into the picture, but because of the chaotic nature of what was happening, I thought it was right on.

This is one hell of an action picture. It is an intense and riveting drama with soft human moments. Just being able to span the range of emotions  stark raving terror, to soft fatherly tenderness for a daughter. Sense of humanity  that's it. That is what this is, a wild ride with a true sense of humanity. Go see this movie. Forget what the commercial critics write, they are bored with life and I think they hate movies anyway  at least they seem like it with their cruel and hurtful language.

It is definitely worth it.

title: a mixed bag
review: Of all blockbusters released this summer, this one is the weakest. This is surprising given that it is directed by none other than Steven Spielberg. He invented the blockbuster with Jaws and added to it with ET, Raiders of the Lost Ark, and the Jurassic Park movies. Recently, however, something has gone wrong. Tom Cruise is simply Tom Cruise and he is more tolerable than his recent interviews on TV in which he comes across as an arrogant jerk. His two children are another story altogether. The usually watchable Dakota Fanning just screams and yells a lot. His son is played by a bland pretty boy who is just annoying. When he disappears 3/4 of the way toward the film, we don't miss him. title: What to expect
review: The whole movie up until the last few minutes is exactly what you expect from seeing the coming attractions. It is suspenseful, intense, and well-made with humorous elements (especially in the beginning), decent acting (especially from Dakota), and good special effects. References to previous Spielberg films are obvious, but not necessarily hackneyed. However, the ending is outrageous, in a bad way. Without giving anything away, I'll just say to be prepared to be shocked at such a poor ending after almost two hours of a good action, sci-fi movie. The message the movie was sending is clear, but there wasn't enough character development throughout the movie (nor should you expect that from this kind of film) to pull the ending off. But you'll have to go see it to see what I mean, so you can decide for yourself.

title: Brilliant Save For a Few Flaws
review:
I'll start with a disclaimer: unlike certain American film 'crickets', I won't claim my interpretations of the film, nor of the intended meanings behind certain plot tactics within the film, are exactly what Spielberg and his crew were aiming for. I am just presenting my own interpretations.

War of the Worlds is a truly frightening and exciting experience. Steven Spielberg and crew should be commended for delivering not only an exceptionally entertaining sci-fi horror vision, but for avoiding so many clichés in a genre plagued by the tacky requirements set by Independence Day. The film is not a direct adaptation of H.G.Wells' novel, however due to being set in the current day, this is excusable. Thankfully, while set in America as with almost every blockbuster disaster film, it doesn't use this to demonstrate the almighty power of the United States, or to promote its supposed status as guardian of peace, democracy and freedom. Nor is this a film with a series of money-shots of world landmarks being blown up, or destroyed. That was once exciting in a purely mindless way (Independence Day), but now smacks of little more than a populist marketing tactic (The Day After Tomorrow) and thankfully War of the Worlds' rises above.

The film's plot and mis-en-scene are remarkably aberrant with the standards in the genre and for that, Spielberg deserves commendation. By eschewing wide-screen, setting the film in dark and grubby, non-descript locations, and avoiding an excess of simplistic proscenium-arch long-shots of 'spectacular effects' action unfolding before a static camera, the film achieves a frighteningly realistic portrayal of terror. Much of the action occurs off screen, and we are left with only the looks on the characters faces, and some intense sound effects and lighting effects to give us a feel for what the characters are experiencing. This is not to say the film is free of spectacular shots of its alien invaders and the destruction they cause, because when it does show this, it is another of the film's strengths. The special effects are quite simply flawless, save for the cheesy microcosm-to-macrocosm shots that bookend the film.

Ideologically, this is not a typical American film at all. Too many US reviews, such as Todd McCarthy in Variety and Jan Stuart for Newsday (there are really too many more to name) want to claim this film for their own political project of demarcating the line between the post 9/11 'West' and the supposedly unified terrorist forces that seek to destroy it, but these people are ignorant fools. Kenneth Turan for the Los Angeles Times argues that every incarnation of this story has been met with a rapturous response because of their timeliness, each arriving at a moment when the 'Western World' is particularly fearful or paranoid due to specific international relations at the time. Turan and his ilk seem to assume the Bush administration has everyone duped into laying awake at night fearing terrorism, and that War of the Worlds apparently taps into this fear. One critic, demonstrating the popular sentiment of US reviewers, actually lies and claims the film uses the word "aliens" and "terrorists" almost interchangeably. I don't remember War of the Worlds even using the word "aliens", and when it uses the word "terrorists", it is not as a synonym for "aliens". When Dakota Fanning's character screams out "is it terrorists?" to her Dad and he says "no it is not terrorists!" this is the film's only diegetic verge towards political exposition. In this crucial moment, the film explicitly acknowledges and then dismisses the 'terrorism' subtext US reviewers mistakenly long to detect. Thus War of the Worlds abjectly resists an interpretation along the lines of the 50s Cold War paranoia invasion films which were ideological allegories against the political boogeyman of the day (once communism, now terrorism). Besides, any interpretation of this film as terrorist allegory seems to rely on a mistaken understanding of what terrorism is: War of the Worlds portrays a genocidal invasion not a terrorist attack. If some of the imagery is reminiscent of people's vivid memories of 9/11, this might just speak more of the strength of memory and the sameness of violence, than of Spielberg's attempt to wield a simple political allegory.

The film does not make this a political war of good versus evil, situating the 'American Way' directly in opposition to those who are seeking to destroy America. It does not imply, as so many other politically troubling disaster films, that the 'goodness' of the world is symbolised in the bastions of the supposed 'West'. When Spielberg and Janusz Kaminski's camera lingers on the surreal image of a church building being torn open, baring its teeth like the mouth of a monster, on the cusp of the impending terror, it is not visually symbolising a dialectic between the 'good' and 'Christian' values that are represented by American soil and the Church, and the 'bad' and 'unchristian' values represented by the aliens. What this shot represents so breathlessly, is a complete paradigm shift; the cultural intelligibility of our world, in whatever cultural niche we may exist in (the Christian church interchangeable for any other culture), being flipped on its head by something truly alien and incomprehensible. The actions of the invaders that follow can not be understood according to the logic of human war, because the culture, history, language and society of these mysterious invaders is truly alien.

War of the Worlds presents a swift, naturalistic, frightening account of a sudden and unexpected disruption of life followed by an even more unexpected return to normal life, free of the worst genre clichés. Save for its tasteless and hackneyed bookend shots, the imperialistic invocation of theism in the final voice-over, and two disastrous instances of product placement (iPod and Tivo), the film is a fresh, original and exciting entry into a genre that sets itself apart through its mis-en-scene and plot.

title: a modern masterpiece!
review:
First off, I have to say that this is a side of Spielberg's creativity I've not seen often, save for JAWS. War of the Worlds is brutal, and merciless toward the easily frightened viewer. However, in all its brutality, its tragedy and horror, it has raw, unbridled, savage beauty, and the simple message that EVERYONE JUST WANTS TO BE FREE. It is, as nature shows in the film, natural for all human beings, and it is our destiny to be free.

Now, for the review. The movie is absolutely terrifying. I, the guy who thought Scream was funny, was trying to simultaneously cover my eyes AND my ears (without much success, I might add). Parts of the film, especially the scenes with Cruise, Fanning, and the crazy guy take a pretty conventional approach to the horror aspects, but to chilling, petrifying effect.

The Special Effects are just that: VERY SPECIAL. You can see this is a Spielberg film when you look at the Tripods (icky machines shooting death rays) and all the ship come out of the ground- or the water-because they distinctly like descendants of the space ships from Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Except for the fact that they're evil.

The Acting is superb, and in all cases (except for Miranda Otto of LOTR fame, and Cruise's son "Robbie") the acting is Oscar worthy, especially for Cruise as Ray and Dakota Fanning as Rachel. This is, in my opinion, Cruise's finest work, since I believe he's actually suited for the role he's in (I'm not really a big Cruise fan except for Minority Report), and if Fanninf were just a WEE bit older, she could be Ann Darrow in Peter Jackson's upcoming King Kong (instead of Naomi Watts).

Overall, the film is an astonishing feat of imagery and emotion, and I believe it's an early runner up for Best Picture. While many rush to call this anti-E.T., I believe it is wiser to say that this movie falls more along the lines of Schindler's list in its feeling of slow and lilting horror, its imagery, and the passion it makes you feel for character you don't much about, but care for instantly (whether the feeling be love or loathing). So go to your movie theater. Prepare for the holocaust, and be amazed and astounded by the War of the Worlds.

title: War of the Worlds
review: This movie was fantastic it is what Independence Day should have been. Spielberg did a great job in telling the heart of the story and avoiding the pitfall that so many movies fall into today and allow the special effects to overshadow the story. Cruies does a great job of reacting the way a human and most importantly a farther would act. So many times in movies like this the main character has to be a hero who unites everyone to save the day but not Cruise he does what you me and any other parent would do and tries to keep himself and more importantly his 2 kids alive. He has flaws but overcomes them the best way he can and in that way you feel like you can relate to his character. Don't get me wrong the special effects are jaw dropping and amazing but used the way they should be a a tool in telling a great story. The other thing I like about this film was the terror felt real it didn't come off as planned or predictable it was truly as scary as it was exciting a fantastic film from a fantastic director.

title: See the movie for the spectacular effects and not for the acting or storyline
review:
(Synopsis) Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise) is a divorced dockworker with few skills as a father. Ray's ex-wife (Miranda Otto) drops off their teenage son Robbie (Justin Chatwin) and 10-year old daughter Rachel (Dakota Fanning) for a weekend visit with their father in New Jersey. Ray is a self-absorbed individual who feels imposed upon by having to baby sit his own children. Then something happens that will change their entire lives. An unusual and violent lightning storm hits the town. In the intersection down the street, Ray sees a huge three-legged war machine rise from beneath the street. The machine begins to fire and incinerate everything and everybody. The Martians have begun the war by attacking Earth with only one goal in mind, destroying everything in sight. Ray becomes a real father when he decides to protect his children and take them to their mother in Boston. They start running for their lives and are just ahead of the Martians, when they get caught up in a frantic mob of people who are also fleeing the machines. The machines have increased in number and are everywhere, and they can not be destroyed by our military.

(Comments) The retelling of the H. G. Wells novel by director Steven Spielberg is only an average one. The story is seen through the eyes of Ray and his children, but there is one major problem, the audience will not be able to connect to Ray as a hero or even a good father. You get to a point where you want the Martians to take Ray out. The movie starts out great, then goes down hill. Dakota Fanning did a better job of acting scared then Tom Cruise. If you want to see the movie, you can, because the special effects were spectacular. (Paramount, Run time 1:56, Rated PG-13) (5/10)

title: Unsatisfying Cruise, Spielberg vehicle....
review: ****Contains Spoilers!!!!**** I tried to like this movie, I really did. I have read some of the other reviews on this movie and I disagree with the majority. I am a huge fan of Spielberg films, he is, in my opinion, the master of developing characters and portraying the neverending battle of good versus evil. This film fails at this and so much more, from the technical aspect of electronic shutdown across the globe to panning the camera into a fully functional hand-held video recorder to the ensuing chaos that is happening behind the characters to the emotionless army to the failed attempt of a homage to 1950's sci-fi flicks. This movie is deadpan and flat. You never care for the humans because they are just as bad as the machines (maybe Spielberg intended this) leaving 2+ hours of special effects, destruction, and watching Tom Cruise move from different situation to different situation trying to sav an annoying Dakota Fanning. The ending is atrocious and abrupt, leaving you feeling robbed of what could have been a good film. I would have preferred to see Harrison Ford cracking his whip at one of the machines or E.T pop out of one of the machines trying to phone home. Fx are decent, perhaps the saving grace of the movie. * out of ****.

title: In this movie, Cruise plays a divorced father with two teenage children trying to evade an alien invasion.
review:
In this movie, Cruise plays a divorced father with two teenage children. Working as a container crane operator, with an obsession of V8 muscle cars, shows up late to meet his ex-family and his wife's new beau. Cruise was to take care of the kids, which he hardly knows, for the weekend as his ex-wife visits her parents in Boston. Later in the evening dark clouds with continuous intense lightning concentrating on the same spot at a distant from his backyard as strong winds rushes towards the area. These lightning are actually aliens sending their bodies down to their tripod all terrain vehicles buried millions of years ago before even humans ever walk on the earth. In the morning, all electrical appliances are dead. The tripods then started to surface and started killing everyone around with their giant laser beams. Disintegrating anything it passes through to dust. As whole movies goes on, more movie extras gets disintegrated, Cruise and his family got moving to Boston. Somehow they managed to find a car that is working. Kind of ridiculous as nobody else in the whole town has another working car. Being the only people with a car naturally they were car hijack by swarms of homeless people. Somewhere in the middle of the movie he got separated from his teenage problem child son who wanted to help the army fight aliens. Cruise and daughter manage to encounter with Tripods in the open as well as inside a basement. There is only two scenes where you can really see the aliens, in the basement scouting at people's photographs and at the end where an alien pop out of his tripod dead. In the end, it is our bacteria that killed the aliens.

Somehow the movie has a rather stale kind of plot. If compared to another recent alien invasion movie like Independence Day. Independence Day has a much better grasps of the alien invading planet earth. Not much of action in this one, a lot of running around. There are only two scenes with aliens shown. Maybe they paid too much money for the Cruise and Spielberg collaboration that they have to compromise on the effects and action scenes. The old series on television was much better don't waste your money.

title: War Of the Worlds... Can definitely call it W.O.W!
review:
I don't like movies that scare me, this one terrified me but I loved it. I am no longer a major Tom Cruise fan but I think he did a fine job in his role. The sound was incredible, the special effects were all too realistic and the suspense was as good as it gets for me. My poor daughter probably has a sore arm from me hanging on to her throughout the movie. I will definitely buy the movie when it comes out but the DVD will be a poor substitute for seeing it on the big screen. I am glad it ended the way it did, kind of reminiscent of the original. I think S.S. has another major hit to add to his impressive resume with this film.

This movie was so suspenseful for me I feel emotionally drained after seeing it. I will have to take a short nap to recharge my batteries so I can meet with a client this evening. I have never had a movie do that before.

title: Good God this film is Bad!
review:
I found this film, quite possible the worst Tom Cruise film ever. There seemed to be No plot, the whole two hours just follows The Cruiser running around the East coast, constantly and conveniently narrowly missing destruction ( despite hundreds around him being killed at every turn).

Don't get me wrong, if you're into pointless, " isn't Tom Cruise clever" running around, I'm sure you'll love it. It was Filled with toe curling clichés, and heavy political agenda. Much of it didn't make sense ( for example all electricity switching off, then cameras working at convenient times).

This film definitely lacks the clever and thought provoking plot of the book and focused too much on the actual Family. One of the many times i wanted to throw up, was when the "typical" selfish, lazy teenage boy Sudden feels the need to join the Army, " for the good of the country" - please! was this film sponsored by the White House?.

However the most Truly awful thing about this film, must be the ending where all of a sudden the invasion stops, - with no explanation as to why or how? ( except some spiel about their being a billion sacrifices or something).

I Wouldn't Recommend this film at all,there was a Shameless lack of explanation that credited this film completely shallow, it may as well have not been called War of The Worlds, at it was not at all following the book. Id suggest you wait for the DVD and watch it in the background of doing something like.. watching Paint Dry!!!

title: Extraordinary DISAPPOINTMENT....spoilers
review:
To say that Steven Spielberg's latest is an extraordinarily dismal disappointment is a HUGEEEEE understatement. From start to finish this movie and it's characters lacked realism, drama, suspense and above all: Common Sense.

I could neither connect to the quarrelsome characters or the movie's disjointed and absolutely idiotic flow. From the emergence of the first alien, the audience is taken on an insane ride that defies physics, probability and sense: Only the main characters' car is functional, only the main characters' home has electricity, and only the main characters are quarreling with each other and behaving in every way as if the world is not being literally vaporized before their very eyes.

Would a child go hundreds of yards away from her father and brother to urinate in the remotest part of a field after fleeing a city where the entire population was running in a panic while building were collapsing around them? And what son would angrily demand answers of his father as they fled this scene though he was as much a witness to the very same chaos? And upon reaching some semblance of safety, who in command of any remaining senses would make sauntering to the kitchen bar and asking 'What should we eat?' their second priority? No surprise/gratitude that the electricity is on in what could well be the only temporary haven in the entire city, no barricading doors, no fear, no shakes, no thought of what to do next, no disbelief at all ... just what should we eat.

And is it even possible fliers for missing family and friends could be posted from end to end at the ferry? By the movie's chronology, the invasion began (at the utmost) a little over 24 hours previous, how and when did this panic-stricken, fleeing-for-their-lives Population of Entire Cities have time to make fliers, leave alone having the wherewithal to secure the materials to do so while in the midst of a Alien & Horrific Invasion? That people would ask about loved ones once their panic and running subsided and they came upon others certainly, but who would grab posters, papers, pens or anything else in the midst of collapsing buildings and vaporizing rays of death and destruction? That stretches the imagination so far that I watched thinking it could not possibly get worse, but darn if the insanity didn't keep coming, with the ferry scene leading the way.

Is it reasonable to think (even for a millisecond) that barring the ferry at the sounds of approaching aliens, and leaving it half filled would save even one life against these 300ft high metal creatures, shooting death rays? The more so when (as one commenter stated), where the heck was the ferry going anyway and was there even a tiny hope they could actually get there with such indestructible aliens in pursuit? But this movie has nothing to do with reason as the subsequent scenes drove home even harder than the previous ones.

For how is it possible for a car to rush head long from a tilted and sinking ferry straight into our water dumped main characters yet propel them only a tad under the water. How could they not safely swim away from what amounted to a playful dunk? Or...

How could a hand full of people literally play tug of war against an alien tentacle and not only win but free the human in the Alien's clasp Intact and Unharmed? One would think the poor guy stuck in the tentacle's clasp would have snapped somewhere between the pull of such strengths. And....

When and why did the Aliens change their strategy of destruction from the overall death ray sweeps (that frankly was working darn well) to the individualized and personal, one on one killings? For that matter why where they bothering to collect them at all? The movie gave not even a hint of a reason why humans were being collected then plucked out of the cages one by one for extermination, especially since the mass killings were going so well. Or...

Why instead of torching buildings and homes they suddenly took to individually checking them. Surely if there was a suspicion of life, the broad laser vapor that instantly disintegrated human flesh, burned earth and buildings but was miraculously ineffective against cloth (go figure that one), should have sufficed. Yet instead we have tiny aliens searching individual basements.

Obviously, a quick invasion was not on their agenda. Nor was a believable or entertaining movie on Spielberg's or the finished product would have at least been adequate. And it certainly wouldn't have ended with the little ex-wife, waiting calmly at home, peering out the window of a very intact and lit house as if she wasn't even aware an alien invasion was going on.

Did the Aliens attack all of the world except Boston...lol

Save your money. This was a major clunker and a major disappointment. Spielberg can and has done far far far far far better.

title: Spielberg Once Again Makes Us Think
review: Enjoyable, creative, well cast, well directed, tight human drama set to a spooky sci-fi background. That pretty much sums it up and I don't want to ruin any surprises. Spielberg is a master at what he does and captures genuine emotion from his cast rather than the overdone: "Hand me that gun and let's go get these suckas" take on man versus space baddies so prevalent in films lately ('Independence Day','AVP', anyone? Bleh.). Spielberg also towers over other directors of apocalyptic near future stories like Armageddon, Deep Impact, etc. He demonstrates the keen sense of character development so prevalent in all of his films and continues to explore what happens to ordinary people in particularly extra-ordinary circumstances. As always this is fun (is that the right word?) to watch and Tom Cruise gives one of his best performances (all my feelings about his very public personal life aside). Dakota Fanning is also superb in her role as Cruise's 8 or so year old daughter. She is the strongest child actor I have seen in a long while and presents a very convincing and multi-faceted performance. Overall, classic Spielberg Sci-Fi. One of his best. I thought it had all of the great buildup we saw in Minority Report and AI without the "My goodness, is this movie still running?" feeling associated with watching the latter. As with those two movies, it should be apparent to Spielberg fans that he's drifted from the nicey-nice movies of yesteryear ("Raiders of the Lost Ark","E.T.") and does explore some material that is inappropriate for the PG crowd (Hence the PG-13), but the worst of the violence is implied and off screen (Ala that guy who gets the propeller in "Raiders"). Though there are several mass vaporizations, hurtling burning vehicles, crumbling architecture, other perilous situations, and a bit of gore, Spielberg focuses more on building the tension from what you don't see (Ala M. Night Shaylaman's "Signs"), but you know is happening just outside that basement window, or door or what have you. If you like Spielberg's work you will definitely not be disappointed with his most recent endeavor.

title: Intense and Good
review: I just saw the first day release of this movie and i have to say that Spielberg builds up good ways to jump you up on the edge of your seat. Surely this movie does not hold up a proper ending, but it still has those great moments where you feel the protagonist is going to go down in total chaos. It starts with the introduction of the Ferrier Family, then after you get to know all the characters and the Aliens come down, things start to build up and get more intense. The special effects and action sequences will leave you dazzled (hoping for an Oscar Nomination after Kingdom of Heaven). The main elements missing are the strength of the script and the direction, other wise everything is just awesome. Tom Cruise is superb as ever, Dakota Fanning is becoming a great star, i was hoping that Tim Robbins would give a good supporting act but he just there for a nice short while. the other technical aspects like editing and sets is well done. i was hoping for some John Williams music in the movie but its only offered in the proper moments. the whole other obstacles in this movie is over the top. if you expect good effects and some thrills and chills, this is certainly the movie for anyone...otherwise you can just sit back and enjoy it. i give it a good 8 out of 10 This Movie is Intense and Good

title: A well worth watch...
review: Going to this film was slightly scary. I had no idea what it was going to be about. The trailers simply mention that "They're already here" and that kind've uninformative nonsense. I sat in one of my favourite seats in the cinema and had to wade through approximately 15 minutes of advertisements. The film is slightly confusing in the beginning. Finding out about main character's situations is simply guesswork. Then you're plunged into a world of alien controlled devices which somehow managed to get underground a million years ago before mankind when they couldn't actually attack earth? The aliens apparently are allergic to the micro-organisms of the planet which, I suppose were there millions of years back... Why did they not die then? Made me wonder. There are only two scenes in the film where the devious plotting aliens actually appear. And after that they die because of immunodeficiency. Just shows how powerful humans are doesn't it? By the way... Did anyone prefer the red landscape to our usually bland green? I wonder if there are any products for dying the front lawn...

title: thrilling and intense
review: Visual effects are so impressive and telling that everything in this story seems real: destruction, hysteria, paranoia and craziness. I thought "Independence Day" was second to none as for the capacity to efficiently render the sensation of escalating terror and the nightmarish atmospheres following that kind of disasters. Well, Steven Spielberg did even better here... it's obviously a piece of pure entertainment but it burdens the alien visitation theme (remember ET) with Holocaust elements and commentaries about war on terror as-well. I believe the director touched the best way the nerve of American psyche, even thanks to Cruise's and Fanning's excellent acting.

title: Not just about terrorism
review:
War of the Worlds is to Sci-Fi, what Saving Private Ryan was to War films This movie isn't just about terrorism (that's so obvious, even the young girl in the film picks up on that), but more significantly (from Spielberg's perspective), it's about Nazism and the Final Solution. Terrorists don't experiment on people, they don't hunt them down and round them up, they don't engage in battle on the battlefields...A brilliant film - I can't understand how people think Scorsese is the best American Director - Spielberg shows with a glance, a mood, a simple reading of a line, what was missing from The Aviator. You know more about these people's motives in 8 minutes then you do in The Aviator's 3 hours. Of course Tom Cruise probably thinks this movie is a docu-drama.

I can't understand why people complain about the ending...that's how the original story goes!

title: Quite an experience
review:
War of the Worlds is an alien invasion movie unlike no other. Most movies of this kind tend to show the story from multiple perspectives, and explain everything that's going on. Not with this one. The movie rarely (if ever) leaves the eyes of Ray Ferrier, the reluctant father who has to protect his kids from the alien menace. The story is therefore tighter and you get a better sense of what Ray's feeling. The movie sort of reminded me of Dawn of the Dead in that the plot rarely explains the background of the invaders or what is going on, but rather sticks to the protagonists' struggle to survive an event that changes their lives in just moments. Having said that, War of the Worlds is certainly the best alien invasion movie I've seen so far because it truly portrays the terror and confusion one would feel in such an event.

Never before has an alien invasion movie creeped me out like this one. The tripod aliens are terrifying to behold, not only because they look so real (kudos to the SFX department), but because their design, their movement, and what they do to human beings is enough to make you shiver when they show up on screen. In the initial scenes, you have to wonder why the people on the streets stare up at the massive alien instead of run for their lives. Believe me, once you see these aliens, and imagine yourself in such a situation, you'd probably stand and stare in awe too. In Independence Day, I just didn't feel that when people on the streets stared at the alien UFO. In this movie, I certainly did.

Despite what you might think, this isn't your typical epic disaster movie. There are some pretty lengthy scenes that take place underground, when Ray and his two kids seek refuge from their oppressors. I found the underground scene with Oglivy to be very unique as there is nearly no dialogue throughout the whole thing. Spielberg also does an excellent job showing the animal-like behavior humans degenerate into in the event of a disaster like this. One of the more shocking scenes was when Ray, driving the only working vehicle in the area, is surrounded by a horde of desperate people. As shocking as it was, it was a realistic showing of how easy it is for civilized people to devolve in terms of their behavior.

The performances are pretty good. Tom Cruise proves that he can play a variety of characters, and as Ray Ferrier he portrays him as a bit of a jerk of a father who still tries his best to be a good parent. After the initial alien attack, he returns home and his portrayal at shock and confusion is excellent here. Dakota Fanning also puts in a phenomenal performance as a rather spoilt little girl who unfortunately has to witness the violence going on around her. Although her non-stop screaming and whining annoyed me at times, you have to admire such a young thing for being able to put in a performance that transcends the acting abilities of her age group.

The film did have some awkward moments, though. Ray and his son get into heated arguments in the strangest occasions, and I really felt the film would have done better without the son because he was acting like a prick the whole time. The ending also comes rather suddenly, too, and it would have been nice if there was a little more resolution afterwards. I've read that people thought the ending was 'ridiculous' or 'laughable', but honestly I don't see anything about it that was strange. You be the judge.

Overall this is a viscereal, hard hitting film. It isn't your typical epic that mainstream audiences will like, because of how it focuses on a single character the whole time, and thus lacks some of the more grand, epic action scenes that has become an expectation of these films so far. War of the Worlds is something different to watch--an alien invasion movie that induces a sense of terror like no other. Watch it with an open mind.

title: Excellent acting and pace, awesome disaster effects
review: I'm not a huge Tom Cruise fan or even a Spielberg fan, but this was a great movie. The acting was excellent and the dialog was very REAL. As always, Dakota Fanning is incredible for a preteen. Of course the effects are awesome, especially the sound (things are often HEARD before they are SEEN, if at all). I don't like a lot of characters in my disaster movies, so I was glad this one just focused on Cruise and his two kids. The plot was fairly solid, if you let the occasional "lucky escape" fly (which you must in ANY disaster movie). My only complaint is Robbie's character was poorly developed. His "angsty, jaded teen" portrayal didn't match with his attitude and actions later in the film.

title: Almost needs a second viewing to get a first impression.
review: I'm not sure if a second screening would benefit War of the Worlds or detract from it, but since most of us only watch films once in theatres, I suppose it should be judged on the first go around. The most impressive thing Spielberg accomplishes here is effecting fear. You might think in our multimedia world that folks would be immune to the manipulation of cinema, but sure enough when I looked down my row, my girlfriend had her hand over her mouth, the guy next to her was absentmindedly chewing on a serviette, his girlfriend's mouth was agape, etc. Whatever you might think about Spielberg, this is an impressive feat. That said, with the weapons at his disposal I honestly think he could have done more if he was willing to take some chances. The Orson Welles' version worked precisely because the world he broadcast to was not plugged in to the media. Welles capitalized on this, playing to an audience that listened to radio for both news and drama. Because they couldn't see the events described they were forced to use their imagination, which we know can be more terrifying than reality. As Marshall McLuhan would say, the medium was the message. But in a world of 1000 TV channels, live Internet streaming and embedded war reporters, a film must truly do something remarkable to transcend the medium. Perhaps this is why Hollywood is in such a slump: they keep trying twists on the same narrative structures, and people are willing to stay home and wait for these stories. If ever a movie called out for some experimentation to rattle the audience's cage, this is the one. Films like Elephant, Gerry, 5 x 2, Memento, Irreversible and 21 Grams are the future of cinematic narrative because they challenge and force a viewer to participate. As impressive as the references and special effects are here, this is a movie you can set your watch to  even if some electromagnetic pulse manages to stop it.

title: Spielberg delivers a marvel to watch
review:
*** Spoiler *** The star of the movie is definitely Steven Spielberg. His direction made the movie a work of art. It was amazing to look at and the graphics and special effects were outstanding. I liked the tripods and I liked how the aliens killed people quite easily.

The acting was good. Tom Cruise's son was a bit weak in my opinion. Really the character only exists to show how bad of a father Tom Cruise's character had been up to this point. Dakota Fanning was excellent. Tim Robbins was hilarious and a pleasant surprise. Overall it was first class.

Having said that, I couldn't help but feel that the movie was kind of a let down, especially at the end. The ending was a neat twist of sorts, but very anti-climatic. You have this whole movie moving in one direction and then within 5 to 10 minutes it swings the other way. I thought the ending could have been more developed. The time frame to which this took place and the explanation how humans prevail is too quick.

The fact that no one of any importance in Tom Cruise's life (ie. the son) died made the story kind of cheesy. This may have been expected, but not as blatant as it turned out. No one in Tom Cruise's immediate or in-law family was sacrificed.

It is a good movie for what it was. It is not another Independence Day type film. No glamorous military victories here. I appreciated that part. It is entertaining. But also the aforementioned flaw of the story itself gives the story and ending a strong anti-climatic tone that couldn't be overcome by a textbook happy ending.

title: Nice Family Drama, Terrible Movie
review:
I must say, its nice to see how Tom Cruise develops from a jerk to a good father over the course of the movie but I DON"T REALLY CARE. Steven Spielberg is a great director, but he has let me down. He has turned a fascinating story about humanity on the brink of destruction, and turned it into a bland, PG-13 film. Parents, be sure to take your kiddies.

For those unaware of the story, the plot is simple. Aliens come to earth, kill many. Its funny how those words seem to sum up the whole film. Actually, I would add a few more significant words. Cruise is Jerk. Bonds with family. The End.

Even though I hated the film, I must admit there was a moment that I enjoyed, and superficial as it might have been, I still add a star to give this movie a total of two stars. The moment I am referring to is when the Jerk (AKA Snooze Cruise) is running from the tripods as the pop out of the earth. The tripods start vaporizing people and there is this one scene where a man's horrified expression melts away as he is vaporized. Purely special effects, but still cool.

As I left the theater as soon as the credits began to roll, there was some clapping. I can only theorizes that the clapping came from people, who like me, were thankful the movie was over. My advice, wait until this movie gets dumped into the $2 bin at Wal-Mart...and then shoplift it. Thank you.

title: War of the Worlds
review: I think this movie was great. There were many funny parts to the movie, especially Tom Cruise, he made the movie have good humor. I liked how the brother Robbie and the sister Rachel really bonded well together. They played good brother and sister roles. I thought it was really stupid how Ray and Rachel got captured in the creature. They portrayed Rachel as being smart and then they had her run outside. I was really surprised at the end to see Robbie because he probably would have died. Everybody probably would have died, in fact. I also noticed that after the first storm the cars were dead and the mechanic had to replace something in order for it to work again. So, after the second storm, at the mom's house, wouldn't he have to replace that same part again because it probably would be dead again? That was just something I noticed. There wasn't much interaction with others, it was just the 3 of them running around trying to survive. Overall, I really enjoyed the movie and thought it was something worth seeing. I definitely recommend it.

title: Pretty good, actually
review:
I think that a lot of people have been unfairly lambasting this movie over silly details. I won't debunk all the dumb criticisms, but it's pretty silly to quibble over what an electromagnetic pulse would, or would not, wipe out in terms of home electronics, automobile starters, etc., or how consistent or uniform the effects would be. (If you're inclined to criticize on that basis, a much bigger plot hole is the fact that alien war machines have been buried under the surface of the earth for an unknown but very long period. Why did the aliens bother waiting in the first place?)

Another silly criticism -- that the movie is derivative. Of course it is, but getting all offended because it has similarities to Signs or Independence Day is just plain dumb, since those latter movies were rip-offs of still earlier movies, most notably, the 1953 version of War of the Worlds. Incidentally, if you've seen the 1953 version, the current version pays homage in several important scenes, including (the much criticized) basement scene.

Whatever. The new movie is quite strong, disturbing in spots, evocative of 911, and thematically complex. People who don't hate Tom Cruise will probably enjoy his performance, which was quite strong overall. If you have children of your own, you'll probably get more out of the movie than if you don't. As others have stated, the end of the movie wasn't executed as well as it could have been -- but keep in mind that the end was written to coincide with the original book. Anybody who's looking for an unhappy, nihilistic ending should instead rent a Romero zombie flick on DVD -- an unhappy ending simply isn't keeping with the source material, however invested you may be in maintaining an analogy to the current war on terrorism.

Note to Steven Spielberg: It ought to be pretty easy to fix the ending for the DVD version, just by recutting, if you're so inclined. Here's my suggestion (SPOILER FOLLOWS):

Stick closer to ending in 1953 version. Send Cruise and daughter directly into tunnel/shelter in Boston area, with renewed threat from tripod, and without telegraphing resolution. Show 30 seconds of despairing Cruise (lifted from basement), possibly with voice-over from a shortwave radio suggesting all is lost. Then have horrendous crashing noise coming from outside -- have Cruise tentatively emerge from tunnel, to discover crashed tripod (not shot down by Army), and dying alien. Then end movie without final scene of family reconciliation. Cleaner and better, IMHO anyway.

title: I was angry at negative reviewers based on my seeing the trailers
review:
Now that I've seen the film, I must only vote a 6. Basically, my problem is that the tripods doing most of the damage are rather ridiculous. They don't make sense physically and seem to be the result of a very poor imagination. I expected a LOT better from this movie.

The scenes of destruction are fine. Those running the tripods aren't bad. But if you can't buy the tripods, the whole concept becomes somewhat silly.

Also, the trailers, which were excellent and showed all the suspense you're really going to find in the film, were in bright colors. The film itself is like a washed out version of the trailer. Since the action seemed just as realistic in the trailers, I don't see that the washed out quality was needed. Every epic, sci fi or ancient, uses a tinted lens or off coloring. Haven't any of these geniuses ever seen a David Lean film? Also The Sand Pebbles and Ben Hur and Khartoum and The Wild Bunch, etc. could show realism in bright hues. Looks like a lost art.

title: An intense disaster movie with action, horror and heart. (SPOILERS)
review:
SPOILERS!!!! (Don't read unless want to know what happens).

WAR OF THE WORLDS sucks you in from the get-go and leaves you terror-stricken and captivated for its entirety. It's been commented on before and it's worth mentioning again that this movie will make you think about what you might do during an alien invasion. Through Cruise's eyes you are right there in the middle of the action as the Tripods arrive and start their extermination. We see the Tripods surface and annihilate, then later search for survivors, whom they pluck and cage before using as fertilizer. The prologue with Freeman's narration is slick and sets the tone perfectly, remarking how oblivious we can be to global change.

Some reviews call some exchanges between Tom and his kids too "touchy-feely", but to me those moments played very realistic--I believed that the characters would behave in such ways during an unthinkable crisis.

I don't have any problems with the ending. That the aliens ultimately found our planet inhospitable was the most believable way to wrap things up. Sure, they had planned on the take-over for millenniums but there were microscopic factors they didn't count on. That solution is better to me than the humans suddenly figuring out some alien Achilles Heel.

Coolest parts: 1. Tom getting the movie's first good look at one of the walking Tripods as he hides behind a house.

2. Tom's ex seeing Tom carrying Dakota down the street, back to her.

3. Our one-side view of a military battle with the Tripods. Tanks, men with bazookas and missile-shooting helicopters charge over a hill. After massive explosions the Tripods emerge from behind the hill w/ out a scratch.

Thoroughly entertaining.

title: W.O.T.W. = Wow
review:

Both of us are huge critics and totally nitpicky about every detail. Well, this was different. I'd say for about 75% of the movie we sat there with our mouths gaped wide and clutching each other's arms the entire time.

Spielberg's Effects were breathtaking to say the least. There were very few points where I didn't feel like this is what it would look like if earth were thrown an extreme level of tumult due to an outside assault.

Those of you into post apocalyptic settings or those based on the eve of destruction will be absolutely enraptured with how realistically this is displayed. Epic catastrophe plays out almost nonstop through this movie. Your white knuckling of the arm rest will be constant. Prepare for a treat.

This is after all a great film, and this is without a doubt the coolest film you'll be seeing this year. The Tripods are truly frightening and the aliens are presented in a fresh and unique manner. Funny how ILM always seem to get their stuff together when Spielberg's at the helm when their results otherwise often vary. Here; all is good. title: Great film released at the right time.
review: That quote broke my heart ladies and gentlemen. This movie was not made into a feature film until it was as equally important to do so, as when HG wells released his classic in 1898. This is where the film maker shows his genius, if you ask me. The original book was published during a time of panic for the British people. Everyone afraid of the invasion of evil forces. THen Orson Welles terrified American audiences on the brink of WWII. Now, Spielberg, our current times celebrated director of all directors (at least in popularity) has given us our own war of the worlds during our war with terrorism. This story serves many purposes. It forces us to re-examine our fear and see what has really changed in the human experience since the late 1800s. Apparently not much. We are still very much afraid of what is coming to get us next. WOTW was not just another remake amongst the fifty other remakes clogging up the theaters these last few years, this was political and social commentary. It's the best kind of remake you could ever do. From the September eleventh undertones of ash filling the air, the knee jerk reaction of revenge as soon as we are attacked...this movie is deep. Deep, but hopefully, accessible to a general audience. Protection of the innocent, protection of our ways of life, the struggles of father and son, the importance of all life, big, and in this case, especially small. I was truly touched by the whole thing. It showed a whole lot of truth, more grotesque and dark as Spielberg has possibly ever gone before. Brilliantly, switching between the bad guys of the aliens to the bad guys of the panicked mob mentality really shows how terrified we really are, as creatures of this planet. As we have always been, and as we always will be.

title: 'Outside the box' movie-making. Magnificent! Atmospheric, human, and artful. A classic movie for future ages.
review:
Viewing this movie from the ordinary 'modern' audience perspective that enjoyed 'E.T.' or 'Independence Day' might have lead some to have been disappointed. Being able to switch your head around, though, and see this through new eyes will assure you a magnificent movie experience! Being true to the original Vicotorian-era H.G. Wells novel, and taking huge and courageous leaps of artistic risks that pay off handsomely for all of us, director Steven Spielberg has created an immense and awe-inspiring movie. He has clearly made a movie from 'outside the box'. Not everyone may appreciate this at first, perhaps, but eventually this will be seen as a breakthrough classic.

I've seen dozens of critic's remarks about this film prior to seeing it today, its opening day in Wales. Some appeared to like it because 'stuff blowed up real good', while others moaned that it was 'too dark', not at all sunny and cheerful, and it wasn't 'E.T.'. Still others criticized the movie because the Martian invasion wasn't 'practical' (which is wasn't), and the tactical and strategic behaviors of the Martian invaders were not logical (which they weren't). Well--- yeah. They are all correct--- the Martian killing machines were definitely Victorian. The sounds they made could well have been London-ish mechanical war sounds from the 1890s or so, if the English had built giant robots and invaded the rest of the planet at that time. Rather than being frustrated at the illogical details, or the evident lack of sound thinking on the Martians' part, I found all of that extremely atmospheric. It was frightening, thrilling, entertaining, and delightful.

Spielberg took a chance, and went in a direction he hadn't gone before. This is definitely 'outside the box' film making. Bravo! May all the critics who so often complain and moan about lack of originality in modern movies and Hollywood please try to reward an originator in this instance. I gave 'War of the Worlds' a well-deserved 10 out of 10.

P.S. Watch for the quickie cameo-homage appearance of Gene Barry and Ann Robinson, toward the end of the movie. They were the stars of the original film, the 1953 version of 'War of the Worlds'. An appropriate, classy, and fun move for Spielberg!

title: Top notch Sci-Fi Entertainment
review:

The film deviates very little from the original novel by keeping the spirit intact and paying full homage to HG Wells' descriptions of the invaders' nature and weaponry. Spielberg and his screenwriters don't sanitize the material by taking the ugliness from the devastation brought by the invaders and the disintegration of human values in its aftermath. There is true despair, horror, and paranoia going full blast in every scene of the film. Every emotion runs high.

Movie lovers around the world should rejoice and appreciate a fine work of art that works as a great action film. Spielberg has once again shows why he has lasted so long in this business. There is fine support by all the members of its cast, particularly Miss Fanning whose range keeps expanding and delighting moviegoers all over the world.

title: An excellent adaptation that gives accurate representation of the book and homage to the old movie
review:
****SOME SPOILERS**** When I first heard that War of the Worlds was going to be released into theaters, I immediately thought, "Great. Someone's remaking the old classic and turning it into the action movie of the year. Pshaw." However, then I saw the trailers and realized that it wasn't remaking the movie--it was adapting the book. The book itself is a thrilling, eerie, frightening story of human nature and it's reaction to a hostile alien threat. Things that were left out of the original were the red weed, the black fog, the alien tripods, and the main character himself--a man, desperate to get back to his wife, whom he'd sent to the hills for safety.

This version of War of the Worlds is the most fabulous and faithful I've seen. The few changes that were made were perfectly acceptable--modern times being the most obvious, as the book was set in 1890s England. What few items were left out--like the black fog the aliens used to suffocate the humans--was all right, as they made the aliens invincible instead of vulnerable, like in the books. Also, the aliens themselves were changed, but were still perfectly awful--also, it paid homage to the old movie, with the eerie suctioned hand dragging itself out of the ship as it died.

The mobs in the movie had to be the creepiest and scariest part of the movie, simply because they were a little too close to reality than one would like to think. People like to imagine that they'd be rational if something like this happened, and like to think that they wouldn't be so animal as to attack people and turn upon them just to get something that they didn't have. However, history has shown the opposite. The brutal nature of the mobs in the movie was chilling and frighteningly accurate--quite possibly the scariest moment of the movie Morgan Freeman as the narrator was an excellent choice--he had already proved himself to be a marvelous narrator with his performance in The Shawshank redemption.

Tom Cruise portrays a tortured man, desperate to save his family and get back to his ex-wife--everything was perfectly in line with the main character in the book.

Tim Robbins was a combination of two of the characters and played them excellently--a man driven insane by the loss of his family and the prospect of being completely drained and used as fertilizer.

Overall, I give the movie nine stars--it was an excellent source of entertainment as well as horror. Very well done.

title: Vintage Spielberg ... from its subtle humor to its child's-eye perspective
review:
You will love it! Tom Cruise, Dakota Fanning, and Tim Robbins are the heart and soul characters that make it all work. H G Wells' famous tale is converted into a "coming of age" film here, courtesy of Mr. Spielberg.

Specifically coming of age are Cruise's son Robbie (Justin Chatwin) and daughter Rachel (Dakota Fanning) (who delivers the best one liners in the film). Ray Ferrier (Cruise) seeks only to protect his family; son Robbie seeks only revenge, first against his Dad and vicariously next against the aliens. Eventually, Robbie joins the battle that his father knows we cannot win. Spielberg touches a modern nerve here in this doomsday scenario.

He delivers a "war" that immerses the audience's angst of natural disasters, terrorist attacks and the anarchy that would logically result when life loses its balance Â– all delivered under dark, dreary skies. The film invests winning elements of Independence Day and Men in Black (without as much delightful repartee - regrettably). It's on par with both as an entertainment barometer.

Tim Robbins is brilliant (!) as the hospitable nemesis, Ogilvy. At one point, he declares: "This is not a war. This is an Extermination," with his flare for extracting all that is bleak and pessimistic from a situation. It's a great role filled by the perfect player.

This is vintage Spielberg, from its subtle humor to its child's-eye perspective. For example, as the city is being trashed by the aliens, the camera pans a "No Littering" sign. The initial attack yields dialog like "Â… is it the terrorists again, Daddy?" And you learn that the average Dodge Caravan is every bit as durable as a Hummer when TriPod machinery is at the height of its vicious attack. No one captures a child's terror and reactions better than Spielberg's lens. He's the Master.

Cruise throws only one tantrum on screen involving an unwarranted peanut butter sandwich. Glib as this standalone scene is, it refreshed my memory of his Today Show antics opposite Matt Lauer on issue of "dealing with psychological imbalance, drug-free". I think he could have used a pill.

When the moment is right, like the story magician he is, Mr. Spielberg taps his magic wand and wraps up the fairy tale for the fantasy ride it has beenÂ…a bit too unbelievably as you will see for yourself - which is why it earns an 8 instead of a 10. See it soon.

title: Truly Underrated
review:
From my point of view this is the best adaptation the War of the Worlds franchise has ever seen. I don't understand the sheer amount of negative criticism this film has accumulated since its release, I'm not saying it is a without flaw, definitely not. But to me it's clear that the positives outweigh the negatives.

Firstly the camera work is stunning. Throughout the film the composition of shots and the cinematography is to be admired, no matter how much you dislike War of The Worlds you must recognise that it is a good looking film. My favourite scene -which presents the camera work at its best- is when our three main characters are in the car, the tension is at its peek here, the camera is sliding in and out of the windows echoing the unease of the situation. I recall there not being a single cut, it is truly beautiful to watch.

Some say the CGI doesn't hold up, I can agree with this statement in some occasions, for example when the Aliens leave their Tri Pods (towards the ending of act 2 and the film's resolution) they do not fit in with the rest of the scenery. In some cases the CGI is a bit too ambitious for its time which can subtract from the realism, however overall I think they did a great job on the key set pieces.

I have also heard complaints on acting. Bad child acting is to be expected although I do believe the child they casted to play Tom Cruise's daughter could have been a lot worse, her over reliance on screaming can be quite irritating at some points however. Tom Cruise does as well as he usually does, he shows his character's desperation very well, specifically when his daughter is in danger.

I still to this day do not understand how Tom Cruise's son survived that explosion within the midpoint of the second act. He shows up right at the ending and I think it would have made much more sense for them to have killed him off, it is just way too unbelievable that he could have possibly survived that explosion, if someone could explain to me their own theory then that would be much appreciated. One more thing which puzzled me is that the aliens had the tools at their hands to create almost impenetrable force fields, however the actual outer casing of their Tri Pods can be completely blown apart with one RPG shot.

In conclusion this film is much to under appreciated and I wish more people would give it a chance as it is very enjoyable. I do recommend you watch this.

title: War of the Worlds battles its way through family turmoil and extraterrestrial invaders.
review:
There was only one director that could adapt H.G. Wells' classic sci-fi novel and make it applicable for the current century. That man is Steven Spielberg. Not only has he made an exhilarating blockbuster intertwining many sub-genres into a sci-fi epic, but also allegorically addresses a society post-9/11. If only that underwhelming conclusion could've maintained the awe and suspense that the rest of the film breathed. The world is invaded by "Tripod" extraterrestrial machines that are exterminating the planet, where a father is dumped with his estranged children. This dysfunctional family must come together in order to survive.

Forget about the colossal alien death machines, the real focus is on this broken family. A father attempting to reconnect with his children within the harsh extremities of an other-worldly invasion. It is during these difficult times that the children are susceptible to their father's authority and start to view him as a figure of leadership. They look up to him, and it gives him a chance to showcase his protective fatherly instincts. Substantial development from all individuals in this family that truly makes for some investing drama. Cruise gives a compelling performance, whilst also running for his life many times. Fanning, well, screams for the majority of the film. It's not her fault that her character is horrifically written, but it does leave her character insufferably irritating. The several lines of dialogue that relate to urban terrorism and several scenes relating to 9/11, particularly the plane crash, thematically presents a society adjusting to events that have changed the entire nation. Spielberg takes this and utilises it to enhance the modern perspective of Wells' novel, and it's effective. The visuals remain awe-inspiring, with the gigantic "Tripods" decimating cities, although some of the green screen was noticeable. Williams' score contains traces of Spielberg's classicism whilst crafting refreshing epic pieces of music, especially when the army are on the hill.

But then we come to the ending, and it just feels so underwhelming given the chaos and fear that preceded it. It's a story about survival, so when these extraterrestrials struggle to survive themselves (despite the advanced technology they have acquired) it diminishes the plot. Is it a remark on current fatty consumerism? Or perhaps pollution? Humans have evolved to survive after thousands of years, able to coexist with the billion microbes that inhabit the planet. However after a day and night, these aliens just couldn't take it. Through all the colourful battles and horrific imagery, the film builds up to a promising final act but misses the mark almost completely. That's without mentioning how lucky Ray was. I mean he avoided death like ten times as he runs, drives or swims away from carnage.

It's a shame that the ending is unfortunately underwhelming, as this is without a doubt one of Spielberg's most underrated and overlooked films within his extensive canon. Not the war that ends the world, but a dramatic battle nonetheless.

title: Fantastic 4/5 of a movie
review:
This review will have spoilers for War of the Worlds AND the film Jurassic Park.

War of the Worlds is Spielberg at his meanest and also his third-darkest (with Schindler's List being first and Saving Private Ryan being second). This film is also sort of a crossroads between what defines a "popcorn" movie and what makes something deeper.

But first, to get the ending out of the way, yes, it sucks. To have Robbie suddenly appear at a pristine Boston home with his parents who, for whatever reason, are a safe haven from the madness of the alien invasion is asinine. But this film shares more similarities with Jurassic Park than any other Spielberg movie and that filmâ€”although people seemed fine with itâ€”had an asinine ending as well when the T-Rex seemingly appears out of nowhere to save Grant, Ellie and the kids. And for those people who say Ray in this movie became too much of a hero, Grant became one as well in Jurassic Park. I feel the two mirror each other closely, even though Jurassic Park (which is still one of my favorites) has just as many problems with it. And anyone who got annoyed with Dakota Fanning here, well, I'd just like to showcase Exhibit B where Lex shines a megawatt flashlight directly into a T-Rex's eyes.

There are also issues with Spielberg ignoring his own rules, so for instance near the beginning of the movie an EMP wipes out all electrical devices but people are still seen in the street with cameras and camcorders. But something similar happened in Jurassic Park when we see the downed jeeps parked in front of the fence right before the main T-Rex attack and the goat, ground, and trees are all basically at road-level. However, after the T-Rex attack and Grant, with the kids, are stuck in the car and the T-Rex pushes the car toward the segment of fence it came out of, there's suddenly a 50-foot drop. There are countless other small problems with Jurassic Park, but again people seem more favorable to that film than this.

So with those problems asideâ€”"rules" issues and the endingâ€”I still give this movie an 8 out of 10 for the sheer darkness it portrays humanity like during a time of crisis. There are heroes. There are also people who want to take advantage of others. I will never forget the shock I felt at seeing Ray's van being stolen from him at gunpoint and almost losing his daughter who was stuck inside. I was also shocked at how closely the film used a 9/11 metaphor when the Tripods start shooting civilians on the street and then the people burst into ash (and, for those who wonder why it didn't destroy clothing, maybe the beams only affect organic matterâ€”I never thought it was a problem, and seeing the clothing go flying off everyone was terrifying).

I believe this film gave Spielberg the opportunity to take popcorn movies like Close Encounters, E.T., JAWS, and Jurassic Park and filter them through the lens of a more mature filmmaker who had done Schindler's List and Saving Private Ryan, and the result is something pretty astounding. So yes, it's flawed, it has problems (as most Spielberg films have), but then again most movies in general have problemsâ€”I mean, think about the actual logistics of a man dressed as a bat in 100-pound body armor crouching on a skyscraper parapet in The Dark Knight and who's fighting a homicidal clown, which, incidentally, is also one of my favorite films. I think people have a hard time looking past the flaws of this film and seeing what's actually a terrifying look at people trying desperately to keep it together during a national emergency.

title: a disappointing remake of a list of bad remakes
review:
I approached this movie with some trepidation but was willing to give it a chance. After all it was a modern reworking of a classic. I DID NOT expect to be slapping my forehead in horror at the pure Hollywood type schmaltzy ending. Also my "suspension of disbelief" was stretched to breaking many times

As soon as i saw the main title "WAR OF THE WORLDS" appear on screen, i was caught up instantly, that added with the fill-of- suspense- trailer, the directors career, and the famed novel, produced me a sensation not felt before by summer blockbusters. title: Irritating!
review: I am a great lover of sci-fi movies and remember watching the original as a child, so what of this modern revisit? Well my thoughts back in 2005 (and 10 years later having watched it again a few evening ago) remain the same - the children of Mr Cruise are irritating to the point of killing the movie, yes folks, the girl is on a scream-fest at every opportunity (and then some), whilst the son is just plain argumentative and unpredictable to the point of being nonsensical. Cruise is still maturing in this movie (I really enjoyed his later sci-fi movie outings: Oblivion & Edge of tomorrow) and still using some of his old thespian techniques such as body language, that 'swagger', light bouncy movements that feel like he is going through the motions of a rehearsal - in fact that term kind of hits the mail on the head - many scenes looked like rehearsal shots rather than what you would expect in the finished product. Throw in Tim Robbins escapades and the whole thing becomes quite jarring. Not a catastrophe - but this really feels like the director lost control of the characters behaviour and the script would have needed work to iron those issues out.

title: dull
review:
I'm very surprised that Steven Spielberg put his name on this thing. Also, why does he use Tom Cruise so much? I won't go through the story. Aliens invade earth, using machines they have hidden below ground for I don't know how long. Everybody goes on the run, and the focus is on one particular family, headed up by Tom Cruise, a divorced man taking care of his young, constantly screaming, hysterical daughter (Dakota Fanning) and his older son who apparently pays no attention to anything his father tells him.

The beginning of this adaptation of the H.G. Wells story was quite good, if you overlooked certain things. I mean, an entity that can evaporate people must be also able to evaporate their clothes. I'm in no way a special effects expert, so I was pretty impressed with the effects in the beginning.

My problem with this movie is that within thirty minutes, I lost interest.

If you move fast and keep an audience entertained with a strong script, good acting, good direction, and good pace, no one will care about the fact that some cars work and others don't, that a videocamera works when everything else doesn't, that a few miles out of town, no one knows about this catastrophe and there is no alien activity - etc. But when you give an audience time to think, they consciously or subconsciously start picking up inconsistencies which gives them a perfect excuse to criticize it.

And what a cop out - to have Morgan Freeman's voice explain the ending.

My real problem is that a great artist like Steven Spielberg should know better. This movie could have grossed more than however many millions it did by having a little more attention paid to it, rather than saying, okay, we've got Cruise, we've got Spielberg, let's throw this thing on the screen, sit back, and let the idiots pay for it.

title: 60 Minutes Of This Film Should Have Ended Up On The Cutting Room Floor
review:
I still watch this movie once in a while, but only by skipping past the insipid parts, which are frequent. The annoying over-the-top drama with Cruise & his kids is just plain distracting.

Spielberg's special effects are great! And I find every scene with the alien tripods to be fascinating. But his decision to go Cruise-family-centric with the film left it cluttered with needlessly annoying scenes of conflict thrown in for absolutely no good reason.

Spielberg should have realized in the editing room that he could still save his movie and make it a real classic by trimming the scenes that were distracting from the REAL STARS of the movie, the ALIEN WAR MACHINES! I think Tom Cruise and Dakota Fanning are great, they just needed to be incorporated with more subtlety. At least the 1953 version showed more of mankind's attempts to battle the aliens.

The only attempt at a real military combat scene we get in this film is one where Cruise's annoyingly waywardly rebellious son is running up a hill towards some aliens we can't see beyond the rise in the darkness. The way the tanks and Humvees were deployed just looked silly and amateurish, as if a giant invisible child was playing with his toys.

I understand that Spielberg apparently wanted to do War Of The Worlds from the standpoint of a father trying to protect his family during the alien invasion. I'm not against incorporating family drama in a movie. I'm just surprised that an experienced movie-maker like Spielberg did not realize the film just really desperately needed some serious editing out of the many scenes that dragged and pulled. That entire scene when Cruise and his daughter took refuge in the house occupied by Tim Robbins' character was a complete waste of time! I would guesstimate at least 60 minutes of this movie should have ended up on the proverbial cutting room floor.

A much better use of those 60 minutes would have been to incorporate scenes showing the military tactical and strategic response to the invasion. Spielberg should have woven in how the world's governments were responding.....something to give some relief to the claustrophobic movie that came out.

title: The Most Thrilling Film I've Ever Seen...
review: Before I begin I just want to say that this is NOT a perfect movie. There are two problems I have with this film.
