By waiting till earth was populated by an intelligent species capable of fighting them the invaders introduced the possibility of defeat. So even though the effects were good and Tom wasn't particularly bad and Steven did his tension and humor moments as good as he usually does them...it just kind of missed the mark. The writer and director got lazy and just went "it's a neat visual, it's doesn't have to make sense." So go for the effects...maybe you won't be as annoyed by the lazy lapses.

title: Emotional
review:
Dakota Fanning is the star of this movie. She is on-screen almost every moment, and never a false touch. Tom Cruise's role could have been played by anyone, but she is in a class by herself.

The family dynamics were realistic and added to my interest. The evolution of the angry son's relationship with his absent dad seemed believable. And the Mom's snarkiness towards her ex also rang true. I liked the realistic New Jersey backdrop. It may have been unrealistic, but I felt that as long as Tom Cruise and Dakota were together, he would keep her safe.

The political overtones also rang true for me. One character says, It's an occupation, and occupations always fail. Hmmm.

Plot holes big enough to drive a jet plane through, but emotionally, this is a winner.

title: War of the Worlds (2005)
review: Middling Spielberg. On the positive side, War of the Worlds boasts spectacular, although not ground-breaking, special effects, and an excellent performance from the 11 year-old Dakota Fanning: the director has always had a facility with child actors, and this is no exception. The film is obviously addressed to the post 9/11 American audience. It's an 'everyman's' experience of disaster compared to the panoramic 'presidents, scientists and quips' scope of Independence Day. Crowds flee in dust-covered terror, more often from a menace heard rather than seen, and there are (very obvious allusion, this) photograph galleries of the missing. The film of course updates and relocates the action from HG Wells novella. Victorian Surrey becomes New Jersey. The source of the threat is not the obviously dead Mars but an unspecified extraterrestrial source. The cinematography is appropriately sombre and dark and the sound effects are very good: the noise emitted by the tripods is a dark inversion of the greeting of the mother ship from Close Encounters. Yet there is a curious lack of imagination here. The film follows the course of the novel, and even the 1953 film version, surprisingly closely, and the aliens, when they appear, are creepy but pure Roswell. More damaging is the director's recurrent weakness of insisting on sentimentality: one either goes for his scenes of family bickering and bonding or gets a little irritated and in a film as brief as this (under 2 hours) and with this theme (apocalypse) one is inclined to the latter. It's also very much a star vehicle, and at one point we're supposed to believe that little Tom has physically got the better of Tim Robbins (whose supporting role is very brief). Worth seeing then  on the big screen  but not in the same league as Close Encounters, or even ET, and certainly not as much fun as Independence Day. But then we live in a different world.

title: A remake but not a rehash - spoilers
review:
Full credit to Spielberg for trying to place a new perspective on this story but, for me, he failed to capture any of the desperation or dread of the original film and his new spin did not do the original material justice The nucleus of the original film is simply that, despite all of human kind's, well mainly mankind's, military achievements sometimes it is the small and apparently insignificant that triumphs.

Spielberg's film simply did not convey how utterly powerless the world's military might was against the alien insurgents. Because the extermination by the machines is carried out so quickly and effectively it is clear that the machines are unstoppable but just how unstoppable is not so clear. In the original movie the decision is finally made to use nuclear weapons, at that time still a relatively new development and so more awesome, but this also proves fruitless. However, in this film we see little of the military's defence of the planet and so cannot appreciate the invulnerability of the alien's machines. The audience could be forgiven for thinking that surprise had been their main weapon. This detracts from the power of the final message. However, I'm also fully aware that a lot of this ground has been trodden before, by the likes of the awful Independence Day, for example. I can completely understand Spielberg's desire to avoid any comparison to that film at all and that could explain the apparent neglect of even a whiff of a military struggle. Also, with regard to the small overcoming the larger and technically superior, I can see that too much banging of that drum could have been seen as an unfortunate allegory on terrorism, even bio-terrorism.

Instead Spielberg chooses to focus on the plight of three individuals. This is a fair direction to take but without a little more reinforcement of the original plot point, humankind's utter weakness even as a united entity, this emotional drama could have been played out against any backdrop.

Of course, having seen the original and so being aware of the aliens final demise I didn't have the luxury of a virgin viewer and so had no real anxiety about how it would turn out. Yet, for example, I watched the end of the Sixth Sense with a vague foreknowledge of the twist and I was still captured by the story.

One minor triumph however is the way events of the insurgency are told, or not told. At no time are we afforded a view of events beyond the immediate experience of the main leads and only then via interaction with another human being. In this way the utter chaos of the situation is portrayed by surrounding them with hundreds of people but utterly isolating them from any information or wider order, a truly terrifying prospect. For me this was not quite carried off but the intention was clear.

In some respects, given this information starvation and the small scale focus, I wonder if it might have just have been better to forego the final explanatory voice over, totally forget the how and why of the alien "defeat" and focus on the fact that Ray and his family survive, rather than having them make it to safety AFTER the turning of the tide. There the finale of the film is confused: did they make it home through tenacity and strength of human spirit or simply because the aliens were defeated? In line with the film's focus it should be the former but due to the "NO shields!" scene and the final voice over it comes across as the latter.

To sum up, I think the original film and story preys on our defencelessness and desperation as a species, and therein lies it's strength, but the new film focuses on the defencelessness and desperation of a few individuals and, in this day and age, I think individuals have plenty in their real domestic lives to threaten their health and well-being without the need to involve an alien insurgency.

title: Minor holes, but overall very real and very scary.
review: OK by real i don't mean that its a good chance that Martians are buried underneath us at this very point in time and will soon come up and destroy us all, but nevertheless Spielberg's War of the Worlds is one of the most harrowing films i've seen come out of Hollywood in a long time. The images of people running away from the tripods (thank god they were tripods and not hover crafts!! Thanks you Mr 'berg) and being instantaneously puffed out is burnt (no pun intended) onto my memory. I'm glad that he decided to focus on a few imperfect human character rather than offering large scale destruction sequences. I can watch Independence Day for that. This time we're given something different in an alien invasion movie - people involved in the destruction to care about! I'm also glad that the demise of the Martians was brought on by bacteria, just as in the book. What i didn't like was the fact that "God in his infinite wisdom" put the bacteria on the Earth. If God put bacteria on Earth, then he created the Martians on Mars. Why would infinite wisdom reside in killing your own creations? Curious. We always need someone to credit and if it couldn't be a gung-ho Yank, then by Joe it was gonna be the next best thing - a Deity which cannot claim sides, because we allocate him them! Yay us. But aside from these little blunders (If the Martians could get here 1 000 000 years ago, why did they wait until there were people to bother them to invade?) this is still a cinematic event, like all Spielberg films (save The Terminal)

title: Surprisingly enjoyable
review:
I went into this film, like many, a sceptic. I was still having bad feelings at the start when Ray (Cruise) is walking around with a gawky smirk on his face. However, once the movie gets going, which is very early on, I discovered that for the most part, all of the actors were very good, with the exception being Robbie (Chatwin) who was wooden basically all the time.

The special effects were, to put it simply, brilliant. The tripods were done very well and looked very similar to what I had envisioned from the novel. The aliens also, were well done, sometimes scary and sometimes cute, for want of a better word.

What I did think was missing from this film was the famous pit scene but still, what they did instead was great.

My main concern was not to do with the film but the classification. In Scotland, this is a 12A which means than under twelves can see it as long as they have a parent with them. I think that very few children would truly be able to cope with it as there were times when I myself was feeling queasy.

That aside, this is very worth while seeing.

review: I enjoyed this movie I might see it again.I went to see it with a very analytical attitude in comparing it to the 1953 George pal movie and the 1938 radio version.I was looking for more narration about the state of affairs in the world during the invasion.Very little of this was in this movie.I also wanted to see more about military preparedness in response to this invasion and more actual fighting between the military and the aliens.I think Spielberg did try but it wasn't enough.The term martians was hardly ever mentioned and more scientists in the movie would of helped.Perhaps the movie was to humanistic in regards to the affairs of one family.Never the less it was a good enough movie and I will probably buy the DVD when it comes out.I would welcome responses to my comments!

title: Earth shattering disappointment !
review:
It is so rarely that you find yourself in the awkward position that the actual ending of a film is so defining for the overall quality of a movie that it actually determines ones judgment of the whole movie. I mean, of course there is good endings and bad endings, but mostly the ending in itself wont influence much on your rating of what actually lies before the ending. Like in 6th sense where you might like the ending, or you might not. But still most people I've met likes the movie for the scary effects and the well played roles etc - and hey, thats a movie all about the ending...

War of the worlds is not such a film! But the complete and utterly crappy ending is just soo lame that the film in my opinion is unviewable, and you should definitely avoid this film for your own sake.

As a sci-fi fan, I tend to like the effects and the interesting visions for the meet up with life from outer space, but there's just too big holes in the story lines and the whole plot leaves you in your seat grasping for your breath. Mr. Spielberg, to leave the audience with such a halfhearted ending is just plain rude. Everything up till the very 5 minutes that contains the abrupt ending is great!!! Really great! Cruise and Fanning gives a performance that is all that, and even Tim Robbins does a more than decent performance as a half crazy story helper. But mainly - this movie succeeds in something rarely seen for a Gollywood/Spielberg production - the actual scenario of aliens invading earth is in itself portrayed very interesting and with great effects etc. But where this movie really kicks in and grasps the viewer, is when it comes to the often brutal portrayal of people, just being people - caught in a horrifying and highly unfortunate situation.

The best portrayal in War of the Worlds is without any doubt his sharply woven picture of the human mind and not least kind. A person can be all that, but "people" are mostly stupid! The human scenarios in the movie is all too terrible likely to actually occur (Not the alien thingy - the human factor). There is no doubt in my mind that the nightmare like conditions arising when people turns against each other in the fight to get themselves and their loved ones to safety would arise. He really makes one believe that should you and I find ourselves in the very same quite unlikely situation, we too would react in the same stupid and extreme manner.

Before the ending the movie had me wondering how far, and to what horrifying extent I myself would go, in order to protect those I love and hold dear.

So far everything is above average for a film about aliens slaying humans on earth. But when the ending in so many words is completely independent of the rest of the movie, I must say that all the setups, all the suspense that is lined up through the movie and even the quite well played characters, is all completely shattered by the ending. What could truly have been a monument of Spielbergs philosophical and ideological interpretation of the modern world, about humanity in all its horror and greatness, is sadly punctuated like a flat tire and left is only the hollow rack of an over inflated rubber tube.

I will not go into why the ending is so terrible and I hate when people starts analyzing all sort of crap to prove that the ending is unlikely or unjust to this and that. I will leave you with this though: What happens between the beginning and the ending of this film, is so nervewracking ridiculously unimportant for the plot as a whole, that it saddens me to the very bone of my science fiction loving soul. Plz go see the darn thing and you will see that I am right!

DISCLAIMER As you can clearly see, English is NOT my native language. If I in any way have offended you by the ill use of this language, please forgive me, as I know not what I am saying.

title: A magnificent metaphor for our time
review:
This is not a science fiction movie. It is not an action adventure blockbuster. It is not a war movie. It is a horror movie about human fears, how we react to the unthinkable, and how humanity may ultimately prevail (with some luck.)

There has definitely been a lot of confusion about the film. Clearly while most critics like the movie, it has befuddled some audiences and left some critics cold. This is unfortunate, because what Spielberg has done is taken a Victorian tale, and projected it effortlessly to our time. So powerful is Wells's myth, that the essence of the story remains intact, while Spielger adds what I believe to be some of the most incredible action sequences and set pieces in the history of film. I confess, I was drained by the end of "War of the Worlds." There is little in the way of a catharsis here. We are just glad to be alive. We are left stunned by the fact that humanity was completely at the mercy of a power that was waging a war of extermination. The power in the movie was the aliens, but it is made very clear it could be any human power as well.

The film has been criticized for "exploiting 911 imagery." This is nonsense. Spielberg as the film maker can go anywhere he want with this tale -- as long as he does a good job, and one with integrity. He does. The imagery is right. It belongs in the movie -- unless we want to pretend the day did not happen.

I have been highly critical of the man since "Schindler's List," (not that he lies awake at night worrying about that), but I have to commend him here. This movie deals with our fears so well that I am tempted to call it the first great post- 911 film. If you see it in the right frame of mind, of what it is intending and not- intending to do, you will be rewarded.

Overall, the film is a technical masterpiece. Every actor rises to the occasion. Tom Cruise especially does a remarkable job as the American Everyman who fights back with brains and extraordinary courage. And Dakota Fanning -- what can I say? The girl is going to have as many Oscars in her career as Streep and Hepburn. Even Tim Robbins, as a man ultimately driven mad by the situation, is first rate.

My only criticism is that the ending is too abrupt. The film should have been longer to ease the audience into Wells's conclusion of the tale. And the "Searchers"-like final shot left me a bit confused. But these are quibbles.

In short, well done, Spielberg and Company. I am impressed.

title: Visually and viscerally amazing, but lacks a compelling narrative.
review:
War of the Worlds is quite a spectacle, dark, claustrophobic, menacing and often quite frightening. Reminiscent of The Terminator, I found myself feeling quite unsettled at times.

However, these aspects can never be the core of a movie, only the dressing to support a real story, with involving characters, plot development and emotional involvement. Unfortunately, this War of the Worlds is significantly lacking in these. There is an odd sense of detachment and uninvolvement of the characters with what is happening around them, and we the audience feel the same. There is no real explanation for what is going on, there is very little science-- it all just kind of happens and it is over.

Since this movie is based on a classic novel, it shouldn't have been hard to do. The 1953 movie, with the best special effects of any 1950s movie I have seen, is really superior in every way.

It's unfortunate, because what is good about this movie is very good -- if only Spielberg had fleshed it out more it would have been a knockout.

title: A re-imagining of a re-imagining.
review:
Wells wrote a good story about a technologically superior enemy colonising our planet and displacing the locals. The goal was to try and teach people who advocated the colonisation of Africa, what it was like to be on the receiving end.

Unfortunately the world has moved on since then. A modern tank (120mm sniper rifle + 60 ton metal heat sink) would be a good match for the original tripods. Gerald O'Neil showed us in the 1980s how then technology could easily be used to create space-colonies which in many ways are better than planets. More to the point, we don't colonise any more.

So how do you update WotW? Well the Iraq War from the PoV of Iraqis wouldn't have been far wrong. Nor would Mars Attacks; that at least addressed the issue of why the Martians would want to attack. Or you don't, and you tell the original story.

Spielberg has done none of these things though. He has taken a classical piece of literature and turned it into a cheap disaster/horror film. Worse than that, he has castrated it by giving it such a low age-rating. The true horror of what such an invasion would mean (and the horror of American soldiers are doing in other countries right now) is therefore safely locked away from anyone who might be shocked by it.

He's taken the 1950s film and warped it still further by revelling in evil and inhumanity of the invaders. Where as the whole point of the original story was that the invaders were doing nothing that the so called 'innocent' country had already done to countless others.

title: War of the Worlds is the best movie of the summer
review:
The summer's biggest blockbuster is already here. I couldn't wait to see War of the Worlds. It was my number one movie to watch in the year 2005. When you have a movie that Steven Spielberg is directing, you know its going to be a terrific movie. I loved all the Jurrassic Park movies, although Spielberg didn't direct the third one, it was still good.

There were no boring scenes in War of the Worlds. Everything is pure fun and it is a wild ride. If only there were more jump scenes. I thought there would be some scenes in which an alien would pop out of no where, but that doesn't matter.

Signs, directed by M. Night Shyamalan, is a brilliant alien movie. It was dark and in my opinion, the scariest movie I have ever seen. If only War of the Worlds would have you scared and shaking. But a movie with disaster like this, I don't think you can expect that. There was only one scene that made me jump. I think there were two jump scenes, but only one made me.

The performances were outstanding. I love Dakota Fanning. I mean, who doesn't? She's so good in all of her movies and she keeps getting better and better. She can act better than some A list female actresses. Tom Cruise also did good. But he always seems to be smiling when there's something serious going on. Maybe thats just his face.

There was a problem with the ending. During the movie, Ray (Cruise) looses his teenage son. He kept thinking he will never see him again, but when the battle was over, he went to his wife's house and to know they were all safe, including his son. It should have been better if they all died and Ray and his daughter (Fanning) survived. The only ones that survived. But the ending doesn't ruin the movie. It's a must see!

War of the Worlds is exciting and a wild ride that would have you on the edge of your seat. If you want a movie with great acting in it and with outstanding special effects, then you should definitely see War of the Worlds. It's one of the best movies of the year. (9/10)

title: A possible explanation for the camcorder issue..
review:
Come on! WOTW is a fine movie, shot with excellent direction. I have never felt in action during a movie despite the fact that I felt threatened by aliens! Spielberg does his job with great respect and wisdom. Sorry 'artistic' people! But he is kind of a genius, always innovating something. I've watched -maybe- a thousand movies, but I go to the theater rarely due to financial constraints, yet Spielberg always makes me stretch my budget. This is why he makes a lot of money! As a fan of many kind movies including 'artistic' ones, I cannot see the reason for the hate against Spielberg. He absolutely loves and respects what he does and more importantly he cares about and respects the audience. Finding problems in a movie is very easy, I count them to double digit numbers for most of the movies.

For the CAMCORDER issue; I should say it cannot be a mistake. I am not a very technical guy but all the things broken down by the lightnings have either connection to the local electrical network or have electrical engines( for example, a watch or a car-cars have small electrical engines to start) But camcorder does not have any of this.. I cannot believe such a stupid mistake exist in a so perfectly shot movie. Still, I can be mistaken..

For the plot, I should acknowledge the weakness of the end, however it is very analogous to the ending of Wells' book. I have always liked the book and as a fan I found the script successful in the sense that it follows the book (secretly). If it were focusing a bunch of people as in Deep Impact, the result will be a betrayal to the book and will lead to another Independence Day.

Cast was fine! Cruise is an intelligent guy, he knows in which movie to play or invest.

Above all, what makes this movie very good is that it is excellently shot. From the first to last 10 minutes, audience, at least me, is absolutely thrilled by the reality of things in a science fiction movie. Everyone should admit that Spielberg is a very talented guy...

I like Spielberg science-fictions..

edit after couple of years: I cannot believe I called Cruise intelligent!

title: Awesome!
review: I enjoyed this movie so much that as soon as it finished, I went outside and bought another ticket to see it a second time right away! I don't know if I have ever done that before (although I may have with the initial release of "The Empire Strickes Back"). It was fun (very few slow scenes) as well as suspenseful and scary (I spent much of the movie with my knees drawn up to my chest and my arms around them). The effects were awesome and well executed (the tripods and other effects did not dominate, as is the case with most of the Lucus movies - Spielberg has retained his ability to emphasize the human experience (both filmed and viewing) rather than focusing on the latest technical display (although I am sure some of the indirect displays of the tripods were quite complex to develop). He is still telling a story about people, not just creating a sequence of CGI shots). I highly recommend this movie, but advise not bringing small children. It is too scary for them.

title: Excellent!
review:
Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise) is a lift driver, divorced from Mary-Ann (Miranda Otto), who, on his way home from work, bumps into Mary-Ann and her new boyfriend, Tim, who are there to drop off the two kids, Robbie (Justin Chapman) and Rachel (Dakota Fanning). When they are bored, Robbie drives off illegally. Rachel orders hummus. Ray is half asleep, until a great storm...well, great until something comes up from the ground.

Loosely based on H.G. Wells' novel, and seeming to borrow more from the radio broadcast, Steven Spielberg's War of the Worlds seemed, from the trailers, to look like a stupid Spielberg summer (ooh three s's!) blockbuster that everyone would think is dumb in five years time. But when I went to see it...far out. From the first word...I was amazed. When I said "borrow more from the radio broadcast" I am quite correct. The first speech is said by Morgan Freeman who seems to be making a big comeback into Hollywood with Unleashed, Batman Begins, and this, War of the Worlds. Freeman reads basically what Orson Welles does in the broadcast, except it was altered to suit the modern times. Spielberg has really done this very well, and I am not a big fan of Tom Cruise (except in Collateral), but a big fan of Dakota Fanning, and these three are great when they are put together. I think when Spielberg said he wanted to scare audiences just like Orson Welles did, he put that statement to justice. Really the second half of the film, though, really scared me. But the scariest part is when Ray and Rachel are "surviving" with Tim Robbins' character, Ogilvy. One of the scariest parts in this whole situation was when Tom Cruise blindfolded Rachel and told her to sing a nursery rhyme, so she didn't hear him do a certain something. There is also possibly one of the scariest scenes when the Ferriers have a car, and many people bash it, and beat Ray up because they have it. The reason it's scary: it's human behaviour. We are like that, we are all scary, wanting things for ourselves. Survival of the fittest, not the ones doing the same thing. This movie, I think, H.G. Wells would approve of, because it is an unusually dark and eerie picture from Spielberg, adding to the level of human emotion, fright, and love. Another part of this movie I really liked: Spielberg focused more on the main three characters than the aliens invading, which I liked very much, and also, the CGI didn't overrule the story, which made it all the more scarier. Justin Chapman, although I thought wasn't a great addition to the production, I must admit did a very good job of being the stuck up son who doesn't give a crap about his father, just himself. We can just glide over Tom Cruise for a second. He was predictably great as Ray Ferrier, and did a good job of being the father trying to take control of the situation he knows he might not escape from. But to Dakota Fanning: AMAZING. If the Oscars don't at least nominate her, I will complain, as I think many other people will, because she was just great in this. Wait, great isn't the word. There is no word for Dakota's amazingly brilliantly tremendously awesome performance. She did one amazing job in this movie, especially when she was frightened. When she sang the lullaby, it made me shiver...and when she screamed looking at the camera...Dakota, you deserve an Oscar for this performance. I am dead serious. If she doesn't win or even get nominated, I will write a complaint to the Academy Awards® to put it lightly. Spielberg did a great job in casting her, I really think he did.

title: War of The Worlds, a thoroughly intelligent and well thought out film
review: I was extremely pleased to see the 2005 version of the War of the Worlds. Its theme was the same as all movies in the time and society we live in, the thought of a world at war with terrorists and an uncertain future, as the theme of the original dealt with Hollywoods obsession with communism, and the American way of dealing with unwanted visitors or believers of different ways of life. A man Tom Cruise, coming to terms with an irresponsible life, and faced with his own mortality. He battles to find the strength to survive and try to ensure a future for his two children, although uncertainty dogs his every move. It was good to see Gene Barry and Anne Robinson, stars of the classic 1954 film of the same name.

title: One of the best yet!!!
review: Now with all the hype about Tom Cruise being a psycho these days, he really managed to once again pull off a great movie! Ignore all the people who bashed this just cause of him and Steve-o. This was one of the best movies I have ever seen, the effects were amazing, the CGI was well utilized, but yet not overdone; at times you couldn't even tell it was CGI. Tom, Dakota, and Robbins' performances were wonderful. Sure most of the movie involves Dakota crying and/or screaming, but it is the subtleties of the rest of it that she pulls off so well, truly showing how badly a divorce, and having a deadbeat father does to a young girl, and how her brother is her only safety net in life... Amazing for an 11 year old. I laughed, I cried a little, I sat wide-eyed a lot, and I loved every minute of it!!! There was one sequence in particular that really affected me deeply, showing a very poetic mirror of a soldier left alone on the battlefield walking home through his comrades own blood... Amazing cinematography!! You only see what the family sees, and it adds to the suspense cause you really don't know what the hell is going on at all until its all over, leaving you to have to back track and think if any of it was even real...

title: AHHHH....some yes, some no with War of the Worlds!
review: OK,to start...for the most part the special effects were pretty awesome, though there appeared to be some "re-use" of some effects from past Spielberg movie's; liked the different "type" of "ground alien/soldier"; liked the "blood veins/roots"; liked the initial "hurry up" and "let's get this movie started", beginning; didn't like the "indoors" scenes too much with Tim Robbins-too long/40-50 percent boring; didn't like Dakota Fanning screaming so much(they should have given her more lines/alien encounter scenes instead- this role was a waste of her potential, I think); A little re-editing might make this movie more quickly paced and "in your face"!

title: Spielberg's summer blockbuster delivers!
review: This movie, while not Spielberg's best work, is the only summer movie you have to see! The special effects are stunning. The music is well produced. There is humor, but kinda misplaced in this extermination. You get a feel that you're there and this is truly is man-kind's downfall. The scale of this movie is epic, and it shows in the amount of detail to everything. Spielberg DID take some liberties with the story, but the ending of the book is intact in the movie. Also, the ending isn't all that great like you would expect from a movie like this... it doesn't give you full closure of the events that transpired on Earth. None the less, it is a great movie not to be missed. If you hate Tom Cruise because of what he's done in the public's eye recently, go see Batman Begins... that movie is well done and has Morgan Freeman in it.

title: one of the best movies i have ever seen
review: I LOVE THIS MOVIE. it is with out a doubt one of the greatest movies i've seen in my life, mainly because it felt real, like it could happen today. i actually own the TV from the movie, which really helped to connect it to the world that i live in. i actually found myself caring what happened to the characters. it managed to keep the focus on the family, while still having a truly epic scale. i was on the edge of my seat from the moment the aliens attacked to the end credits. it was one of those movies where you walk out of the theater in awe. another thing that helped make it so believable, was that the beginning was actually pretty funny, the baseball scene in particular. i don't want to say any more, but it also showed me that this guy had the same kinds of problems we do. the only real negative was that the ending was a little weak, however the rest of the movie more then makes up for it. everyone should go see it

title: Don't believe the (good or bad) hype
review:
Early reviews of War of the Worlds suggested that this was a movie for the cinema history books, an amazing, relentless, and terrifying spectacle. Later reviews came out, blasting the film as a disappointing clunker. Still more reviews praised the movie for its opening sequences but discounted its ending as a colossal disappointment.

I didn't feel the beginning of the movie was as strong as the raves suggested. Nor, however, did I find the ending of the movie to be as disappointing as I'd anticipated.

War of the Worlds is not a great flick. Neither is it a terrible one. It's good, though. It manages to remain entertaining. No more, no less.

title: Movie was FABULOUS!!!
review: This movie was excellent! I was on the edge of my seat, pretty much the whole movie. Your heart is pumping, you don't know what's going to happen next....and it's funny too! I thought the effects were great! I would totally recommend this movie! Tom Cruise (despite his latest antics) was really good, great in fact! Dakota Fanning was wonderful....and for those who complain because they think she screams too much in the film....HELLO!!! She's an 8 year old girl being chased by aliens! Wouldn't you scream!?!?? She is just great, interacting with Tom's character. I'm very happy with the movie, and I hope you all enjoy it too!

title: Spielberg Shows Us Aliens Aren't Just Cuddly and Trying to Phone Home
review:
May contain spoilers.

I'm probably one of the last people you want to go to when asking about a Steven Spielberg film, because I'll always tell you they are always good. Or great. Or awesome. Or spectacular. I think there might be one other director who I'll make myself like their films. One.

I mean, Jurassic Park made me choose two career paths: 1. a paleontologist, and 2. a filmmaker. So you can blame that movie for everything. But seriously, Spielberg has changed my life with most of his films, and even his weaker ones I'll make myself like if I have to.

Whenever I walk into a Spielberg theater I think, "Okay, I'm just going to immerse myself in this world you're presenting and even if the largest plot-hole ever exists, I'll believe it." And it hasn't failed. I've never had to make myself like a Spielberg movie, either. I always have. He obviously is very much in control of his material. Self-proclaiming directors like Lars von Trier don't have anything on him.

Tarantino should quiver in his presence. The only other filmmaker almost on par with Spielberg in Scorsese. Seriously, Spielberg was named the greatest filmmaker by a British magazine. Hitchcock and Kubrick are excellent as well, but. . . . I don't know, basically I have a bias towards Spielbergian films. I always will. I have had one since 1993 and it hasn't gone away, even when I've gone through my different phases and whatnot.

So, on to War of the Worlds.

I loved it. And it is, by far, the best film of 2005. Batman Begins, Star Wars, Cinderella Man, and all those other films have nothing on this.

First of all, Spielberg gives us believable characters. He is going to make you like these guys, because, if you don't, you won't care what happens to them. And that's what tension is all about. Second, he gives us a story. Actually, it's H. G. Wells's classic masterpiece story, though vamped up a bit. The ending and events are all relatively the same, but just in a different time period. Finally, when characters and story are out of the way, Spielberg knocks us out with the visuals.

It's a running movie. Tom Cruise and his kids run away from the alien creatures. And just like Spielberg made it seem like they could be our friends, he turns around and shows us how they can rape us as well.

The tension. Man, some of those scenes are incredibly intense, I can't even describe (though one of them mimics Jurassic Park, but that's all good). I couldn't take my eyes off the screen, I was engulfed in what was going on.

Then, I squirmed in a few places. Like the red mist scene.

Brilliant film.

And we get performances out of everyone that is actually worthwhile. Cruise proves he can act and isn't always just a pretty face (think the Mission: Impossible films). I'm not a big fan of Dakota Fanning, but she was excellent.

Again, the story gives us plenty of moments of intensity. And great, and loud visuals. Kaminski's cinematography always makes you think that the entire thing is surreal, but very real, like the worst adrenaline rush ever.

The ending was kind of a bit off, but it can be forgiven by the brilliant scenarios that proceed it.

Anyways, I still think this is the best movie of 2005 by far. See it now.

***1/2 /****

title: Kick Ass Movie!
review:
To Why all the rave? - Bad Special effects?!! Thats the last thing to complain about the special effects were amazing! This movie is great fun, it has one or 2 little problems sure, but nothing that ruins the non stop destruction fun! Forget batman begins, go see this!

The movie does a great job of creating tension, its not a horror movie, startle people by having things leap out at them movie, but it has a constant tension throughout the movie, and it shows how people will act in disasters.

Three major emotions throughout the film are pity, fear, and amazement at the epic catastrophe scenes. I would give this a 9 but am lowering it because it could have been a bit longer in order to explain things a but more throroughly.

title: Very Disappointing
review:
OK, this was an exercise in two movies...the first half being riveting, intense and genuinely well directed. The second half is rehashed Jurassic Park cheap setup thrills, incredible suspensions of disbelief and a very rushed and hacked on ending. I say this not because I did not know the ending...most of us do, but because it was even more abrupt and disorienting than the book and the original '54 film, almost tacked on.

What's worst are the many...and I mean many plot holes...I won't go into them but there are things that happen in this film that make no sense within the guidelines of the world Spielberg has created...rule #1 of films...you can bend the rules of the real world, but adhere to them within your own film and no one will buy it...he broke that rule.

As far as entertaining...yes it was, but after-wards I found myself very upset at how much of a missed opportunity this was. It was not bad but so filled with holes it annoyed me when thinking back over the film.

The effects are top notch. I mean top...the tripods themselves are so realistic I could swear they were models...they have none of the typical glossy CGI look to them, especially when shown in broad daylight with sun reflecting off of them. The only effects I did not enjoy were the tentacle arms in the basement scene (which incidentally lasts wayyyy too long, cops most of its choreography from Jurassic Park and is just plain silly)...as well as the aliens themselves. We did not need to see them at all and when we did they were a let down...but those tripods were insanely realistic.

All in all, a fun movie, but certainly not the triumph critics would have you believe. Not sure why but this and Land of the Dead are getting great reviews. Land of the Dead just plain stunk and this one is a major letdown yet critics adore them...hmmm, could they be trying to get more butts in the seats based on the long slump the box office has been in???

title: Incredibly tense, frightening... and very real
review:
With the fact in mind that my review is but one of hundreds, I nevertheless hope to put the more skeptical of viewers at ease by stating that THIS IS ONE HECK OF A GOOD MOVIE. Steven Spielberg has put his trademark touch on the classic H.G. Wells story by incorporating a struggling family into the plot, and it works quite well. The special effects are outstanding, but most importantly, they don't rule the screen - they supplant the story with incredible effect, through the use of handy-cam effects, mirror reflections, events occurring in the foreground and background in parallel... It all serves to put you right into the middle of the action and make you believe it is all real - no matter how far-fetched the story may seem. Humanity's reaction of turmoil and panic is frighteningly real, and so are the alien tripods and their behaviors. I literally sat there sweating with my heart racing during most of the film.

To address some of the more common issues brought up by negative reviews... Things such as cars and camcorders working again after they first fail is NOT a goof. For one thing, who knows how thoroughly an EMP pulse really destroys all electronics? Some things survive it and/or recover after a while, so I saw nothing wrong with the guy filming the first attack, or the main characters driving off in a working car. Tim Robbins' character is well-acted, Tom Cruise is quite good and Dakota Fanning just about steals the show with her great acting. Who said all she does is scream? Bottom line, if you go into this film without a sense of cynicism and wanting to nag on every little detail... you will find that this is an incredible movie to see. Intense through and through, and worth seeing right to the end. (Which, to be fair, DOES come just a tad bit too suddenly, but doesn't ruin the movie in any way.) This movie is all I expected it to be, and then some.

title: A very entertaining thriller with some really creepy moments, some outstanding visual and sound effects, and some good performances by the characters.
review: This was an excellent film. I found it to be entertaining and thrilling, which was the intention of the producers. If you are expecting an educational film with no plot holes, then you will be disappointed. If you are expecting a typical Spielberg spectacle, then you will be in for a treat. The visual and audio effects are truly amazing. Not bad for a 7 month project. The tripods are very much like those described in HG Wells book, complete with an ominous war cry and a very convincing death ray. This film pays homage to both the book and the original 1953 film. Gene Barry and Ann Robinson, who starred in the original film, have a cameo at the very end of this film. Tom Cruise, despite his controversial public persona, does an effective acting job here. Dakota Fanning, who plays his daughter, has an Oscar-worthy performance in the film. While the film has some references to 9/11, the terror mainly comes from the realization by the characters that the only thing left to do is escape the onslaught. A very entertaining thriller with some really creepy moments, some outstanding visual and sound effects, and some good performances by the characters.

title: Fantastic spectacle - shame about the dumb scenes though!
review:
On the positive side this is one hell of a spectacle. The opening 20 minutes build the story around the fractured family headed by a less than dutiful father Tom Cruise. Spielberg is a past master with building personality into his movies but however hard he tries I just don't think he builds the human characters enough to make them credible or believable.

The first views of the doom laden sky point to something amiss when bizarre lightning storms consume the planet. From the first signs of potential trouble the film then moves up a gear to continue at a frantic pace as Cruise and his two kids try to keep one step ahead of the alien invaders.

It is a real shame that such a masterful filmmaker as Spielberg allows this spectacular film to fall down on a number of stupid 'gaffs' or unbelievable sections where the dialogue is so daft or stilted that it made me cringe.

The references to terrorism and the picture boards of the faces of the missing are misplaced as is the same old tired notion of the dysfunctional family eventually pulling together.

Overall though I would recommend you see WOTW although be warned that it may well leave you feeling a little hollow

title: Not just an entertainment movie, though it seems to be
review: "War of the Worlds" may seem a lot like the typical summer blockbuster that you eat along with your popcorns and you forget right after you get out of the theater, as you've done with the last ten summer blockbusters. It's not. Worldwide hated Steven Spielberg redeems of his last flaws ("Catch me if you can", "Artificial Intelligence" and the somehow incomplete "Minority report") with this hell on earth caused by an alien invasion that has more in common with "Saving private Ryan" than it has with "Independence Day" (for example). At first, when we get into the life of Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise) and his selfish, childish and rather inexistent relationship with his two kids, old-time Spielberg emerges from the shadows and, for the first ten minutes or so, the spirit of "Jaws" or "ET" comes back to life. His ability to depict the apparent routine of real life and, then, break it with the unexpected is superb, and in "War of the worlds", he does his best. The scene that breaks it all up (literally) and starts the journey is the one with the electric storm and the lightnings, probably the most terrifying scene filmed by Spielberg since "Close encounters of the third kind" (it makes you start to sweat with just some lightnings). After "uncle Steven" reminds us all he still knows how to frighten us with two bucks, the CGI madness begins (yeah, it begins with a camcorder that shouldn't be working, but that's, you know... madness): Brooklyn blown up, people disintegrated, trains in flames, corpses floating in the river and families destroyed. But throughout all these catastrophes, we slowly see a man, lost with his children somewhere, who is forced, little by little, to assume his responsibilities and to become an adult. And as being an adult means loosing, he has to go through the worst of all losses (he apparently sees his son die) to truly look into the eyes of his daughter and see his only salvation. Of course most people will say this film is mushy and shallow (they say that about any Spielberg movie), but that's just because they don't make the effort of looking more deeply. But Tarantino and Robert Rodriguez, Guy Ritchie and Kevin Smith, they are the great directors of our time, and they're profound and complex. Of course, Kill Bill is profound: Uma Thurman spends the entire movie kicking the hell out of 239 people in a yellow suit, man! That must be deep!!! Not like Tom Cruise stylishly closing the door behind him, ready to kill a human being in order to save his daughter, while she sings the lullaby he wasn't able to remember, his worst fail as a father redeemed. We should remember that Hitchcock, Hawks, Walsh, and other directors were underrated and even hated in their time, until Cahiers du cinema, with Truffaut, Chabrol, Goddard and the others rescued them as critic sacred cows, and the same will happen with Spielberg. But who remembers George Stevens or Lewis Milestone? Who will remember Tarantino?

title: A very good movie!
review:
Having read the books, and heard the radio show, I was really looking forward to this movie. As a movie, it's a great movie, the cinematography, editing, acting etc etc are all brilliant. Spielburgs use of tracking shots is always pretty amazing. As an adaptation of the book - well, considering they transplanted the action 19th century London to modern-day America, it's an OK adaptation. Not amazing, as they seemed to use the book as an outline or synopsis, and they changed quite a lot of it. As with Lord of the Rings (2001), you have to look at it as a film rather than a adaptation of the book.

Tom Cruise plays Ray Ferrier, a divorced docker, father to two children, and the central character. Dakota Fanning and Justin Chatwin play his two children, neither of them close to their father, and Robbie Ferrier (Chatwin) spends most of the film fighting his father in a typical teenage manner, preferring to fight as opposed to flee. Fanning is excellent as young Rachel, who is completely dependant on her brother and father.

It's a rare sort of action movie where the hero runs all of the time, and isn't entirely responsible for the downfall of the enemy. But this only makes this movie seem somewhat more realistic (for a sci-fi movie), and the composition of the family unit makes it somewhat easier to identify with the characters, especially facing his feeling of inadequacy compared to his ex-wife's new husband and his frustration with his rebellious teenager.

All in all, a very good movie!

title: Spielberg again graces us with his genius!
review:
*Now I should forewarn everyone who reads this review it is a bit slanted because I am a huge Spielberg fan and believe he has never made a bad film*

Here Steven Spielberg again gives us a brilliant Science Fiction film which has the power to scare an audience almost as much as the Orson Welles broadcast. I mean there is no way this film will cause a nationwide panic.

Spielberg although presents us with shocking visuals that truly induce fear into an audience. Tom Cruise gives his usual great performance and was supported by the wonder Dakota Fanning and Tim Robbins.

Although many will say this film is Jurassic Park with aliens, Spielberg still manages to frighten us. Some of the most frightening scenes do not even come as a result of the actions of these invaders but by the actions of people. Spielberg accurately portrays how people would act in these times of desperation and insecurity.

title: Surprisingly disappointing
review:
When H G Wells wrote the War of the Worlds, it was meant to be a critical look at the British Empire and its rather idealistic self-appraisal as the Greatest Empire in the World, which is shown to be so comprehensively inconsequential when the Aliens invade and start destroying Earth, with Humanity (and the British Empire) seemingly powerless to stop it from happening.

Since the British Empire has been dead and buried for the better part of the last 50 years, a new Empire was needed as the main protagonist for an updated version of the War of the Worlds. Steven Spielberg chose the only real empire left in the World today, the United States of America. This modernising of the story is understandable, yet it is hard to ignore the fact that this movie tries to put into perspective America's dominance of the world and the fact that when thinking of the universe as a whole, America and the human race in general are inconsequential.

The updated Story revolves around the character of Tom Cruise, a crude and egocentric father who's life centres around himself. He's taking care of his son and daughter for a weekend while his ex - wife (Miranda Otto) is away with her husband on a trip to Boston. Unfortunately for him, that weekend happened to be the time a group of Aliens decide to attack Earth. The Story is easy to follow since Spielberg keeps it surprisingly simple, concentrating on the 3 main characters as they attempt to flee the strange tripod-like Alien machines.

This movie is not about confrontation, it is about escape. Only at the very end do we get to see Tom Cruise slip into Ethan Hunt mode and try and fight back. The ending of the film is the same as the book's, but while it worked for the book, when employed here, it seems to cut the story short rather than finishing it. At the beginning, Spielberg chooses to spend no time developing the story preferring to jump right into the action. The ending suffers similar problems; it ends all too quickly, considering everything the protagonists have been through. As for the acting itself, there's nothing spectacular, though there is a wonderful cameo by Tim Robbins, as a man who has lost his family to the Aliens and who now stubbornly believes that fighting them is the best course of action. There is more than a hint of Irony about this role. Dakota Fanning plays Cruise's daughter; yes, I know she's only 11 and that she's supposed to be a great actress for her age, but she seemed to be overacting here. Either that, or I'm not making an allowance for the natural exuberance of a 11-year old girl.

The special effects are all standard fare, as you would expect from an accomplished director like Spielberg, but he doesn't really do the story justice. This movie gives me the impression of having been put together in a hurry, in a rather hotch-potch way, which is not surprising, since the release date was brought forward by almost two full years. There is a marked difference between this movie and The Terminal, which was Spielberg's last film set in post September 11th America. In The Terminal, Tom Hanks attempts to approach his predicament with optimism, despite the mess he finds himself in. Here, there is no optimism, just plain fear and desperation. I was disappointed, though the story deserves credit for its pace, never slacking anywhere, especially in the middle, when films tend to slow down. For that and the fact this is not bad overall (I was more disappointed with Spielberg that the movie itself), I'll give it 6 on 10.

title: Biology Saves the Earth
review: I loved this movie up until the end. First off it happened out of no where. What was the point of Tom Cruise pointing out the birds flying around the ships? I realize this was in the original story, but so what...these beings have the science to travel light years to Earth and defeat us without a problem but they forget to get vaccinated before traveling abroad??? Advance parties didn't catch this germ(s)? The planning for such an attack would have considered an alien world having alien germs. Maybe this wasn't thought out when HG did it originally, but maybe this should have been thought of now. Have earth use it as a defense by contaminating them. The door is open...

title: The movie was alright.. but not the greatest and here is why.....
review: The movie was okay but not the greatest. Like everyone else, I loved the original. I went to see this version with the notion that it will be like the original except with a lot more special effects. However, I was a little disappointed. Number one, why did Steven Spielberg dress up Dakota like Drew Barrymore in by beloved movie of all time E.T., with that 79 style shirt with rainbow strips and fluffy jacket. Number two, if bacteria has been around for millions and millions of years, how did the aliens get to bury the machines on earth without dying. Number three, once the lighting hit the floor, everything went dead, the TV, phone, car, light. So how did the old guy in the intersection with the video camera (when the first machine rose near the church) have power to shoot the machine. The video camera should not be working. Number four, okay so you suck with the original a little bit, but the part where Ray had to kill Ogilvy was uncalled for. I mean yea, he had to be silenced so that he would not make noise, but come on, to kill him!!! I did not like that idea that the aliens buried the machines in the ground. It would have been a lot better if they came from outer space. Number five, I doubt very much that aliens foresaw the future in that humans would one day populate the earth. There is a line in which Ogilvy said "It's an extermination." Why would the aliens bury the machines to one day enter them to kill humans if they never even knew of their existence. Number six, did it not occur to anyone writing the script that Ray drove from NJ to somewhere upstate NY without stopping to get gas for the car even once. HA! When the hatch opened up in the end and the blood came out, why did it look orange. Come on in this day and age, you can make blood look so real... Just look at Dawn of the Dead =) Even thought I knew how the movie ended, it was kind of stupid to have Ray and his kids drive all over the east coast when the real lesson was to "Stay in your basement and wait it out until the bacteria killed the aliens." Do you know how many people would have lived. So, all in all, I was a bit disappointed with Steven's version. I expected more than this. I loved the original. Another reason why the original and classics should never be messed with or touched!!

title: Quite good, but not brilliant!
review:
Actually this is an entertaining movie, somewhat of a cross between Independence Day and Signs. Not as action-orientated and not as burdened with heavy-handed patriotism as Independence Day, yet presented on a bigger scale than the events that take place in Signs.

While astonishingly not really superior to these movies, War of the Worlds is an acceptable and entertaining current adaptation of H.G.Wells novel to the big screen.

If you like Independence Day, Signs or Tim Burton's hilarious Mars Attacks you will likely enjoy the movie. Do not enter the cinema with excessive expectations, though!

War of the Worlds is certainly not a failure, yet similar to A.I. and Minority Report is also not a film that will leave a lasting impression.

I will not tell you about the film's ending here, but rest assured that Mr. Spielberg does stay true to his usual habits.

title: Even with the mistakes - it's just okay - spoiler alert too!
review:
Tom Cruise - totally unrealistic as a father trying to bond with his children, any father would have tried harder to get his kids attention.

The son of Cruise - I'd want to run away from Cruise as well if he was such a horrible dad, he was of the age when he could have said to the mom and step-dad, I don't want to go.

Dakota Fanning - how wonderful is she - that face, eyes, and scream. She's just so amazing for such a little lady. And it's too obvious that Spielberg wants to have her as the next Drew Barrymore, she can easily do it...she's just that much of a talented actress to go places that Drew could never have gone at such a young age.

The Plot - interesting concept, carried off rather well, but the movie needed more explanation as to the action.

Morgan Freeman as the narrator should have played a bigger part, his voice could have carried along some of the "dramatic scenes" to a more logical conclusion.

Tim Robbins - hysterical as the mad man in the farm house basement. Though the death scene was played nicely.

Now for the big F'd up ending: don't read anymore this is a spoiler! How the heck did the son live through the inferno that came over the hill? The father and daughter leave him behind, two seconds later, where he just was is a blazing inferno and he's not seen until the end of the movie...what a rip! I know it's just a movie, but the dramatic impact could have been done to bring the mother and father closer together with the loss of a child...but Spielberg just had to have the happy ending...how sad is that? Let a lead character died for once...he could have even gotten away with killing off Cruise at the end of the movie, the last alien strikes him down as his daughter is reunited with her mother in Boston.

Overall, special effects were nice, but the general consensus as everyone left the theater - what a stupid ending to a good movie.

title: Little disappointed but still good film.
review:
I went to the movies to see this film, after being bombarded with trailers for many months. I was sold at first sight of just a small teaser. But That may also be why the film give me a small disappointment. Yes it was a cool film, but great it wasn't. Much fancy stuff, but not the best story. I mean a girl screaming throughout the whole film, a father with kids trying to run away. We get to see the Aliens and suddenly they all just die because of small things in our water. Aka the film Signs. So the only defense our planet have is small things in our water. Yeah right. If they had studied us for millions of years, I would think the aliens also would know about everything on this planet. And it ended so stupid. So fast just in the middle of the good part - bang - the film is over. Come on! that sucks. hmm must adjust my voting down to a 6. The best was all the great effects, and no one can make aliens like Spielberg. But the ending destroyed my good mood. Almost everyone I have spoken to says the same in Norway at least. It was just to fast ans stupid. Short the film is this:

Scream - run - Scream - scream - run - scream - getting interesting - the end. the screaming of the young girl was just too much. And I get furious about using $12 for the movie ticket when I get ripped off like that. The ending sucked and that was that. Could at least have made a better story out of it, changed it a little. Never renting it on DVD, so it was just worth a one time look nothing more.

title: Interesting but what the heck?
review: This has nothing but spoilers: A lot of this film doesn't make sense but it was entertaining? What were all those red root/vein like things for? Why did aliens fry a lot of humans only to seem to need them as some kind of fuel later? How did the son make it through the intense conflagration? Why are the houses in Boston unharmed? What was the purpose of attacking earth anyway? Why would aliens bent on world conquest be wasting time on an a abandoned farm house, more than once? A lot of the movie is implausible, however it does have some great imagery. I liked the approach of taking the refugee approach which is not as exciting at say the "Independence Day" approach of military it was pretty interesting to see what happens to ordinary people. How people react during a crisis? What are the issues to face? Given our world and war a lot of what was explored was indeed relevant to basically refugees in war against a hostile, exterminating force. For this I gave the movie a favorable review.

title: It is not a great movie by all means
review:
This movie is obvious not the masterpiece of Mr. Spielberg. It suffers from several factor which lead the movie nowhere. The original book the move might have based on have more contents than what was expressed in the movie.

First part of movie, people are running scared. However, the fact that people under pressure will do should be more overwhelming that it showed on screen. The sense of tension is not felt through the movie most of the time. Only near the end when the little girl was lost can we sense a little bit fast paced.

As always, Tom didn't deliver any good performance by all means.

The movie also suffers from several logic flaws. We can't feel anything brought from Internet application and/or modern communication benefits. Though the original book was about 19th century, we should see that.

The aliens (from Mars?) did very inefficient job of killing. Not knowing exactly why they chose to keep people one by one ... for 6 Billion times? The ending is like in ID4: all aliens suffer from our human's flaw. Hey, maybe we should have fed them with some serious illness? Like ... HIV or TB or something? Or maybe it is because of that?

title: worth the admission but not for kids
review: I saw this movie last night with my 9 yr old son. I was expecting something along the lines of Independence Day or I never would have taken him - he had his eyes closed for half of it. This is a very intense and serious movie with very realistic graphics. There are some slow bits but all in all it was very enjoyable. title: Good show, but not nearly as 'earth-shaking' as you might expect...
review:
... It reminded me of "Titanic" in a lot of ways; you can see where all the money's gone; and a number of the visuals are quite simply fantastic. We know Spielberg can handle a set-piece; but for me, since the early days of films like Jaws he's comparatively lacking in the ability to marry such talent with the due care and attention required for a script. Give him a 'little' film, and he'll explore wider issues; let him loose on a blockbuster these days, and he goes for the showier moments to the detriment of other pleasures. Those of you who've seen "The Lost World" might get what I'm trying to say.

"Titanic" was a big film where the script took a backseat, and so is the case here. Of course, that doesn't mean there isn't some enjoyment to be had from what's on offer - and those just looking to marvel at the spectacle won't give a hoot; but why assemble a cast with such big-hitters, when there's not much thought behind their actions beyond 'look panicked'? At times it feels like a loosely disguised retrospective of Spielberg's past numbers, too; riffing on all the things you'd expect, like "Close Encounters" and "Jurassic Park". Why 'revisit' though, when such ground has already been covered? I hate to whine too much when something looks as good as this does; but it sorta feels like a step backward for Steven, after the looser, more 'experimental' style he's shown us with his recent work...

title: A very good interpretation from a master storyteller
review:
First thing to say is that this is a very good interpretation of the book. I think it remains very true to the feel of the book, obviously the time-line and country is different but the precept is the same. The worlds biggest power overwhelmed easily by superior forces and the confusion and panic that ensues. I think the way Spielberg makes us realise the way we take things around us for granted and that in an instant that can all change was superb, one minute Ferrier is watching a lightning storm and maybe 30mins later he is running for his life not knowing what has happening was great. The tripods were brilliant and true to the book and the combination of Ogilvy, the curate and the artilleryman in Tim Robbins character was genius as far as I was concerned. Also Ferriers determination to shield his daughter from the horrors was a nice human touch. In closing I would advise people to read H G Wells original book as Spielberg has obviously done, listen to Jeff Waynes Musical Version (very loud!) just re-released and watch the film.

The best thing about the film is that Spielberg keeps the focus on the characters and the emotions they are going through and ONLY uses special effects where appropriate, for example the battle scene on the hill could of been a major use of special effects with the images of war going on but you are left with being positioned just below the brow of the hill only able to hear the noise and see the flashes whilst the camera focus on the people and their reactions so you are left only with your imagination to fill in the detail. Very good A+

title: Wow
review:
This movie rocks big time.

I would say it's probably Spielberg's best film since Saving Private Ryan, in terms of being just a blistering assault on the senses.

Spoilers start here: The movie kicks into gear immediately with the first tripod appearing about 15 minutes in and it just does not let up. The CG is brilliant and not overused,(wait till you see the death rays blasting everyone in sight). There are also some powerful moments too involving Dad's desperation to protect his kids and Cruise really nails this role and is very believable. He is certainly no action hero in this, he's just as helpless as everyone else, at times he just seems confused and afraid.

What makes this film works is that is avoids the obvious army versus the aliens clichÃ© over and over, it sticks right with the Ferrier family and I only remember seeing jets and tanks in one scene and the odd soldier in a few. It also has great acting, great camera-work (check out the freeway shot) and very inventive set-pieces that put tension and fear before flashy visuals.

The only drawback is that the opening hour is so great it can't be topped in the second and unfortunately the end feels flat, although the same goes with the book, so I'm just nitpicking really. Overall I would call it one of the best blockbusters you are likely to see, and probably up there with Sin City in terms of being the best film this year.

Go see it you owe it to yourself.

title: What a movie!
review:
This is a must see awesome film that puts Spielberg back as undisputed master of the blockbuster.

Direction, special effects and tension are handled perfectly.

This is a movie that will grip you from the first few minutes and will linger in the mind days after watching.

There are some truly shocking scenes that will bring back emotions from recent real-world disasters that Spielberg uses to tap into those primal fears we all share.

The best action adventure movie of recent years.

George Lucas should take note!

title: Good, but not Great
review:
This Spielberg film is no Jurassic Park or Jaws as far as action yarns go, but it is good entertainment. I am a fan of this genre, both sci-fi and alien invasion actioner, and I have been a lifelong Spielberg fan, but I could not say that War of the Worlds is worthy of the hype. Like, I would probably not even buy it on DVD. Also, the audience reaction was tepid at my screening... no applause or spontaneous cheering or laughing. People just filed out as soon as the ending credits started.

(spoilers) I felt that after an excellent and exciting opening act (with plenty of destruction and a thrilling chase), the film goes to sleep in a too long middle act (hiding and in-fighting among the humans), and finally limps to the well-known conclusion (I had hoped Spielberg would do something creative here, something like the Independence Day twist). Also I thought that there were too many lucky coincidences experienced by the main characters (like repeatedly surviving close proximity encounters with the very deadly, very scary alien vehicles). There is much maneuvering and drama surrounding the Tom Cruise character's imperfect relation with his kids, who remain consistently and frustratingly uncontrollable throughout the film despite the obvious peril and mayhem around them.

title: Very good--Very disturbing
review:
I have been a fan for the most part of Steven Spielberg's work. I enjoyed the 1953 "War of the Worlds". I have read Wells' novella several times. I like sci-fi and horror, and have never really been bothered by sci-fi gore and fright.

Having said that, I think Spielberg's take on "War of the Worlds" is quite good (yes, fans of the picayune have repeated about the camcorder). I am impressed by the cinematography (Janusz Kaminsky again doing a great job). In fact, in certain regards, it is much more true to Welles' novella than the 1953 film was (down to the design of the alien machines as tripods, and the focus on a small group of people as the world comes to an end while watching your species get savagely wiped off the face of existence....and all are powerless to stop it). The 1953 film focused a lot more on the military's lack of success (mimiced to a certain extent in "Independence Day". Save for one scene, this is not a factor in this film.

Welles' original novel dealt with the forecasting of mechanized 20th century war, and how destructive it would be. I don't think this film makes quite the same statement about 21st century warfare, though it is intereting that Spielberg chose to ramp up his film a full two years in advance of its original release date...Orson Wells did his radio play as World War II was preparing to kick off, and the 1953 film was in the wake of Korea as the Red Scare swung into full swing. In a sense, we are there again, and I suspect that Steven Spielberg is taking advantage of the national mood to make a film that ten years ago would have lacked the resonance.

I think of any film that Steven Spielberg has ever directed, this film has far more in common with "Saving Private Ryan" than "E.T." or "Raiders of the Lost Ark". I found the imagery to be incredibly disturbing at times. I don't mean to make this sound negative....just a comment from someone very much not used to feeling that way in a film. I felt very tense while watching it, and hours afterwords still had some difficulty clearing my head of what I saw.

I was not crazy about some of the acting, and felt that there were some technical holes that developed in the plot. If you are the type that watches sci-fi for the technical aspects, you may be dragged out of the theater after yelling at the screen too many times. This is not that kind of sci-fi film.

I was amused by a comment claiming that the alien machines resembled those from previous sci-fi films. Considering that many of those films turned to H.G. Welles for inspiration, and that this is where Spielberg returned for his inspiration, this is not a time to be criticising Steven Spielberg.

After watching "Saving Private Ryan", I felt empty because I was left at the end with an "incomplete" feeling. I decided later that perhaps the film was not supposed to have a clean ending where there is a tidy message and lecture on what it all means, except that war is chaos...confusion...obliteration...insanity: a human experience that leaves you empty. This film left me with that same feeling.

I strongly urge parents to see this film before allowing younger children to watch it...this is not your average PG-13 film.

title: A war movie to remember
review: I saw the old 1955 movie, the other day and couldn't wait to see this. I love the movie, the only complaint was the shortness, and no meteors as in the old movie and the book, and the question of how a teenage boy walked all the way to Boston by himself. The movie went by the book very well, as compared to the old movie, which had UFO's, this had tripods which made you think differently about "alien movies". It had the same "3" stuff for the aliens like the old one, and the alien prob looked just as it did in the old one. Some people complain about the aliens dieing by (SPOILERS) germs, well READ THE BOOK! This also makes a good ending by "God protecting mankind". The cast was pretty good, but at some points it seemed like a script read line, but was pretty good. The feel of fear in Fanning was awesome, and she had a perfect role as Cruis's little girl. Over all not as WOW as Independence Day or as much action, but with a perspective of a normal person trying to survive, it is different than any other alien movie. Despite some unanswered questions and little changes from the book that was "bad" (the aliens being here all along), it was one of the best movies I've seen, and finally a change from the overboard superhero movies.

title: Ah, an apocalyptic philosophical science fiction movie with no environmentalist ravings...we haven't had one of these for a while.
review: I have been looking forward to this movie for some time but I still expected something along the lines of the dull Day After Tomorrow blockbuster from last year. I was pleasantly surprised. This is not everyone's film. You need to have a real appreciation for decent science fiction, and some people may find the characters too homely for their taste. I found the family relationship pumped the film with emotion because they were real characters, rather than the stereotypical gorgeous scientists and heroes that most apocalyptic films favour. However, I did find many scenes in the film disturbing because of the (deliberate or accidental) references to the atomic blasts of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, such as the bodies floating down the river and the separation of the family. But I don't count these against Spielberg, as every moment was treated with respect. The plot was enduring, but imperfect. Nitpickers will welcome a chance to point out every flaw in the logic, and I agree that (as in Shyamalan's Signs) the aliens did seem strangely ill- prepared for their invasion, which had supposedly begun thousands of years ago. The suspense was executed well: the terror was bitingly real. All over, War of the Worlds is well worth the viewing.

title: Great Movie!!!
review:
This film is so far (since its midway through the year) the best film of the year. Spielberg gives u everything: Suspense, drama, action, horror, in this one film. From min the tripod rises till the end, Spielberg leaves u on the end of your seat. I haven't been this scared since the Sixth Sense( and I was 12 when that was out) The only thing that was like ugh was at the end (which I won't spoil for u but book fans, ur be happy) but otherwise great and entertaining film.
