title: Cruise + Spielberg + Fanning = Amazing film
review:
WOW. that's simply the best of explaining this movie, WOW. I watched this film with a bit of apprehension after reading other reviews but I honestly cannot understand why it's got the critical bashing it has done.

Spielbergs work with the camera is amazing from start to finish. As another review stated (Sorry I can't remember the reviewers name) the camera almost seems to be part of the action in so much that it appears to be 'afraid' of what is happening, throughout the film this makes you feel as if your actually there next to Ray and Rachel which scores big plus points in my book.

Cruise is absolute perfection in this role. For the first half of the film he is easily hatable for the way he is with his children but, as the film progresses, he manages to do something many actors seem to have trouble with when playing the bad father who comes good, He makes the transformation between 'idiot' to 'good dad' seem believable, it doesn't seem forced as it does in SSSOOOO many other films.

Fanning, Where do I start. If this girl can keep going the way she is then she will be one of, if not THE, best actresses in Hollywood in years to come. I've watched her grow as an actress since I first saw "I am Sam" and it's just remarkable. Pretty much any other young actress would have been more than annoying in this role, always asking for mom and always putting themselves in danger which they have to be bailed out of but Dakota manages to bring a charm to the role that, instead of hating Rachel, makes you sit and pray that she will be OK. She actually managed to bring a few tears out on my part (I'm man enough to admit it) in scenes such as when she is stuck in the car and she's crying for her brother and father and at the end.

Now for the one downside to the film. The section with Tim Robbins in just drags, it didn't help that it came directly after such elaborate action pieces such as the Boat, It's ashame really as it drags the entire movie down from being damn near perfection.

Overall this movie is absolutely brilliant and doesn't deserve the bad reviews it's been getting. I bow down to Cruise and Fanning for some of the best actors these eyes and ears have ever witnessed.

title: One of the best sci-fi movies I have ever seen.
review: Hello, I am 33 and a big action/adventure and sci-fi movie fan. I try to give every movie I watch the "innocent until proved guilty" mentality. In other words I try to see the good in most movies unless they really suck. I have had my fair share of nearly walking out of theaters or putting a rental back in it's case after an honest 20 minutes of trying to like it. I would never put this movie back in it's case. I did walk out though...because the theater I was in had a bad front right driver that popped like a firework when a bass note hit -like with explosions and what-not. I got my refund and free pass from AMC and went 10 miles to another AMC theater and had a great time! The day before I actually saw it for the first time however and loved it then even though I stumbled upon what I believe to be the last theater in the universe that only had STEREO!!! NO SURROUND!!! What the f*ck is that???!!! After the first 2 minutes of what I hoped was them just testing the center channel with the previews, I glanced around the walls and saw lights and the, well just walls. No speakers. But the movie mesmerized me so much (and no not because it was secretly programming me for Scientology) that I actually could stand to sit thru the stereo -which is the A.M. Radio of cinema. But the next day I was on a quest to watch it with this new fangled thing called surround! What a neat concept. So after the speaker popping and crackling at one theater, some additional driving, and telling an 8 year old kid with A.D.D. and nervous twitches from a Ritalin overdose to quit kicking my chair whenever the action came (which, by the way was nonstop in this movie), I really, really have to say War of the Worlds is VERY entertaining and actually sorta scary. My mouth hasn't hung open that much since I saw a stripper do a weird thing with a Darth Vader Pez dispenser. The only reason I give it a 9 and not a 10 is because the climax wrapped up to abruptly and fast and I guess I would add lame to that too. The rest of the ending after that was fine again, but when you see it you'll understand my and many others complaint. The cheesy and horrible 80's band called Climaxx was better. But I have to say in all it was a great movie even though I feel Spielboyg cut a better climax out for time or some stupid thing. After 2 1/4 times of seeing it in 2 days, I can't be wrong about it being great. Well maybe I should go again tomorrow to make sure.

title: Best disaster/alien movie I've ever seen !!!
review: What can I say about this movie... It was awesome... stunning visual effects(CGI) and sound( the best I have ever heard -but I saw Wotw as usual in a kinepolis cinema which has outstanding sound-system ), superb acting between Cruise/Fanning-good family dialogue/humour... For the first time in my live I felt a little anxious during and after this movie because not like in the day after tomorrow or independence day, this is not extermination of buildings but this is an extermination of mankind, you can feel the anxiety/despair of the people in this movie... One negativity : the movie had a (happy) ending, I'd hoped for a total defeat ... but it happily had a clever ending :)

title: Great Movie
review:
After reading the book I knew what would happen in the movie and that disappointed me a bit: I knew that the aliens where going to die because of diseases and when Ray kills Ogilvy, because in the movie he killed the priest in a basement with only a little 'window' to the outside and all those moments that are really close to the book (which I don't think is a problem because Spielberg did it best this way).

I think that the movie is awesome. The special effects are really amazing I didn't know that those kind of effects could be made. I loved the part when the bridge falls apart over the houses. Tom Cruise, Dakota Fanning and Justin Chatwin are a great trio. One thing that made me look forward to see this movie was to see Tom Cruise and Dakota Fanning, (I'd never seen a movie with Chatwin before) because they are my favorite actor and actress, and I was not surprised when I saw the great acting of both.

I think that the fact that the cameras are almost always pointed to Ray and Rachel is awesome because after the lightnings (where the action starts) you can know exactly what they are thinking and if they are scared, sad or angry. Thats Spielberg's objective, to show us how terrifying it must be to run from those monsters and to loose someone that we love, and the way Ray always tries to protect Rachel and struggles for her love.

The film is not scary (and it wasn't supposed to be) it's all based in a family trying to escape alive from those invaders, exactly like in the book. And also like in the book this film shows our arrogance when we believe that we are alone in the universe (like H G wells wrote in his book) and no one is prepared for a strike from anyone outside the Earth. I personally think and I hope we are not alone.

In my opinion this is the best movie of the year so far, and I think that it is the best about alien invasions and attacks. Spielberg has now made 2 movies about both sides of an alien invasion, the friendly alien (ET) and the bad aliens. I prefer War of the Worlds even that the possibility of an invasion scares me.

Spielberg, again, showed how a great director he is and I'm waiting to see him directing more movies with Fanning and Cruise, because after War of the Worlds and Minority Report (between many others) he is now my favorite director too.

title: One of Spielberg's grandest, most horrifying films
review:
The movie event of the summer has arrived: War of the Worlds, and it doesn't disappoint. First off, let me state that I've been a fan of Spielberg's work since I saw Jurassic Park in theaters at the age of 5. Regardless of people's opinions of some of his more recent films (The Terminal, or A.I. even though the latter was more Kubrick's than Spielberg's), Spielberg is undoubtedly one of the most influential directors of our time. In creating a modern day retelling of H.G. Wells' sci-fi classic, The War of the Worlds, the director had his work cut out for him. Who else but Steven Spielberg could pull it off? Onto the movie itself, which as I've said before is excellent. Tom Cruise plays Ray Ferrier, a blue-collar dad who has part-time custody of his two children, Rachel (Dakota Fanning) and Robbie (Justin Chatwin). Not the greatest father, Ray doesn't even bother to cook dinner for the two. This all changes, however, as Ray and his family realize that the lightning storm occurring just outside is not your average weather.

I don't want to say much about the plot, for fear of ruining anything for people, but needless to say, it probably sounds a little contrived. Alien invasion? Lame, right? WRONG. This movie is so much more than that. A great sci-fi/horror, a political and social commentary, and just a wonderful movie in all. The special effects are of course amazing, but what surprised me was just how important sound proved to be in War of the Worlds, as some of the more terrifying moments are made using unearthly sounds that chill to the very bone.

See this movie, see it now, it is something not to be missed.

title: Spielbergs Cruise missile hits target prematurely
review:
By now everybody knows the HG Wells story, and everybody knows about Orson Welles's radio play that shocked a nation. And even the first movie has become a textbook example of 'how-to-make-a-sci-fi-B-movie'.

So I didn't quite understand what drew Spielberg to this project. It's like Van Sant remaking (or rethinking or reinventing, or whatever they want to call it) Hitchcock's "Psycho" or Jackson doing "King Kong" all over again. But I have to say that I'm surprised what the summer blockbuster 'meister' has done with this one.

I absolutely loved the first Spielberg/Cruise team-up (Minority Report) so it's safe to say I had high expectations for their next project. And most of those expectations have been met. Spielberg has made another great movie. The only flaws this film has have to do with Koepp's screenplay reworking.

Strangely enough he stays quite true to the original. Now some would say that's a good thing, but you have to understand that some elements from the old movie simply don't have that much impact anymore in this century. And that's where the film's main problem lies. Spielberg tries his best to make everything feel real. It seems getting older has made him more cynical, and this film has several scenes that are gut-wrenching simply because you don't expect them in a 'popcorn' movie. But however gritty and painful he seems to want to make it, Koepp's B movie script prevents credibility in any way, drawing more attention to the ridiculousness of the whole thing. And by the time we're introduced to Tim Robbin's character in the last half hour, the movie seems to have run out of steam, dabbling along to a sudden and anticlimactic ending. Probably because Spielberg had run out of money turning the first hour and a half in such a roller-coaster ride.

But in a time where all of Hollywood seems to suffer from a permanent writer's block, this is a relief. Despite its faults it's a more than decent 'reworking' of a well known story. The visuals are superb, William's score is almost 'invisible' to the ear (knowing that he's used to over-scoring every single frame you see) and the Cruise/Fanning team-up works beautifully, both of them proving once again why they're hot and wanted in LaLa land. It may not be another "Minority Report" hit, but it's definitely a close second. 8/10

stephen

title: Finally...
review: A mega blockbuster that uses FX to move the story - instead of as space filler and eye candy? Who would've known such a concept could work? I've skipped most blockbusters within the last five years (right after Independence Day sucked the soul right out of me). But gave Spielberg a chance at redeeming the genre (mega-blockbusters should be its own category despite being action, drama, comedy or horror). The genius director delivers. He came through on just about every level (story, visual, pacing). Other than "Tom's" annoying, whiny, cloying son and daughter (I wanted to reach through the screen and slap the #$%! out of them more than once), the movie was pretty much flawless. I'm still mulling over the ending (not sure if this is how the book or not) but WOTW is great summer escapism that won't lower IQs.

title: A fun and exciting summer popcorn movie!!
review:
I know there are lots of Spielberg and Cruise haters...but after reading some of the reviews here, I'm wondering if there aren't 2 versions of "War Of The Worlds" released simultaneously the way some have reviewed this movie. It's unfortunate that, in this day and age, most moviegoers have to watch movies, such as this, in those pint size theaters with marginal sound and tiny screens. I saw it at the Ziegfeld Theater which I recommend for anyone living in NYC. That's how I wanted to see this movie as I did Raiders, Star Wars, Empire Strikes Back, Jaws, Die Hard and Jurassic Park.

The acting was good enough, the visuals were excellent, the sound was incredible (at the Ziegfeld) and I'm truly grateful that Spielberg didn't conform to the "now" style of action directing...which I despise. Nowadays, most action directors continue to use that horrendous flash/quick editing style for the action sequences. Unfortunately you can't tell what the hell is going on, so ultimately it's just distracting.

One of the big pluses of the movie was that it was UNDER 2 hrs....yippee!! I wish more action and sci-fi directors would follow suit. After watching the sleep-inducing and overlong "Revenge Of The Sith" and "Batman Begins", "War Of The Worlds" was a breath of fresh air. There was more suspense and thrills in the first half-hour of "War Of The Worlds" than both of those aforementioned pictures put together. Remember, this is a summer popcorn movie. See, I wasn't looking for something thought provoking or with loads of character development....watch "Crash" if that's what you want.

"War Of The Worlds" was loads of fun, despite the smarmy ending....reminiscent of the 70's and 80's summer flicks.

For all the people who nitpicked this movie apart for unbelievability and plot holes...who cares? Did you do the same to "Die Hard", "Raiders...", "Temple Of Doom", "Jaws" and "Back To The Future"..all great summer popcorn movies with more holes than a 10 ft. wall of swiss cheese.

Lastly and sadly, for all the people who said it's unbelievable that the people in this movie would watch the alien invasion instead of running away...remember 9/11? I was there and everyone was watching the horror and even filming it...no one ran until the buildings started collapsing. Spielberg did it in the movie just as it really happened. And to those nitpickers who keep ridiculously asking why so many people in the film aren't running away from the tripods...well, they've seen people zapped right next to them whether they ran or not...maybe not running is a good thing.

A fun summer blockbuster film!

title: Dissed by Spielberg: you, me & HGW
review:
Okay, I'm used to big studio movies being big, loud, stupid and full of plot holes  spectacle over substance.

But WotW was unnecessarily so.

Here we have one of the great science fiction classics and a prior movie that had some reverence for the source material. And Spielberg's "enhancements" are the main thing wrong with this 'new interpretation.'

SPOiLERS!

If the "aliens" buried their machines in the soil in the past, they would already have been exposed to the "bacteria, microbes and viruses" that have been here long predating man.

I'm quite sure Mr. S. knows nothing about cars, but he can afford someone who does. An "EMP" would fry the engine management system of the late model minivan the mechanic was working on. True, it might fuse the solenoid or coil, but that's the least of the problems. It's integrated circuits that are dead meat. So most older cars (including Ray's Mustang) would have been fine with little or no work.

When the machine appears, the nice little 'hands' unfurl and shoot the 'death rays' at fleeing, unarmed people. Does it seem logical to you that beings that advanced would have planned to come to earth and individually shoot 6 billion people? I mean, the ones they don't put in their picnic baskets...

Let's say that we'll suspend disbelief because the aliens are 'so advanced' we don't understand them. There's still one aspect of this movie you cannot avoid. You can see the specific scenes where the Universal Studios WotW ride is being previewed: the cracking pavement, the tipping ferry boat; the shaking basement of the house hit by the falling airplane...

And speaking of falling airplanes: when was the last time you saw a jetliner crash that distributed large sections of plane over no more than 150 feet? The plane crash scene  again  looked like it was designed to be part of an amusement park ride rather than be realistic. But it was nice that the wreckage left a clear path for the minivan to exit.

And the ferry scene. Bad pacing for a Spielberg movie. Plus, we're expected to believe that with a limited number of machines to take over earth, four of them (breaking the 'pattern of three') show up to ineffectually menace our fleeing hero and family.

I'm sorry, but there's something plastic and contrived about Spielberg's 'adventure movies.' And I, for one, am getting tired of it.

title: My thoughts on 'War of the Worlds'
review:
Not knowing whether or not you've seen it yet limits me to how much I can say, suffice to say, that the film rates 8 out of 10 for me, quite acceptable entertainment, and where the changes to the story are, in general, are understandable. Not totally happy with the start of the film, i.e. I wouldn't have bothered with showing the title of the film, I would've just gone into the story a small continuity error which surprised me a bit, a scene where daughter to Ray is having a conversation about who is going to make dinner, early in the film, she sits down on the couch and leans back into the arm of the couch, very next scene she is sitting up right, toooo obvious! I know Spielberg was aiming the story mostly at the "human element" in the film, and that's OK, but it would've been a nice to show a little more of our Tripoded aliens blowing up things, even though Spielberg does a pretty good Job at showing us just how menacing these creatures are, a little more devastation would've been nice, perhaps showing us the mayhem being done around the world. I wondered how Ridley Scott would have handled it or James Cameron maybe? But at the end of the day I'm still very glad that Spielberg took the project on, there are more that just one moment in the film that has me going, Spielberg is good at getting the mood and atmosphere just right. I'm certainly looking forward to seeing it again. There were even some scenes that took me by surprise, not by much, but still had its effects! I didn't want to see any religious overtones in this version, and pretty much that's the way it went, however the reference to 'God' in the closing dialog I guess was acceptable. There were definitely some scary moments in the film, the sound is absolutely amazing I think my sub woofer is going to work overtime on this film, that's for sure What else can I say, I reckon Spielberg could have done more to the story, sure it would've added more time to the length of the film but at 116 min I think it goes for, I'm sure Spielberg could've spent more time in adding to the story but still keeping in homage to H.G Wells story line, I agree totally in not referring to them as "Martians" as we all know now that there are no Martians and as Carl Sagan once said, "Humans will be the Martians". I felt the ending was a little shallow, but then we all know the ending, like the Titanic, we all know it sinks, we all know the 'Aliens' succumb to the bacterium that we have come to enjoybut I dunno, a little more embellishment to the ending might have felt likea victory, we defeated them!...we wonmaybe a little cliché, it's not going to go down as one of Spielbergs greatest films partly because it's a remake, but also because, I felt, the film didn't have that Spielberg touch, the love that he can put into his films, in this case, he might as well have enlisted Tober Hooper as the Director! I think you know what I meanstill a bloody good film, directed by somebody else but Spielbergs influence all over it

AnywayI enjoyed it, 8 out of 10 I figure is about right

title: An amazing movie for all to enjoy
review: Personally, I loved this movie. I thought it was a good idea for a movie. I do not see how you could not like seeing a brilliant man's view on an alien invasion. I thought it was clever how the aliens grabbed up humans with huge tentacles and kept them in those little cages, picking them off one by one. title: Great nostalgic entertainment
review:
My whole family went to see Spielberg's "War of the Worlds" this past weekend, and the two big hopes I had for the flick were amply met. I first saw the 1953 version in the summer of 1953 at the age of eight--in other words, at generally the same time that Spielberg himself (we are coevals) no doubt was first impressed by the 1953 George Pal version. I have since then seen the '53 version several times, and I have read the Wells novel close enough to have taught it several times in a science fiction class.

My first hope was that Spielberg would communicate the same sense of nostalgia that runs through all his action flicks. The cameo appearance of Gene Barry and Ann Robinson (the original leads in the 1953 version) was like icing on the cake--and a huge wink from Spielberg to communicate his real motivation.

My second hope was that the flick would primarily be an entertainment, with any BIG STATEMENTS strictly subsumed to the plot dynamics. The inconsistencies noted by other reviewers seem to me trivial and without dramatic consequence. This movie, like the earlier version and the original novel, is primarily a mood piece, and Spielberg beautifully captures the sense of foreboding and attendant suspense that belong to the original conception--so that Spielberg's version is deeply resonant to the wellspring of his own creative energies. In other words, this film communicates the childlike wonder at the heart of what we call "classics." That kind of wonder is possible when the lead character is a vaguely defined Everyman (as in the 1898 novel) or a research scientist (as in the 1953 film version) or a vagrant dad (as in Spielberg's version). The choice of character may communicate something about the era in which the novel was written or the film produced, but in no way distracts from the mood at the heart of the conception.

Even the apparently more serious inconsistencies (okay, the invaders are ethically and religiously challenged mental giants, but is it plausible, for example, that a race of creatures so technically advanced in physics and engineering could be so abysmally ignorant of microbiology?)--even the fairly serious inconsistencies easily dissolve in the willing suspension of disbelief effected by Spielberg's faithfully recollected childhood wonder.

At age 60 I left the movie house with the same agreeable sense of dazzlement that I can recall feeling at age eight. Spielberg's version is, of course, quite a bit more technically sophisticated than George Pal's 1953 version, but it has the same magic connection to that wellspring of foreboding wonder. If you care for that kind of connection, you'll love "War of the Worlds."

title: Incredible. Best Picture sort of stuff; yet no record-breaker
review:
Before concerning myself with the film, lets start with a recap. In a pre-release interview for this film, Steven Spielberg insisted that this film would be bigger than Titanic, and would be then biggest movie of the decade.

Now, there are two problems with that comment. Firstly, Lord of the Rings has already taken that stance, whether we like it or not, earning somewhere near to $2billion in worldwide gross, 30-something Oscars, and a huge cult following between the three films. Secondly, what made Titanic so spectacular was the fact it had a teen heartthrob, a massive scene of destruction at a level not seen since "The Towering Inferno", and was so riddled with production problems that we just had to make sure that it was really as good as it seemed back then (excusing all who now regret that moment in their lives).

Yet while watching this film, you feel that it could have had all that and more.

Unless you viewed and truly understood "The Passion of the Christ," this really is the first film to send you out of the cinema feeling distraught, scared and truly entertained since the three-hour marathon about Leo and the Unsinkable ship. The only difference is is that this time around you probably wont be regretting it.

For those who have read the novel of "War of the Worlds," the movie follows the basic outline, with the obvious changes for the modern world. Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise) has gone from London social worker to New York docks laborer. He's divorced, and his kids hate him (especially his son, Robbie, portray by Justin Chatwin). Constantly neglecting his children, his ex-wife (Miranda Otto) and her new husband give most of the care. A fact that falls on his face when they're left at his place for the weekend. The parallels to modern society are too many to mention, with Cruise, Dakota Fanning and Jutin Chatwin (with some help from screenwriter Daivd Kopp) coming together in a sort of anti-family chemistry, that reflect the real "modern family." It's at this point that it all goes haywire. Aliens that have buried their ships here millions of years ago (I thought it'd be easier to kill dinosaurs?) come along, take their tripod-ships off "park" and hit the acceleration pedal hard. The plot becomes non-existent, a point proved by the fact that Cruise is constantly escaping certain death (and always finding a working car, an empty road, a way onto an overcrowded ferry, etc.), but our connection to the three characters grows, as we see them through experiences that we all know would happen if suddenly aliens start coming out of the ground and sucking all of our nutrients. The experience is made more distraught through some of the best camera work in years, that doesn't focus on the aliens (for too long), just on our heroes.

The only let down was the lack of plot to bring it together, and a really poor end. Yes, these are the thing that we usually complain about when watching something by Michael Bay. But Michael Bay would never be able to pull something like this off.

All round, Spielberg has yet again done something too spectacular for his own good. The film plays almost like a Hitchcock in protruding fear, shows that Spielberg is back on Roger Federer-like form that brought him "Jaws" and "Jurassic Park," and will probably the summer representative for Best Picture, come February 2006 (considering all the problems surrounding "Cinderella Man").

Yet will it break records, it worth a second viewing, but no.

title: A Holocaust Allegory
review: I was struck how much this movie was an allegory of the Nazi occupation of Poland and the subsequent Holocaust: the overwhelming blitzkrieg of the Aliens(Nazis); the migration of the Jerseyite(Jews); the hiding in the house as the Aliens(Nazis) searched for occupants; the rounding up of Humans(Jews) for later extermination; the killing of a fellow Human(Jew)to prevent the detection by the Aliens(Nazis); the separation of the family and post Holocaust re-unification. Even the rendering of Humans(Jews) to ashes...need I go on? This movie, these scenes have all been done by Spielberg before in Schindler's List and a host of other directors in the Nazi/Holocaust genre.

title: A Harryhausen Sense of Wonder...Congratulations!
review:
See this film for the technical advances alone.

The fan base of the Wells story is extensive worldwide. Byron Haskin who directed the 1953 Paramount version of this understood that to attempt a movie of this required and deserved the very best technical and visual effects available. (Gordon Jennings won an Oscar for his FX).

To ensure the sense of wonder embedded in the Welles book,(and to subscribe to that felt by readers when they read the book at the time of its publication over 100 years ago), requires the very best technical advances available to today's cinema. Last but not least, this story deserves no less than a full cinema presentation to convey the full visceral impact of H.G. Wells intentions. Anything less is an affront to the story and Wells' memory.

The sequences showing the first Tripod revealing itself near the beginning of this version are awe-inspiring and taken directly from the subconscious nightmare region we all harbour. It bypassed straight to the visceral. The machine was alien, towering, intent, evil and unstoppable. The sequence was breathtaking, conveying quickly that mankind was in real trouble from an unimaginably malevolent superior power. This is cinema. A masterly marriage of the technical to the emotional which was always attempted and oft-times actually achieved by the great Ray Harryhausen. (Not to mention Willis H O'Brien with the original King Kong).

Excellent performances from all the principals, notably Tom Cruise whose interpretation of a man trying to be a better father under duress was outstanding. Tom Cruise in "Minority Report" also showed a new side to this actor's talents. Mr Cruise has worked hard to get where he is today and is not afraid to take chances with his performances and it shows.It was not many years ago that "stars" of his magnitude would not have touched science-fiction cinema with a bargepole. Tim Robbins also deserves mention. Dakota Fanning, (from "Taken"), has a screen presence beyond her years.

A film is made up of "moments" with everything else serving as framing for those. Much like life.

Steven Spielberg obviously understands this.

See this film.

One related.

Haunting, jaw-dropping stuff.

title: About the EMP
review:
The following comes from a Northwestern University website devoted to the study of electromagnetic weapons:

Although the electric field created from an EMP lasts for only a short time, its effects can be devastating. ... Electrical systems connected to things that can conduct current like wires, antennas, and metal objects will suffer significant damage. EMP effects on electronics include interference of radio frequency links, irreparable damage to microcircuits, and even the disabling of satellites. Fortunately, electronic equipment that is turned off is less likely to be damaged.

So if the video camera was *off* during the EMP pulses (which it was; the guy with the camera didn't start taping until well after the tripod emerged from the ground), it is possible that it wasn't effected by the EMPs at all.

Consider that one plot hole plugged.

title: Oddly paced action flick
review: First off, no thanks to the theater, the aspect ratio was off, and the sound wasn't tweaked for a good viewing. Spielberg wastes no time getting to the point, and introduces the hostile takeover with all the speed of a meteor. However, where many of his films allowed you to take a breath every now and then, this one seemed to go in and out of hyperventilation and asthma and at odd times. For a first time viewing, I left a little bewildered, not so much by the ending and the cheesy dialog, but I left thinking that if I had all that money to spend on a flick like this, I may have chosen a different pattern to it's telling. A worthy release, but not quite Metropolis.

title: Occupations Always Fail
review:
My whole family loved this movie.

The effects are as cool as you'd expect. In particular, the bone-shaking noises the machines communicate with are highly unsettling.

The plot follows the H.G. Wells novel somewhat closer than the 1950s movie, for what that's worth. The tripod war machines are the most noticeable example. There is at least one touch you won't appreciate at all unless you've read the novel: the aliens' interest in a bicycle wheel in one scene is a nod to Wells' improbable conceit that the Martians (for that's who they were in the novel and the George Pal movie) had never invented the wheel! - their machines ran on a complicated system of sliding arms and cables.

Dakota Fanning, who plays the little kid with her emotional problems and trendy coping devices ("This is your space. You are safe inside it.") is the best thing in the movie, by far. She gives a professional, nuanced, performance. But Tim Robbins delivers the best line in the movie: "Occupations always fail."

What with all the ghastly bad publicity about him lately, it's a little tricky at the beginning seeing Tom Cruise and not thinking, "That's Tom Cruise. He's insane." But you get used to it after a bit.

title: Excellenyt
review: I went to see War Of The Worlds this weekend and it blew me away! Actors all brilliant, storyline brilliant, everything brilliant! The way it was shot was v. good, and the bits of humour injected were a welcome relief from the amazingly tense moments. Cruise is fab as Ray, and his 2 kids in the film are also excellent. It really did have me on the edge of my seat all the way through. I was shocked that it was only a 12A rating, a little girl was taken out by her mum covering her eyes half way through-think its a little scary for the younger members of the audience. It is definitely going to become one of my favourite films of all time. I would definitely recommend this film and would tell everybody to go and watch it.

title: It's not a war, it's an extermination - of talent on screen!
review:
Before I even start on the review - I believe that the man named Spielberg has brought more path breaking movies to mainstream cinema than any director anywhere on the planet. Movies that make us smile, cry and gape in wondrous entertainment. And more importantly - movies that sometimes make us think.

War of the Worlds is definitely not the latter.

The premise of the movie is razor thin simple. Aliens who've planning extermination of the Human race for more than a million years finally decide to move into the implementation stage of their mega-project (Maybe the funding for the war was tough to come by on their home planet. Alien government procedures, if anything, would be presumably more complex!). Logically their observation and study of humans would not make so much sense. As a man named Darwin put it (in slightly different words) - a path in natural history could have ensured Aliens would have had to fight T-Rexes instead of soft puny humans. But, I guess the tripods would have blasted the T-Rexes out of oblivion too.

The-most-saleable-face-in-Hollywood-cinema is a blue collared worker (despite the character being obnoxious and harsh on his kids, the girl sitting with me ended up saying - so cute! I guess Mr. Cruise does have his advantage right there). Now, saving his kids, saving his life and fleeing the Tripods that burst out of the ground are top on Tom's list of To-Dos. In typical Hollywood panache (which hasn't changed much for the 100 years when we puny humans started making movies) he does all three! He gives a controlled performance - Thank you for that Tom. Dakota Fanning does a good job too. All critics I've read are raving about her performance - but honestly, am I the only one who found her continual shrieking annoying? Then again I've never met a 10 year old kid fleeing alien tripods with an estranged dad - so maybe that's what they do.

The best-director-in-the-world does get one thing bang on target - the human drama. The interaction between the estranged father, the newly pregnant with someone else's child mom, the kids who do not have any regard for their biological dad are real. It's nice to see real. Even if it is in the background of the human race trying to flee from blood sucking tripods.

There are some gaping gaps in the story line. For instance, the aliens who're technologically advanced enough to build force fields, undetectable anti-rust tripods deep within Earth's surface and invisible mother ships forgot to invent one thing - Gas Masks! Jeez - tough luck that they plan their invasion on a planet which has more microbes than humans. Another one - they're drawing human blood for some reason - food, drink or maybe even radiator coolant for their Tripods. Wouldn't you expect alien guys (who, BTW as we are often reminded, have been planning this for a million years) to have subsidiary material for all this during an invasion? And if they somehow where biologically stupid enough to do this (I told you - I love that Spielberg guy! I'll give him the benefit of doubt any day) wouldn't a sensible military tactic be to send a first wave of soldiers to an unknown terrain - and then depending on the success of the initial wave bring in the full force to wipe puny humans clean? Ask any soldier anywhere on the planet.

But, at the end of the day - its a movie. We're not supposed to ask too many questions like that. Some say it's great that the book is "true" to the book. The very term - "remake" or even "based upon" mean that it has to improvise on the original. If you would like to be so true to the book then set it in 1890s when the book was written. Mr. Wells would've radically changed a "re-write" of his book had he lived today.

War of the worlds is entertaining. That's what counts. But, a request tough - do not package and market movies as something they are not. When I went to see Independence Day a decade ago, I knew exactly what to expect (and I enjoyed it!). That did not happen with WOTW. For all you critics who have panned ID4 with the cheesy Feel-good-American ending - girls running towards victorious guys and hugs/kisses follow. Please revisit your reviews after seeing the ending here.

See the movie. It's a summer time blockbuster. And that's all it is.

title: Ignoring his performance in the media, Tom Cruise's performance in this movie was sensational!
review: This movie had me on the edge of my seat the whole way through. The whole idea of being in pursuit of these ominous, threatening beings added to the stifling horror and delightful thrill that is this film. Tom Cruise did an amazing job going through the emotions of a father agonizing over the safety of his children. Once the audience puts his self-absorbed cries for attention on Oprah or other talk shows out of their minds and gets into the movie is going to be swept away. Dakota Fanning is one of the best child actors I've seen in a long time. She just captures every scene she's in. And this was probably a challenging role for an actress her age to be in constant, paralyzing fear throughout the movie. I'm most likely going to see this again, and would highly recommend it to anyone who hasn't had the chance to enjoy this remarkable film. Just knowing Spielberg directed it was all I needed to know. Great acting, great filming, wonderful plot--it's definitely going to win some awards.

title: Tom Cruise can ACT
review:
Y'know, it's all too easy to watch a Tom Cruise movie these days and just think "that's Tom Cruise." In this movie, I found his character to be believable. Annoying and frustrating at times, but believable. And Dakota Fanning is wonderful.

The story is pretty much the story, and if you know WOTW, then it's familiar. This remake, with up-to-date effects (aliens and their machines), is well done. The mystery and incomprehensible nature of the aliens and how they prepared and why they're doing this remains from Wells's classic.

Well worth the price of a ticket.

title: Impressive film, but misunderstood
review:
I was expecting the worst when I heard that Spielberg was taking on WOTW, but I was wrong. I have not enjoyed his films of late. Hated AI, Minority Report was average, catch me if you can was dull. Having now seen WOTW, I can understand that he is obviously a real fan of the source material. He has made the story modern day and in USA, both of which were unnecessary, but was probably a financial decision most of all. Aside from that, I was completely absorbed by this film. The acting was very good, the script worked fine with the film, the sound was amazing and the lack of music only increased the atmosphere. The special effects were incredible.

Having sat through 2 hours of CG in Revenge of the Sith where no one is really in peril as everything is blatantly CG, WOTW was an absolute work of genius. Nearly all of the effects were really there in the film. I rarely thought 'nice effects', as it was all there, with the actors as if there actually used giant tripod props and carved up buildings and streets.

This is a well made film and understands the source material very well. It's not the popcorn summer blockbuster that people expect when they see the two big names, but a more personal film. I would probably give it 10, but it deserves to lose a point for the last 2 minutes.

I have read through a number of comments here and much of it seems pedantic or irrelevant. What a lot of people are forgetting, is that this is essentially a science fiction B-movie. It doesn't have to be 100% accurate.

You don't have to have everything explained to you. Who cares if someone had a camcorder? Yes, the ending seemed like the result of focus group feedback, but I can forgive it based on the overall quality of the film. There are lots of unanswered questions, but if you read the book, it may make more sense. Not all of us need everything justified and explained to us in simple terms and for this I am grateful to Spielberg.

title: Unusual and Great
review:
Well, after so many diverse critics I went very skeptical to the movies, not expecting much. Now after seeing this film, I am amused about the bad reviews of some people. Sorry folks, this is not your typical popcorn-flick. Spielberg gave the genre a whole new dimension with this masterpiece. Okay, I agree: some parts were just illogical and this got mentioned enough by reviewers, so I don't have to go into it again. But despite that excusable fact, he created something new and not another "Independence Day"...Dirty, dark, dusty and yes, creepy.

I loved the original novel, one off my all-time favorites is the Musical Version by Jeff Wayne and yes: maybe he shouldve set the story in its original time but than again, why not show us that even as advanced as we think we are today, for someone else we might just be as worthless, than our animals are for some of us, and we get treated that way. Being not more than food and fertilizer. So, I could live with the fact that it plays NOW and not a century ago. Staying close to the novel, some little differences were programmed.

That the camera does never leave the main characters was also a very special fact, that made it for sure very uneasy to watch for people, expecting another ID4 or regular catastrophe flick. But some of the scenes are staying in your head and some pictures are "burning" themselves into ones brain, haunting you after the movie is over.

That scene were the mob is going for Rays (Cruises) Car was intense, terrifying and it showed how mankind is a threat to itself when it comes to the point of survival and how egoistic we are. We are not better then this alien invaders, was one thought of me and some friends at this point.

Something that bothered me, though, was the end. Not that quick end, that some are criticizing. That stayed true to the novel. No, the fact that the son survived was just a little bit to much and there Spielberg failed, not daring to give up the idea of a happy end. I usually love happy endings, but that one did not work out after all that terror, he showed us before.

As for the acting: it was alright. I don't like Cruise, never did, but he did a good job not being the hero he is used to play. Dakota Fanning is amazing and lets see how her career develops.

"War of the World" was a movie that dared to be different than the mainstream and other movies of that kind. For that I give it a 10 and forgive the few plot holes.

For the DVD I hope for an extended and unrated directors cut that will make a great movie perfect.

Enjoy and expect a new kind of sci-fi-horror....

title: Totally gripping
review:
What a roller-coaster ride of a movie! Hoping for the best, but expecting the worst, I was relieved to be witnessing a number of totally enthralling moments in the cinema on Saturday.

Whoever tries writing this movie off as another Independence Day rip-off, obviously did not allow themselves to enjoy this movie before they saw it. With a distinctly personal storyline, and no ounce of patriotism anywhere, 'War of the Worlds' is a disaster movie like no other.

Steven Spielberg and Cast deliver a movie which engrosses you right until the somewhat 'Hollywoodised' ending. I can tell you now, that I was genuinely quite scared at two points in the movie and I could feel for the characters when the terror became too much for them.

Tom Cruise and Dakota Fanning were brilliant in their roles. I know many people accuse Cruise for not being able to act, but surely, if you can sympathise with his character Ray and find him believable, then how can he be a 'bad' actor.

The effects were of course out-of-this-world, but as you can tell my review is focusing on the characters, as that is what makes this movie so different from the other disaster movies you might have seen.

Now, the ending Having already read many reviews for 'War of the Worlds' last week before I saw the movie, I was fully aware that I should beware of the ending. I can honestly say that during the movie I was aware of the shift from 'stylised terror' to 'Hollywoodised conclusion' 15 minutes before the end. However, it was not as bad as I was expecting. If you haven't seen the film yet, don't let the ending put you off from seeing it. It isn't unnecessary, but admittedly, it could have been rendered better.

title: Not your formulaic action flick.
review:
I went into this movie slightly skeptical, if anything just because I was tired of seeing the previews during every commercial break and Tom Cruise's face on the cover of every magazine with Katie Holmes. Once the movie started, all of that went away and I realized that I should've known better than to doubt the ability of Steven Spielberg.

Given this is an action flick, so you can definitely expect top notch action sequences combined with the best SFX in the world. What you might not expect is Steven's direct approach in making you feel the blind terror, panic and chaos the people feel in the movie. That from the moment people began dying, all anyone could do was run and try not to look back. The magic isn't in the action or SFX, but in the terror you feel triggered by the most basic of human functions, self preservation and the desire of an average Joe parent trying to protect his young. This is what the movie is about in the end. There will be times in this movie where morals would be a joke, where courtesy and virtue -not to mention abiding by the law- are lost in the face of annihilation. Then there are other times, times that aren't necessarily critical turning points in the movie but are important nonetheless, where you'll see a much needed helping hand. During a time of alien movies where the human always wins in the end, it's nice to see what might happen if the human race lost, and nature won out.

What is also trademark of Steven's movies is the brilliant acting. I'm not a fan of Cruise, but his performance as the average Joe/less than ideal parent is no less than superb. No where does he overact or undervalue this character who is in no way a hero, but a man willing to do what he needs to in order to survive with his kids. So imagine my surprise when he should be outshone by the 11 year old Dakota Fanning. Frankly, she is the star of the movie and she acts it every second as the claustrophobic child scared out of her mind while running for her life.

Plain and simply put, this isn't formulaic. You need to think with this movie. It's not Independence Day where we beat the big bads with a computer virus and we're left cheering and congratulating each other. Steven doesn't lead us by the hand like a toddler. We were loosing from the start and he drives this home in a brutal way. Through his use of camera angles where you feel like one of the people running, you won't see big battle scenes b/t the military and them over the hill. You see our people going in and never coming out. Big bright flashes and then flames. In showing less, he has us feel more terror because our imagination takes over. In this, he honors Well's book, which also tried to instill that same fear.

Honestly, this couldn't have been any better.

title: A Superb Alien Film
review: I recently saw another take on this movie, starring some actors you've never heard of and the special effects in that one contained little violence that was believable. This film, however, seeing last Thursday, was excellent. It was very violent, indeed, for a PG-13 film. I think Steven Spielberg really preferred it to be PG-13 because a lot of young 13-15 year old boys are dying to see a movie about aliens. I was glad when I found out that Steven Spielberg was directing this film because his other alien films were spectacular. And, finally, like in his other ones, you get close-ups on what the aliens look like. In the movie, Signs, you rarely saw the alien's anything. This one shows a lot of aliens and even a scene where they're playing with a bicycle wheel. Anyway, Tom Cruise was good, but Dakota Fanning--GEEZ! She's in every movie you see nowadays, am I right? She's been in fourteen films now! In four years! But even that didn't stop from enjoying this film, which has humor, violence, tragedy, and an awesome beginning, middle, and end. Everyone should see this film. Well, whoever is a fan of bloody violence.

title: Gripping Study of Humanity (Watching with envious eyes)
review:
As a searing indictment on human nature during crisis, this film works wonderfully. It really paints the horrific of how desperate people get in doomed situations.

This is really Spielberg working on all thrusters I think. There is such a genuine feeling of despair running through the movie, and the characters all act realistically. Dakota Fanning is a great addition to 'Spielberg's Children', particularly since he hasn't really squeezed good performances out of children for a while now (Jurassic Park anyone?). I loved the depiction of this story. I was so worried when I heard it had been transplanted (again!) to the USA for this film version, as I had hoped a historical setting in England 1898 would've lent the film a unique perspective. However, I soon was involved deeply in the film as it is. I'm no fan of Tom Cruise in general, but he works fine in this flick, particularly because he spends most of the film panic-stricken and not displaying his usual square-jawed All-American heroism. Apart from the occasional performance like the harrowing one in "Born on the Fourth of July" (Oliver Stone, 1989), "War of the Worlds" and Michael Mann's "Collateral" surely signify some sort of turning point in roles for Cruise. He comes across as very vulnerable and human.

I was also glad to see Spielberg didn't take the opportunity to pepper this film with jingoistic overtones, and any patriotic devour, which does come from this film is true to the characters represented. But thankfully it is in short supply and the film is more about how humans (not just Americans, though it is set in the U.S.) cope and change in desperate times.

From a production and directorial point of view I have to say there are some great Spielberg moments. There's a scene where characters are running through mist as clothing rains down around them, and I also have to say I have never seen (or been taken off guard) by the ferocity at which people were 'vaporised' as in this film. It's quick and startling.

There is also a VERY Hitchcockian moment when one character watches a body float past down stream only to then be followed by a mass of bodies. The way it was shot was just pure Hitchcock.

Everything rolls along fine in this film. John Williams' score is brooding and dark, and the pace works well: action packed, yet still time for human moments. And it's the human moments which make this film memorable (i.e. The crowd and the car-jacking scene).

If Independence Day appealed to teenagers, then this film will appeal to the over 25's. Intelligent, thought-provoking and gripping.

SPOILER FOLLOWS: As a creative choice, If I had directed this film I would've 'realistically' not had one of the characters survive by the film's end. But then again, this is Hollywood, and considering the mainstream effect which usually seems to guide Spielberg, it is great to see that for the most part he delivers a movie which stays very true to the original story and shows Mankind at its darkest hour - not just against an unknown enemy, but against itself.

title: This movie was AWESOME!!!!
review: I thought this movie was great!!! I think it had great special effects and the actors were really good. When i saw the previews for this movie i did not expect to much out of it but i thought what the heck might as well go see it. I was much surprised, the movie left me guessing all through it and it was pretty intense (which i love). The thing i like most about this movie was that it was a lot like the old version but with more effects, it was not like a lot of movies that are remade that are nothing like the older versions. It is one of the best movies i have seen in a long time and i would recommend this movie to anyone who loves a good science fiction movie.

title: Very good, if not great.
review: This is the best movie about alien-invasion I have watched. It has a fascinating vision, a chilling atmosphere and great action, which is destined to stay as a classic. Based on H.G. Wells' masterpiece, it tells the story of malevolent aliens, who attack the world. The main character, played very well by Tom Cruise must save his kids from the apocalypse, unleashed by the aliens. The film is really great. I think that its strongest point is the atmosphere of lurking doom and despair, which floods from the movie. If aliens really attack humans, we'll be like this. Without stupid heroics like in "The Independence Day". Just stunned and very scared people.

title: Save your family before save the world
review: I have seen the B/W film 30 years ago. The same ending as before. I have lived in the time asking everyone to be hero to sacrifice himself to save the world. I was born in the date that communist threatened to bury us. I saw the movies about the heroes in world war II. When I was in university, I saw anti-hero movies. Anti-Vietnam war. Rambo started hero again. And you, people of United States, try to tell the world that you are the heroes of human beings (like ID4). In this film, hero must save himself first. Then saves his children. Do the duty of a father first. And keep the rest to God.God has created a world to keep human to survive. But human should protect themselves for enough time.

title: If you're going to see it...see it on the big screen!
review: In my opinion, this was a magnificent adaptation and modernization of the original. It capably carries the foreboding feeling of impending tragedy and the will-sapping desperation that comes with the realization that humanity's best efforts are futile. Humans are extinct...we just don't know it yet. Unless you have a gigantic television or projection TV - preferably with surround sound and a decent sub woofer, a DVD just won't do this justice. The enormity of inexorable destruction and horror, the subsonic bass rumblings that herald human doom...these are best experienced on a big screen and stereo. Do yourself a tremendous sensate favour and ignore the hype for a couple of hours; immerse yourself in the first-person perspective. You'll find yourself in a waking version of those dreams we all have had: running and running from some implacable and inescapable *something*.

title: I liked it...but sometimes it didn't make any sense!!!
review: When i went to the movie theater i expected to see a really good movie...i mean..after watching the amazing "Batman Begins" This summer and actually having a dream about the end of the World i was more than ready to see Mr. Cruise save the planet. Don't get me wrong, i have always loved Spielbergs movies (Not Amistad...never seen it, hopefully never will) to me JAWS is my all time favorite movie,but for some time now he has changed, he's got old and his movies are not as cool as they used to be. I mean come on,He had in his hands a perfect recipe for disaster on biblical proportions and i say that in a cool, action-packed, adrenalin rushed way, and what does he do...he makes it a movie from the point of view of only one man and his family and the quest to take care of them...BORING!!! There is a small moment when even "THE AMAZING" (To a lot of people) Dakota Fanning came to be really annoying and said a line that not even the little boy in Episode 1 (Jake Lloyd) could have acted worse. Tommy Cruise is Tommy Cruise with his pearly white and his running skills that put an Olympic runner to shame, he does it well, he has a serious scene..a very..very serious scene that made it for me..i mean..that final scene with the other survivor (Tim Robbins) was what made me like it...it was crude and well played...even for Spielberg...it makes you think that the situation is not a joke...well played. The ending was a head scratcher for a lot of people i saw it with so I'm giving it a poor 8 on a good and o.k scale. Definitely you have to see it to talk about it.Tons of plot holes and more.

title: Overall Disappointing
review: I've been fascinated by WOTW since a child. I own the original book and have read it countless times and it is a book way ahead of its time. The images from the book captured me and never let go. The film when I saw it is exactly as I could have guessed.I'm not going to go into technical details or pull the film apart it is an overall feel of the movie to me. The opening of the film to the point when they enter the basement with Tim Robbins is superb. It catches the panic and hopelessness of society perfectly, although the film only concentrates on the invasion from the point of Tom Cruises family. You do not see anything on a global scale which disappointed me personally. When you do see the Tripods they are just spectacular. But where in the book they are a main part they are not really seen enough in the film for me, and I felt somewhat unsatisfied. I'm sorry but I felt the aliens were just laughable, they were almost cute like but the worst thing about them I thought they were remarkably similar to the aliens in independence day. Except the aliens in Independence day were truly menacing and disturbing ( the captured one ) they just did not cut it in this film. The basement part with the eye I thought copied too much from the 1953 version and was not very original. From this point in the film it felt rushed and lacked anymore imagination at all, the ending came very quickly and kept to the book exactly, and even the hand coming out of the fallen tripod again copied exactly to the 1953 film, and I thought this scene was laughable and no better than the 1953 WOTW. So to sum up its a film of two halves. Excellent first half, abysmal second. Dakota Fanning was the star of the movie and Tom cruise was even OK. Does this film do any justice to to HG Wells and his book? No it certainly doesn't. So with the other versions out too ( which I haven't seen yet, but going by other reviews ) it does not look like I'm going to see a truly excellent version of WOTW in my lifetime. How sad!

title: It was great entertainment
review: I did not know anything about this movie. I didn't see any trailers nothing. And I must say I thought it was just great entertainment. OK If you don't like sci-fi or even a bit of sci-fi, don't bother to go see the movie. But if you do, then you should see the movie. I thought even the story was nice. Tom (major hunk) Cruise as an ordinary guy, that was nice for a change. No fighting the aliens by an ex-navy seal or an ex super soldier. No just an "ordinary" guy (as far as Tom Cruise and ordinary go) trying to survive. Well done Steven Spielberg. It is what the man does best. Great movie, pure entertainment. Thank you Steven for entertaining us. Fantastic!

title: Best Movie I Have Seen This Year
review: POSSIBLE SPOILERS AHEAD: I read the H.G. Wells book as a kid and saw the George Pal movie a few years later and was familiar with Orson Welles' radio play. However, for me, no one has ever REALLY made WAR OF THE WORLDS. One of the biggest things missing was the tripods. Those cool walking machines are on the cover of almost every edition of the book that can be found and I wanted to see a faithful adaptation of this wonderful book. When I read that Cruise and Spielberg were making this film, I was kind of dreading it but when I heard Dennis Muren, one of the greatest effects men in the history of cinema was on board, I felt a lot better. I knew Spielberg was doing a modern update so I felt it might stray from the book too much but I was amazed to find this movie is remarkably faithful to the source novel, including the ending so if you do not like how the book ends, don't expect to like the movie's ending either. For the fans, Spielberg includes nods to the original 1953 film (look for Gene Barry and Ann Robinson in clever cameos) and some scenes are almost straight out of the original and one great line spoken by Les Tremaine from the '53 version is said by a news reporter in this one. If you are familiar with both films, you'll know what I am talking about. This film is dark and scary in tone and closer to SIGNS than INDEPENDENCE DAY. Spielberg shows once more that he is a master of suspense and dread. Cruise is at the top of his game here. He is totally convincing as the struggling father trying to keep himself and his family together in crisis. He is no hero...just a regular guy facing a deadly test of his will to live and carry on. The cinematography is absolutely gorgeous and some beautiful scenes suddenly turn into scenes of horror, such as the one where Dakota Fanning approaches a beautiful river in the morning. Spielberg's editing turns it into one of the most horrifying scenes in the movie. Tim Robbins is also excellent playing a character from the book, who is a little warped but likable at the same time. All the acting is excellent - there is not a bad performance in the bunch. Score by John Williams is also good and the special effects alone are worth the price of admission. Dennis Muren and ILM deliver the goods here and their work blows away even STAR WARS: EPISODE III. I fully expect them to get an Oscar or at least a nomination for their work. The tripods themselves are beautifully designed and completely menacing. The scene where they first appear will someday be remembered as one of the classic suspense and horror moments in cinema. They make a sound that fills you with dread to hear it and you really feel what the characters are feeling. The only weakness is the red weed. It's a nice addition from the book but it isn't explained so it leaves audiences wondering why it is there. Still, that's a minor gripe and I was so impressed that I saw the movie twice in one day and will be going back again. I highly recommend it. Spielberg and Cruise made this film better than I ever expected they could have. Everyone involved with making this film should be proud.

title: great!
review:
i loved it.

and just to clear up a few issues we keep seeing... EMP will only affect devices that are currently ON at the time of pulse. so a camcorder could easily be on after an EMP. and EMP is not forever. devices will recover. so no nationwide blackout for too long from that. the filmmakers really wanted to put you, the viewer, in the shoes of the terrorized people. therefore, you must concede that not all will be explained to you. you only know what they know, which is absolutely nothing and let's just keep running away from the monsters. so expect not to be spoon-fed for once, it's a nice feeling. but also expect some unanswered questions. it's OK. i liked it. and not everybody's a genius. they're not all going to run. some will stop and stare. it's called Darwinism, these things happen. and some people will be hysterical. especially nine year old girls. it's perfectly natural.

overall, i thought it was fan-freaking-tastic. i'm going again for a second viewing now, 3 days after the first.

title: Dakota Fanning Stole The Show
review: I normally never write movie comments but felt the need to do so this time around. Dakota Fanning is truly a talented young actress. I was already a fan and find it nice to find that with each successive film her talent and skills become honed and right on the mark. I would go as far as to say that she stole the spotlight from Tom Cruise in this film. Her emotion is real and comes very naturally. Despite the negative reviews I had heard about the film, I felt that overall Spielberg did a great job with the direction. There seems to be so much commentary on the fact that there is a goof in the film in regards to the camcorder. I did not see this as so. Why? Because by replacing the "Solonoids" in the car the mechanic was able to get the vehicle to work. Every system per se has its glitches and faults. If you noticed Tom Cruise grabbed a flashlight with batteries to be used later on. The initial reaction is that all CARS and Lighting went down, but there were instances were these goods were available for use even after the tripods made their presence.

title: A curious effort... big BIG spoilers
review:
Like many, I have been looking forward to this film for a long time. I saw it with friends, and as soon as the film ended, one friend turned to me and said "I didn't like it", and began to catalog changes from the book and the movie. I pointed out that the story was updated, and you can't really hope to stay faithful to a book that was written 107 years ago.

My immediate opinion of the film was that the first half was good, but the second half faltered badly. In WotW, Spielberg is at at his best when capturing the panic of the whole situation. But when the panic gives way to paranoia, this is where the film caves in, undone largely by the tokenism of Ogilvy (a vague, pointless character), and by the lack of explanation of various things seen in the film. As someone who has never read the book, what the hell were the red weeds growing everywhere? And how could the tripods have been buried underground for so long? Surely mankind would have found AT LEAST one of them at some point. Or maybe not, minor gripe.

Of major concern for me - as I'm positive it will be for most people - was the ending. Not about the "defeat" of the Martians (if they are indeed from Mars) but the more "personal" ending of Ray and family. The closing reunion begs the question... How in the hell did Robbie survive??? He went running headlong into the fire thirty seconds before things went to hell. Big mistake, filmmakers.

For that matter, how did the rest of the family come out so well? Maybe that will be told in the sequel. Usually Spielberg's trademark optimism doesn't bother me the way it does most, but this ending was 2 points off for me. In many films - good ones - the Hero is faced with a decision, and the decision he makes defines his character. Ray made his decision, for better or worse, and that decision was to sacrifice his son to save his daughter. Great. But then his son survives anyway. So much for character-defining decisions. He had his cake and ate it too. It smacks of the decision Neo was forced to make in The Matrix Reloaded: "save your girl or save the world". He made his decision, but was still able to do both. Doesn't sit well with me.

Praise. The first half of the film, I have mentioned, is virtuosity. There is wonderful work by Janusz Kaminski, expertly executing Spielbergs direction on such shots as the opening shot coming in from a helicopter to a closeup of Ferrier (which might have been achieved with CGI) and a marvelous extended shot of Ferrier and kids driving down the freeway with the "camera car" having to move around cars and weave in and out to keep track of the dialog. Watching this, I turned to the guy next to me and said "how the heck did they do that?" My friend had no answer.

The music by John Williams was uncharacteristically unobtrusive, containing no memorable themes and musical moments. This suited the tone of the film perfectly.

The tripods look great too.

In summary, a great opening showing much potential is undone by a weak second half, terrible coda, and the sudden onset of the ending, with nary a climax to speak of.

title: Visually Entertaining! Worth Seeing!!
review: I went into this movie expecting something along the lines of Independence Day, Day After Tomorrow, and A.I. I suppose that when you have that combination within your expectations, it's going to blow it right out of the water. Tom Cruise, Dakota Fanning, and Justin Chatwin were excellent! There was never a dull moment, there was never a part where you know exactly where the movie is headed (unless you've seen the original or have read the book). This should be the movie of the summer! Love it! Some people have said that they had left the theater thinking "what was the point?" It made me leave the theater asking myself. . "Would I be able to survive had this happen?" Again, this is a great movie - highly recommend everyone see it! It will suck you in!

title: Surprisingly good!
review: Over the past several years I've come to dread the release of Spielberg films. The man has created some wonderful stuff - "Raiders of the Lost Ark", "Jaws" - and yet has created some truly awful junk too - "A.I.", started out so well and yet smelled up the theater by the awful and merciful end... On the other hand, H.G. Wells novel "War of the Worlds" had a tremendous influence on me as a kid - got me truly interested in astronomy *and* reading. Wells' image of the Martian tripods towering over the English landscape has stayed with me ever since. So imagine my mixture of excitement and trepidation to learn that Spielberg was filming "War of the Worlds", starring Tom Cruise. Would it be another "Jaws"... or another "Minority Report" crap-fest... Just saw "War of the Worlds" tonight - and it is truly great! Yes, the setting has been changed from 1895 England to modern-day New Jersey. Yet much of Wells' story remains intact... trapped in the ruined house, creepy alien wailing ("Ulla ulla ulla..."), and of course those fantastic tripod fighting machines! The acting was also quite good. Tom Cruise may be an ass in real life, but I must say that his single-dad character came off as quite sympathetic to me (Hmmm... what does that say about *my* character, eh?) Loved this movie.

title: Truly one of Spielberg's greatest films
review: Seeing the trailer one would think this is a mindless action movie that in turn, like most are, will be bad. This is completely incorrect. The plot in this movie is amazing, and though it varies from the original in many areas, it still will have you on the edge of your seat. There is non-stop suspense, and you will be surprised in every single scene. The Alien tripods are extremely realistic, and invoke much fear whenever you see them. The sound they make whenever they are about to attack will make you scrunch up in your seat and feel like shouting at some of the stupid people in the movie. Finally when you start seeing the tripods go down and find out that 1 billion have died in three days, (177 people die a second if think) you are amazed and shocked at the same time. The narratives by Morgan freemen in the beginning and end and are truly spectacular, and you will wish you had a remote to rewind the narratives, and the entire movie! Over and all if can see one movie this summer make it War of the Worlds!

title: Opens well but ends poorly
review: While it would be unfair to give this movie an entirely bad review, I must say that it is another in a string of Hollywood blockbusters that simply fails to live up to its own potential. And while the first two thirds of the film are actually quite good, there is a distinct point in the movie where it goes irrevocably south and becomes silly and disappointing. The final revelation is so embarrassingly heavy-handed (it has nothing to do with the aliens) and under-explained, the only way to overcome the staggering letdown is to remind ones' self that it is, after all, a Spielberg movie. Naturally, it is going to have an icky-sweet-sentimental ending that makes no sense whatsoever in the context of the story. Since his over-riding theme is about parental responsibility and the importance of family, he has no choice but to show everyone happy and united at the end, even at the expense of forgoing any sense of the movie's own logic and the opportunity for a truly profound and emotional ending. The substitution of a comfortable sentimentality for real emotion at the end is, perhaps, the film's greatest flaw. Alas, not the only flaw, but the others are more forgivable. There is a whole sequence with Tim Robbins that could almost be completely excised without harming the plot, but sadly it contains a few key elements that lead to the awkward and silly climax (though actually the film could lose that whole section and possibly make better sense). While the action is well staged, the effects impeccable, and the bulk of the movie is engaging, at the end it is still a typical disappointment.
