title: Best invasion film ever (so far)
review:
So, if you read the novel, one must admit, that it really is a very good interpretation (or adaptation) of the book. The novel, set in the late 19hundrets, has a simple message: mankind is arrogant. We used to see ourselves as the "center of the universe", the "crown of creation" and like to think, that our machines and technology can deal with any problem - even with technological superior invaders from space. Well, if an invader is superior, the invaded culture has no chance of survival. Look to the history-books and see, what was done e.g. to the indio-cultures and to the American-natives. So, if an alien invasion would occur, they would blow our tanks and jets to peaces in a minute. The film is very honest to this part of the story.

The only thing that saves mankind in the end is not technology, but the fact, that we have adapted to the environment of the planet earth - we simply have "earned the right to exists by evolution" - and the invaders haven't. So, they all die simply on a flu. No big heroic battle like INDEPENDENCE DAY ;o) we would have lost, if it wasn't for the microbes, that save mankind.

I must say, I liked Spielbergs other "Alien" movies - CLOSE ENCOUNTERS OF THE THIRD KIND and E.T. - more, because they were the few examples, that say "Well, they could be our friends". But, if invaders would some day arrive in orbit, the won't be.

So, if you like big action-disaster-alien-invader-films, this is the one to watch.

title: What the heck was THAT about ?!?
review:
I went to see this movie with my wife in a fantastic cinema and was looking forward to seeing it.

The trailers had looked exciting and the main part of the movie didn't disappoint with some excellent special effects and some thumping sound effects too.

The main characters were OK - the little girl was excellent.

The aliens first arrival was as expected really gripping and I couldn't' wait to see what would happen next.

But you just have to ask what the HECK was that bit about where the boy comes back from the dead at the end ? Ruined the whole entire movie It was a sad ending to a decent movie.

title: Well worth watching
review: I was reluctant to watch this movie, primarily because Cruise seems to fit better in some movies than others. However, curiosity prevailed primarily because I had seen the original as a kid and had to see what difference fifty years made in terms of special effects. I wasn't disappointed. Spielberg puts a bit of a spin on the original, but it works well. Special effects are fantastic. Although I have a 55 inch screen at home, I am sorry I didn't see this flick on the big screen. Cruise does a magnificent job. His lines are limited, but what he says with facial expressions alone, well, is nothing short of genius. I started watching this film 9:30 pm one night and figured I'd nod off. Not. I was glued to the screen until the end.

title: War of the Worlds
review: Open your eyes and you are watching this movie. You can not even turn your face for a second,cause you are absorbed by the special features of Spielberg's masterpiece. All you can see is Tom and his family in a bad condition of poverty and the aliens attacking our planet. If you have not seen a movie which makes you stuck in your seat,go and get this movie,brilliant performance by Tom Cruise,Dakota Fanning,and a great picture by Steven Spielberg:War Of the Worlds. You cannot believe your eyes,there is no way out of this mess caused by aliens,who have been in our planet ages ago and have planned to destroy our race. Just watch the movie,you will never get bored.

title: They are Already Here!
review:
Their Already Here

War of the Worlds is an amazingly terrific movie, and if you have any liking for Action/ Sci-Fi movie, then this film is a must see. This movie mostly targets the teenager to adults. It has everything a young boy could want, but yet it still remains to be a movie that will keep you on the edge of your seat at all times.

Prior to me viewing this extraordinary movie, I was lucky enough to have seen the original film, released back in 1956. Even though the newer version is quite a bit different from the original, I still enjoyed it immensely. In the 2005 version there was much more use of foreshadowing and technical camera anglings. In doing this, it give the audience a better sense of what it would be like to be experiencing what the characters feel. The uses of CGI's in the newer version also help heighten the reality factory in the film. Compared to the 1956 version when you can actually see the wires that suspends the spacecrafts in the air. Using these CGI's most definitely helps captivate the audience and put them into the film. Being a teenage when I viewed this, I could find every thing a teenager boy would want in a movie: aliens, death, lots of action, and even some humor. Having the aliens and their space ships look so real can really capture and bring the viewer, no matter what the age. The use of CGI's where excellently used in that fashion. These had to be some of the best CGI's I have seen in a long time. This film can also be very intriguing to an adult due to the fact that it was based on a novel written by H.G. Wells. If that will not capture an adult's interest then I don't know what will. If they do not like suspense and scary scenes then I would not recommend this film to them. It only takes about fifteen minutes for the movie to get real exciting. Once all the excitement starts, it is non-stop until the very end. The CGI's again are so well done that you don't even have to use you're imagination on anything. It shows you real live looking aliens and total unbelievable events that seem as real and believable as you are I. Further more in this film it has great casting. All the actors in it did any excellent job on making the roles they played very believable. Even the little girl, Dakota Fanning, had a very important role, and if she could have screwed up the entire movie if she hadn't acted so marvelous. The other actors/actress's cast for the film where chosen equally as well as little Dakota. It must have really taken true talent to act completely horrified by the aliens, when in real life there was nothing there. Over all I think that cast, filming crew, and everyone else who participated in creating this film did very admirable work.

title: Another Tom Cruise Film!
review: I can't count how many people I came across who wouldn't go to see this film because Tom Cruise was in it! Is this the way it's going to be, I wonder? A film gets made and people decide to not see it because it has this guy in it. Looks like his antics this year have put people off massively! I for one thought the film was very good (chilling, scary etc) and the reason for this was the quality of the film, not the star. It is safe to say that he was a passenger, which is the way it was supposed to be (powerless, frightened, pathetic). To those who have a bit of TC problem at the moment, I would say that you should see it, if only to see Tom Cruise at his most powerless and pathetic!

title: Five Points Newark NJ
review:
In 1953 I was 9 and lived on Ferry Street in Newark, NJ a few doors down from Five Points. I went to the Rivoli Theater, across the street from that church to see "War of the Worlds." The Rivoli Theater is no longer there, but has been transformed into some other business. Actually most of the other buildings on Ferry Street have also been transformed, but that church still remains. This was the church that breaks apart as the machine emerges from the center of the street.

It was such a treat for me to see Five Points again in the new remake of "War of the Worlds." I assume the Five Points in the movie was a Hollywood set, or maybe even enhanced by computer graphics. But the street signs and the buildings were so remarkable in reproducing the Five Points of my memory of those early 50's buildings. I was so taken by this scene of my childhood, that I want to revisit the place to see the changes and to compare the movie set with the current Five Points.

After that moment down memory lane, the rest of the movie was anti-climatic for me. I still enjoyed the movie, but was just so impressed at how many details were preserved of Five Points. Great job for the set designers!

title: Nice job Spielberg ! Fitting of the 'turn of the century' book that Wells gave "our world"
review:
I thought Spielberg succeeded in finding the right level of blending today's special effects with the incredible book that HG Wells gave to "our world", while giving the 1950's screen version it's due.

I'm a special effects junkie, BUT, this movie would have been ruined if Spielberg had yielded to the temptation to turn this into Star Wars. The enhancements he made to the plot were subtle enough to maintain the intent, theme and overall sense that both the book and earlier movie gave us all.

The acting was fine. I liked Robbins the best, but Cruise was believable, too. Hat's off to finding a way to get Gene Barry on the screen.

Overall an enjoyable movie for all ages, and all "ages".

title: No Credit to Tom
review: I, too, was disappointed in this much-hyped film. I gave it a 7 because of Spielberg, not because of Cruise. Many of today's top movie stars could have played the lead role. Cruise was, in no way to me, necessary for the success of the film. Spielberg is the one who deserves the credit for what's good about this film, which is in large part the special effects. When I think of the people, I just think of running and screaming. Of course, that's what I'd do, too, if these aliens were destroying my world. After I watched it, I sat there and thought about Peggy Lee's song, "Is That All There Is?" It was just kinda empty. My favorite part was when three human characters were in the cellar (Cruise, Fanning, Robbins) because the aliens' actions were captivating to me. I rented the DVD and watched it on a nice sized TV screen. It was worth the $3-4, but I would have been irritated had I spent $7-10 to see it at a theater.

title: Hmm?
review:
If you've seen the older version or read the book, you know know it ain't gonna be the same!

The characters in this movie were all so lame, you actually would have preferred them to be dead. The little girl should have been the first one killed and then every whiner after that!

The premise for the movie was so-so, alien's invading Earth.

Unfortunately the movie starts slow and ends quick! The first 20 minutes were horrible and probably could have been skipped, but then finally the action starts and things improve.

Although I may complain about a lot of different aspects of this movie , I still enjoyed it enough to watch another 5 times for the great sights and sounds.

Even with all the negative marks on this movie, it's still well worth watching as long as you can stomach the cheesy start to it and don't mind 1940's SCI-FI child-like imaginations.

In this day and age, if someone made a similar type movie, it would be far more violent and futuristic.

title: Very Poor
review: I just finished watching War Of The Worlds, which is one of the worst movies I have seen in a long time. There are movies that are not my personal taste though I can still accept as a decent movie, but this movie was nothing but one filled with nice special effects, and bad acting. It had extreme over acting, over dramatization, and totally irrational responses to almost everything that happened. It was worse that the the old disaster movie where one emergency followed another with no stopping. This was sort of like the old Clint Eastwood movies, slow moving with extreme facial expressions and very little plot. The movie even ended with out a clear explanation of why the Aliens died. If I hadn't seen the original movie, even I wouldn't have had the foggiest idea. The stars just seemed to pop out of every seemingly tense situation, with no apparent reason, or explanation of how they survived. One minute he is in a sinking ship, and then he is in the water. Another moment he is in an alien machine, a basket falls, and then he is walking on the ground. I would tend to blame Tom Cruze, because he tends to do that in a lot of his movies, except for the fact, that almost every actor in the movie was the same, even to the little daughter, who had to be the most over protected spoiled brat on the planet. The son was also behaving like a moron, and the movie never really gave a reason for most of what he did. The movie just seemed to drag on with them moving from one basement hiding place to the next. If you want even a better idea how lame it is, just turn off the sound :) I guess I would have to blame Spielberg, because he directed the movie. I watched the whole long movie, with a couple dozen of my friends, and half way through the movie they wanted to put in another movie. If it weren't for one girl who couldn't see how dumb it was, the rest of us would not have even seen the end of the movie

title: An anti-Close Encounters but something good here anyway
review:
In Spielberg's "Close Encounters of the Third Kind", he gave us aliens who arrived in spacecraft covered with clouds. They stabbed the night with blinding spotlights, communicated in tones, and hovered over Devil's Tower. Awestruck earthlings contemplated the arriving ships while bathed in heavenly, alien light just before the aliens emerged and turned out to be nice. It was a transition from a universe full of horror to a benign one.

"Independence Day" overturned that universe when it gave us aliens who arrived in clouds and hovered over buildings that seemed to vaguely resemble Devil's Tower. After a few scenes of awestruck people bathed in heavenly light, the aliens blew the daylights out of all of them. Since I never got over that sacrilege against Spielberg, I was prepared to hate his "War of the Worlds" in which he committed the same sacrilege against himself.

I should have become ill when the aliens in "Worlds" arrived in clouds, occasionally stabbed the ground with blinding spotlights, and communicated in tones all in the service of a genocidal war against humanity. But the film won me over when I realized that it is primarily about the horrors of becoming a refugee from such a merciless foe. It is no "Grave of the Fireflies", that gut churning Japanese film about the aftermath of the fire bombing, but it does poke into the territory.

We see how refugees will protect their families and sometimes help others but also sometimes sacrifice others for their own safety. They make stupid decisions out of ignorance and even kill to avoid danger. The theme is true to the novel, because H.G, Wells wanted "War of the Worlds" to show what it was like for primitive people to be overrun by advanced weaponry that they could barely understand. He expressed this by writing early on that the Tasmanians were entirely swept out of existence by European immigrants and asking "are we such apostles of mercy as to complain if the Martians warred in the same spirit?" Now that weaponry is more advanced than ever and sometimes used as ruthlessly as ever, the theme is timelier than ever.

Spielberg's film makes us inhabit the minds of one family and experience their terror as they flee the mounting atrocities. Because it grabs us with the emotion of their danger, it is a good movie. However, it is not a great one because it missed too many chances to drive home what "Worlds" is supposed to be about. Wells' book contains the above quote; the movie does not. Although it has been criticized for various logical flaws (how did that kid survive the big fireball, anyway?), its main problem is in not following its theme through to the end. "Fireflies" was mainly about hunger after someone destroys a society; "Worlds" barely touches hunger. Probably Spielberg thought he was making a movie to warn us about terrorism rather than the one I saw.

But it grabbed me anyway, and many of the logical criticisms can be avoided. The camera might have been shielded from the EMP behind some cars. I suppose the machines rose from an impossible million-year underground hideout to exploit our fear of sleeper cells. But how, in the movie itself, do we know they were there that long? We have only the word of half-crazed people, and they had no way of knowing anyway. We saw the machines rise but not how or when they were buried. Part of the horror is that one day life goes on, and another day brings unexplained terror. People on the run would probably concoct explanations by the bucketful.

Where could the machines have come from? Maybe all the lightning was a Star Trek-like transporter that beamed them in only moments before they arose. The ground could have provided protection for powering them up and raising the shields.

The final family reunion does break the spell, but after all, Wells ended his book with one and the film would not do much business otherwise. I am, at least, not surprised that the aliens missed the microbes. They were probably so obsessed with their invasion, that they even thought that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction.

title: Devoted HG Wells fan but I enjoyed this one
review:
Despite some inconsistencies that have obviously delighted the 'goofs' buffs I thought this was a pretty good rendering of the original story but with a 21st century setting. Far more faithful to the HG Wells classic than the 1954 Gene Barry effort (although nice to see him and Ann Robinson again in this version). The heat ray, the red weed and humanity's hopelessness were all conveyed convincingly and the ferry attack was a credible substitute for the Thunderchild sequence in the book. Nice too to see the baskets of captured humans and the Martian feeding.

If only Dakota Fanning had been zapped in the first reel I would have scored this an 8.

title: Who would have believed...
review:
Who would have believed, that in the early years of the 21st century, they would remake a movie that was based on a book, that....

Here is the story, unbeatable aliens attack earth. We see the story through the eyes of a Ray and his two children as they travel so he can reunite his children with their mother.

Spielberg is certainly a great director, especially of special effects. For once there are none of those terrible panoramic CGI shots, everything is at ground level, yet you still have a feeling of awe about what is happening.

Yet having said that, this update on HG Wells landmark Science Fiction novel fails in a number of ways. In fact, the only original addition to the story is that of a family dealing with the Aliens, rather than anything else.

The design, script and story all fail to come up to the level of the original book. It is a pity, but this is mostly because it was a rushed project and so the result is mostly entertaining with characters that feel very real.

title: Really exciting and a bit scary too
review:
It is nice to see some social realism in a science fiction movie. Cruise is doing a decent job there. It is easy to feel that you are that main character because he is not a super hero, he has flaws and does not always know what to do in a given situation.

The movie was very tense at moments - actually most of the time. And a bit scary too. There were scenes where I was truly scared, especially because I have children. Spielberg is a master at creating scenes where you as a spectator is sitting at your hands, because you want to interact NOW in the movie, and not wait so long time as the actors do. This is so cool.

I remember I was furious two times during the movie, where I wished to do something differently. The movie makes you go up and down, so you find yourself in fear, happiness, anger, etc. And this is what I think is a good movie.

title: brilliant film
review:
i thought this movie was very intelligent. out of all the science fiction movies Spielberg has done, this was the best one yet.

The characters were well-chosen. The music score was perfect. i haven't read the book, but i believe it was quite accurate.

the whole cinematography made me feel like i was getting the feel of the movie. This film seriously made me think deeply about this issue .. what if it was really supposed to occur and how the whole world would be taking it.

I believe it should've gotten more than just three wins and one nomination. this movie was unbelievable. it struck out to me in no other way any other Spielberg movie could have.

title: Good movie that gets a bad rap
review:
First, I think the people that are saying the original movie is better are giving it too much credit. Some have reffered to this movie as a disgrace to Wells, well the 53 movie strayed further from the book and was loaded with religious and anti-communist slants which were not in the book at all. If either is a disgrace to Wells it's the original.

With that said I liked this movie. The acting was good, the effects were great, the movie seemed more real than Independence Day (some have said ID4 had a better plot to which I laugh at), and I like how Spielberg and Koepp tried to avoid all the clichés that would have made this into another ID4.

Some people have said that this movie has no plot to which I say: Did you even watch the film? The plot is about a father that is trying to protect his children during the midst of an alien invasion, does that sound like no plot? *SPOILER* And to the people ripping on the ending: So the son lived and it was a happy ending, big deal, get over it. Doom and gloom endings get old after a while. *ENDSPOILER* Finally, the only thing that would have made the movie better would have been one or two more scenes with the Tripods and their heat rays but it's fine the way it is.

8/10

title: A very involved study of divorced families and how one guy copes
review:
We get a chance to study all the dynamics of a divorce. The acrid innuendo between husband and ex-wife, the ravings of their hypochondriac daughter, the tired old saga a son rebelling against his father, the meddling in-laws, ...

Spielberg has caved in to "going for the money" and has abandoned film as an art expression. Spielberg tries too hard to relate to all the divorced families and tries too hard to relate to the children. I suppose this is all in an effort for ratings and dollars.

Even with all the exploration, there is nothing new to be learned about the relationships of a divorced family. Yes, they will unite against outside threats. Yes, the prodigal son comes home. Yawn.

Oh yes, there is some sci-fi in it also.

title: Good movie, but you need to know your history
review:
This is my first comment, so please take it easy on me. Anyway, I just finished watching the DVD and listening to the Radio broadcast of War of the Worlds, from mecurythearter.info. In order to appreciate the movie more you have to have either read one of the novels or listen to the radio broadcast of it, then you'll understand what Spielberg was going for.

The movie is more or less about a single man named Ray. His ex-wife drops off his kids to watch for the weekend. Now many people didn't like the whole, family sub-plot. But it was put in there for a reason. Anyway, the movie is well made, it has mistakes, but those people just want to ruin the movie for everyone. When you're watching the movie you have to look past it, don't think of it as an alien movie, think of it as a survival movie, okay, maybe they go hand in hand, but try and you might see what I'm talking about.

*WARING ENDING WILL BE DESCRIBED, AND POSSIBLE SPOILERS*

The only gripe I have with the movie is that the ending just happens. Ray finally reaches Boston and he sees that Robbie is safe with his mother, stepfather, and grandparents. Then the camera pulls back and shows the destruction and the narrator, Morgan Freeman, talks about how the bacteria kills all of the aliens. Now many of you will say "What?! Germs killed the aliens, that's bull!!" But you have to think about it. The "tripods", the aliens attack vehicles, were buried under the Earth millions of years ago, and it's safe to assume they were buried pretty far down to avoid detection, back then there probably weren't any bacteria deadly to the aliens at the time and they thought there wouldn't be any new germs on the planet.

*END OF SPOILERS*

So other than that I enjoyed the movie, and I recommend you see it at least once.

title: Steve hits the spot again
review: I think I speak for everyone when I say Stevie Spielberg has still got it, about 2 hours ago I just finished watching War of the Worlds and man was I on the edge of my seat. The effects were great, the storyline interesting, and the suspense was tense, when it first was released I was thinking "great this will just be aliens killing everything they see" and yes that was in it but there was also a storyline, you see the problems between Ray and his children (particually his teenage son)and your guessing "where on earth did the aliens come from". Acting was great, Dakota Fanning is just amazing and shes still so young, I've never minded Tom Cruise as an actor but as a person he's just a warped science freak who's up himself, so he is the only reason I didn't give it a 10.

title: Brilliant but highly annoying in parts!
review: Well... it's kind of hard to know what to say with a summary like that! This was a really great movie! Shocking and at some points totally terrifying in it's own way and yet I felt it was spoilt by the totally unnecessary role that Dakota Fanning had to play... there is nothing more irritating than the screaming child who remains totally helpless to the end and in the script must be quoted every few lines as saying *screams hysterically*! On the other hand the rest of the cast remained strong to the end with Tom Cruise proving the perfect lead. Ray Ferrier is a real father, although at the start he appears to take very little interest in his children's welfare and approaches parenthood with a half hearted attempt at making things work, by the end he proves himself to be a devoted and loving father. Human kind will be tested physically, mentally and spiritually. The question we all must ask ourselves is how far would we go to survive and see to it that the safety of our own is secured? The film goes so far as to see humanity teeter on the edge of destruction. Yet whilst there are still people to carry on the fight hope is never truly lost, which brings us to a sudden and unexpected conclusion. This would be a 10/10 for me if it were not for all the high pitched screams coming from Rachel Ferrier (that to be quite frank would be enough to drive even the aliens crazy if they could hear her from all the way up there in their weird tripods!) All in all however this is an amazing movie and definitely worth a viewing!

title: Spielberg and Cruise hit it out of the park again!
review: The same people who hated this movie, hated "SIGNS". Why? Because instead of showing wall-to-wall scenes of Earth being destroyed, it actually dares to take the P.O.V. of individuals who are running or hiding from the attack, which generates actual psychological thrills instead of mindless explosions. Yes, the ending is a tad abrupt (however faithful to the original material), but between this and "BATMAN BEGINS", I have actually had my faith restored in the idea of intelligent and thrilling summer blockbusters. Almost everyone who has expressed disappointment with the film complained that it wasn't what they expected it was going to be. Since when is that a valid point of criticism? I wish more movies would shatter our preconceived notions of what the plot will be, instead of spoon feeding us the entire story arch within a 2 minute trailer.

title: War of the Worlds
review: I have to admit the first time I saw this I wasn't very impressed, mostly because the performances by the leading actor and the daughter, but the second time I really saw why this remake by director Steven Spielberg (Jaws, Raiders of the Lost Ark, E.T. the Extra- Terrestrial, Schindler's List, Saving Private Ryan) is a good one. Basically Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise) is looking after his two children, young daughter Rachel (Dakota Fanning) and teenage son Robbie (Justin Chatwin) while their mother, and Ray's ex-wife Mary Ann (The Lord of the Rings' Miranda Otto) is in Boston. Ray isn't enthusiastic about looking after his kids, but his self-absorbed attitude is soon to change when a lightning storm approaches, and it seems bolts are hitting the same place numerous times. Then a large machine, known as a Tripod, comes out of the ground and is attacking everything in its path. Ray and the kids are now on the run with everyone else to escape the alien extermination and get to safety. Along the way they encounter an angry mob wanting their working car (all vehicles, electricity and communication has been killed off), Harlan Ogilvy (The Shawshank Redemption's Tim Robbins) obsessed with stopping the aliens in whatever way possible, and capture by one of the ships. In the end, after breathing and eating our planet's stuff, the aliens die of sickness, and Ray gets the kids to their mother safely. With opening and closing narration by Morgan Freeman. The special effects are of course fantastic, the story is pretty good, and even though the characterisations of Cruise (nominated the Razzie for Worst Actor) and Dakota may get on your nerves, you can believe their reactions. It was nominated the Oscars for Best Sound Editing, Best Sound Mixing and Best Visual Effects. Very good!

title: A worthy tribute to the classic tale!
review:
I am a huge fan of H. G. Wells' classic War of the Worlds, the first and penultimate tale of an alien invasion from space. Smart, witty, and terrifying, it is a story that has never been matched by any sci-fi authorever. So, when I discovered that Steven Spielberg, America's reigning genius of the cinema (and I don't use that term lightly), was crafting his own version of this classic story, I was greatly excited.

My verdict? Pure genius---but not perfect. Let me explain.

War of the Worlds (henceforth, WotW) is a remarkably complex film---so complex that it almost resists classification. Is this a science fiction film? A horror film? Poltergeist meets ET? Hitchcock meets Wells? The truth of the matter is that it is all of these elements, each blended masterfully by Mr. Spielberg into something that can best be described as a psychologically-harrowing cinematic experience. The plot of WotW is so ingrained in our culture that no real explanation of the premise is needed; suffice to say that aliens, hell-bent on the extermination of mankind, launch a surprise global attack that sweeps all before it. The original story had the aliens, Martians to be exact, landing in meteorites which also contained their mechanical killing machines. Mr. Spielberg plays with this original concept a little by positing the notion that the alien war machines had been pre-positioned below the surface of the earth some millennia before mankind arose. However, the alien operators (Spielberg offers no explanation as to the origination of the invaders) of these tripod machines arrive via massive EMP-generating (electro-magnetic pulse) lightning storms.

Needless to say, in the wake of the lightning storm, aliens run amok murdering all that cross their path. Into this maelstrom the movie's main characters are thrust. Tom Cruise plays the blue-collar and somewhat irresponsible single dad Ray Ferrier. After witnessing the terrifying arrival of the first alien tripods, he rushes home to retrieve his teenage son, played by Justin Chatwin, and young daughter as portrayed by the always superb Dakota Fanning. The trio quickly find themselves swept along with untold thousands of other refugees from the alien onslaught, thrust into life-or-death situations that would have been unimaginable a mere handful of hours earlier in their pre-invasion humdrum lives.

At this point, I need to pay special respect to Mr. Cruise. Even though he is quickly becoming the self-righteous thespian all the world loves to hate, Mr. Cruise's performance is absolutely brilliant. His "flawed everyman" portrayal is dead-on, serving to humanize events that are often portrayed with the clinical coldness of epic-history (in this case, pseudo-history). To watch Mr. Cruise is to empathize with him as he battles both aliens and his fellow humans in his desperate struggle for the survival of himself and his family. Mr. Spielberg also deserves a pat on the back for, at long last, bringing some depth of character to a science fiction flick. In a genre often littered with protagonists that are little more than two dimensional heroes, WotW brings the fantastic down to the level of ordinary humanity, allowing an all-to-rare breath of fresh air into the oft stale environment of sci-fi. Again, well done!

WotW also defies the genre in other ways. This film could have easily been yet another vehicle for mindless special effects and action sequences. Mr. Spielberg defies the trend by deliberately taking his film down a very different road, a path more in keeping with Orson Wells' War of the Worlds Halloween broadcast of 1938. Instead of a big budget light show, we get a very frightening movie that plays out in the deep recesses of our minds. WotW is very Hitchcockian in nature, at times more akin to Psycho than Independence Day. The movie dwells not on fireballs and big battles, but on the horrific nature of being hunted by aliens and their machines. Not content to stop there, Spielberg also taps, very subtly, into our contemporary fears by using our disturbing memories of 9-11 to punctuate key moments of the film. These clever techniques, combined with the perfect musical score of John Williams (again, also very Hitchcockian), combine to make a film that resembles Poltergeist (also by Spielberg) more so than it does any previous telling of Wells' tale.

I have few criticisms of the film, and those that I do have are more matters of preference than an actual disapproval. For example, as a purist, I do prefer Martians and their meteorites to unnamed aliens and their bolts of lightning. To me, there is nothing more properly sci-fi in nature than an invasion begun by a meteorite storm from Mars (as well as being plausibly realistic).

I also would have preferred more scenes of outright battle between the aliens and the armed forces. Again, I understand how Spielberg wanted to keep the film pointedly focused on the intimate plight of ordinary citizens just trying to survive another few hours. However, what is the point of imagining an alien invasion if not to provide at least one grand battle? As such, the aliens always seem to be more of a shadowy threat just over the next hill than an actual, tangible enemy force. Disappointing, but only minimally so.

So, what does this all add up to? Is Steven Spielberg's War of the Worlds the ultimate cinematic version we fans have been awaiting since the release of its dim-witted sibling Independence Day? Alas, no. Mr. Spielberg's interpretation is truly excellent, as well as innovative, but George Pal's 1953 version still reigns supreme as it maintains the best balance of end-of-the-world calamity versus personal horror. Nonetheless, Mr. Spielberg's film is a fitting tribute to this classic tale as well as a worthy addition to our shared science fiction cinematic heritage. By combining two disparate genres, sci-fi and horror, WotW becomes something very original and worth watching. I give it 8 out of 10 deathrays.

title: Pretty good roller coaster ride...
review:
I think people are mistaking this film for sci-fi, when in actuality it's a pure summer action blockbuster with little science fiction content.

If taken as such, it's very entertaining indeed and "edge-of-your-seat." I was especially taken by the plight of the little girl in the film, and her near descent into catatonia produced by all the stress. An interesting examination of how almost unbearable stress can affect people.

The special effects were first rate, although not 100% convincing... however, they were convincing enough to enjoy the film and be able to sustain disbelief.

Overall, a fun roller-coaster romp that requires no brain power whatsoever. Hey guys, we browse the Net so much... what's wrong with relaxing the gray matter at a film once in awhile? 6/10.

title: An underrated Spielberg spectacle.
review:
After the disappointing "AI" and the bloated "Minority Report", I figured the last great Spielberg sci-fi film would be "Jurassic Park", so I decided to skip this movie during its theatrical run. What a mistake! "War of the Worlds" has everything that made Spielberg great in the first place.

The director fails in this genre when he has a hidden agenda, force-feeding the thematic undertones of the material to the point where we forget what brought us to his flicks in the first place. That is not the case here. "War of the Worlds" is everything you should expect it to be: spectacular thrills and breathtaking visual finesse.

Is that all you get? Yes, and thankfully so.

This is one of the most action-packed movies I've ever seen. Literally, there are thrills one right after the other. Don't think that I'm calling this a Michael Bay movie, now. Unlike anything that odious director has ever tried to make, "War of the Worlds", despite its continuous action, has style. Not very many movies scare me anymore, but there are countless scenes in the movie that are downright terrifying.

And believe it or not, Tom Cruise doesn't ruin the movie. In fact, I think it's one of his most accomplished performances. This is the cool Tom Cruise, not the one that makes me want to pop Ritalin. Both Cruise and Spielberg have been rather disappointing in their recent theatrical offerings, so "War of the Worlds" is a refreshment.

Of course, every movie has its lowpoints. The ones here are easily-forgettable logistical errors concerning very insignificant plot points.

I expected "War of the Worlds" to be typical SpielSchlock. And I got a riveting action tale. I was impressed, unlike "AI" where I expected deep sci-fi themes, and got lame, fairy-tale sentimentality. That was a disappointment. This one isn't. Wake up, people! This deserves a better score.

9/10

title: Spielberg's new take of the original 1953 is an interesting new telling.
review:
An over-worked construction worker by the name of Ray (Tom Cruise), who never had time for his troubled teenage son (Justin Chatwin) and his bright young daughter (Dakota Fanning). Since his ex-wife (Miranda Otta) left him for another man. Since Ray might have a chance to get along better with his two children for the weekend but the world has changed. When Aliens has taking control of the Planet and trying to destroy the whole population of Earth. Ray and his two children try to run to Boston to join his ex-wife and his ex-parents in laws. But they meet all sorts of troubles, they witness an wave of mass destruction and death. Now the human race must have new ways to destroy this aliens before taking over.

Directed by four-time Oscar Winner:Steven Spielberg (Jaws, Schindler's List, Murich) made an vivid, science-fiction thriller with elements of drama and horror. Cruise gives an good performance here. Which Cruise rarely plays a father in the movies. Fanning is terrific in the picture and newcomer Chatwin is also fine. Oscar-Winner:Tim Robbins has an small but credible role as a crazed man. Spielberg does gives you a real feeling of hopelessness and it is also quite haunting in this picture.

DVD has an sharp anamorphic Widescreen (1.85:1) transfer and an terrific:DTS 5.1 Surround Sound (Also in Dolby Digital 5.1). This Single Disc Edition has only one featurette as an extra. This might be far from Spielberg's best works but he makes this film feels real with a certain doom that makes this remake worth seeing. This picture is Based on a Classic Novel by H.G. Wells (The Food of the Gods, The Island of Dr. Moreau, The Time Machine). Oscar-Winner:Morgan Freeman narrated the film. Watch for Gene Berry and Ann Robinson as Ray's ex Parents-in-Law at the end. Screenplay by Josh Friedman (The Black Dahila) and David Koepp (Carlito's Way, Panic Room, Zathura). Screenwriter:Koepp is no stranger working with Spielberg before. Since Koepp also wrote Jurassic Park and The Lost World:Jurassic Park is both directed by Spielberg. Strong music score by five-time Oscar Winner:John Williams (Fiddler of the Roof, Saving Private Ryan, Star Wars). (****/*****).

title: Looked Real to Me
review:
Ray (Cruise) a divorced father of two receives his kids from the mother for the weekend and all hell breaks loose. The War has started.

I have no idea what they used or how they did this, but the special effects of roads buckling, buildings simply losing their adhesion and collapsing, Alien Tri-Pods walking thru brick buildings, bridges separating and turning over, and cars flying thru the air like they had some place to go was unlike any special effects I have ever seen. And, it all looked very real.

My thoughts went to the Orson Wells' broadcast (I read about it) in the late 1930s when Americans really believed they were being invaded by beings from Mars. That must have been scary stuff. This was scary stuff too. No one knew what to do, or where to go when the Tri-Pods the aliens used came to life obliterating everything in their way. Ray needed to get his kids to their mother in Boston and it seemed as though everyone else had someone in Boston to see also as there were miles of a ribbon of human flesh headed that way.

After the initial attacks, things quieted down for the rest of the movie. That was a mistake because the second half of the movie sort of died. Yes, there were still some scary moments, but not on the scale that opened the movie. Oh, there was the human interest story regarding Ray and what a lousy father he must have been, but still he fought to get his kids to Boston. Then, some uncomfortable scenes with Tim Robbins comes into play as he tries to help Ray with the girl (Fanning) now since the boy had to go to the front to see what was happening for himself. Teenagers!

I couldn't figure out why Dakota Fanning was in this movie. There was nothing striking about her performance and I still believe she will be one of our best actresses in time. No, I think she is on a mission to work with all the biggest names in the business before she is 15. I could be wrong. Speaking of being 15, Fanning looked every bit 10-yrs old in the beginning. By the end of the movie she looked like a young teen-ager. Hmmmmm.

Where the Aliens came from was never explained. Mars was never mentioned. Everything seemed to happen on the way to Boston, as there was no mention of anything being shown in other countries and yes, the power outages may have had something to do with that.

How did it end, you ask? How did we beat the unbeatable alien race hell bent on exterminating us when everything our army did was of no consequence? Well, as smaaaaaaart (we're in Boston now) as the Aliens were, they overlooked one thing.

Overall, pretty good and worth going to see if only for the special effects. Looked real to me.

title: Better than the Original... but not the Definitive Version
review:
H.G. Well's sci-fi novel has had  to some  quite a good year. Not only have three different versions of his book been made into celluloid renditions but Jeff Wayne's cult classic musical version has been fully restored and re-released. But I'm not here to badger about the musical version.

I'm a massive fan of the book and Spielberg has done a good job with the atmosphere and horrific loss of life of the masses. The tripods are tremendous as is the CGI effects for them and the SFX for their ominous war-cry. There are faithful nods back, not only to the 50's original, but to the book itself. Whilst the film boasts a mixture of "Saving Private Ryan" style filming and "Independence Day" alien invasion (without the sickening American patriotic tosh, and Will Smith one-liners) it has something else, something that has never been done before. Whatever it is you can decide for yourself because I don't want to give too much away.

Whilst it is a cut above the rest so far, Spielberg's adaptation of the survival-horror / sci-fi classic was actually not due out until 2007. The executives must have got hot-pants for the project and green-lit it too soon. It created the con's result as thus. One of them is employing superstars and not actors. I like Tom Cruise and respect him as a professional but not even his talent was enough to make a convincing unsteady family guy (especially Dakota Fanning), unlike the Freelander's from "Poltergeist". Whilst Spielberg captures Wells' inspiration of a world super power brought to its knees by invading Martians (or to Mr Spielberg Aliens *groan*) and their monstrous fighting machine tripods, the flick's failing point  the same with the 50's version  is the ending. The film literally ends half-way through the story. Had the film not have been so rushed would we have a better and much more of a bitter-sweet ending, like the book? And could we have had more footage after the army's bitter defeat? With Steven "They-All-Live-Happily-Ever-After" Spielberg at the helm, I say, probably not. But he has surprised me so far.

But all hope is not lost, until 2007-8 that is. Remember Mr Wayne? Well with the success of his album he is due to release a CGI animated movie so will that be the definitive version and zap the others with its silver screen heat-ray out of the lime light? Let us hope so. Let the Martian war-cry ring out true ULLA!!!

title: War of the Yelling Family
review:
Although I think a small handful of his films are gems, I'm not the biggest Steven Spielberg fan, and this film is a typical example why that's the case. Spielberg is someone who tends to be great at concepts and the "look" of a film, but his writing and directing tend to suffer from a plethora of peculiar problems; War of the Worlds is no exception (I know that Spielberg doesn't get a writer's credit here, but it's obvious that this is a Spielberg story and script--his marks are all over it). In my opinion, Spielberg is someone who should be in the film business as a lead technician--overseeing special effects, production design, cinematography, and so on. He's one of the best at those aspects. Judged on those elements, War of the Worlds may very easily get a 10, and if you're a fan of that stuff, you should definitely check this film out.

The first 10 or 15 minutes I actually thought were worth a 10 overall. The film begins closely parallel to the superior 1953 version. When we're first introduced to our stable of characters, the film is interesting. Tom Cruise's character is a bit different from his usual stock. He's a working class curmudgeon who, if this were 1953, could pass for Bruce Springsteen's father. The setting is oddly surreal. And the initial appearance of the alien menace is certainly gripping and intense.

But then we get more into characterization and a story meant to develop it, and the film goes into the toilet. The focus isn't really the alien invasion, its effect on humanity, or the science behind trying to understand the aliens and fight them, as was the focus in the H.G. Wells book and the George Pal film. The focus here is on Tom Cruise's character, Ray Ferrier, and--surprise surprise, given Spielberg--his kids, played by Dakota Fanning and Justin Chatwin.

Spielberg has never been someone who cares too much if his films make logical sense, as long as each scene has the "right affect" (and yes, I definitely mean "affect" there and not "effect"). Sometimes it can work, and I certainly am not averse to surrealism and dream logic, but this isn't a modern Asian genre film like Karisuma (1999), this is a film that should make logical sense. The worst offense here is that Cruise and his kids just happen to survive and be in the place they need to be in to perpetuate the story, even though most of the transitions from scene to scene would require machinations amounting to, " . . . and then a miracle happens". Sometimes we're shown the miracles--such as when they just happen to break through the police line to an escaping boat, and sometimes we're just given them, such as the fact that even though an airplane fell on the house (in a scene that seems stolen from Donnie Darko (2001)), the car remains unscathed--why? Because they need the car to get to the next scene. Likewise Ray Ferrier needs to be the only person in New York City outside of the military who can get a car running after the aliens disable all other devices that work on electromagnetic principles, such as electricity, telephone service, watches, and so on. Among the tens of aspects of the film that make no sense in this way are the fact that in the opening, one guy just happens to have a video camera that still works; there are people in the immediate vicinity of the opening scene, including Ray's kids, who seem to not have the faintest idea what is going on, even though a very visible "monster", hundreds of feet tall, just tore up half of Bayonne, New Jersey; and Ray and a number of other people seem to "just know" that the alien machines had been buried under the ground for hundreds or thousands of years. The film is littered with almost incoherent items like this.

But if the story and script were good, if the actors had been directed well, those incoherent aspects might not kill the film. For example, yeah, it makes no sense that someone has a video camera that still works during the opening scene, but it does provide an interesting way to see some of the action, so it is almost excusable.

Like always, Spielberg wants to make this a human story, centered on a family and their problems. The ingredients are there for it, and it might not have been a bad idea. But in trying to develop characterization, he makes just as many illogical, inexplicable leaps as he does elsewhere. Why does Ray's son suddenly want to run off with the military (who just happen to be in a ridiculous place at the time they're needed for this scene, by the way)? We're not shown anything that would ground or justify this for the character; in fact, the opposite seems to be true. Why is Ray's daughter an emotional basket case? We don't know, she just is, because Spielberg thinks it will make the film more emotional. Why wouldn't Ray tell his kids what is going on in the beginning? It seems the only reason for this is to perpetuate some tension in the film. Most of the "characterization" is along these lines.

Worse is Spielberg's direction of his cast. He seems to have told everyone to overact, and then overact some more, just in case the folks in the next town over couldn't hear them. There is a lot of yelling/screaming in this film. People yell no matter where they are. They yell at people to be quiet, otherwise the aliens might hear them, and then once they quiet them, the next scene has them yelling anyway. Everything is for maximum manipulation, including the clichéd John Williams score, but most of it doesn't work.

title: Expected more
review: This movie is a showcase for special effects. Unfortunately, and amazingly, the widescreen DVD is NOT encoded as anamorphic widescreen - which means that if you watch on a widescreen TV, you'll see a small picture with black letterbox bands above and below as well as black panel bars left and right! The story is weak - but you didn't come for that. The character development is very thin; only twice are characters with any depth imperiled, and somehow I couldn't muster any emotion for them. And in a plot filled with barely believable angles, the ending is very weak. The most interesting part of the DVD was the documentary on development of the concepts for the tripods and aliens.

title: Not about a Hero
review: When I first saw the trailer I thought that I will see another hero who will fight against the danger and saves the world but the real surprise in this movie is that it is not about a hero who saves the world. It is about a simple man like many of us who can get in the middle of a global disaster and has only one target that is to save his beloved ones. He does not understand or care about why that is happening or how to fight this, he only thinks about how to protect his family and reach a safe place with them. Tom Cruise Really did great on playing that man. If you are looking for a kind of a movie that has the hero who saves the world then this is not the right movie for you but if want to see a real man like most of us and feel thankful for the peace you live in, I recommend it to you.

title: Reason to Recall the Impact of H.G. Well's Apocalyptic Book
review:
The real dazzler about this reincarnation of an old story is that it IS the reincarnation of an old story. H.G. Wells published his scary sci-fi novel in 1898, Orson Welles terrified the country in his 1938 radio drama version of the book, in 1953 the book became a film, and now in the time of terrorism Steven Spielberg makes the story not an invasion from Mars but an enemy from within the bowels of the globe. Quite a fest for a book over a hundred years old to still seem pertinent.

Steven Spielberg once again proves he can outdo most anyone with costly productions. His style is evident from the first moments when the actions seems centered on the broken family of Ray (Tom Cruise) and his ex-wife Maryann (Miranda Otto) as she leaves their children Rachel (Dakota Fanning) and Ray (Justin Chatwin) with Ray in New Jersey while Maryann and her new husband take a trip to Boston. The tension is obvious: Ray is not a father-type and finds communication with his children tedious at best. The Spielberg family drama recipe is set.

The action starts almost immediately with newscasts of electrical field disturbances on the media and then the occurrence of lightning without thunder in New Jersey. In rapid motion the etiology of the altered weather is seen to be the emergence out of the ground of huge tripod machines that destroy everything in sight ("Is it terrorists?" Rachel repeatedly asks, driving home the underlying tone of Spielberg's intention of making the story relevant to our time). New Jersey is destroyed but Ray and the kids find a car that works and drives toward Boston for reconciliation with Maryann. What happens between New Jersey and Boston is a battle to end all battles during which time Ray discovers the importance of his fatherhood, the love of his children, and his own humbling recognition that he is but one member of the planet earth.

The stars of the film are the extraordinary tripod machines, though Cruise and Fanning hold their own. One leaves the film feeling it could have had more impact had it stuck more closely to the book, but then that's been done before. Grady Harp

title: Somewhere in there is a fantastic flick waiting to get out
review:
What really disappoints me about this film is that somewhere in there is a fantastic flick waiting to get out. It has scenes which are highly impressive but these are equaled by those which are just ridiculous.

First of all my bugbears with the movie:

1) Tom Cruise  Bad casting. Loved him in Minority Report, his last collaboration with Spielberg; hate him here. He doesn't convince as a father, even an irresponsible one. You can see him trying but that's the problem; a real actor doesn't look like they're trying.

2) The kids are annoying. I know I know, little Dakota Fanning plays traumatised pretty well. Except I think here she overplays it. The son meanwhile, well, personally I'd have tied the little turds hands behind his back, found a gun, and told him to march 6 feet in front of me if I had to.

3) I don't get the "they've been planning this for over a million years" thing. There's about 100 things wrong with this. The worst being that the aliens somehow overlooked innoculations for local bugs. Sheesh, even when you fly to Asia or Africa you get shots!!! And it didn't take a million years for us to work that out! Or maybe a million years just wasn't long enough to do any research into it!?! Here's an idea for the sequel: Aliens get sick & die. Other aliens (in protective suits) come down; grab one of the deceased ones; take it home, dissect it; work out an antidote from its blood; vaccinates its entire military; then invades again. Jeez, don't let a little bug stop ya guys!!! There's a planet at stake here!!!

4) The aliens have awesome technology that can zap people, destroy buildings, terraform the planet; but their hearing abilities are terrible, both biological and mechanical. I mean, how much noise do the Cruiser & the Timster make in that basement while that snake scanner thing is snooping around?!?! Hello!!! It's not a big basement people!!! And you mean to tell me the scanner misses the lit lamp that they extinguish just before the aliens come down for a look around in case it "might give them away"?!?

There's more but to be honest they border on the trivial. The special effects themselves are fine tho not outstanding in this day and age of "the next movie topping the previous one for jaw dropping fx".

I would've have liked Spielberg to focus more on the complete social collapse, something rather briefly hinted at during the mob vs car scene. It would have brought the movie much closer to home; a lot closer than say, the endless September 9 references, which while poignant still left me somewhat emotionally distant from the groups predicament. There wasn't really a feeling of horror here. Everything seemed rather paint by numbers as a matter of fact. I realise it's a remake and a rather loyal one that adheres to the originals framework. I just believe the potential could've been expanded on rather than only the special effects.

It's quite alright for some remakes not to be submitted to the "high concept" or "alternative view" approach (i.e the need to starkly differentiate the latest version from the original). For the latest Batman the alternative view approach worked extremely well. However the meat & potatoes of War Of The Worlds is about Human survival against Alien invaders. While it may be a parable of the Holocaust or other examples of mans extreme inhumanity to man, what this movie should be about is what we would do to survive & the levels we would sink to against impossible odds. It didn't need to be about a family. It needed to be about Us as a species. In this case it should've been made much more simpler tho with more pathos and introspection. What we have instead is just a simple movie with characters we care not a jot about.

title: Brilliantly Visualized and Gripping
review:
Having been a fan of the novel, George Pal film, and Orson Welles radio drama for years, I waited with eager anticipation for the release of this version on DVD (having missed the theatrical release). Overall, I found Spielberg's rendition to be brilliantly visualized and gripping. While remaining true to the spirit (and some of the technical details) of the novel and subsequent versions, he and his writers have managed to highlight some of the horrific aspects of the story that are underplayed in previous versions.

The result is a suspenseful journey through a rapidly alienizing territory, beset by terror and tragedy, but also offering hope.

While paying appropriate homage to the lineage of this powerful story, the filmmakers weave together a visually stunning and humanistic narrative that comments upon major events of our day.

title: Excellent, but surprisingly dark.
review:
Sitting down to watch War of the Worlds recently on DVD, I was expecting a return to the type of movie Spielberg would happily make throughout the eighties and nineties, before becoming the more experimental and more thoughtful filmmaker he is nowadays. To be honest what I was expecting was basically Jurassic Park with aliens, but what we get is something very, very different. Instead of it being a fun packed thriller with comic relief spread throughout, what one gets is something very dark, very serious and at times downright distressing. This is basically a big budget blockbuster from the man who has brought the world Schindler's List and Saving Private Ryan, not the man who brought us the Jurassic Park movies and Jaws. This is not to say that the film is bad, because it's not, in fact it is very, very good. Terrific in fact. It has all the usual aspects one should expect from a film like this such as budget busting special effects sequences, thrilling action set pieces and a genuine sense of terror, but what makes the film more than that is the way that instead of focusing on characters that are mere fantasy figures like a fictional president or smarter than thou scientists, what we get is the invasion of earth by extra terrestrials from one family, in this case the Ferrier family as played by Tom Cruise, Dakota Fanning and Justin Chatwin. The whole movie is played from their point of view and it makes it a treat. As Spielberg said in a lot of the publicity before the film was released, it is the biggest small film ever made. Like Batman Begins (the best film of summer 2005), more thought is put into the script and characters, so much so that we truly care about them. One truly distressing sequence has Cruise and his family being car jacked, but Fanning's character being left in the car and Cruise struggling to get to her. It is a moment of pure suspense, but one that is very distressing and almost full of despair.

Technically the film is also superb, as it should be. The invasion sequences are some of the best put to film and best of all they don't look like special effects, something so rare in the movies of today. The tripods are terrifying, equally so the aliens themselves. Janusz Kaminski's photography is eye catching, as always. Much like his work in Minority Report and Saving Private Ryan, he goes more for a washed out look, with a tendency to shoot at a higher number of frames. It gives the movie a beautiful and ugly look, mostly at the same time.

In a summer blockbuster season that has given us some of the best blockbusters in some years (Batman Begins, Sin City and Revenge of the Sith), War of the Worlds is more than equal to stand alongside some of the output of this year. It is in effect an old master doing what he does best. It amounts to one thrill packed ride.

title: read me
review:
1898..one of the greatest books I have ever read was first published. 1938..A little known narrator (at that time) by the name of Orsen Welles performs a rendition of the story in the format of a radio broadcast. The chaos that ensued due to people believing the invasion was real prompted government studies on mass paranoia to take place. 1953..A George Pal produced motion picture captures an Oscar and brings the Wells classic to the silver screen for the first time. There have been way too many TV versions for me to count.

I remember picking up War of the Worlds by H.G. Wells for the first time when I was about 8 years old. Some would consider an 8 year old reading that kind of stuff horrific, but I was into Stephen King as well. I remember as I read into the book I was thankful that this never really happened, because humanity was screwed. The ending in my opinion was poetic justice. To this day War of the Worlds is one of my favorite books.

2005..One of the greatest directors of our time decides to take his shot at the classic story of man versus alien. Spielberg has done a superb, but not flawless job. I was excited when the movie first started and there was narration from Morgan Freeman (uncreditied to boot). The book was narrated in past tense by the main character (who I believe was unnamed if I'm not mistaken) and it was my hope the whole movie would have such narration, but it only happened at the beginning and the end. Of course the setting has changed, with the book the setting was England circa 1900, the movie places us in modern day New York. I was a little miffed that Spielberg didn't stick with the original story completely, but I understand most people here in the States wouldn't feel much for London being burned to cinders. Granted it's stated in the movie that the aliens are attacking all over the world and that this is truly a global disaster. The one thing Spielberg did right by the book was telling the story from the view of the main character, our charming Mr. Katie Holmes himself...Tom Cruise.

Tom Cruise plays a divorced father named Ray Ferrier. In the book the main character was alone, no wife no kids. I thought the addition of a family was unnecessary, but I guess that's why I'm not a filmmaker. His son Robbie is a reclusive yet headstrong man and his daughter Rachel, played well by Dakota Fanning, is the scream machine in this movie. Ray is obviously the bad father who spent more time worrying about himself than about his marriage. The whole movie revolves around Ray trying to get his family safely to Boston, where he hopes to find his ex-wife. There were many things I liked about this movie. I liked how they never really explain the alien's motives a la Independence Day. To the audience or me in particular, the aliens are nothing but cold-blooded killers. I have to admit, this is a dark side of Spielberg we haven't seen since 'Saving Private Ryan'. The death is catastrophic. And while I kind of 'geek out' a bit as the alien tripods belch out a loud echoing "uuuuuuuuuuu-lahhhhhhhh' (just like the book!!!), I felt really a sense of dread as people were hunted down and killed mercilessly. I admit this movie scared me a little.

The first hour of the movie is intense. But to my utter disappointment it slowed down quite a bit with the introduction of Tim Robbin's character Ogilvy. The movie kind of dragged here and I can't help but wonder if they should've introduced the 'black gas' (like in the book) instead of dealing with this strange character.

That was the only real flaw other than the screaming kid of course. What is good is that Spielberg stuck with the general ideal of the book. And anyone who has read the book knows how it ends. But anyone who reads the book will never know if Ray succeeds in reaching Boston or not.

Great book, good adaptation of a movie. But I would still love to see a direct adaptation, it's high time a movie should be as good or better than the book! 8 out of 10 stars. Nice work Steven.

The story and interaction of the characters is excellent, and well balanced with the great special effects which for a feature of its kind is surprisingly not over bearing (with no (or little) product placement to ruin it).

The problem with the film is though that the dialogue can be quite frustrating and irking, and personally i wish they would have just got on with the film at points. The kids do a fair job (especially the girl who for her age was excellent in the role) but really their script could have been better written. Also the ending ruins the film and is not necessary in the way they did it, what is Spielberg like with movie endings!!!! Maybe without knowing it, this movie was a warning about human behaviour as much as invasion or attacks.

Overall, a good film, but walk out with 5 mins to go, else the ending will spoil the whole thing for you.

title: Not deep, but extremely well made
review:
Ordinarily, location choices and set management are barely considered when a big-budget CGI action flick is made.

Happily, this film revels in the opposite extreme: the outer boroughs of New YOrk City, the frumpy clothes, the rain and cold misty breath, the textures and dirt... are all so vivid, so REAL, that we can readily accept something as ..well.. PREPOSTEROUS as an alien invasion.

Heck, I even found myself thinking "Tom Cruise... is acting ? I didn't know he could do that !" The lack of plotting is quite nice, adding to the whole panicked atmosphere of the film rather than detracting.

Small touches, like photographing little Rachel (Dakota) through a screen door or showing an alien ship through the maze of bare tree branches, made me really enjoy the textures and realism far more than I have in any other recent movie that comes to mind.

If you see this film, you'll enjoy comparing Tom Cruise's frumpy, lumpy, messy house and fractured home life to Will Smith's overly-clean, overly sensational similar home scene in Independence Day. Where Will Smith is asked to play a smarmy, too-clean, all-mighty guy sleeping with a sexy stripper in a fairly well set-decorated house and neighborhood, Tom Cruise is a delight to watch as a divorced, grungy dock-worker whose setting is so believably portrayed as to make me, a New Yorker, nod almost continuously while thinking "Yeah... that's the way it really is." More about the acting: Tom Cruise, like WIll Smith, is almost always asked to play a good-looking, all-mighty, smiling near-superhero. It was refreshing in the extreme to see him here with tears, an almost droopy face, and filthy fingernails....a less than average man, surviving only by coincidence, and completely convincing as "just another guy from the hood".

Dakota's performance as his daughter is even more engrossing. While she isn't yet being offered roles with the impact of Haley Joel Osmet's childhood films, I'm mentally crossing my fingers and hoping that this budding actress will continue to bloom as she has in this film.

Tim Robbins' brief role is riveting, and his realism is engrossing. He's truly got star acting power.

Little incidental touches, like a woman and her daughter whom TOm Cruise's character sees just before boarding a ferry -- or another character who picks up TOm Cruise's fallen gun, who is nameless and wordless and only on screen for seconds-- are nonetheless producing powerful reactions in the audience.

Happily, the script is filled with good lines that are alternately powerfully wise or comical and accidental-seeming bits of real life. Watch for Tom Cruise saying "Cound you come up with a plan that doesn't involve your 10-year-old sister joining the army ?" or Tim Robbins saying "It's no more a fight between them and us as there is between men and maggots".

The alien machinery is particularly noteworthy. You'll particularly enjoy its unexpected steam-engine blasts, foghorn sounds, gritty dirty industrial look, and unexpected weakness (it vaporizes people, but leaves clothing intact). The designers succeed brilliantly in delivering an imagined alien technology that is believable, yet entirely unlike anything we've seen before.

Walk out before the final scene, though. The Hollywood happy ending is just... too damned silly, and doesn't belong in this film. It's completely unnecessary, ignores the spirit of H.G. Wells' novel, and tears the veil of realism away from this film like someone stripping wallpaper off of bare brick.

You'll also be annoyed at the darned silly inclusion of a virtual commercial for the army, toward the end of the film, when a band of army men get to use their bazooka with good results. This is an anti-war movie, but some damned fool on the film's crew decided to turn this and several other scenes into recruiting commercials for the army... completely out of place, like a damned Spice Girls song during a Mozart revival concert.

title: An Epic Blockbuster
review:
War of the Worlds is a typical Spielburg film. He drags you in quickly and almost never lets go. WotW is an a big time Summer movie that anyone can enjoy.

The film starts off quickly and you're pulled in faster than you can say Tripod. The acting is amazing and the writing is good too. The only problem is, it slows down too much at the end and the ending comes abruptly and unexplained. Only Morgan Freeman's sign off narration can explain it properly to confused fans.

Aside from some small errors on the part of the director (digital cameras working during electronic blackout), WotW is an enjoyable film. Tom Cruise andDakota Fanning steal the show and make this a truly amazing experience. The visuals are astounding as well. This film is easy to pick apart, and if you're a picky movie watcher, chances are you won't enjoy this. But if you can sit back and simply enjoy good entertainment, then WotW won't disappoint.

title: War within our Worlds
review:
As a science fiction movie, I thought it was the worse - it lacked the scientific details that make good science fiction; the film however, excels as an exploration of familial values and the war within our worlds.

This review deals explicitly with Spielberg's adaptation, because I haven't read the original novel.

Many people who watch the movie will find it a great piece of escapism. Indeed, it is tribute to Spielberg's virtuoso ability to manipulate the audience; great music, which does much to instill tension, and at the same time, can easily be blinded over because of its very orthodox sound. Now, the latter is especially important because in doing so, the audience is not distracted - one's attention is fixed upon the events unfolding before one's eyes. There's much more to the directives; the fact that he got most of us at the edge of our seats is testament to that fact. But I won't comment.

In the opening scene of Cruise's character, Ray, we see him as a man of contradictions; his qualities tend towards the irresponsible, yet he exhibits the skills of a man who can only be responsible - one who knows his work. This contradiction shows itself literally in a myriad of ways. The fact that he is a divorcée; and in possession of disarrayed home and a vacant father-child relationship - he is even unable to play a baseball game with his son without making quirky comments about hats, or discussing the aspects of divorced life. Fact is, this contradiction reveals Ray to be character which is not so much childish, but rather, incomplete and unfulfilled. In a sense, he doesn't even feel like a real person. He sees his ex-wife's present husband, and feels little obvious jealousy or pain; he shamelessly throws himself under the table when lightning strikes, then he laughs - its almost surreal. Having said that, even his actions seem a little odd. He wanders off, pushes his way pass the crowd, and stares into the hole made by the crash; there's no dialogue, no indication of what he might be thinking, so we can't say that he's simply adrenalin hungry, or that he is a satisfying curiosity. Anyway, the overall effect given is that Ray appears to be lost, and searching. His world is filled with contradictions and incompleteness; a fact that is central to the movie.

We will see that he undergoes certain revelations... certain changes in character that ultimately quells the 'war in his world'. A pivotal scene in the movie is when he meets with the seemingly gratuitous nobody in the underground cellar. One could argue that the just-arrived character is in fact the Hyde in Ray; or in a way, the person we see working in the crane earlier in the movie. He yearns to strike at the enemy, a scenario that one could involve Ray in if he was still in the role of the contractor. Clearly also, he is irresponsible as he lacks concern over the possible repercussions of his actions. So it is because of this that Cruise's attack and murder of this man is significant. In his murder of the man, he has effectively eliminated his other half. He turns responsible and becomes conservative in action, because he feels an obligation to protect his daughter.

However, it is not specifically familial love that saves Ray from the same fate as his Hyde brother. Rather, I'd like to think that the main theme is responsibility and devotion to ideals; it is this which stills the conflict in the people's worlds. The mother for example, is unharmed. Which seems strange at first... but in accordance to the previous point, one could argue that she is unharmed because she stoically maintains her ideals of marriage, love and family; she marries again after divorce, and yet, still trusts her ex. In contrast are the people who thwart Ray and his children in their escape: the 'masses', who attempt to steal our hero's car, and even use guns in the process. Such people have no integrity/responsibility and hence, do not survive their/the war(s). As for Ray, there is devotion/ responsibility to his children reinforcing his will to survive. All of which is reflected in his drive to reach Boston; a place not to be taken literally, but rather, symbolic of family and home.

I hope that the latter point helps to ease any 'discomforts' over the strange and abrupt ending. When Ray reached Boston, the movie HAD to end. Oh of course, seeing aliens die would be fun. But again, just *seeing* an alien would ruin the movie by making it thematically pointless.

Robbie's disappearance and appearance is also interesting. His apparent death is a necessity to the movie. If he had not disappeared, then there would be no way in which the middle scene (previously commented upon) could be inserted into the movie. And that scene was quintessential to the movie. On a metaphorical level, one could also view the son's temporary departure as further indication of that restless, child in Cruise's character, leaving to be replaced by the mature albeit paranoid character displayed by his daughter. And at the end, he had to 'become alive' because Boston as mentioned before, is symbolic of family. If he doesn't return, then there would be the complication of his mother's feelings, and etc. The family had to be whole to convey Cruise's character's fulfillment.

I hope I've done something to change your mind about the movie if you thought it was bad. I know many people walked out cursing, expecting aliens. In that sense, I guessed the title and trailers were misleading... especially since its a Wells piece. One wonders if they could have put the movie under a different name and gotten away with it. Chill guys!
