title: These Aren't Friendly Aliens
review:
Where the 1953 War of the Worlds movie was terrific sci-fi, this movie is more effective as a horror film. Steven Spielberg's aliens aren't the cute little E.T.s or even the mysterious invaders from Close Encounters. These aliens are here to kick some ass and destroy every little thing in sight. The aliens, which travel in giant tripod machines are relentless. They keep coming and coming and coming. Nobody knows why they are here and nobody can stop them.

Tom Cruise plays Ray. He is a dock worker who is sort of a deadbeat dad. His intentions are pretty good but he can't seem to get it right. When he is left in charge of his two kids, a rebellious teen, and an innocent 10 year old girl, he must take on the responsibility he has been pushing off for so long. Cruise does a nice job as the dad trying to protect his two kids (Justin Chatwick & Dakota Fanning). The kids do everything they can to give Cruise a hard time including running off and starting arguments.

What War of the Worlds accomplishes what it sets out to do and that is to entertain. The film is loaded with great special effects and terrific sound effects. The audience knows when the machines are coming. Spielberg uses loud shrieking noises and loud thunderous weans that indicate that you better run. Spielberg also has a knack when it comes to showing children in danger. Dakota Fanning is constantly in danger. Like films such as the Jurassic Park movies, Spielberg likes to use kids to get to the audience.

The movie isn't without its problems. The sequence with Tim Robbins seems to go on too long and some of the movie doesn't make a whole lot of sense, esp. where the aliens intentions come to play. There were some continuity issues as well.

If you can get past some of the films flaws, you'll enjoy this movie. It really is a great summer popcorn film with a lot of great things to take in. (***)

title: Not bad, but read the book, it's 100 times better
review:
I just saw this movie this past Thursday night. Upon the rolling of the ending credits, my friends and I were not sure how we felt about this movie. The movie is relatively faithful to the novel in many ways, which is a good thing for fans of Wells' science fiction such as myself. My biggest problem with the movie lies with how the aliens die.

As in the novel, the aliens catch earth viruses and die. Now my problem lies here: In 1898, when Wells wrote the novel, science was just touching the surface of the nature of viruses and bacteria. So Wells having the aliens die from infection was a brilliant stroke of realism. However, in the present day, we have infinitely greater knowledge of viruses and bacteria than in 1898. We know the dangers of being exposed to unknown viruses and bacteria. So thus the Aliens in the movie should have also known the dangers. Hell, they should have sent a probe (just like the probe we sent to Mars) to test the planet for dangerous microbes.

However, I did enjoy seeing the tripods of Wells' novel brought to life. But you should probably read the book before seeing this movie or the 1953 version.

title: More "WOW" than "wow"
review:
The combination of director Steven Spielberg and actor Tom Cruise - last paired in "Minority Report" - promises much and the vehicle of the 1898 H G Wells novel "The War Of The Worlds" seems like an exciting basis for their undoubted talents. The basic elements of the original story are retained, notably an alien tripod invasion of Earth with a Morgan Freeman opening narration quoting the first words of the novel and the ultimate defeat of the invaders through the same mechanism as offered by Wells. The transposition from late 19th century England to early 21st century United States is understandable commercially, but the abandonment of any mention of Mars and the absurd notion of aliens descending down lightning bolts to inhabit huge vehicles buried long, long ago weaken the credibility of the plot. A sequence involving Tim Robbins as a crazy survivalist (especially a cringe-inducing effort to sing a children's song) is also misplaced and unpleasant.

However, Cruise as always is very watchable and here dispenses with any special bravery or skills to portray a confused father desperately trying to save his two children, constantly scared, confused and on the run. Eleven year old Dakota Fanning is so good as his daughter that she is in danger of becoming the star of the movie. Where "WOW" scores big time - and I mean BIG time - is in the 400+ special effects generated by Industrial Light and Magic The opening sequence when the first tripod erupts from the city streets is brilliant and other scenes - notably the crashing of a Boeing 747 - are the exciting visions and sounds that beg to be witnessed on a large screen. This is Spielberg much more in "Jaws" and "Jurassic Park" mode than "ET" and "Close Encounters", but in the end it is more a case of "WOW" than "wow".

title: Cinema as an art-form
review: I just saw War of the Worlds after reading and hearing countless accounts of people who either loved it or hated it. Well, for those who hated the film because it didn't have a good plot or an idea to drive it forward, you missed the boat. Literally. Spielberg makes a lot of important points throughout the entire film. His main characters, Ray and Rachel are very well defined and his key scenes are priceless. Lets take, for instance, the scene in the basement. We see a little self-referencing when the alien machine goes down there - easily reminiscent of Jurassic Park's kitchen scene. We see very real character development - Ray committing murder to save his child. And, above all, there end of the film is foreshadowed - yes, through aliens drinking water and going through "earthly things". What many skeptics don't seem to realize, that these three aliens were not the only ones going into houses and drinking water and eating food - that's what happened to the entire army. The speech on occupation is not incidental either - Spielberg is quietly making a point on Iraq - NOT the war on terror. People, always viewed from Ray's perspective either get "heroic", "frightened" or "crazy" as they would in real life - each instance well defined by the filmmaker. But even if you refuse to acknowledge all those subtle touches that give the film a third dimension, the cinematography is breathtaking. A film, unlike a book, needs more than just a plot. In fact a "simple" or a "weak" plot can be saved by the film-making process itself. As Hitchcock said before, each shot is there to evoke emotion, Spielberg does a fantastic job of that, continually refining his craft. Film as an art-form (and especially of this genre) is a spectacle to be seen and Spielberg provided us with a spectacle in the best sense of the word.

title: Was there some dark but topical subplot in this movie?
review:
Recall what Ogilvie (Tim Robbins character) says at one point about how the Japanese in Osaka managed to take down a couple of tripods. We never learn how. Later, he asks "what is their weak point?" The question is never, directly, answered...

There is actually one fearsome technique that could have been used to attack the tripods as depicted in the movie: Their one weak point was that they had a habit of capturing humans alive and taking them onboard - inside their force-shields. In fact, Ferrier (Tom Cruise's character) almost does it, although the movie shies away from the conclusion and allows him to escape...

It's something the Japanese were very famous for - the kamikaze.

title: Better than expected
review:
This is another example of a film which I watched where my preliminary expectations were quite low. I was pleasantly surprised. While I'm not an expert or the original novel, it does seem to stick to the basic plot. I think the director modernized it a bit, enough to be engaging, realistic and true to the original plot. Of course some changes in characters, and their relationships were made, but it all seems to fit well.

The suspense is built up well, and the story develops nicely, without a lot of rapid-fire explanations. The depictions of the way society breaks down in the face of the invasion was really very powerful. I was impressed with the way the monsters were presented, the special effects were very good, and the aliens had enough face-time to be pretty scary.

I'd been bummed out by most of the dribble to come out of Hollywood lately in the sci-fi vein, but this was a change of pace. I'm glad I saw this one on the big screen.

title: Amazed at the lack of thought...
review:
I felt the movie was a very good, if not imperfect, adaptation of the H.G. Wells novel. It strayed in some ways, but one could argue the use of creative license and making the story more relatable to a 21st century audience.

Two points of concern, however. Notwithstanding the fact the I have, indeed, read the book, I thought it was still obvious, although subtly presented, that the aliens die as a result of their exposure to the natural bacteria and atmospheric differences that we are acclimatized to. I was dumbfounded by the number of audience members who left saying that "there seemed to be no end", or that they didn't understand the conclusion. We have been conditioned to the Hollywood "formula" that explains all at the end. It's amazing to think that some didn't have the capacity to think for themselves.

The other thought is the atmosphere in which this movie has been released. Wells wrote and published the book at a time where it was seen as an allegory for the decline of the British Empire. It reflected the "fear of the future" that was felt with the diminished power and prestige that the shrinking Empire brought about. Could the movie's release as a Hollywood blockbuster be a metaphor for something a little closer to home?

title: Enjoyable up to a point, but not a masterpiece
review:
Because it has been so many years since I experienced any of the older versions of this story, I did not feel overly compelled to compare. Therefore, I looked at this film on its own merits.

From that viewpoint, this film did an adequate job of entertaining, though something clearly was missing, but I struggle to exactly put a finger on exactly what that is.

The acting was reasonably good, though a little shaky at times. The story moves along apace, and few scenes feel drawn out or unnecessary. Visually the film is very engaging. For reasons that are apparent once you have experienced the two, I found the visuals to be greatly reminiscent of the video game 'Half-Life 2'.

I think if anything, the disappointment comes in the lack of a build up to the climax. I don't begrudge that the writers chose adhere to the basic structure of the established story (I guess that's what makes it a remake), but I did feel that it was not executed in a way that provided a release of built up tension that should have been the big payoff for sitting in a cinema seat for two hours.

As well as the obvious sci-fi theme, this film also has strong elements of the horror genre. If, like me, you have a soft spot for both these kinds of stories, then you'll probably enjoy this film. But if you can take or leave films from either of these genres, then this film is marginal enough that I don't recommend it to you.

title: Terrific special effects - usual Tom Cruise acting
review:
In many ways I found this movie to be very similar in the way it treated the subject to the older 1950s version. Neither has much in common with the book beyond the title and the basic premise of alien attack. At least the alien machines are more similar to the book and it also included the fast-spreading red plant.

What irritated me with both this film and the old one was the seeming need to make the alien machines invincible. In the book with concentrated artillery attack the 19th Century humans do manage to destroy one or more alien machines. I think it spoils the story and seems unbelievable to set the action in modern times and with all our modern technology to not be able to bring down even one machine except when Ray gets captured.

It also seems unbelievable that the machines could have been buried underneath the cities on Earth for hundreds of years without us noticing. I would also like to have seen some scenes addressing the political, scientific and military response to such an attack as well as the response in other countries. There is a brief mention that the Japanese managed to destroy an alien machine but there are no details given. It might have heightened the suspense to see such scenes as were included in Independence Day not to mention the 1950s version.

However, I rate this movie as well done because the special effects are pretty good. The CGI graphics don't pixellate too much, except when the camera is panning. Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise) is pretty unsympathetic and Tom does his usual workmanlike job, neither good nor bad. His daughter is cute and well played by Dakota Fanning (who invents these names?) but his son, Robbie, is a brat. The action doesn't drag and it isn't too long. It might have been nice to explain how Ray and Rachel get from the river crossing to Boston on foot? How far is that?!

title: Surprisingly Excellent
review:
I admit I had low expectations going into this: I am not an especial fan of Mr. Spielberg, find Tom Cruise to be a gifted but limited actor, and don't understand the fuss over Dakota Fanning. I'm not a huge fan of alien invasion stories and figured this would be very thin gruel all around.

In fact, it's genuinely excellent, easily the best of the Summer movies I've seen in 2005. Unusually hard-edged and rough, with clear references to 9/11 -- I found the usually pro-forma shots of cities being destroyed unusually powerful. Cruise is a very fallible "hero", we never get much more than a small piece of the whole story (which I found exceptionally believable). For the most part the kids behave believably. Certain moments of mass hysteria (especially the van sequence) are as hard as anything I've seen from Spielberg. A couple of small but niggling weaknesses, but all in all a remarkable achievement.

title: Sick political undertone of ending??? (+Poss Spoiler Alert)
review: I have read in a lot of reviews that WoW is somehow Spielberg's commentary on the 9/11 attacks. This is a very obvious reading - "oh my god! horrible attacks out of the blue from a foe we don't understand that brings devastation to our city!" But if indeed this is the main theme of the film, it has no clear resolution. This is partly due to the fact that the hero Tom Cruise has no relationship with the aliens other than to flee a lot, nor does he do a single thing to bring about their downfall - there's no dramatic relationship whatsoever. (Why everyone from New York is fleeing towards Beantown, by the way, I have no idea - do the aliens enjoy Cheers, why would they leave Boston in any better shape than New York?) Anyway, my main point is about the ending (which, as stated, Tom Cruise did nothing to hasten). We are told in a tacked-on, voiced over appendage, that man has earned his right to live on earth through long millenia of dying and evolving to live with our micro-organisms (why the Martians did not take their shots before coming to Earth I cannot fathom). "No man dies in vain", we are told, or words to that effect. Well Mr Spielberg what about the thousands of people in third world who die from *preventable* diseases??? Or are we meant to salute them as "taking one for the team" and acting as a mass petri dish to fend off future Martian attacks? This is a muddled film - bring back that crazy British musical version say I!

title: Pretty terrifying!
review:
Wow, well I was surprised at this film. I did not expect it to be as chilling as it was.

Some people don't seem to have the same reaction, but I'm gratified to find one or two people who were as affected as I was. I thought the film was brilliantly put together, the "harvesting" of humans being one of the more hair-raising things. I think it depends on one's personality; I am the sort with rather a vivid imagination and if you're a bit apathetic, it's not going to affect you. Indeed, there were some moronic teenage girls giggling behind us the whole time; but if you let the atmosphere of the film take you in it's pretty amazing.

Possibly the scariest part of the film was nothing to do with the aliens; the scene where the main family are the only people with a car, and suddenly mass hysteria grips the mob around them as they try to be allowed in with them, they are dragged out of the car bodily, a man tries to rip apart glass with his hands, people are shot just for the possession of it, etc etc. I was quite amazed at how powerful this scene was.

The ending was a tad strange, and a tad sudden. But I will finish by saying this - this is the ONLY film I have EVER seen where I genuinely thought every single main character was going to die. I have never thought that before. I've always thought "eh, they'll survive somehow, they don't kill main characters." But I just thought they were totally screwed here!

title: Good book, fair movie, lousy science.
review:
*CONTAINS SPOILERS*

This film, somewhat based on the H.G.Wells classic book, fails it's namesake because of poor writing, bad science, horrible continuity and unbelievable characters. First let me say that I was surprised that Steven Spielburg would copy someone else's work, namely the movie 'Them' (not the one with the giant ants. In that movie the aliens traveled by use of lightning. Samething with this film. And the idea of the alien machines already being here is ludicrous. Someone would have discovered them because of excavation, exploration, or just the changing of the planet due to earthquakes and erosion. Spielberg should have used H.G. Wells premise from the start. Other flaws in continuity is that when all electrical devices stop because of some so-called electromagnetic pulse, why did it not affect video cameras? And the idea that cars won't start because of the solenoid burning out wouldn't stop cars already running. To stop them the electronics in the vehicle would need to be fried and if that was the case, how could Tom Cruises character start the minivan? And since diesel power vehicles don't need a spark, why aren't they all running? Next time Steven that you decide to make a movie based on the book, please follow the book.

title: Sorry Steve, Just Can't Let You Get Away With that Ending ...
review:
This film seems to have everything going for it ... brilliant action sequences, unnervingly horrific scenes, a dab of political commentary and just a smidgen of character development ... make no mistake this is a Spielberg action/sci-fi effort not to be confused with 'serious-Steve' who made Schlinder's List and Saving Private Ryan ... then we come to the end of the film.

WHAT HAPPENED THERE!?! Fair enough this is Hollywood. Maybe everything has to be tied up nicely (perhaps to his credit Spielberg didn't go too over board and totally reunite his on-screen family of the times). Perhaps I would have felt let down with a totally downbeat ending that would have seemingly tied in with the grim tell of survival that had proceeded. The ending though just comes off as rushed, ill-conceived and a total let down. The original Wells' ending could have been handle much more positively ... the final 'battle' scene and subsequence Freeman (king of the v.o.) voice-over just leaves you wondering what really might have been.

What proceeds that though is great entertainment. Popcorn flies through the air, loved-ones cling to each other as Spielberg delivers a series of high-impact shocks and hands are held over eyes waiting for the next jolt ... OK well maybe not quite but this borders on horror at times ... honestly it does! The scene where Cruise ventures out into the newly harvested world of strange vein-like creations is awesome (in the non-surfer and totally intellectual way!) and brilliantly created.

All notions of horror aside this is an action flick dealing with the grim notion of survival at all costs. The first appearance of the 'tripods' is particularly impressive; buildings fall, the earth heaves and people ... well they basically fry! As the story progresses we see Cruise's (he may be a jerk, but he sure does Hollywood blockbuster well) dock worker, Ray, tries to build bridges with his estranged children (awwwee). Eventually we see Fanning's (a talent I'm sure well be hearing about for years and years to come) character become drawn to him, but Justin Chatwin's (just a tad annoying) Robbie relationship with his father is slightly confusing ... just when he seems to have made a connection he runs off to join the army! I guess these are minor details; the real drawing points of this film are Spileberg's use of SFX, the set-ups created for these action scenes and Ray's tale of his grim efforts to save himself and his children. These all hold up well to scrutiny ... but the ending, OH, the ending ...

title: Like a relationship that ends in a break up
review:
I thought long and hard about whether to include the spoiling details, but since all the bones I'd like to pick with this movie relate to its ending, it seems pointless writing this comment without it.

There are plenty to like about this movie. Steven Spielberg revealed in a recent interview that this is the first movie he's made that doesn't involve some sort of interaction between aliens and humans. His past classics have all featured kind and peaceful aliens. Then what compelled him to do this one, with aliens hunting humans without any apparent reason, I have absolutely no idea; I didn't finish reading that interview.

What is clear, however, is that it's a refreshing change from his usual formula. WotW has tapped into the best of current CG technologies, so much so that ironically, CG scenes look even more real than the actual full scale models which look rather amateurish by comparison. There are plenty of spectacular and exhilarating scenes for both young and old. If every aspect of a film is this good, then the reasons behind the alien race's invasion doesn't have to be fleshed out in order for the film to be enjoyed. On top of that, the entire cast delivers a flawless on-screen performance: Tom Cruise as a protective father to an absolutely terrified daughter (Dakota Fanning) who's more terrifying to look at, and a rebellious son (Justic Chatwin) who's wrapped in heroism. Tim Robbins also displays his usual high calibre performance as a slightly warped guerrilla sworn to fight these uninvited guests. The characters don't spit out smart-ass one-liners, and do manage to develop during the course of the movie. Developing casts has always been Steven Spielberg's forte.

Then what's wrong with this movie? Everything else you don't see on screen. Why are they harvesting people? Is it like Matrix? For food, or as fuel to run those machines? What are those vein-like structures everywhere; perhaps an assimilation of everything alive? Why are they then on rocks as well? It would have made more sense, and more gruesome, to show just a blood-soaked earth.

There is also an uncanny resemblance to those critters in Independence Day - shame on you, Steven! Also, why do they have a cute face? They're annihilating humans and they've got baby-face... Having skinny long legs alone doesn't make a creepy creature - just look at those catwalk models. What disappointment I had when I finally saw their face after all that anticipation!

They are also incredibly stupid. The scale of their invasion is so puny. Within three days, we find how to defeat the walkers. How much damage have the walkers caused by then? Not much because they're WALKING! If they happen to be related to the long-legs of Independence day, then the ID cousins did a hell of a better job. Huge saucers on top of major cities, fast jets, magnificent destructive power - they gathered intelligence on local environment and invested tirelessly on preparation.

Which brings us to the biggest bone of all - the ending. They had apparently planted these walkers millions of years ago, which means they must have known at least a little about this planet. Surely enough, they know our atmospheric content because they casually walk around breathing our air. Furthermore, their assimilation of humans and live-stocks means they are aware of their constituencies as well, and have devised a use for themselves accordingly. Yet, they didn't know about the trillions and trillions of microscopic organisms, bacteria and viruses that are present, say, everywhere, and died from them? Have they missed them during sample analysis because they're so small? Do they not carry microscopes on board their ships? Perhaps that's why they invaded earth - to gain knowledge on how to manufacture microscopes. If, by chance, they fired their walkers from outer space with a view to come later, then it's just plain bad preparation, and they all deserve to die. But if they were that stupid, there wouldn't be a movie. Yet, here I am, discussing it.

These are all reasons as to why I have described this film as a relationship that ends in a break up. Everything is wonderful in the beginning and there are lots to love about this relationship, but the terrible last few minutes before the break-up shadows everything good of the past, leaving you with the sour taste of memories of what could have been better. And not even the most logical reason behind their invasion could save this movie.

title: Powerful film from Spielberg
review:
War of the Worlds is far from perfect on aesthetic grounds, but scrapping the whole thing because of a few minor plot problems is laughable in itself. Of course the audience is asked to accept a few improbable happenings, but let me remind you, this is a film about aliens invading our planet. This is hardly a realist drama. Quite frankly, rather than being critical of clichés in the character development, I feel more inclined to be annoyed that so much emotional weight was given to developing the characters period. But without some sort of development we would feel disconnected from the individuals involved, and the conventional angst and resolution of the family drama act effectively as a counterpoint to the less everyday component, understated perhaps but unquestionably central, that is, again, based on the premise that aliens are invading the earth. In other words, it's a trick, enhancing the emotional intensity of the film at the expense of aesthetic merit. The ending so many people were critical of was meant to be perfect on critical grounds, but to give the audience a certain feeling upon its departure from the theater. One may criticize Spielberg for undervaluing the audience's desire for aesthetics, but such criticism would be irrelevant - the overwhelming numerical success of his films stands for itself in proof. Spielberg offers his audience not film as an art product, but as a sensationalist/emotionalist escape - he creates film as a craftsman does, not an artist. I am certain that Spielberg knows his stuff, and his decision to overlook certain aesthetic aspects his films is a conscious one.

If you go to see War of the Worlds and view the film with any sort of critical eye whatsoever, you will undoubtedly realize that it is a deeply flawed film in several respects. That should not, however, interfere with the film's power to move, its sheer emotional intensity, an intensity which, I believe, would be less effective if it were not free from the constraints of art. The images produced here are among the most powerful and disturbing yet to emerge from the CG age - in fact, until a certain point near the end involving Tom Cruise and a strange blood-draining mouth in a metal cage (hopefully I do not give anything away here), I wondered if perhaps this does not qualify more as a horror film than a sci-fi. I cannot honestly remember the time myself and the audience around me was more engaged by the movie screen - not uncritically mind you, or unconsciously, but engaged nonetheless. Neither can I remember the last time I observed the effects of such a catharsis, as the audience emerged from the theater giggling at its own spent emotional investment.

For what it claims to be, War of the Worlds is a highly effective film. That's not to say it is a great work of art, or that its effectiveness will not soon expire. Nonetheless, tonight Steven Spielberg took me for one heck of a ride.

title: Exterminating consequences?
review:
Since SAVING PRIVATE RYAN, most Steven Spielberg fans have been looking for something more, something worthy to talk about for days, not just hours. That's not to say the films he has produced the past few years have been garbage, they're just not up the caliber most of us look for in a Spielberg film. In films like A.I.: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE and THE TERMINAL, there's nothing that jumps out and grabs me like SAVING PRIVATE RYAN did. And, then you have the "popcorn" flicks like MINORITY REPORT and CATCH ME IF YOU CAN; both of which were fun to watch, but not as fun as previous gems like INDIANA JONES AND THE LAST CRUSADE.

So, no matter what type of Spielberg film you look at, he's been a little off lately. Maybe I'm being a little hard on him, but we are talking about arguably the best director of his time and one of the best directors Hollywood will ever see. In saying that, you can see how excited all of us fans were when the idea of WAR OF THE WORLDS was released, especially considering Spielberg's resume with aliens. And even with all the hype around Tom Cruise's personal life, it still comes down to the movie, and that was where all my expectations sat. Like most people I was looking at WAR OF THE WORLDS being this big spectacle of a film and although it came very close to that, it wasn't what I had hoped it would be in the end.

When Tom Cruise is in a movie, does anyone else really matter? After seeing most Tom Cruise films, you don't remember who played opposite Cruise; you just remember what Cruise did and how he did it. That's the world Cruise lives with, in and out of movies, but when you're good, you're good. And Cruise once again was good, but that's almost a given in any of his movies if you ask me. The question is, was anyone else worthy of praise, and in this one, I would have to say not really. This film wasn't really about Cruise or anyone else, as it was about the ideal of an invasion of earth. That even goes for little Dakota Fanning, who even with all her talent, had a role that could have been played by any 10-year old girl. And then there was Tim Robbins and his role, which again was played well, but most actors not as talented as Robbins can pull off the role of being a refugee on the verge of madness. But, I realize if you bring a guy like Robbins in for this small bit part, he will do it well and be memorable, so I can understand Spielberg's thinking, but his role doesn't make or break the story.

Recently we have been privileged to see some insane special effects from Steven Spielberg's films, and WAR OF THE WORLDS is no different. With tremendous sets to back up some of the CGI special effects, nothing bad can be said about the action and overall intensity oozing from this film. The opening 20 to 30 minutes is about as tense as it comes, where you are literary on the edge of your seat watching these machines terrorize our world. And, that feeling lasted for quite awhile too, right down to when you got your first glimpse of the aliens. But, like many of its predecessors, this film started to fail shortly after the appearance of the aliens on the screen.

I don't know what it is about seeing the aliens that ruins films like WAR OF THE WORLDS, but it does every time and according to Wells' story, there wasn't a true need to do that until the very end. But, I guess with his fascination of aliens, Spielberg just could not resist the temptation. As tense as this film was, to not show the alien until the last shot would have improved this film dramatically, especially since that was where this film took a fall and never recovered.

So, as highly anticipated as WAR OF THE WORLDS was, I would have hoped for something a little more. And at this point, I can't really put my fingers on exactly what that would be, but this film had the potential of being "one of kind" for a very long time. However, just because WAR OF THE WORLDS, in my mind, could have been a tad bit better overall, it doesn't change the fact it was an event to see and something I would never deter fans from seeing.

title: A big, expensive disappointment. What has happened to Steven!
review: I am not a particular fan of sci-fi or loud action films. Because of Spielberg and Cruise, though, I was anticipating this one--maybe they would get it right this time(after the equally disappointing Minority Report). That outing was pure genius compared to this melange of clichés--adolescent ex-husband, still sympathetic ex-wife,devoted and resented new husband-father,angry and insolent children,an automobile that never runs out of gas, crazed "old" codger(here the not so old Tim Robbins) ad nauseum. Does the world really need another one of these overblown, overlong disposable entertainments? Did the mind of the same man that surprised and delighted us with Close Enounters and ET(Not to mention Duel,Jaws, Sugarland Express)conjure this weary accumulation of special effects? Where is the imagination and adventure of the earlier film-maker? War of the Worlds is not only trite and tired,it is very boring. title: A triumph of Spielberg schmaltz over substance
review:
Spielberg and Cruise are for some reason regarded as some awesome pairing of epic proportions. In terms of box-office receipts, this is empirically true but this film demonstrates that both actor and director are greatly over-rated.

This attempt to update the Welles classic is something that, on paper should work. The characters, plot and overblown special effects are all there to make this a watchable popcorn flick. However, it's as if the framework of a film has been constructed but someone has neglected to infuse it with any life.

Despite the fact the film spends most of its time looking at the main characters, there is no real sense of character development. They're either running or hiding. There is no real catharsis for any of them and no real tension.

The special effects are what one might expect of a summer blockbuster but they aren't really all that impressive as they lack any real purpose except to be there, much like the rest of the film. It's a popcorn flick that falls flat on all fronts.

It's not bad per se but simply lacks a certain energy, a joi d'vivre as it were that condemns the film to be nothing memorable and a rather hollow viewing experience. Suffice to say, that your time and money could be spent better elsewhere.

title: Brilliant!
review:
What a brilliant film. Easily one of the best 'aliens coming to earth' thrillers I have watched! Very rarely do you watch a film so tense the whole way through. This really had me on the edge of my seat for the entire film.

I loved how the film got started straight away. A short narration brought you up to speed and it was straight into the action. Great - there's nothing more annoying than a huge long history of how a story gets to the point where it actually begins (great example of this - Spiderman).

I thought Tom Cruise was great in the part. A hero but by no conventional means. I loved the fact, single handed, he saved his children but I also loved the fact he didn't try to save the entire world single handed. Like any normal person his priority was his own and of those closest to him. How refreshing. It pulled the film toward the 'what would you do?' perspective. And the answer to this for most people would be to take care of your family. The emotion from Cruise was immense and I loved the scene when he held his hands to his face and the look in his eyes was of sheer terror.

The only part of the film I didn't particularly like was the ending. Not so much because it was a happy one - I do love a happy ending - but more because of the way it was shot. The mother, grandparents and even Tim appeared at their door in Boston, not a scratch on them, clothes beautifully clean as if they had been quite safe in their little house. Meanwhile, devastation is all around them, Ray has gone through hell to get there, thousands are dead, but the mother's hair is intact and looking lovely! Bit of a shame they hadn't looked at least a little stressed and dirty! Also I'm sure as a mother she could have shown a little more gratitude to Ray for saving her daughter. 'Thank you' was a bit lame.

Overall though I loved this. The time spent in the cinema flew in, I think I was actually holding my breath for most of the movie as it was so exciting and one of the first films in a long time that I would immediately watch again.

title: Steven Spielberg can do better
review:
I was so looking forward to seeing this movie. A Steven Spielberg movie, means a lot of meaningful entertainment...not the rubbish we usually get which are excuses in the name of entertainment, or so i thought. For, though not the 'rubbish' i mentioned earlier, the movie is nowhere near Spielberg's standards. The movie starts with an introduction of how humans have stayed totally ignorant to the fact that they are being watched by extra-terrestrials always. Then, it moves from an intriguing introduction to the highly uninteresting character of Tom Cruise. He is a father who has to tend for his two kids, who have no particular liking for him. His ex-wife(who is pregnant with the kid of her next husband)is off to Boston to be with her parents and leaves the children(the elder one looks like cruise's younger brother)with Cruise. Then suddenly all hell breaks loose and a weird storm takes over the place. Tom Cruise who goes to the heart of the city to investigate is in for a surprise. Sinister machines emerge from the ground and start zapping people all over. I must admit. These bits are extremely well done and Spielberg's genius, absent in the rest of the film, shows here. And then, Cruise, one of the lucky survivors, reaches home and takes his kids to their mother, the reason for which, i'm yet to decipher. He takes the only car that works(since everything stops working due to electromagnetic impulses). I think Cruise's car worked because it was a solar charged battery or something. I missed that bit.The rest of the movie has no story that can be put in words. It's just action and the action does work in most of the places. It is good, but not great...not something that made my jaws drop or anything. Just good enough to keep you engaged.

Well, that's the story. Now, the positive points of the movie. Good action sequences...especially an initial storm sequence and the fist attack by the alien machines. Stunning visual effects. The aliens were done creatively. That's it. The negative points now. An extremely unintelligent screenplay which is determined to push the patience of the audience beyond endurance. Tom Cruise is one of the most ungifted actors i've seen. Dakota Fanning is totally wasted. She seems to have had a bet with her friend about how many ear drums she can destroy in the cinema hall, for that's all that she does. She screams throughout the film. The main problems of the movie is that the story of this father trying to save his kids is extremely poorly done. It could have been shown in a much better way, but Spielberg fails at this dismally. Last but not least, THE CLIMAX! I'm sorry to be saying this, but this movie has one of the worst climaxes ever. The movie drags in the last half an hour and then the climax happens even before you realise it's come. title: "War of the worlds" takes intensity to the next level
review: War of the worlds is an amazing film, not revolutionary per se, but amazing. Once the mood is set, it never stops, the atmosphere and level of intensity is amazing. Even at the rare parts where they start lulling you into a sense of safety, it throws something at you that reminds you of what is really happening. As an example, when they're all going to a ferry that's supposed to be taking them all to safety, a train signal starts up, and every one stops, and a flaming train (If you look closely you can even see a human hand hanging from one of the windows) goes by. This isn't the greatest movie ever, and I know many people aren't going to like it, but when it comes to intensity this is the perfect movie for you. This adaptation isn't too amazingly close to the H. G. Welles 1898 novel, but they get the idea down pat and even people who are looking for a near perfect adaptation may not be seriously let down. This film is just a great time to spend at the theaters period, but don't go looking for the best film ever.

This movie is scary! I think the 50's version probably scared that times audience, but it is laughable today. I was probably more scared because I wasn't expecting it to be. But trust me, it is! It is made so scary because of the great suspense. And also the aliens actually look scary (no little green men!). Plus the machines the aliens control are actually very scary because the seem so life like.

Overall I thought it was a brilliant movie. I was pleasantly surprised. Make sure you see it!

title: A Zombie movie but with war machines... aka. "It's still better than Jurassic Park2, which isn't saying much"
review:
War of the Worlds, the Spielberg version, I must add, wasn't one of the movies I was most eagerly waiting to watch this summer (trailer reminded me of some Michael Bay movie). To add, I've already seen the classic 50's version, which I really liked, and didn't think it needed a remake (I sort of have similar thoughts about the upcoming King Kong, but then again, that movie would really test Peter Jackson's skills as a director--it's like redoing Star Wars). Can remakes be good? Yes, if it's more like an adaptation of the original source material (if it's a book) than a remake of a movie version of that material.

As mentioned, I did finally decide to watch this film on Sunday evening, after hearing a plethora of poor reviews from friends and critics, knowing that I can now watch it without all the hype and expectations. To add, my friends just wanted to see it (which is usually a good enough reason for me)... AND it was matinée, after all.

The movie starts off with the alien invasion (perhaps Martians) on Earth, and with many parallels to the 9/11 terrorist attacks, the citizens are attacked unexpectedly, seemingly without reason, by gigantic alien war machines referred to as "tripods" (they resemble walking tripods with lasers that destroy everything in its path). As destructions ensue, much of the movie is spent around the Tom Cruise's deadbeat dad character and his kids, facing many near misses, and running away most of the time. There are some interesting character developments, however, as Tom Cruise's character do take more of a parental role as the movie progresses. Cruise, despite the fact that he looks a bit too movie-star-ish to play the average joe, does a pretty good job, and the young actors (who play his kids) do their part, as needed, in a movie like this.

Meanwhile, as the public is in chaos, normal people start to turn against each other, sometimes killing each other, just so they can survive the massive annihilation. Certainly, the movie does touch upon the darker aspects of human nature (which I found interesting), but just briefly. Majority of the focus, however, is spent on Cruise's plights and the visuals. In terms of look, in the 50's version, we had flying saucers (which indeed looked very alien, cold, sleek, and fairly well-designed, I might add). In comparison, it would've been cooler if the tripods in this movie looked more alien as well--as it is, they look rather retro, metallic, somewhat antiquated (something akin to a steam-engine). The way the machines operate just don't seem as cold and efficient.

Overall, I liked the movie for what it was (a chase movie--think "Zombie movie," but replaced with gigantic alien machines--though Zombies might've been less costly, and more entertaining). However, there's a bit of disappointment for what could've been. There is certainly a lot of budget to work with here, but they hardly seem to service the story, or enough thrills, for that matter. What's kind of missing is the sense of wonder Spielberg alien films like Close Encounters and E.T. had. There was a sense of mystery and had that other-worldly atmosphere. It's creepy because you're not exactly sure what to think. This movie rather relentlessly throws it all at you. Although I knew how it was to end, the movie's ending felt rather abrupt (without a certain feel of progression) and doesn't really wrap it up as well as it did in the 50's version.

Yes, it's kind of unfair to compare this movie to the classic, but that's what one must expect whenever you have a remake. As mentioned, I enjoyed it for what it was, a series of destructions and CG-laden action sequences and the character development is fairly good for the first half of the movie. There are parts that seem longer than it should be (particularly the scenes where Cruise and his kids are hiding in someone else's basement) and parts that don't really amount to much other than serving up for more action. As a Spielberg film, it's not as tight, nor as stylistic, nor satisfying as his previous works. It's still better than Jurassic Park 2, though.

(I have heard some rumors that Spielberg didn't get enough time from the studios to really work on it, which might explain why the film felt a bit like it was rushed)

title: Another triumph for Spielberg.
review:
While we have seen countless variations on the alien invasion movie, Steven Spielberg's does here what he previously accomplished in "Saving Private Ryan": putting us on the inside in a way we've never been before. Consequently, there is a palpable sense of realism and fear in "War of the Worlds" that was missing from "Independence Day" and "Signs".

Spielberg, making his most overt popcorn film in nearly a decade (one which nevertheless features some sophisticated subtexts), utilizing all of his tension building skills much in the same way he did in "Jurassic Park". While this is not likely to go down as one of his greatest films, it is a top-notch thriller with strong performances from Tom Crusie and Dakota Fanning, and a welcome addition to the filmography of Hollywood's greatest director.

review:
I gave this film a 2 out of 10 because it is slightly better than the film "Signs" starring Mel Gibson.

If you are thinking about going to see this movie... DON'T. It is a waste of 3 hours (note that the 3 hours includes travelling time and waiting time). I found several discrepancies in the film, which should have been thought about, one main one is the video camera people have mentioned, where after everything else electrical doesn't work, after the EMP, magically the video camera does work.

I have several other problems with this film, many of which have disgusted me. One such example is the problem I have with the son. We see him charge over a hill while tanks and infantry are desperately firing at whatever is on the otherside, then.. CRASH! A huge alien tripod thing comes over the brow of the hill into view on flames crushing everything. Then at the end, you see the son has made it to his mother. Pardon my language but what the f*ck!? I mean, where was the plot at this point? In fact, the plot was absent throughout the whole film. Another thing that made me want to get up and leave was the horrible shrill scream of the little girl. There was absolutely no need at all for her to shriek so much. She shrieks while they're in the car, and refuses to shutup for a brief moment. However when she is faced with mortal danger after being picked up and caged by a tripod she doesn't make a f*cking sound.

Also, this movie was almost as bad as Signs, War of the Worlds had the same lack of plot as Signs, and made about as much sense. There are only three things I can say about this film which makes it better than signs:

1) The way they die in the end is to do with micro-organisms and bacteria, which is slightly more plausible than water, however is just as ridiculous.

2) The special effects, this area was successful with some very good stuff despite the non-sensical ideas that inspired them.

3) The Weaponry, at least this film had a few rocketlaunchers.. but not many. Which is a real disappointment. you would think since the aliens were killing everyone anyway some nukes would be involved, or better stuff.. the most advanced thing we saw of the "huge" American military was the squadron of harrier jumpjets that attacked one of the tripods. If an old balding mechanic can fix a car in a couple of minutes, then the U.S. army can fix a few planes in 2 days.

In conclusion, this film was horrific. It was the sequel to Hiroshima. Also, another small point to make, if you are considering watching this film, then note that the beginning sets you up well... it sets you up for a further 2 hours of filler, so you can get ready for the nerve wracking 2-minute ending where they all just die. Enjoy.

title: The quintessential post-9/11 blockbuster.
review:
50 years hence, film-studies essays will cite Spielberg's *War of the Worlds* as the movie best reflecting the prevailing mood of post-9/11 America; Spielberg ensures this with his "authoritative" visual symbols and direct references to the real-life disaster ("Is it the terrorists?" Tom Cruise's teenage son asks early in the proceedings). But we've come to expect this from Sir Steven, who apparently feels that any Major Event or any Major Issue has not been fully documented until he makes some self-important summarization of said Event or Issue. Earlier in his career, he was more prone to telling original stories that were INFLUENCED by the stuff he loved as a kid, such as sci-fi monster movies and adventure serials. But these days, his ego has clearly grown to such proportions that even his beloved original inspirations, such as, well, the 1953 movie version of *The War of the Worlds*, don't seem good enough for him. He must make the AUTHORITATIVE version. The Spielberg Imprimatur of Approval.

The 9/11 references get cloying very quickly: the hero covered in ash while dodging the marauding tripod that has been incinerating panicked people with a laser beam; the silent cascade of discarded clothes falling from the sky; Tim Robbins, in a role he must have relished, mouthing Bushian tough-talk about taking the fight to the aliens. But damn, Spielberg sure makes it all LOOK magnificent, doesn't he? This is his best picture since *Saving Private Ryan*. The gigantic tripods, first of all, are an absolute triumph, almost entirely free of the fake sheen and unnatural movements of CGI creations. Lovingly sticking to Wells' original vision, Spielberg insists on maintaining their rather low-tech, 1898-imagined grandeur. Their fog-horn blasts (usually preceding some act of devastation or other) are memorably chilling. Several set-pieces are very well done, particularly the lightning strikes early on that announce the aliens' arrival, followed by the first tripod erupting from a busy street. And Spielberg has always had an uncanny knack for the offhand scene that generates acute psychological disturbance, such as the scene where Cruise's little girl (Dakota Fanning, in another unnatural "child-actor" performance indicating too many acting classes) takes a bathroom break in the woods by a river. Suddenly, a dead body floats downstream. And then another. And then a small town's worth of them. From idyllic to ghastly in a moment: Spielberg remains a talented showman.

He also remains an egregious sentimentalist, troweling on the unnecessary histrionics. For example, there was no good reason for Cruise's teenage son to be separated from the rest of his family. Bet on it, a sappy denouement will be forthcoming. If the point was to focus on the deadbeat dad's wobbly competence in terms of keeping his little girl safe by putting them in close quarters with the psycho Robbins character, then the teenager should have been written out of the story entirely. (Besides, it's too unnerving to see a movie in which Tom Cruise, Mr. Risky Business, is old enough to have a kid in high school! Rust never sleeps, eh, my fellow GenXers?) There are also curious lapses in simple logic, despite all the mind-blowing visuals and suspenseful situations. Why, for instance, does a cell-phone camera work early in the film, after it has been established that the aliens have managed to short-circuit all electrical and even magnetic devices (including wristwatches)? When Cruise gets his kids to his ex-wife's house from his own place, he complains that the teenager brought only salad dressing and hot sauce for their provisions (Dad is a TV-dinner kind of guy, obviously) . . . but why don't they simply open the ex-wife's refrigerator? And don't get me started on how thousands of tripods could lie buried in the earth for a million years without detection . . . or how supposedly brainy aliens would not have long ago figured out that our filthy, bacterial planet might possibly kill them. (The latter blunder is Wells' boo-boo, to be sure.)

Well. Despite all this, there IS something to be said for a movie that cost $185 million dollars that also dares to focus its energies on one family's story so as to demonstrate a general story about the end of the world as we know it. The movie, in other words, has the sense to avoid being just an empty spectacle: the lives of people we come to know are actually at stake. Spielberg is eminently commonsensical when it comes to the basic narrative, even as it never occurs to him that a middle-class woman's refrigerator will likely have some food in it.

And on that six-of-one-half-dozen-of-the-other note, I'm giving *War of the Worlds* 5 stars out of 10.

title: Let down!
review: When I sat in a cinema some months ago and saw the advert for this movie I was in heaven, Spielberg remaking War of the Worlds with Tom Cruise, wow!!! I saw the movie today, and.. well, I feel like a limp you know what. title: Good effects, lacking story,
review:
If you've grown up with the music as a child then you'll have certain expectations of the movie  and most likely you'll be disappointed. I was. If you knew nothing about War of the Worlds, then you may find it an interesting action movie.

So what was disappointing? It's hard to pinpoint exactly  aside from saying that it feels soulless and unbelievable. Firstly, there's no music of any note (excuse the pun). Secondly, the story line feels almost non  existent. By the end you know you have gone somewhere and a lot has happened  but you are left wondering what exactly it was. It feels somewhat pointless, and simply a series of special effects strung together.

The special effects are great, at times, but I couldn't help feeling that a good portion of the budget was spent in the first few minutes and then they had to skimp to keep to budget.

War of the Worlds is a classic, but this movie is not. I've heard that Jeff Wayne who composed the original soundtrack is considering making a version  now that would probably be a good film  especially if he teamed up with Peter Jackson

title: Good, but not great
review: Why can't Spielberg (or the majority of major American filmmakers for that matter) leave well enough alone? There's no argument that he knows how to make a film, but why, for god's sake WHY, does he have to put the stupid, schmaltzy, out of context with the rest of the film bits in? Two glaring examples of this: Tom Cruise gets sucked up the alien's back passage (let's face it, it looks like one), pulls the pin on some grenades and is pulled back out again. Wrong wrong wrong. The character is not an action hero, don't give him stupid things to do. And by the way, why don't those same people try pulling other unfortunates to safety, or does only Tom count? Two, the annoying son. There is no way, given the manner of slaughter we have just been shown, that he could have survived, but no, Spielberg had to have his happy ending. How much stronger would it have been if there were some personal casualties? We'll never know.

title: Weak just weak, irresolute even.
review: There are some spoilers in here but much like the film they are vague. I'm a big Spielberg fan, who isn't, but come on! This movie had some good moments, but they were few and far between. Yes the original was great, the book great but having only one an A story to follow that builds up this huge enemy and their immense power and then tagging on a bunch of un-established conclusions in the last ten minutes to wrap up the film sucks. I'm sorry it just does. I had to explain to those I was with at the theater why the aliens were dead! And the son just suddenly appears back at the house in Boston, "hey Dad, remember that big ball of flame that killed everyone well not me, I made it home on my own, don't ask how, just accept it". Plus I would have been a bit more frightened of the psycho in the basement if he didn't start out with the cheesy B movie -I'm frightening so I'll step into this spooky light and stand here for an unnatural amount of time to establish that fact- shot. I'm all for that kind of thing in a 'Sin City' vibe or a ' Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow' feel. It was a shot that didn't fit for me. But who am I right. Not Steven Spielberg, but this movie isn't either. The film struggled to get me to suspend my disbelief and as soon as it did it gave me the (expletive-est) ending ever. I could care less about Tom Cruise, I love knowing that a Spielberg film will never disappoint, will be a complete well paced story. I left this movie feeling robbed. Fine, be true to the original story but please, please, be honest to the audience above all. This was a bad movie.

title: Should have been better
review:
War of the Worlds could have been a good movie had it not been bogged down by whiny kids and plot holes. The movie starts off great. Unexplained weather phenomenon, very good atmosphere setup and special effects that make you believe this is the real thing.

First problem with the movie was that I didn't feel any of the characters. The young boy was annoying at best: the best scene with him in it was definitely when they were tossing around the baseball, definitely the ONLY scene I recall where I felt chemistry. Other than that, his character was dry, linear and not at all believable. Would that girl shuttup??? She fricken screams for anything. Little storm AHHHHHH, seeing the alien camera after already surviving numerous larger scale attacks AHHHHHHHH, dead bodies floating down the river... oh wait, the one place she forgot to scream. Tom Cruise's character wasn't any better, but at least he didn't annoy me throughout the movie.

Second problem was there was too many things unexplained or that simply didn't make sense. These striders seem to have an attack range of a small city and can kill anything in it's path, yet, 10 of them stand around in a remote location together, tons of people manage to keep enough distance to not even see one while others encounter dozen in a 2 day drive, I must say for an advanced alien race, they're pretty stupid when it comes to strategic military planning. Another thing - these strider run off of humans??????? WTF!?!?! How did these aliens (who planted striders in the ground before the world really started) know how to design their machines to run off of humans? And if they could run off of humans, why couldn't they run off of trees, or dirt, or cement with the same tech??? How does that kid survive what was surely an inescapable death (that disappointed me)??? Overall, the movie started great with a lot of mayhem, destruction and brutality. But then turned into run and hide and scream for the next hour and a half. The special effects almost make it worthy of theatre watching, but definitely wasn't complimented by it's acting, character development, or story line.

6/10

title: WOTW - With Out The Wow factor
review:
Over the past few years Spielberg has come out with A.I, Catch Me if you can, Minority Report and The Terminal, none of these are really vintage Spielberg (Indiana Jones, Jurassic Park, Saving Private Ryan) and as for War of the Worlds well it sits some where in between this list. As a film that strikes terror and fear into the viewer it succeeds in part, well at least the first hour does. But then Mr Spielberg decides to go into the fantasy land he exposed us to towards the second part of A.I, which just blows apart all the hard work used to build up the atmosphere in the first part, and the story spirals out of control from this point and ends abruptly ! The story centres around a troubled family, Ray (Tom Cruise) is a divorced father with an estranged teenage son and a 10 year old daughter he never even knew was allergic to peanuts ! As the kids are dropped off with Ray for the weekend the film exposes us to Ray's strained relationship with his kids, but before we're able to say "what a bad father he is" all hell breaks loose and the streets of New Jersey begin ripping up beneath our families feet.

From here on Ray takes charge and takes his kids and flees the town, whilst watching innocent people being vaporised in his rear view mirror. All Ray wants to do is keep his kids safe, this is where the film does a very commendable job, you really believe Ray wants to make up for all the years of bad fathering and neglect he's put these kids through and if he can do one thing its at least keep them safe.

The terror of the earth being attacked by Aliens is not a new theme (Independence Day, Men in Black) but rarely is it explored for the "fear" point of view, and the widespread panic and evacuations of the cities is filmed really well, I was really enjoying watching the panic stricken people creating such a manic atmosphere up until we're introduced to a troubled new character who has little justification to the story (Tim Robbins), then we are suddenly almost rushed into being introduced to the aliens and their reason for invading the planet. From the scene where Tim Robbins character is introduced to where Ray takes down one of the Alien's Tripod machines the film feels rushed, unexplained and looses all the suspense and thriller aspect Spielberg had done so well to create in the first part.

It really does the job of leaving a bitter after taste in your mouth, Tom Cruise can't be blamed, he does his best with an inadequate plot line, Dakota Fanning as the terrified daughter plays it well and really hooks you in with her performance, its not the worst movie of the year, but it certainly ain't the "summer Blockbuster" we were all expecting.

title: The end of the world!
review: The War of the Worlds Dreamworks/Paramount 2005 Color 117 mins. Sci-fi/Action Tom Cruise, Dakota Fanning, Justin Chatwin, Tim Robbins and Miranda Otto star. Directed by Steven Spielberg Written by H.G. Wells Rated PG-13 for terror, brutality, violence and gore. OK so who knew Mr. Speilvberg still had this in him. After the lame lineup of films he's turned out lately. It's surprising for him or even a big studio to go forth and make mega budget Horror flick. And thats what precisely this is. Don't be fooled this film is brutal like Saving Private Ryan brutal when Spielberg makes a film about way, he makes a film about war. While their mother and her new beau head on over to her parents in Boston. All in the same day he gets off work and comes home to his resistant kids and the invasion begins. The aliens attack in their 50's movies inspired vehicles and decimate the population while him and his kids race cross country to find their mother in Boston. The movie is a sweaty palm inducing nightmare that only loses its nerve in the last act. Had the film had a bleak ending like everyone thought it may have been of the most disturbing films ever made. Spielberg has accomplished a glorious feat by taking the prospects of an alien invasion and making them seem real through holocaust and 911 references. Truly terrifying stuff here people. Tom Cruise I've a wonderful and Oscar worthy performance as the after and Dakota Fanning joins him in the same caliber. Another standout in the film is hottie Justin Chatwin who does an ice job by making his character memorable. i'm telling you right now when going to see War f the Worlds you have no idea what to expect, no matter how much I or whatever others tell you. Just be Read to cover your eyes and grab hold of your seat. A-

title: What summer movies should be  Entertaining.
review:
This is the best movie I've seen in a long time.

Right from the beginning you're drawn into this movie. And really you're into it the whole way through. The action, F/X, storyline and pace are near perfect. And i suppose there are some plot holes, but I didn't really notice them or cared to dismiss them. And I'm a pretty cynical guy  always cutting up bad movies. But the movie is relentless and I got so into it that I didn't notice or just said "who cares this is great, a movie I like!"

Usually I don't like Tom Cruise, I mean actually I can't stand him, I've always found his acting over the top and distracting to the point of ruining movies. But in this one he plays his part well. Pretty believable as a self centered jerk, who eventually turns into a hero. Of course there are some scenes of trademark over acting, but I didn't care.

Also the sound and movement that these giant alien craft make are super creepy. It reminds me of how I felt when I saw Empire Stricks Back for the first time  the size of the snow walkers was super cool  same with the tripods.

title: Spielberg can't make sense of 9/11/2001
review: The film I saw with a sparse matinée crowd here in southwest Michigan reminded of better treatments that offered audiences surprise, novelty, and more toned-down pleasant amazement. This, after all, is the same filmmaker who brought us CLOSE_ENCOUNTERS_OF_THE_THIRD_KIND and E.T. in his heyday and now that he is a "message" director he apparently felt he could team with hyperactive celebrity/mogul Tom Cruise and bring some sort of answers to our troubled times of war and terrorism. For those of you deciding whether or not to see the film, I'd recommend to wait for the DVD release. It cannot see "forest for the trees" of its visually overstimulated usage of effects like all our worst nightmares (tornadoes, mass transit cataclysms, spy intercept and machine killing technology, earthquakes, even some U.S. military impotence against foes that won't surrender!). The scenes that deal with the wrecked planes and missing persons' posters were heart-wrenching for those of us for whom September 11, 2001 is still a foundational date of destiny. Shame on you, Mr. Spielberg for trying to insinuate something about destroyers "buried" ready for activation (sleeper cells of the al Qaeda variety) and the young boy/rebel thinking that joining vigilante-style in the Army/Reserve assault that seems rather disorganized and knee-jerk will "solve" the confrontation between the destroyers and those about to be destroyed. This film certainly was apparently rushed in some ways to meet a "gap" in the Hollywood schedule as far as a 2005 blockbuster. Its "framework" narration does give one pause. Certainly for those of us aware of the levels of material utilized by those drawing on past versions of this tale of the 1890's by H.G. Wells the WAR is won by forces humanity has taken for granted, apart from any sort of prayerful plea for help like the 1950s version of the WAR. Maybe this S. Spielberg creation will look better to me later when I see it and can stop and start the puzzling sequences. For me, a 8* out of 10*.

title: Great spectacle with no ovation
review: This movie is a good representation of today's mainstream Hollywood productions - tons of money spent on visuals, leaving the plot obsolete and bleeding far behind. To be quite honest, I was disappointed - through 3/4 of the movie I was picking up my jaw from the floor, but what is wrong with this terrible, clueless ending? First the invaders take us to the ground and beat us to pulp. The human civilization is literally dying, with no chances whatsoever to stand up to those robots. And what happens? For some unspecified reason we win! I mean it's good, but how? We didn't do anything! I was expecting Tom Cruise to accidentally find a solution against the aliens, and save the world - that's what I have expected. And I have also expected Spielberg to surprise me and do against those every men's expectations, if you know what I mean. And what happened? Nothing. Nevertheless, the first part of the movie, especially when seen in a high quality audio theater, is breathtaking. And of course Tom Cruise - I think he's found some kind of magic potion for eternal youth :) Go and see this movie, and judge for yourself - I think Spielberg, though surely still able to build a tension (see the scenes in Tom Robbins' cellar), is now over the hill with his talent.

title: Effective, but mindless entertainment with creepy morals
review:
The imagery and tone of the action sequences in this latest Spielberg offering are truly the stuff nightmares are made of. The scenes in which ten-story, three-legged killing machines stalk the countryside and appear back-lit on the horizon just when you think you've escaped truly taps something primordial in us all. The special effects in this film are some of the most artful I've ever seen. The menace is palpable and terrifying.

Beginning in New Jersey, the story chronicles the flight from Martian invaders of Tom Cruise's Ray Ferrier and family to Boston by way of march and minivan.

But from shades of 9/11 where Cruise becomes encrusted with soot (like so many emerging from the Twin Towers disaster), to the wreckage of downed jet-liners, to an indifferent media, to a holocaust-like river of bodies and wholesale hunting of humans, the story is more a showcase of what frightens Americans the most in 2005 -- at least according to Mr. Spielberg. Just as the original film adaptation of the classic H.G. Wells novel reflected a Cold War paradigm, and, as with so many sci-fi films over the years, this picture, I believe, will become a snapshot of our national mindset at the time of its release. Whilst Ferrier and family flees New York in a panic, Ferrier's daughter screams repeatedly, "Is it the terrorists?"

We meet Cruise's Ferrier on the job, hard at work moving cargo containers from ship to shore. Clearly taking his job seriously till the clock runs out, he declines his super's request for a little overtime in a flourish of working-class "not my job" palaver before peeling out in his muscle-car.

Upon arriving at home, he is greeted by his ex-wife and her new, far wealthier husband. Ferrier's children are less than impressed with Ferrier and, like so many children these days, seem wholly persuaded by the notion that respect for one's parents must be earned and not compelled. Woefully, the rest of the dramatic arc in this tale is the standard critique of the working-class slob we've seen spewing out of Hollywood from Archie Bunker to Homer Simpson. Ferrier, as anyone might expect, must transform himself from disillusioned Al Bundy to Super-Dad in the wake of Martian death-rays.

Leave it to Hollywood to make a movie about how the only way a white, blue-collar man can redeem himself to the wife who left him, the children who chide him, and society in general is by running a gauntlet of humiliation and violence to meekly relinquish his children to the care of his ex-wife, her parents, and her new rich husband. Of course, THEY are all somehow immune to humiliation and violence as is evidenced by the fact that, despite living in a major urban center, have escaped unscathed in a gorgeous Boston brownstone. You see, they're cute, rich, and responsible and everyone knows Martians only target slackers. Where, after all, would working-class men be without rich Bostonians, morally superior wives, disrespectful children, and SUV-driving second husbands to all look down their noses at him? And by the way, Tom, while you're out there redeeming yourself, could you stop off and MURDER some of the flakier, more liberal, more paranoid elements of our little superiority club? You know, the ones who make us look bad? Let's make it Tim Robbins, shall we?

*** Huge spoiler alert! ***

In a scene remarkable for its political undertones, the vocally left-wing actor Tim Robbins is offered up in sacrifice to a perceived mainstream mentality by being killed off by Cruise ( arguably a symbol of mainstream America ) in a segment many agree belongs in a different movie altogether. Robbins' character, Ogilvy, is a fear-mongering fruitcake who can't seem to grasp the gravity of the situation -- rather the way pro-war "liberals" view the pacifist hippy wing of the embattled Democratic party at the time of the film's release. Ogilvy's hysteria threatens to alert the aliens to their hiding place. So what does our sympathetic protagonist do? Tie Robbins up and gag him? No. Cruise finally decides to kill Ogilvy in Ogilvy's own home! That home into which Ogilvy had invited Ferrier and fawn and offered up as shelter from the evil aliens when everyone else was beating the Ferriers senseless and stealing their minivan. I'm sorry, but Ogilvy's murder sickened me and caused me to stop caring whether or not Ferrier and his precious, smart-mouthed little daughter got stomped into fertilizer by Martian robots. Robbins' character was a sad, pathetic figure of a man who was guilty of fear, not evil.

Yet another cultural critique from this reviewer may seem like over-thought hand-wringing and needless hair-splitting, but movies tell powerful stories on giant screens that seep into our consciousness and subtly ( sometimes not so subtly ) affect how we view the world and how we react to it. Anyone who doubts that TV and movies affect our behavior hasn't been paying attention to the amount of money advertisers spend to do just that. And anyone who thinks filmmakers don't advance social and political agendas from time to time obviously haven't seen 'The Stepford Wives,' or 'The Sullivans.' And anyone who thinks movies don't affect popular culture just isn't paying attention. And anyone who hasn't acknowledged that popular culture recreates norms for what most of us consider acceptable behavior hasn't consulted the latest edition of Merriam Webster for the definitions of either the words 'popular,' and/or 'culture.' And anyone who hasn't weighed the notion that, occasionally, what may seem like an appropriate new norm turns out to be grievous, short-sighted tom-foolery, obviously hasn't looked at the latest statistics for divorce and mental illness.

Further, there are a number of logical flaws I understand may have originated with the novel, but entirely defy rational thought.

But if the present picture is any indication, Hollywood has stopped encouraging us to think altogether.

This movie review by Erik Gloor

title: far better than Independence Day, but...
review: There's a spoiler here, as I'll refer to the way this movie ends... so don't read this review if you still haven't seen the flick. If you have read the book, you know that it was placed by the end of the 19th century, and we should consider that Pasteur's discoveries were still a revolution. To say back then that our own diseases were a great defense against an outer space invasion was innovative... but not today: we know about biochemical warfare, and to imply that all the military could do during an invasion was using conventional weapons is a bit naive. Of course one could say that the point of view of the leading characters was that of the common man, but I'm sure that the common man could have suffered the by-effects of those new weapons. I'd say that's the best thing in this movie: Tom and Dakota's point of view, people who don't know what's happening, how or why. But still I think some more substance to the fight could have been added without losing that (ie, that could have been accomplished by a meeting with surviving soldiers). Also, to believe that beings that probably left high-tech machines waiting under the ground for at least several thousand years do not expect our humble Terran flu, is a bit far fetched. There's another issue: this ets did not arrive in meteor shaped cannonballs from Mars, they probably have their mother-ships in orbit, and this was just the first wave that earth people have defeated by the end of the movie. Another loose end... Anyway: good movie, good acting, nice effects, lots of suspense and scary at times, this is worth seeing. But I left the theater wanting more.

So, enjoyable but after watching it I couldn't help but thinking it was sort of a rush job. Set my hopes too high; for great director+great story I expected more.

review: I don't it get. The alien machines just died? Or the aliens inside them just died? Or both? What happened at the end of this movie? And the whole sequence in the basement got on my nerves. Suddenly a decent action movie has to become a Tim Robbins acto-thon? Stupid waste of time, if you ask me. Basically this movie needed to do a whole lot more explaining. What were those bloody vein-things all over the ground? The aliens were consuming blood or just spitting it out on the ground? The aliens waited a million years to launch their attack, but they never did any surveillance to realize that they would all die in a week or so? It just didn't make any sense.

title: Winning WAR
review: That Mr. Spielberg really knows how to churn out a great summer flick. This adaptation of WAR OF THE WORLDS nearly manages to make us forget the recent public TOMfoolery between our hero and a certain babbling Brooke. Watching Bayonne eaten by tripods did provide certain thrills for this Jersey boy - pay day for all those hours spent in bumper to bumper traffic. Cruise is in control, but pint-sized thespian Dakota Fanning is this film's key - she provides both the requisite humor ("I have back problems" she whines sardonically when asked to bunk out on a cellar floor) and the warm and fuzzies. Indeed, the relationships between Cruise and his kidlings is the film's bedrock with the tripod Aliens providing the scary chills and thrills of a sci-fi roller coaster. 'The crazy loon in the basement scene' (a staple of every WAR) pays off nicely thanks to Tim Robbins as said 'loon'. Like most treks, it all ends in Boston - but if you've any common sense at all, leave before they reach Beantown. The film's confusingly simplistic ending is not only dumb but sentimental. Its nearly enough to do the film in. But luckily it's only the battle thats lost - not the WAR.

review:
Well before I say anything in particular about the movie I have something to say about the rating. This is supposed to be a PG-13 movie.
