title: Still don't really get it
review:
I was really looking forward to this movie, and I gave it a lot of chances throughout, but it just doesn't bring much originality to the table. I have not read the book nor do I know how much the movie is like the book, but comparing this to other spaceship/alien movies, I did not come away feeling like I was awed by anything. The special effects are pretty good. I feel like this movie took a lot of ideas from other movies including The Abyss (the probe in the basement scene), Independence Day/Star Wars (the 'impenetrable' field on the alien ships), Jurassic Park (when the alien probes are looking for Cruise et al in the basement as well as the constant noise of the tripods moving about outside), Signs (the entire basement scene), Signs/Alien/Predator (the look of the alien beings themselves), Twister (the storm at the beginning), Titanic (the boat scene).

I was entertained by the beginning of the movie. The lightning storm was pretty cool, the disintegration of humans by the aliens was kind of unique, but I thought the fact that Cruise somehow has the only working car to get out of town was pretty dumb. Unexplained things in the movie that irritated me: why Cruise's son was so stubborn about taking on the indestructible aliens and then how he survives in the end. Do the aliens die because of the earth's atmosphere, our diseases? The end talks about the smallest pieces of life and have paramecium floating on the screen-is it bacteria or other organisms? Why is Tim Robbins and Spanish from Old School in this movie? What was the significance of Cruise destroying the tripod with some grenades (which also reminds me of something I saw in Raising Arizona/the Professional with the pin on grenade in Cruise's hand). That metal crate of people falling to the ground after the thing blows up and everyone is OK? How did the Japanese figure out how to kill them, but in the end they seem to die not from our figuring something out about them but because they are able to adapt to the environment?

This is pretty much a stream of consciousness now as there was just too much trying to be done in this movie and it ends up being pretty boring with the exception of a few parts. The Tim Robbins basement scene should have been 10 minutes shorter. They also could have done without Dakota Fanning disappearing all the time (I think she would want to stay with her father rather than be on her own hiding from aliens). I don't even know why I gave this thing a 6. I guess because I have always liked Cruise and Spielberg and I hate to admit that this one missed the boat.

title: "They've been planning this for a million years. And these are only the first. They'll keep coming. " - Harlan Oglivy
review:
Whenever Steven Spielberg comes out with a new movie it's always a big thing. I mean, although Spielberg is a little bit of a sell-out in my book (that thing he did with E.T. was absolutely insane), he's still an extremely talented film director. He's given blockbusters such as Jurassic Park and Jaws, and has given us Oscar-contending masterpieces such as Schindler's List and Saving Private Ryan. It seems no matter what film Steven Spielberg produces or directs, whether it is great or kind of so-so, they are always entertaining. Well, 'War of the Worlds' has it's number of flaws, but one thing you cannot say about it is that it isn't consistently intriguing and entertaining.

'War of the Worlds' is a remake of the 1953 film with the same title (which was based on H.G. Wells' legendary novel), and it is pretty much about the end of the world. It follows two children, Rachel (the undeniably talented young Dakota Fanning  Hide and Seek, I Am Sam) and Robbie (Justin Chatwin  Traffic: The Miniseries). It's their weekend to be with their deadbeat dockworker dad, Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise  The Last Samurai, Minority Report), who lives in the beautiful state of New Jersey (you sense the sarcasm in my tone?). The kids stay with Ray, while their mom, Mary Ann (Miranda Otto  Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King) and her new boyfriend go to Boston to visit Mary's mother. The kids have kind of a rocky relationship with their father; Rachel is kind but distant, and Robbie has nothing but contempt for his father. In the middle of a family emergency, mysterious lightning strikes and changes the world we live in forever. Enormous battle ship type machines emerge from the soil of the earth and start firing lasers at random citizens that turn them into ashes in a second. In the machines, are aliens who have been beamed down from the lightning and into the machines to exterminate our race and have Earth for themselves. Needless to say, Ray's problems with his family become kind of mute when blood-hungry aliens start attacking earth. Ray, Rachel and Robbie take off to Boston to find Mary Ann in a battery-powered minivan, while desperately trying to escape aliens (they have the only car that works because everything gas-powered and electrical has stopped working). The film becomes for-the-most part an entertaining adventure flick, but kind of drags during some unnecessary family feuding between the three. During their journey, Ray and his kids hide in a farmhouse basement in upstate New York that is inhabited by Harlan Oglivy (Oscar Winner Tim Robbins  Code 46, Mystic River), a deranged/paranoid conspiracy theorist armed with a 12-gauge shotgun.

'War of the Worlds' garners extravagant and eye-popping special effects. The designs of the alien machines and the aliens themselves are very inventive and interesting to look at. I think it's safe to say 'War of the Worlds' will get some Oscar nominations for visual effects, sound, makeup or even art direction (set decoration). It's entertaining for the most part, but really drags during unnecessary and extremely boring conversations that try to be heartfelt between Tom Cruise's Ray and Dakota Fanning's Rachel. It may be the writing, but something tells me the problem was with the acting. Not to take away anything from Dakota Fanning, she does a remarkable job as to be expected, probably delivering the finest performance of the entire film. The problem lies with Tom Cruise. He's a terrible actor, and he stumbles through his role. He never really makes you believe he's in real danger, and that really kills a lot of the movie's would-be tension. Cruise always seems to play the same smart-ass cocky son-of-a-b*tch role, and it kind of gets to you after a while. I believe whole-heartedly they could have found someone better than Cruise for this role, Mel Gibson maybe (although he just did 'Signs'). Tim Robbins is perfect as the whacked out conspiracy theorist armed with a shotgun for the unfortunately limited amount of screen time he has (he doesn't show up until over half of the film is over). Miranda Otto is okay in a kind of a nothing role, but I wasn't too crazy about Justin Chatwin's stiff and disengaging performance. Morgan Freeman provides his voice for narration at the beginning and end of the film and that is a definite plus. Steven Spielberg does a good job directing this, and the screenplay is kind of alright for this kind of picture.

All in all, 'War of the Worlds' turns out to be a pretty good movie and a decent fare to see while it's on the big screen. It has it's flaws, but the good outweighs the bad in this action summer blockbuster. 'War of the Worlds' is worth seeing for the amazing special effects alone. It may not have Oscar-worthy performances, but it's a hell of a lot of fun if you just sit back and enjoy the ride. I recommend 'War of the Worlds'. Grade: B (screened at AMC Deer Valley 30, Phoenix, Arizona, 7/1/05).

my ratings guide - A+ (absolutley flawless); A (a masterpiece, near-perfect); A- (excellent); B+ (great); B (very good); B- (good); C+ (a mixed bag); C (average); C- (disappointing); D+ (bad); D (very bad); D- (absolutley horrendous); F (not one redeeming quality in this hunk of Hollywood feces).

title: Technical beefs dismissed (maybe)
review:
I've read many negative posts here, many attacking "scientific" flaws in the story. I'd like to offer a counterpoint to those criticisms.

1. Why would aliens who want to take over the earth bury drones rather than fly right in with "manned" vessels? Answer: Don't we do the same thing, by sending unmanned craft into space to check the environs before we send our life forms out? 2. Why didn't anybody detect the drones underground? Answer: What if they were buried so deeply as to defy identification. Most of the inner earth is rife with metals anyway, so how would man have ever known they were there? 3. Tripods are inherently unstable platforms, so any life form would be better on legs divisible by four. Answer: Take a chair with four legs, chop most of one leg off and try to sit on it. You'll fall on your keester. Now take a a bar stool with 3 legs, shave one down... it remains fairly stable. That's why cameras use tripods, not octopods.

4. The tripods should have died underground after exposure to our germs before the aliens arrived. Answer: The tripods are machines in this movie, so only after the life forms arrive do our germs have effect.

5. The electro-magnetic pulse (EMP) is not properly depicted. Answer: Correct, but other than a newscaster or two using the term EMP, are we really sure that's EXACTLY what the aliens are using? Is it possible their technology disables electronics in a different way from what we're familiar with? You betcha! 6. Why don't the aliens employ infrared sensing during the probe scene in Ogilvy's basement? Answer: This movie isn't "Predator." Where does it say in the Sci-Fi handbook that all aliens can see heat? Besides, it makes for one of the better suspense scenes, and a nice homage to the book and the 1953 film. (Wasn't it nice to see Gene Barry and Ann Robinson at the end, BTW?) In summary, enjoy the entertainment. Watch the amazing camera work as the Ferriers drive their van out of town. It's one long take orbiting the vehicle, culminating in a fantastic crane shot. Also savor the achievement in sound by Michael Babcock and his team. One of the best ear drum workouts ever!

title: Excellent and horrific introduction of invaders, but never reaches that plateau again...
review:
Horrific, shocking, and edge-of-your-seat movie-watching is what I remember about this film. Great build-up to the introduction to the alien invaders, but the terror doesn't ever regain it's heights from there. I would have given the movie a 9 out of 10 if it had done so...maybe even a 10, because I haven't been that scared in a movie for quite some time.

I expected much more panic from the crowds of humanity later in the movie. We do see a glimpse of this panic when Ray's family arrive at the first town, but afterward there is very little confusion/wide-eyed panic that would cause hundreds of deaths in a real-world situation. The first "invader" scene is awesome, but the crowd reaction in the following scenes weren't as believable to me.

The alien machines were quite fantastic and the sound effects were brilliant. The "war call" of the machines were down-right chilling. I only had one problem with the alien machines and that was when they showed the human captives and how they were freed. I suppose I'm nit-picking, but I didn't need to see vulnerable aliens. It diminished my terror-filled experience. When I go to see an alien-invasion flick, I want to be terrified. As the movie went along, I went from terrified to interested. Yeah, I'm hardcore.

Top notch visual and sound effects. Not much more to say about that. I had read quite a few reviews of this movie and wondered what I was going to see. I have read the book and seen the original and pretty much knew what was going to happen and how it was going to end. I don't understand how some people are disappointed in the ending of this movie. Either, 1) they have never heard/read the original or, 2) expected Spielberg to put his own twist on the end of this Sci-Fi classic. I liked the end quite a bit and it was true to the original ending. Kudos for Spielberg for keeping with the original material. He can always try out his "twist" for the DVD edition.

I plan to see this again when it's out on DVD. I don't know whether I'll buy it or not, because I'm very critical of my movie collection. I'll have to decide once I watch WOTW on my set-up. I would recommend that people see this movie in the theater for the effects and in-your-face factor. But, I would also recommend that they do some homework on the original and not expect an "Independence Day" type of movie (which I hated) where the hero doesn't punch an alien in the face and deliver a line like "Welcome to earth!"

title: It's official: Dakota Fanning is scary good!!
review:
If ever there was a sure fire, safe bet kind of a film this year, it was always going to be War Of The Worlds. You have the ingredients there for a great movie. We have Spielberg multiplied by Cruise which is the square root of Dakota Fanning. It is a simple mathematic equation; that these elements combined will make at the very least a good movie. War of The Worlds, while not the best addition to Cruise or Spiely's catalogue is still a top class summer movie and the best Alien invasion movie so far. To sum up War Of The Worlds you could say that the first 2 acts are classic, top draw stuff, perhaps the best this year, while the third act drops the standard when introducing a needlessly cast Tim Robbins, before ending, some felt, rather abruptly. More on that later however.

Firstly the films strength's. This film has amazing action. Really amazing action, the best use of CGI this year. The CGI is used so effectively and made to look so real. The camera never sits still and lovingly gazes at the computer imagery to the point we see that it is fake and see the seams as it were. Spielberg uses the camera to disorientate and give flashing glimpses of massive killer tripods zapping people into dust while Cruise and his fellow publicans run like the wind. The effects are astonishing but we don't focus on them too long in each shot, allowing us to keep the feeling we are seeing something genuine. As the action ripped along I was on the edge of my seat. The effects, the sound, the direction all combining to create some truly chilling and pulse pounding sequences, especially the first sitting of the tripods. As well as the action we have a core family story we care about. Now of course they have raided the cliché box as this is after all a disaster movie made in Hollywood, so Tom Cruise plays the bad father who eventually comes good, while Justin Chatwin is his angst ridden teenage son. Thankfully young starlet Dakota Fanning is given a character a bit different to the norm, a freakishly intelligent and quirky daughter. Of course this is due to the fact that Fanning is a freakishly good actress and plays a role 99% pf child actors couldn't play, so generally the play little hyperactive brats. At times Fanning is the heart of the movie thanks to having a fairly unique character combined with a unique level of talent for someone her age.

The movie is helped along by it's primary cast. Cruise is superb. He really delves into the character again and it's not the usual heroic and faultless character again that Cruise plays, it is another departure for him for this type of movie, much like the flawed character in Last Samurai. Cruise can act, no question and here he gets to stretch, while the chemistry between himself and his kids, Chatwin and Fanning, really make the family dynamic engaging. Cruise could be an outside bet for an Oscar nod this year, having been unlucky in previous years missing out for Samurai and Collateral. Justin Chatwin is excellent as well. He pulls of a stretching role for someone fairly new to the business. Then there is the frighteningly good Fanning who just darn well scares me because she is too good for an 10 year old. Remember feeling that way after seeing Haley Joel Osment in The Sixth Sense? A performance of such intensity and maturity that it seemed like it had come from a veteran of 40 years. Fanning is the same, and in some ways too good and mature to be a realistic kid. However her character, like Osment's in Sense, is a strange character with strange tendencies and the part is good. It's a character actors part in some senses. I still find it scary though. Elsewhere Miranda Otto has an extended cameo and little to do, while Tim Robbins seems to serve little more purpose that to have some extra complication and to add a star name.

Spielberg is on fine form and goes quite dark in parts. The central character Ray for example steals a car at someone else's expense, who were probably left to be zapped to oblivion while he also beats another guy to death. The action is also top notch as I mentioned earlier but for as much as Spielberg goes dark, he does end up playing it safe. Where he could have wiped out a few characters he chose to have the happy ending for the Ferrier family. Also while the film was a departure for Cruise, we still had a few super Cruise moments, with him being the first person to both damage and destroy one of the aliens machines. The film ended abruptly and felt like a good 15 minutes was chopped. Not so much the explanation which I liked and which stayed faithful to the book, very much an ode to Darwin, but the way it shifts from one setting to the sudden end of the film without necessarily having a final showpiece. The ending itself was good and the explanation worked but what was slightly off was the pacing of it.

Overall despite some off moments this is still a great movie that won't disappoint. Fine performances combine well with cracking action. Technically as well this is superlative from the music, to the cinematography and effects, absolutely top class. ****

title: Spielberg delivers again
review:
I have usually regarded "master story-teller" Steven Spielberg as a man who was overrated. Every movie he made was just one everybody loved and he really didn't care that much about the movie at all. I believed him just to get a profit. However, Spielberg delivers us a powerful new film that strays away from his usual style.

Like most that know the story of alien invasion, the plot of Martians coming to the planet Earth and beginning a quest to destroy all forms of Earthling life is a familiar story. But Spielberg gives us something more. Using film-making materials as his brush, he paints a well conceived, intense, vibrant, and at times frightening and disturbing portrait of alien hostile takeover. From the first moment with the Martian spaceships (called Tripods) arrive, we already know it won't be a fun ride. And as their laser beams blast to disintegrate people without will in a matter of seconds and tentacles that reach to grab already frighten humans, we the audience are at the edge of our seats. Bitting our nails as we feel that we are also running from these Tripods that let out a simple low horn-like sound that delivers a powerful effect of sending fear and chills in our body.

Since Tom Cruise is starring in this picture, his character is like most of his in the past. The character has a large ego and a cocky presentation and throughout the course of the film he tries to amend his past ways to try and evolve into a better person. Even still, with Cruise's clichéd character, he doesn't hurt the story that much and all actors put in a good effort to the intensity of the film. The only complaint is that Robbie, Crusie's son, is not a well acted character. His lines sometimes seen scripted and the actor tends to overact his character.

This film is made even more terrifying and disturbing because we are now living in a post-9/11 world where we feel an emanate terror can strike us and we may feel powerless to stop it. This film has now changed my outlook on Spielberg's work. No longer do I see him as a conventional filmmaker who only delivers what studios want. He can make movies that stray away from light and happy situations and that lead to dark and disturbing road. Likewise with "Schindler's List", I hope Spielberg continues to stray from his usual path of happiness because his best work comes from the truly dark films.

title: A blockbuster with real human feelings
review:
The level of this movie is far more higher than all the other alien movies. Not because of the special effects, which were great, but of the humanity of the movie. This is not about soldiers who are fighting the aliens but about a man who is trying to save his family. The movie really starts of really quickly. You get to know the characters very fast and then the worlds turns into a real hell. Fantastic. Sometimes some typical Spielbergs emotional moments, but thats OK i guise

The special effects were great, but what really stood out for me, was the acting. Tom Cruise and Dakota Fanning were just perfect together.

What I don't really like is the ending.

title: A great summer popcorn flick!
review:
Spielberg's remake of "War of the Worlds" is an action packed extravaganza that should leave most viewers a little shaken, if not stirred. I do not understand the negative reviews of this movie, and I think these reviewers a looking a little to deep within a movie that is strictly for entertainment value.

Luckily for us, this movie does not have any of the cheesy White House/Capitol Records blow-ups and destructions as its wimpy predecessors such as "Independence Day" or "The Day After Tomorrow". Instead, Spielberg keeps the action much closer to home; and right in your own backyard! The plot is basic and straightforward : Ray Ferrier (Cruise) is a single father, who doesn't have the closest relationship with his two children. In fact- they are a bit "estranged" to say the least. On a typical weekend drop-off of the kids is when our martians began invading and Ray's parental instincts begin to kick in.

It starts out as a weather storm that looks rather cool - & then things begin to go horribly wrong. Lightening bolts began shooting out of the sky, and then from the ground, giant three legged mechanical tripods began to emerge. At first nobody knows what to make of them- until they suddenly start vaporizing humans and destroying every building on the ground ; and that's when the panic, anxiety, and fight for survival begins! The rest of the movie centers on Cruises struggle to keep his children alive and get them back to Bostonwhere there mother is hopefully unharmed. In between, we get fantastic action sequences as cities are destroyed and the true nature of the visitors is revealed.

"War of the Worlds" is not sugary sweet like some many other Spielberg films- and if anything- the film invokes a sense of panic and fear with the audiencebecause this is something that possibly could happen one day. And of course, this would be our civilizations worst nightmare. The film proves itself to be kind of creepy, if not downright scary- and this is where Spielberg succeeds marvelously.

All in all, "War of the Worlds" is an instant sci-fi classic- and one of the better (if not THE best) movies we will see this summer. The direction, photography, acting and affects are all top notch.

The perfect summer movie definitely recommended!

title: Does the Spielberg/Cruise combo get it right after the muddled and half-decent "Minority Report"?
review:
Having neither read the novel upon which it is based nor having viewed the 1953 cinematic outing or heard the classic Orson Welles radio play I pretty much walked into "The War of The Worlds" only knowing a handful of things:

  • It's directed by the bearded genius Steven Spielberg. - It stars the world's number one Scientology spokesperson Tom Cruise. - His co-star happens to be the terrific little actress Dakota Fanning who happens to always get cast in the same type of role - the annoying troubled child. - It has plenty of explosions courtesy of our neighbors - the evil aliens hell bent on destroying all of mankind. - Mr. Cruise repeats his couch stomping act when faced by the movies main antagonist.


Okay fine, one of the above isn't true. I'll let you find out for yourself after viewing it on the big screen. You know you're going to. The two names the producers are using to promote the movie (H.G. Wells? Who dat?) are enough to ensure enormous numbers of enormous bottoms in cinema seats.

As mentioned earlier I have no detailed knowledge of the story so I can't tell you how accurate this interpretation is. In this modern update Tom Cruise stars as Ray Ferrier a divorcée asked to take care of his two children Rachel Ferrier (Dakota Fanning) and Robbie Ferrier (Justin Chatwin). The first act does a terrific job of flashing the character relationships no matter how cliché they are. If you haven't already guessed from viewing the trailers (or the multiple movies with similar character types) Ray isn't the "#1 Dad". In fact he's a pretty harsh especially towards his son and doesn't even know how to start dealing with his daughter. I'll let your imagination (and superb memory of movies with similar characters) help you figure out how his story pans out.

Soon after the invasion begins and we're treated to some of the best scenes of destruction Hollywood has put on the screen. The craft and alien designs are excellent and how I wish they had more detailed action pieces. However, since most of the characters do noting more than run away from the mechanical monsters the action starts to tire out real quick. This is where screenwriters David Koepp and Josh Friedman try to get creative.

I said try.

The real downer of the whole plot comes as soon as we're introduced to everyone's favorite political mouthpiece Tim Robbins as Ogilvy, a stranger who offers Ray and family shelter in his underground bunker. Again I'm not sure if his character was in the books but he most definitely is not a welcome addition to the proceedings. By this point of the movie Ray's motivations for getting his kids to their mother become crystal clear to us therefore the whole interaction between the two and the outcome of it feels pointless and repetitious.

With nowhere else to go the movie finds a convenient end. I'm guessing they kept the books original ending but in my humble opinion if they were going update it they should have also crafted a much more effective and smart ending. The whole thing just looked far to silly especially when the antagonists, who've planned this invasion for centuries, are far superior species than humans.

Like many I had high hopes for the Spielberg/Cruise pairing after the muddled, half decent "Minority Report" but sadly they don't get it 100% right this time either.

title: All other alien invasion movies prostrate and forget themselves before this one
review:
It really is that good. ID4, in all it's box-office glory, was still just a campy piece of entertainment that didn't take itself too seriously, and that was in it's favor. The original 50's WotW, well, I simply don't think very many people KNEW how to make a good movie back then. The original version was naive and ill-constructed, like a kids comic book from that era, but still had intrinsic value in it's writing (I am willing to acknowledge the films importance of special effects development, as well). But this NEW version from Spielberg, who shines like he hasn't in a while, blows those other movies away. In fact, it disintegrates them as easily is the alien's heat-ray disintegrates humans. It has a thrilling action sequence in the beginning that punches you in the gut the same way Saving Private Ryan did in it's first half hour. It leaves you breathless and hardly gives you a chance to breath until the movie's over.

After the initial shock of the alien invasion, the movie takes a drastic turn. It becomes a holocaust movie, focusing on the escape of Rey Ferrier (Tom Cruise), and his children from an ex-wife (Justin Chatwin and Dakota Fanning). Here is WoW's main source of drama, and it is compelling. Spielberg brilliantly uses 9/11 imagery along with his lessons learned while filming Schindler's List. The effect is emotionally devastating and almost on par, if not on par, WITH Schindler's List. It feels that raw and real. This isn't you're traditional happy "mankind unites under tremendous adversity" tale. Oh no. Cruise's character has to spend as much time fighting off humans as he does running from aliens. Little bits of family values moments poke out here and there, but they never seem forced or contrived, and helps the over-all story arch. The real heart-wrenching moments come whenever Rey attempts to hide the terrible reality of the situation from his daughter by many means. "You're gonna wanna look around, but you're just gonna look right at me," one might remember from the adds. Dakota Fanning could easily get a supporting actress nomination. She is that good.

Few people, but many internet trolls, will find things to nitpick over in this movie, such as how the aliens got here. The implication is that their machines were buried under the earth for god knows how long, just waiting for the aliens to arrive. I can see the problem with that, but alien invasion movies all come with many inherent glaring technical discrepancies that much can be forgiven. For example, advanced alien races are not likely to be hostile, and if they were, they would never put themselves in danger. They'd use robots or a subservient race, or possibly creatures that they designed at the genetic level to be really nasty. At any rate, they would never do it themselves for their own safety. In the face of all that, my dis-belief for a movie like this is very flexible.

Some people will complain about the ending, and this will only show how illiterate they are. Knowing the book really does help on'es appreciation for the movie. The movie ends the way it does because the book ends this way, plain and simple. It may be hard to swallow that advanced alien invaders can be done away with microbes, but Wells himself, as the surrogate hero of the book, remarked at how astonishing it was. He postulates that somehow the Martians (they were Martians in the book) had wiped out their own diseases centuries ago, and simply didn't factor it into daily life or their plans for Earth. Spielberg didn't have time to include that whole paragraph in the movie, but those who read the book have that masticate. Naysayers will also complain about how unlikely it is that none of the family dies and they're found in Boston with their house untouched after all the aliens died. Again, from the book. For the movie, you can just replace London with Boston. Same thing here. The aliens pushed on as far as London, and then died. People immediately began repopulating the place. Perhaps they simply returned to their home, or perhaps the aliens never made it so far as their house. It's like in the book when he's reunited with his wife at his home, which is also miraculously still standing.

There are a lot of internet trolls out there just aching to make a name for themselves by blasting WotW. The truth is, this movie is too mature for them, and they would rather make fun of something that's quite beyond their grasp than except the fact that a filmmaker may be ahead of them. Another problem is that some people are far to cynical for a Spielberg movie these days, no matter how dark and gritty he makes it. My advice, if you're reading this, is don't listen to anyone who says this is a bad movie. They're just plain wrong.

title: If you want to see a typical blockbuster flick, avoid this film
review:
If you want to see a story about a man trying to survive the end of the world, this is definitely your thing. There are no heros, there is no grand battle scene,there is no scene with Will Smith dragging a dead alien across the desert.

The film stars Tom Cruise as Ray, a divorcée from NJ. He's pretty much your typical 'average bachelor' - he has a job that he hates, a place with no food to eat, and an ex wife he thinks he's pretty much the scum of the universe... Not to mention the kids who harbour feelings of resentment towards him.

Enter the martians (Although it is never mentioned they are from Mars - more on this later); here we see some incredible special effects as machines come up from the ground (apparently had been put there about a million years ago) and start destroying human life left right and centre.

What follows is pretty much Ray trying to save himself and his children from the aliens. There is no big battle scene, and Ray is definitely not the 'hero' that saves the world. I think this is what separates this movie from other alien blockbuster movies. It is shot completely from Ray's perspective, which means little information is given about the aliens, and what is going on outside. I thought the performances (especially by young Dakota Fanning) were outstanding, and Tom Cruise (although not usually a fan) did a great job in this role. There were a couple of goofs, and people have complained that there was not enough backstory. I think this was the intention of the film, to be shot from someones perspective means (unless he was military intelligence or whatnot) he really won't know jack. All he knows is that he needs to protect his kin.

My one complaint is that, although I realise that it was shot from his perspective, they should've been a little bit more detailed about the ending - and how his wife and son were still in tact, in a building that was relatively untouched when the rest of the world was pretty much in ruins.

Other than that an unexpectedly gripping and entertaining film, that was well worth my $13.50.

title: Spielberg Doesn't need Cruise for this action packed 'War'
review: 'War of the Worlds is a very impressive remake of the very impressive original. The 1953 classic starring Gene Barry is equally as spectacular when placed in the perspective of its own era. The 2005 version stars superstar Tom Cruise as everyman Ray Ferrier. A divorced father of two who is hosting his teenage son ( Justin Chatman ) and his ten year old daughter ( Preteen flavor of the month Dakota Fanning )for the weekend. While their mother ( Ferrier's ex ) is vacationing at her parents house with their wealthy stepfather. Cruise's teenage son is not too happy with this arrangement or with his dad for that matter. And there are various references to Cruise's irresponsibility and selfishness and right away you know that Cruise will end being a hero based on the criteria of this formula. Well it isn't long before the weather anomalies associated with these types of disaster films line the sky. And the Ferrier household turns from fighting each other to staring in awe at the late Autumn sky which is full of black cloudy vortexes. You know the rest. The invaders take the city by storm. And here is where we begin to see Spielberg's spectacular touch. These effects are nothing short of breathtaking. As the hidden aliens ride gigantic tripods, which are sort of reminiscent of the 'Imperial Walker's' in George Lucas's ' The Empire Strikes Back'. Only much more frightening and foreboding when placed in a real scenario like New York. Actually the effects themselves are the star of this film. Cruise might be too fine of an actor for something with this much action. Just check out some of his sublime performances like those Oscar nominated rolls in 'Magnolia' or 'Born on the Fourth of July' if you need a reference point. Someone like Gene Barry, who has a cameo as the Grandfather in this adaptation. was more than capable of doing the work without distracting us from the film's excellent special effects. That's not to say that Cruise doesn't have some scenes which require difficult acting. One of the best scenes of the film involves a mob attempting to steal the van which the Ferrier family commandeered from their local garage after all things electrical are blacked out by the aliens. Cruise handles the panic, fear and rage like the seasoned veteran he has become. Even though he could be accused of overacting at times, the whole premise is over the top. Eventually the family makes it to the cellar of a burned out farm, where the encounter the reclusive surviver of a wiped out family, portrayed in an extended cameo by Tim Robbins. Here Spielberg and Co continue to dazzle us with fantastic other world visions. And when a snaking eye comes into the cellar searching for survivors of the carnage above, we are reminded of the suspenseful kitchen raptor scene in 'Jurassiac Park'. Genarally the film is pretty dark. From the insidious intent of the raiders to the execution of their evil plan, some parts may be too frightening for smaller children. Over the years Spielberg has proved to be one of the greatest, if not the greatest film makers of any era. One of his specialties is the Summer blockbuster and he executes that genre to perfection once again here. Although even the mighty Spielberg isn't immuned to the occasional clunker, you will find no such worries here. It's a good film to see on a Summer Saturday night. It's a good film period. 7 out of a possible 10 T.H.

It's a good blockbuster you should be looking for the night you go to the theater! Don't expect anything else. Sit down, fasten your seat belt and let the ride kick off. From the first minute on, you're totally drawn into the movie and Tom Cruise is very convincing as a dad who doesn't qualify. That's the main reason you go along within the family issue which 'carries' the movie. It has been a long time since I've had the feeling to 'wake up in the real world' after a movie, so I'm very positive.

The feeling there's more to come will constantly keep your eyes on the screen. And there is. My only complaint is the ending, which comes suddenly and not with a final 'blast' or something like that. The story can't allow itself to move to far from the book, off course, but still... It would be nice in this genre..

Finally I'd like everyone to realize this isn't a Magnolia, American Beauty or whatsoever. Its just a blockbuster, so compare it with equals!

2. Yes the ships were planted here millions of years ago, the aliens live millions of years because they come from a highly radiant planet and radiation is the mediator for weak genes and petty diseases that plague our species. A pure race on a pure planet doesn't take into account other planets species', kind of like collaborating with another country on software for putting a rover on the moon and forgetting to add a program to convert metric to English. And no, they didn't have to come to the planet to dig a hole for the ships, if you send something fast enough to a planets surface it's going to go a little underground.

3. The ships lost their shields because they were organic vessels that also fell victim to single celled organisms. And you can critique this answer with my first question and all I can offer as an answer is that this is a science fiction movie ending the same way as the book and people are trying to read too much into entertainment.

There were some scary parts-the loud 'honking' noise that sounded every time the aliens were about to attack was truly frightening and kept running through my head the day after I saw the movie. If I ever hear a noise like that in reality, I think that I may jump out of my shoes!! The tripods were quite scary as well. It was interesting and a good plot line that Spielberg chose to show the aliens as actually being very curious and timid once they exited their tripods and explored around the house. Apparently they could only be menacing inside their tripods. My problems with this film: it wasn't at all explained how the aliens were able to harbor underground to begin with. Was this explained in the novel? I also felt that it should of been shown how Tom Cruise killed Tim Robbins. Why did the door close without the viewer being able to see how he did it, and not even a scuffle or other noise? Spielberg can show countless people being zapped and guts being blown out but not one person killing another?? There was also no explanation given as to how Tom Cruise's son survived and made it back home. He headed into the fight and somehow survived the huge, fiery inferno that killed everyone else? How extremely milquetoast and unrealistic. Overall, the movie is scary, it has amazing special effects, and keeps you on the edge of your seat throughout, but is not flawless nor the best action/scary movie you will ever see.

title: A Bit Silly !
review:
Besides the air conditioning being broke in our theater,the movie was great for the first 30 minutes ! Then it somehow became a bit silly ! Why was Tom's car the only car in the area that worked- how true could that be? why could the Army not even kill these Aliens but somehow Tom did with one hand grenade ? title: Tightly wound tension with very real FX and strong story line.
review:
One measure of how much I'm enjoying a movie is how aware or unaware I am of the passage of time while sitting in the theater.

During War of the Worlds there was no sense of time whatsoever. It flew by as I remained riveted to the wallop this movie delivers. When it ended I realized I had been leaning forward literally sucked into the action.

The presentation was realistic sticking to pure Sci-Fi, never slipping into comic bookish fantasy.

The acting, from Dakota to Tom, is believable in conveying the sense of desperation and terror an alien invasion would invoke.

For pure entertainment this is the summer of '05 movie to see!

title: Won't be liked by all, but a magnificent and profoundly important film
review:
I am a great fan of HG Wells' original novel, and was mortified when I first heard that the names 'Spielburg' and 'Cruise' associated with this project. However my concerns were misplaced! This has turned out to be a tremendous achievement and one of the most important films to have been released in recent years.

There were, I admit, minor plot-holes, but this is not your traditional Sci-Fi story. The emphasis is not on the concepts or technology, but on the characters at the centre of the story. Ray (Cruise's character) is so *human* in his behaviour - he is lost, helpless, frequently defeated and reduced to tears. This isn't some cheesy effects extravaganza designed to promote the 'human spirit', this is an honest story about the frailty, selfishness and pettiness of humanity.

Magnificent performances all around, with special mention for dear little Dakota who was absolutely mesmerising, and Cruise who played well out of type. Great cinematography, direction and special effects along with a truly spell-binding soundscape. The Tripods were magnificent  breathtaking to behold, but also chilling.

This film is true to the spirit of the original book in so many ways that I think HG Wells would be proud. I suspect that it won't appeal to everyone as it lacks the kind of grand finale that most Sci-Fi blockbusters have, and it is painfully honest about how weak mankind really is. But in an age of arrogance and ignorance, I would like to quote Mark Hadley and say that this is the invasion we had to have!

title: 2005 W.O.T.W draws on all 3 previous
review:
The current version draws on ALL 3 version of War of the worlds. H.G. Wells chilling novel - Jeff Wayne's Musical Version and the 1950's movie version. Example. the 'Fog horn' sound emitted from the tripods in dual-tone. very similar to the musical version's tripod drone of "Ul-la". For those unfamiliar with the Musical Version. Find it and have a listen, and NO, It's not a musical like Moulin Rouge or Sound of Music.

As for the movie (2005) the ending was too abrupt which in turn renders it SH-T! Awesome Special effects and sound. Shame it ran out of puff after an hour.

title: A good enough film with good acting, but does contain some flaws.
review: I have been a fan of the War of The Worlds story for a long time. I liked the situation of the radio broadcast causing panic in America because it was believed to be real events. The 50's film was well made even if it is a little dated now. As for the Geoff Wayne album... I laughed the first time I heard Uuullaaa (as I was young), but soon came to love it. Forever Autumn was fantastic. When I heard Steven Spielberg was going to make a new version, I could not wait. I watched it last night, and I must say, it did not grip me quite as much as I would have liked. I know the camera style was very well done in following the main characters and having events going on around them, but it seemed to be missing something. Maybe it was a lack of dramatic music used to heighten suspense, I can't say. Anyway, it was not a bad film. Tom Cruise, Dakota Fanning and Tim Robbins in particular were excellent. The new concept of the alien craft being on earth for a million years was novel if a little hard to believe, as wouldn't the aliens be able to create better machines during the million years and how would they know where the cities would be? I know most people picked up on the camera inconsistency, but 2 other things that were a little hard to swallow were the fact that after a passenger jet landing on their estate and causing a blast of flames and leaving destruction everywhere, they were still able to get into their intact van in the middle of where it landed and drive off. Also, when they were being pulled out of the van, and Tom pulls out a gun, only one other person has a gun! In America!, with an invasion going on! Get real, I'm sure there would have been a few mini guns etc... :) I did feel that some things could have been explained a little more and that the film could have used about 20 to 30 minutes more to do this. By the way, did they mention at any stage that they were Martians? That aside, I did enjoy the film on the whole. The heat rays were very well done. I am sure I will get this when it come out on DVD as I have everything else on the story.

title: Frightining Effects
review:
CONTAIN SPOILERS: This was a great movie, I don't remember the old movie well, but I think this contained much the same material. The tripods were much like a strider in PC game "Half Life 2" with Dr. Octavius tentacles. The mostly I liked sound-effects. The tripod noises were very disturbing, even frightening. title: A War Drama with UFOs
review: If this movie will not be as a big blockbuster as e.g. Independence Day then it will be because it is not really a dull audience-serving popcorn. This is a war drama about a father who learns how to protect his daughter; it's a war of worlds not only between aliens and the Earth but the father and others, the father and himself. We can see lots of typical Spielberg moments in this movie (from his war, adventure and also sci-fi movies) which shows it is way more efficient (viscerally) to show explosions and flying cars in their actual speed than the very slow-mo spectacle that Emmerich's movies show. The keyword is "realistic" this case: the sights make us remember all human catastrophes from our memory (from wars and holocaust to 9/11 and tsunami) and righteously so. In the end the movie becomes a bit more popcorn-y as the father becomes a hero and helps in the war against the aliens but still not in an Emmerich-style dumb way. Maybe my only concern is that we could not see anything "revolutionary" or fresh and new - but maybe that's too much to ask from an adaptation of a hundred-year-old book.

title: gadgetry, Cliché'd plot, Mutilated Characters, Fair Special Effects
review:
*** Spoiler Warning *** So I had everything done for the weekend and an afternoon to kill, I figured I'd gamble that the crowds had abated nip on down to catch a matinée showing.

I appreciated the opening and closing narration by Morgan Freeman, but the obvious CGI water drops were a bit tacky. Why not just shoot an actual leaf with water on it? That theme of overdoing CGI was persistent throughout the film, Alien warships too gadgetry, though overall appearance was good, I wondered why they looked like they all had a giant car headlight on the front.

The energy shields were rather idiotic, the tension would have been better served if a few were shown going down, as in the original book, but they still succeeded by their overwhelming might. I didn't appreciate the Astronomer/Curate/Artilleryman combined character who looked like some sort of child molester. What was up with that? People around me laughed quite a bit, like where there's a convenient path to drive through every time they needed one and various script holes, like why are these craft planted under the cities and only now the aliens arrive? That one's a real head scratcher.

The general feeling was the film suddenly stopped with the only living family left in Boston intact. I thought the "disfunctional-family-united-by-common-cause" was really a bit of a stretch. Most characters were fairly shallow, which was a real shame considering the material this originated with, but seems par for the course these days. But people will call pretty much anything a blockbuster now, including the truly regrettable Cat In The Hat.

Not the best of Steven Spielbergs work, but not his worst either. I'm not in any particular hurry to see this again. Undoubtedly this film will serve as some inspiration for others to check out the 1950's classic. Hopefully many will sit down and read H. G. Wells' book which inspired all this.

Also, do give a look at the other War Of The Worlds, directed by Timothy Hines, which was released earlier this year on DVD and attempts to tell the story in its original setting on a much smaller budget.

title: Best and most authentic Alien invasion film yet! Will be very different from what you expect!
review:
No, Spielberg fortunately abandoned all these clichés and emphasizes suspense and realism. He has accomplished something, no other director of an alien film has before:

"War of the worlds" is very, very authentic, everything seems real in such a way, it is like a nightmare that could happen every day, every time.

Spielberg's directing as well as Cruise's and Fanning's acting brilliantly show the hopelessness and the helplessness of humanity. The characters more and more realize that there is no way out, as the film goes on. Cruise's character does what every other human being would do in such a situation, he runs, but every time he thinks, hes escaped the Aliens come after him and he realizes that there is no place on earth where one is safe and there's no weapon or instrument made by human hand, that could harm these invaders

No Alien- or disaster film had ever had such a scaring impact.

Yes, other such films might me about nothing more than running and screaming and "War of the worlds" is running and screaming all the time either, but the way, it is illustrated is different.

There are neither hero-clichés nor unnecessary love stories.

Other comments I have read criticize that there is no plot at all. Okay, there might not be a complex and emotional plot like in Drama films or thrillers like Fight Club or Schindler's List, but that's really not the claim Spielberg raises, it is solely the helplessness, Spielberg focuses on, and this works perfectly.

That might be the point why one half loves the film and the other half is totally disgusted by it. But I unfortunately cannot tell if one will like the film or not. I myself am more a fan of demanding dramas and sophisticated thrillers, but nevertheless I really enjoyed the film.

WARNING: minor SPOILERS following:

Unfortunately Spielberg isn't bold enough to consequently follow his style until the end. He regrettably lets Cruise heroically rescue his daughter from the aliens and shows the whole family happily reunited in the last quarter of the film which bedims the excellent impression.

Another downer was the fact that the aliens were actually shown, past alien films should have made clear that the showing of the unknown and scaring somehow let drop the suspension, so that was a little negative aspect.

SPOILERS END

Moreover the visual effects are stunning as expected, one shouldn't be put off by some bad reviews, my result is that the film is definitely worth watching, but "War of the worlds" is such a film that is liked by one group and hated by the other group and one cannot finally tell why. Give this film a chance, if for the single purpose of joining the discussion.

title: A worthy blockbuster!
review:
Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise) a crane operator has to look after his two children (Dakota Fanning and Justin Chatwin) for the weekend as his ex-wife (Miranda Otto) and her new husband are visiting her parents in Boston. Later on during the day Ray and fellow neighbours are out on the streets watching dark clouds forming up in the sky and there's lighting strikes too. Because of this everything that runs on power becomes dead and including phones. Then suddenly all of the confusion changes to horror when an alien machine comes from the ground and starts terminating people. This causes crowds of hysteria and Ray rushes home and starts on a trip with the kids to get to Boston. Though, these malevolent beings in their machines are popping up everywhere and our out to destroy mankind.

This is an adaptation of H.G. Wells classic story of an alien invasion (maybe a metaphor on the wars in the British Empire at the time) which was published in 1898 and well, what can I say about Spielberg's film? It was far better than I expected to be. This blockbuster truly delivered what it was meant to do grand entertainment and nothing more. I wouldn't class it a masterpiece, but still it's very good film and Spielberg at his best. These aliens were far from friendly like those in his earlier films " Close Encounters of the Third Kind' and "ET- The Extra-Terrestrial". There was a lot style behind this film, but it was kind of mediocre on substance.

The story concentrates on the family than what's actually happening globally and somehow it still felt a bit thin (probably because the plot is basically hide and go seek) and you can see elements of 9/11 attacks, subtle WW2 images and references on terrorists, but anyhow it had heart and it tells a gripping and unnerving tale. The acting wasn't great in my eyes but it was reasonably fair. It's nowhere as bad like some people make it out to be. Chemistry between the Cruise, Fanning and Chatwin was believable and to you start to care for them the further along the film goes. The witty humour between the three is incredibly enjoyable too. I thought Chatwin's character was by far the most interesting and it was a little disappointing that his character departs halfway into the film. Fanning's performance was good (well, her constant screaming wasn't annoying) and you can see why she hyped to be the next big thing. Cruise came across rather deadpan and lacking bite, especially when his character is the one who carries the story. Maybe a stronger actor would have added something greater, but hey what am I complaining about the film it delivered what it was meant to do and overall you could argue that his performance fitted in with the bleak mood. His portrayal is that of a average block and not of a clean cut hero or ingenious scientist and hardly an ideal father figure too. As he has let down his family in the past, but when this chaos occurs he's someone who focuses on his two children then that of someone trying to help everyone that he passes and he isn't here to save mankind either. His got only one thing on mind and that's to get his children to their mother and he would literally do 'anything' to keep it that way. Tim Robbins plays a traumatized father who lost his family and is hiding out in his basement. He basically plays the nut and does a good job of it, if sometimes a little too over-the-top. I thought some of the scenes involving him did kind of drag on for too long.

Though, saying all of that and explaining some minor glitches. I was too entrenched and amazed in the film for those things to really bother me. Starting with the chilling opening intro which is narrated by Morgan Freeman, it just pulls you into an emotional ride with destruction a plenty and surprises, until we get to the sour and overly sweet ending. The astounding special effects are mesmerising and have great impact on the viewer. The sprawling camera-work truly captures the magnificent imagery e.g. the burning train that speeds by. Something just keeps you glued as the disturbing scenes involving the alien machines chasing the humans create such terror and tension. The moody atmosphere of the film is superb in creating such a feel of doom and dread. I just really enjoyed the grim and dark tone of it. It just held such a disturbing vibe to it all. The first half of the film is incredibly gripping and paced very well, but it does slow down in the second half with some extended scenes that went on for too long. When it came to the end I thought how the aliens were defeated and how mankind survived was just too brisk and it turn out to be somewhat of an anti-climax. But after thinking about it more I came to except the reason. Well, Morgan Freeman's narration to end the film truly does convince you of why mankind's fate was spared. Though, the happy but odd family ending didn't work and came across a forced, but that's what you call a small hiccup compared to the rest of the engrossing film. I guess Spielberg just can't let go of a happy ending well, not happy but sappier.

For what its worth it's a fairly striking and highly enjoyable ride that has only a few bumps.

title: (May Contain Mild Spoilers) Close Encounters of the Nastiest Kind
review:
Literally the other side of "Close Encounters", this film uses many of the same techniques as did that film to work on our emotions and forebodings.

I consider this Spielberg's best genre film since "Jaws", and for much the same reasons -- he delivers the scares and the gotchas with verve and precision.

The plot is a bit slight, but the point of films like this -- and of Wells' original novel -- is more to portray the collapse (or not) of civilisation on a broad canvas; in fact, i believe that there may well be MORE "human-interest" type plot in this film than in the novel.

My biggest gripes are the sorts of gripes i always have with a Spielberg film -- his inability to stand back and let the situation or action carry its own weight, the need to "punch" it up, to play on our emotions, or to force the plot rather than allowing it to develop it naturally.

Thus, in, for instance, "Close Encounters", the REAL reason ROy Neary throws dirt in the window is that Spielberg's plot requires his wife to leave and Spielberg doesn't have the time or patience to come up with a good reason. In "Schindler's List", the little girl in the middle of the B&W cinematography is there to point up the pathos of the whole thing and to twist our emotions a little more.

There are several such moments in this film -- all of which completely defy logic and violate reality in scenes when the director should be trying his hardest to make it look realer than real so that when the stuff that's flatly NOT real turns up, it will SEEM more nearly real because of the surrounding reality.

Also, sadly, there are a couple of scenes where the effects -- mostly "practical" effects rather than special effects like CGI -- fail to stand up to the rest of the film, and one important sequence looked to me like one of the worst-executed "outdoor" soundstage sets in the last twenty years.

And, of course, the film demonstrates Hollywood's complete inability to understand anything remotely technical, in its portrayal of the effects of EMP.

ALl of which said, i didn't feel at all as if i had wasted my $5.50 senior-citizen ticket money.

title: Very Good adaptation of the original source materials
review:
I have been very skeptical for some time about the ability of Spielberg to pull of the remake of the WOTW. I grew up in England where the original book was mandatory reading for English lit classes, besides that, I was an avid lover of Jeff Waynes musical version..and a disappointed watcher of the 1950's Hollywood flick .

Just reading the criticism's so far leads me to believe the viewers have never read the book and most only have passing notions of the insights into the Book... Spielberg cleverly weaves his way through the magical story of the Worlds first invasion story, masterfully recreating Horshall common of the Victorian England era into New Jersey residential situ of the 21st century. The tripods true to form could almost have been drawn up in the mind of HG Wells himself, with their giant Hissing Fire weapons and baskets of human trophy's. Cleverly Spielberg keeps the Alien invader 'shields' intact aka 1950's movie in lieu of having moved the episode from the 1890's to 2005, see what Cruise can do with a few Grenades and figure what could be done with a Stealth fighter bomber without shields. He maintains the view of impending doom and savage extinction of mankind very boldly and very eerily, we have become the hunted. I could almost hear watching the movie Richard Burton narrate 'It was like watching the beginning of the route of the extermination of mankind..'

A few little items peeved me though, and being English and the movie not being set in England, funny enough was not one of them ! But the idea of the lightening bolts sending the 'pilots' into the ships, was somewhat absurd..I kept thinking half the movie, surely in all this time the Aliens craft would have been discovered with things like building codes, road development, water pipes, London being bombed during the war, etc etc... The idea of the original Martian pods landing and the aliens building their machines in the impact crater, as Wells originally wrote, was how it should have been..and that brings me to peeve number 2..

This movie was earth vs the Martians..thats how it was, and should have remained, Steven Spielburg, man, don't you get it ! we understand its a movie, we would not have chastised you for using the word martian, or complained that we know Mars is Lifeless, its a movie dude.. Not once, was the word martian used in the whole movie, and that was kind of funky as this was THE STORY, where the word Martian emanated.

Couple of things I loved, the Film perspective, it was like saving Private Ryan, slower shutter speed action cam in your face style..great shooting, and yes I loved the tripods evil buggers they were, finally I loved the perspective of the family Ferrier, and that is how it was written. Wells did not go for the whole Government vs Aliens shoot em up scenario,aka Independence Day, it was based on one man avoiding and evading the aliens, Cruise holding his sons foot begging him not to go, whilst having the choice of seeing his daughter whisked away forever made a lump come to my throat, especially as I am a father of a boy and a girl, I could easily put myself into his situation of just trying to give them one more day of life.

Spielburg could have done far more with this movie, but then it would not have been War of the Worlds, it might have been revenge of ET ! but Spielberg kept remarkably to the spirit of the book and thats what I don't get from the detractors of the movie.

What i did not like, the movie is typical of Hollywood timing, guys I can last more than 1hr 50 minutes, an additional 30 minutes would not have stretched the movie out.. Not enough destruction of the major City, London was wiped out in the book, please, I could have watched NY City being razed to the ground, without whimpering about 9/11, its only a movie for goodness sake. The ending was abrupt and true to the book, it sucked. Thats it, we are getting our bums kicked all over the World, no chance of survival, totally exterminated and then thats all folks, we win. The end. Lets all thank God, just as HG Wells did. I did not like it in the book, I hated it in the movie. Spielburg chooses to keep to the spirit of the book where it was important, but digressed where he needed it, and I thought a movie should have an explosive ending not a whimper, Steven one Fighting machine getting a rocket up its ass was not exciting, you could have at least had a better David and Goliath feel good victory for the poor bloody humans watching the movie..

That all said, Well bloody done, I have asked why nobody tackled this movie before as a modern project,especially as its the First Invasion story ever ! Its the daddy of em all !

I am glad Spielberg did it proud.

title: Left me wanting...
review:
Firstly I find the acting very good and consistent throughout. Whoever watched the movie (or trailer) will not forget that look of fear in Dakota's face. That girl is someone to watch out for in the future. Cruise is also pretty good, he really had come a long way since Cocktail.

The graphics and sound effects put together were mindblowing especially, the "coming out scenes" at the beginning of the movie. Pretty scary stuff. However, I find the alien tripods similar to a British TV show in the 80s called (what else) Tripods.

So what exactly went wrong with the movie? Firstly, the bad script. I don't know about the rest of you guys. Some of it just don't make sense especially the narration (that sounded so much like Morgan Freeman) at the beginning and the ending of the movie - it's like watching a badly-done documentary. There were good moments like when Cruise's son asked "Is it the terrorists?" but they were few and far in between.

Second, Spielberg seems so bent on blowing us away and shocking us with the graphics and effects that he forgot all else, like the logic and storyline. When the movie ends, I am stumped. Am I the only one who don't get it? What happened? Was it the birds? Or was it the human blood? And what the hell was the root-like thing that spread all over the ground? What was it purpose? And how come Boston was not affected when all other parts of the world were in rubbles? All of these were unanswered. And who could not see that camcorder goof? And how come the military helicopters, tanks and lorries were in working condition? Were they from Boston? I also hated the last minute effort at ending the movie in a peachy note - the tears, the hug and everyone is safe blah, blah, blah...it's so...typical.

So, if you stripped the movie off its effect, you will left with good acting and not much else. There were parts of the show which I got quite restless because it was so boring and slow moving.

I think I rather rent the 80s "Tripods" and read the book.

title: War of the Worlds has 'meaner', 'rougher' aliens
review:
War of the Worlds is quite a powerful, intense tale guided by master director, Steven Spielberg, who knows how to move things along so fast that you barely notice any inconsistencies in the plot. As summer entertainment, it serves a tasty dish. It shows wunderkind director still at the top of his game.

A father, Ray Ferrier (Tom Cruise), gets to keep his two kids for the weekend as his exwife visits Boston. He barely knows his rebellious teenage son Robbie (Justin Chatwin) and is not much better with his younger daughter Rachel (an adorable Dakota Fanning). Strange phenomena begin to occur over New Jersey as mysterious sounds, lightning, clouds, and wind emanate from the skies. What follows is the shocking appearance of an alien machine from beneath the ground that shows incredible power and fires deadly rays that disintegrate humans. Curiosity turns into panic as the machines begin a reign of terror that will destroy the community. Ray switches to survival mode and thus begins a desperate flight to safety. What started out as an estranged, dysfunctional group, becomes a frightened, desperate family whose members begin to rely on one another for survival and hope. And there is not much hope as the aliens are invincible to any military force that can be leveled at them. Soon it becomes clear that the aliens are also using humans as a living resource. When they lose contact with Robbie, Ray and Rachel seek refuge in the basement of a farmhouse where a mysterious loner, Ogilvy (Tim Robbins), is willing to make a last stand. There, they play hide and seek with the aliens. Eventually Ray and Rachel come face to face with an alien machine, and what Ray does to save his girl and himself leads to the film's climax as it shifts locations to Boston. .

Spielberg pays generous homage to War of the Worlds' three previous incarnations including the original H.G. Wells novel (with its eerie horn-like sounds that precede the aliens, the crazed Ogilvy, the look of the alien machines, and the ending), the Orson Welles 1938 radio broadcast (also set in New Jersey with its unseen news reports and dark mood), and George Pal's 1953 cold war film adaptation (with its apocalyptic destruction and farmhouse sequence).

An antithesis of his kinder, gentler alien epics, Close Encounter of the Third Kind and E.T., this film features an evil menace that gives no reason or explanation as to why but rather how quickly the human race can be exterminated. There are obvious parallels with the Holocaust in the mass extermination of humans which has influenced Spielberg in recent years (Schindler's List). This has the meanness of his early television movie, Duel, with its relentless enemy. While there are thematic similarities with Independence Day, by focusing on the one family from beginning to end as opposed to a half dozen groups of characters, Spielberg draws a more intimate portrait of people we care about.

What is good about this film is that Spielberg wastes no time and gives enough exposition of Ray's fragmented family before the alien terror begins. He shows how good he is at suggesting violence. You get teased with glimpses and sounds of something unusual and frightening before the real threat reveals itself. Sometimes we only see evidence of massive destruction and death without having the event played out. It is as if we are standing on the sidelines catching enough of the event to know what is happening. The film's pacing is very good, and the production values are outstanding. Of significant note, this mega-budgeted film took only seven months to make, an incredibly efficient shoot! Spielberg knows how to utilize state-of-the-art special effects in an organic, believable way without being artificial or self-conscious of its technique. The effects, spearheaded by veteran Dennis Muren (Terminator 2 and Jurassic Park), are extremely impressive, and they all look convincing. Nothing looks phony, and anything that is an effect looks like it is really happening.

The acting is strong, and Cruise and Fanning are delightful in their energetic, emotional performances. Robbins registers in a creepy supporting role, and Miranda Otto (Lord of the Rings:The Return of the King) is effective as Cruise's exwife. Chatwin (reminding one of a young Jake Gyllenhaal) seems weak and doesn't show enough of his character while interacting with Cruise, but this may be a fault of the script.

Surprisingly, the strong emotional ties that characterized E.T. and Close Encounters are not as evident here. We see Fanning's character traumatized by her surroundings and we see Cruise's character trying to connect with his kids as he fights to save them at every turn. Spielberg needed a bit more interplay and meaningful dialogue between father and daughter, and it would have been a perfect realization of paternal bonding.

The final scene, however, does not ring true regarding the fate of Ray's family-the only glaring fault of the film that seems unrealistic given all that has transpired. Its resolution seems almost a nod to the classic western, The Searchers. There are also other film references like a brief scene from The Greatest Show on Earth or a familiar sound effect from the 1953 War of the Worlds. Watch for cameos of Gene Barry and Anne Robinson near the end; they starred in the 1953 classic.

War of the Worlds is a tense, exciting amusement park ride through a scary funhouse, and when it ends, you are glad to have survived the event.

title: Could have been funnier

title: Excellent movie that brings to life the spirit of the book
review: Spielburg has paid particular attention to the spirit of the original novel and captured it brilliantly on film. H G Wells original vision dates from the end of the nineteenth century, but this film updates and brings a twenty first century spin on the story. If you have not read the book, doubtless you will be disappointed with the ending. Visually Spielberg gives a massive clue to what's coming from the first shot panning out from a single drop of water. Other visual images (Dakota standing next to the river and the "ash" clouds falling) give scale to the momentous events occurring on the screen. The film centers around the struggle of a single family to survive, but it is set both in large scale again the mass destruction of lives and civilizations surrounding the family, and in small scale, against attempting to hide from the aliens in a farm basement. As expected, the special effects are both well conceived and credible, and contribute to the real tension that builds as the story progresses. Both Tom Cruise (cast as an everyday dock worker) and Dakota Fanning are excellent, along with a gritty cameo from Tim Robbins. This is not the usual run of the mill science fiction yarn. Like any good story its told on a number of levels and there is enough complexity to have an English lit major essaying for many thousands of words. The sustained level of suspense and action, makes this a film that will be enjoy a wider audience than just the science fiction aficionado.

title: Another update on a "classic" sci-fi book
review:
To start off, I must say that I'm not a fan of Steven Spielberg's films. Not to say that I hate the guy, I'm just not a fanatic of his films like most people are. In the case of "War of the Worlds" I must say that this is, without a doubt the best Spielberg film that I have seen to date.

Even though this film is a remake of a remake, this film work well on many different levels. For one, all of the performances in this film were flawless, the effects were excellent and the story is beautifully modernized to fit in our time. I would even go as far as to agree with one critic when they said that this is one of the best summer blockbusters to come out in recent years. This is quite true. This is perhaps, in my opinion, the best disaster film since the 1998 critically panned sci-fi action flick "Armageddon" which happened to be virtually released in the same weekend as this film.

All in all, go see "War of the Worlds." Fan or no fan of Spielberg, you should definitely be pleased.

title: Spielberg does it again! Utterly Amazing!

Aliens from a far away world have planted machines in the ground of Earth to one day enable them to emerge and take over. The effects for the movie are unbelievable as the weather patterns take course, as lightning strikes the beasts in order to have them react. The destruction of buildings, of the ground, the aurora of weather, the fire train, everything, builds for tension. The deep blast of the machines' sound makes for an eerie setting, which is perfect for the mood.
